# Handover — The Remote Support Program

Rewritten 2026-09-09, updated 2026-09-13. This is the current state of the build, not a plan. Read
it before changing anything; everything here was paid for once already.

The health check work is **finished** — see §17. Open faults are in **`docs/BUGS.md`** — check
there before diagnosing anything that misbehaves.

---

## 1. What this is

A from-scratch Windows remote support suite plus a job/ticketing system, built for Anywhere IT
(Clint, clint@anywhereit.co.za) and designed to be resold to other IT companies as a multi-tenant
SaaS called **The Remote Support Program** (domain: theremotesupportprogram.com).

Location: `C:\Users\Clint\Desktop\Remote Support`. A git repository since 2026-09-09 — see §14 for
what is deliberately not tracked.

Nothing is bought in — no RustDesk, no third-party remote engine. Screen capture, input
injection, file transfer, script execution, the protocol and the portal are all ours.

---

## 2. Projects

| Project | What it is |
|---|---|
| `RemoteSupport.Shared` | Protocol, `SystemSpecCollector`, `WsConnection`, `DeviceIdentity`. Referenced by everything. |
| `RemoteSupport.Platform` | **The live server** — multi-tenant ASP.NET Core: WebSocket hub, Razor Pages portal, EF Core/SQLite. |
| `RemoteSupport.Server` | The original single-tenant server. Superseded by Platform; kept in the solution. Fixes often need applying to both. |
| `RemoteSupport.Client` | Customer tray app (WinForms). Requests support, shows consent, chats. |
| `RemoteSupport.Agent` | Windows service for unattended access. Runs in session 0, spawns Host.exe into the interactive session. |
| `RemoteSupport.Host` | The thing that is actually shared: capture, input injection, files, scripts. |
| `RemoteSupport.Technician` | Technician console (WinForms) — device list, sessions, chat, tickets. |
| `RemoteSupport.UI` | Shared WinForms theming/branding (`Theme`, `Controls`, `BrandIcon`). |

Build: `.\build.ps1` with `-Platform`, `-Installers`, `-Linux` switches.

Diagnostic harnesses live in `tools/` and are not part of the product — see §7.

---

## 3. How it fits together

Three WebSocket endpoints on the server:

- `/ws/device` — customer machines (tray app **and** unattended agent)
- `/ws/tech` — technician consoles (dashboard connection: device list, calls, chat)
- `/ws/session?role=host|viewer` — one per live session

The server is a **relay and message hub**. It never stores screen data.

Protocol is polymorphic JSON (`Msg` with a `t` discriminator,
`UnknownDerivedTypeHandling.FailSerialization`) plus three binary frame kinds:
`BinKind.Tiles` (1), `BinKind.FileChunk` (2) and `BinKind.Audio` (3).

**Screen capture:** GDI BitBlt to 128 px tiles, FNV hash change detection, JPEG per **changed**
tile. This matters when debugging: if nothing changes on the remote desktop, nothing is sent. An
idle desktop sends **one** frame and then silence, so a single missed frame looks like a permanent
failure. `SubscribeMsg { On = true }` sets `_forceFull` on the host, which is how to demand a
complete frame.

**Input:** `SendInput` with absolute virtual-desktop coordinates (0..65535), derived from the union
of the monitor rectangles — the same source the capturer uses. Do not go back to
`GetSystemMetrics`; that was a bug.

**Unattended:** the service uses `WTSGetActiveConsoleSessionId` + `CreateProcessAsUser` to put a
host into the interactive session. Since 2026-09-09 it launches the host **as SYSTEM** — see §4.

**Multi-tenancy** is *structural*: one `TenantHub` object per tenant, `HubRegistry` maps sessionId
to tenant. The tenant key is baked into the installers and presented in the `hello` message.
Tenants cannot see each other because they are not in the same object.

**Session start:** `StartSession` prefers the device's **Agent** connection and falls back to the
**Client** connection. Both register under the same `DeviceId` (one `device.json` in ProgramData),
so on a machine with the agent installed the agent hosts *every* session — a technician-initiated
connect and an accepted customer call take the identical path. `FallBackToClientAsync` (12 s)
covers an agent host that never connects.

---

## 4. Integrity levels and desktops — read this before touching input or capture

Two Windows mechanisms decide whether remote control works at all. Both cost a full day on
2026-09-09 because they fail **silently** — no error, no return code worth checking.

**Integrity levels (UIPI).** Every process has a rank: Medium for normal apps, High for anything
elevated, System above that. A process may not send input to a window owned by a
higher-ranked process. Windows discards it without telling anyone. So a Medium host cannot drive a
UAC-elevated app, an installer, or an admin PowerShell.

**Desktops.** A session is not on one desktop. `Default` is normal; `Winlogon` hosts UAC prompts,
the lock screen and Ctrl+Alt+Del; `Screen-saver` hosts a secure screensaver. Capture and injection
are both **per-thread-desktop**. A thread pinned to `Default` keeps returning the last picture it
could see, and its input goes nowhere, the moment the user hits a UAC prompt. **Only SYSTEM may
open the Winlogon desktop** — elevated is not enough.

What the code does about it now:

- `RemoteSupport.Agent/SessionLauncher.LaunchAsSystemInActiveSession` duplicates the service's own
  SYSTEM token, moves the copy into the active console session with
  `SetTokenInformation(TokenSessionId)`, and starts the host with it. `AgentService` prefers this
  and falls back to the old user-token launch if it fails, logging which was used. SYSTEM
  outranks every elevated window, so this fixes the UIPI half too.
- `RemoteSupport.Host/DesktopFollower` attaches a thread to whatever desktop currently has input,
  re-checking every 300 ms and only re-attaching on an actual change.
- `HostEngine` runs **capture, cursor and input on dedicated threads**, each with its own
  follower. They cannot be `Task.Run`: desktop attachment is per-thread and `async` continuations
  hop threads, so a pool thread loses its desktop the moment it resumes elsewhere. Input arrives
  on the socket receive thread and crosses to the input thread through a `BlockingCollection`.
- `RemoteSupport.Host/UserContext` supplies the interactive user's name and profile folder,
  because SYSTEM has none. Without it the Info tab says "SYSTEM" and received files land in
  `C:\Windows\System32\config\systemprofile\Downloads`.

**Consequences to keep in mind:**

- **Scripts run as SYSTEM**, not as the logged-on user. Usually what you want for support work,
  but a script reading `$env:APPDATA` sees SYSTEM's. Making them run as the user needs
  impersonation with hand-wired stdout/stderr pipes. Not done.
- The product holds full machine rights on every customer machine. That is the normal posture for
  remote support tools and is what makes UAC prompts work, but it is a deliberate decision. The
  cleaner answer for the *elevated window* half alone is `uiAccess="true"`, which needs a signed
  manifest — code signing is deferred (§10).
- **Never launch a user-facing app from an elevated installer with a plain `Start-Process`**: the
  child inherits the elevated token. That is exactly how the customer's own tray app ended up
  blocking remote control. `Install-Client.ps1` now starts it through a one-shot scheduled task
  with `-RunLevel Limited`.

## 5. Running it

Server (listens on `http://0.0.0.0:8090`, LAN address `ws://192.168.1.115:8090`):

```bash
dotnet run -c Release --project src/RemoteSupport.Platform
```

Portal: http://192.168.1.115:8090/ — technician login clint@anywhereit.co.za.
Owner portal key is still the development value `owner-demo-key`.

`demo/technician` and `demo/client` are branded, ready-to-run copies. **They go stale** — refresh
them from `dist/` before a demo, then apply live tenant branding, or you will test yesterday's
binary. That has already wasted time twice.

**Client deployment** lives in `deploy-client/`: the three binaries, branding, the PowerShell
scripts and double-clickable wrappers:

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `Install-Client-Unattended.bat` | Client + unattended agent. The normal case. |
| `Install-Client.bat` | Tray app only; someone must accept each session. |
| `Uninstall-Client.bat` | Removes everything, with a Y/N confirm. |

Each wrapper re-launches **itself** elevated (`Start-Process -FilePath '%~f0' -Verb RunAs`) and
then runs the `.ps1` with its own fixed options. Nothing is forwarded through the elevation step
on purpose — passing arguments through cmd → PowerShell → cmd is where these break on a path with
a space, and the real path ("Remote Support") has one. Advanced options (`-InstallDir`,
`-NoAutoStart`) go through the `.ps1` directly. New wrapper files must be added to the installer's
`Copy-Item ... -Exclude` list or they get installed into Program Files.

## 6. The test machine

`192.168.1.113` / `DESKTOP-L2B85US`, ticketing client "Roger Rabbit", user `DESKTOP-L2B85US\User`.
Client + unattended agent installed at `C:\Program Files\Anywhere IT\Remote Support`, pointing at
`ws://192.168.1.115:8090`.

Verified end to end: unattended session, monitor list, screen frames, remote mouse and keyboard,
chat to customer, file browsing, script execution, ticket recording, pop out / pop in, full screen,
and remote control of elevated windows.

**Security debt on that machine — must be reverted before it is done with:**

- Windows Firewall is OFF. Turn it back on.
- `LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy=1` was set:
  `Remove-ItemProperty -Path HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System -Name LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy`
- Delete `~/.rs-target-cred.xml` (a DPAPI-encrypted credential file) when finished.

Credential rule that must not be broken: **never take Clint's passwords in chat.** The agreed
pattern is `Get-Credential | Export-Clixml`, so the plaintext is never seen.

## 7. Diagnostic tooling — use it before changing code

Clint wants things proven, not asserted. These exist because guessing sent fixes to the wrong file.

**Traces, both always on and cheap:**

| Log | Written by | Contains |
|---|---|---|
| `%LOCALAPPDATA%\TheRemoteSupportProgram\technician-trace.log` | Technician console | Build stamp at startup; viewer socket connect/fail/end; **outbound messages dropped because the socket was not up**; **inbound messages lost before the UI thread** (`BeginInvoke` throws with no window handle — the old `catch {}` hid it); every `MonitorsMsg` with indices; every `SubscribeMsg`; pop out/pop in; and in `ScreenView` the canvas resets, first three `OnPaint`s, applied frames, a counter per rejection reason, mouse/key counters and a one-line reason whenever input is **suppressed**. |
| `%ProgramData%\RemoteSupport\host-trace.log` | Host (on the customer machine) | What identity the host runs as, whether it can open the input desktop, and every desktop switch. |

The console's closing line is the single most useful thing in the file:

```
session window closing — frames=11 applied=11 tilesDrawn=145 rejMonitorMismatch=0 rejNoCanvas=0
  decodeFail=0 mouseSent=1708 mouseOffPicture=6 mouseDisabled=0 keysSent=24 ...
```

`mouseSent` climbing while the remote machine does nothing means the fault is past the console.
`mouseOffPicture` is **not** a fault — the view letterboxes, so a pointer in the grey bars is
correctly rejected.

**Harnesses** (all need the Platform server running locally; all log in as clint@anywhereit.co.za):

```bash
# Decodes tiles with ScreenView's exact logic and writes the composed canvas to PNG.
# Waits for MonitorsMsg and subscribes the way SwitchMonitor does, so a missing
# subscription shows up as "no tiles" rather than being papered over.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/blackscreen/blackscreen.csproj -- DESKTOP-L2B85US out.png

# Drives the REAL SessionForm, shown the way DashboardForm shows it. Screenshots docked,
# popped out, popped back in (via a real WM_SYSCOMMAND/SC_CLOSE X button) and full screen,
# feeds each one a real WM_MOUSEMOVE and reports whether the remote cursor moved.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/viewprobe/viewprobe.csproj -- DESKTOP-L2B85US <out-dir> 6000

# Runs tools/hostinfo/hostinfo.ps1 on the remote machine through the product's own script
# execution. The script is a child of Host.exe, so its own token IS the host's token.
# Reports identity, integrity levels, process parents, device identity and the foreground
# window. Joins a live session rather than starting one if a session is already open.
dotnet run -c Release --project "…\tools\hostinfo\hostinfo.csproj" -- DESKTOP-L2B85US

# Proves file transfer BOTH ways by checksum. Pushes a file of random bytes, lists the folder it
# landed in, pulls it back and compares SHA-256. Names the first differing byte when they do not
# match, because a wrong offset and a truncated stream look the same in a hash comparison.
# Cleans up after itself unless --keep is passed.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/filecheck/filecheck.csproj -- DESKTOP-OPHQIDH [--mb N] [--keep]

# Runs tools/hostinfo/audioprobe.ps1 through the same script execution, so it answers the audio
# questions AS THE HOST'S OWN TOKEN: every render endpoint in every state, the default device per
# role, volume and mute, which applications hold the device open and whether any are muted in the
# per-app mixer, and device-manager problem codes. --tone plays a 2-second 1 kHz tone on the
# customer's speakers; without it the probe is read-only.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/audioprobe/audioprobe.csproj -- DESKTOP-OPHQIDH [--tone]

# The CAPTURE half of the same question, and a different permission from rendering: opens WASAPI
# loopback with the host's own token, plays a known 1 kHz tone while capturing, and runs a
# Goertzel filter over the samples — so it is a pass or a fail, not "I think I heard something".
# Also answers what arrives when nothing is playing (nothing at all, not silence) and what a
# muted endpoint does to loopback (nothing — it is taken before mute and volume are applied).
# --unmute briefly unmutes the customer's speakers to measure that directly, and puts it back.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/audioprobe/audioprobe.csproj -- DESKTOP-OPHQIDH --listen [N] [--unmute]

# Proves the whole audio feature over a real session: tells the host to listen, makes the
# customer's machine play a 1 kHz tone, records what arrives at this end and checks it for that
# tone. Reports sequence gaps, received duration against wall clock (which is clock drift in its
# raw form) and bandwidth. --screen subscribes to a monitor too, so audio is measured against a
# socket that screen tiles are competing for — the case the codec decision turns on.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/audiocheck/audiocheck.csproj -- DESKTOP-OPHQIDH [--seconds N] [--wav out.wav] [--screen]

# Tests the audio engine on THIS machine alone — no server, no session, no customer machine.
# Ten seconds. The machine plays a 1 kHz tone at itself, the REAL host-side capture, resampler
# and framing carry it, the REAL parser reads it back, and a Goertzel filter says pass or fail.
# --play also feeds it to the console's own player. Everything genuinely hard about audio is
# hard here rather than on the wire, and this is where to look first when sound goes wrong.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/audiolocal/audiolocal.csproj -- [--seconds N] [--play]

# Does a session survive a dropped socket? Answered on THIS machine alone — no customer machine,
# no live server, nothing installed anywhere. It runs its OWN platform on port 8099 against a
# throwaway database in the temp folder and pretends to be a customer machine, then kills viewer
# sockets with Abort() — no close frame, no EndSessionMsg, which is the whole point; a clean
# CloseAsync tests nothing because the server sees a tidy goodbye either way. Counts tiles before
# and after. --grace also waits out the 90-second hold (~100 s), which is what proves a held
# session cannot leak a host forever. Clint's live server on 8090 is never touched.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/reconnectlocal/reconnectlocal.csproj -- [--grace]

# The same question over REAL hardware, which the above deliberately cannot answer.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/reconnectcheck/reconnectcheck.csproj -- DESKTOP-OPHQIDH [--grace]

# Does anything on the session toolbar cover anything else? Opens the REAL SessionForm at 1280,
# 1320 and 1600 px with no server at all, COMPUTES the overlaps rather than eyeballing them, and
# screenshots each — plus the reconnecting, disconnected and restarting states. It exists because
# the Listen button half-covered the connection pill and only a screenshot caught it (§18); this
# is that check, automatic, and at more than one width. It found three real faults the day it was
# written.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/toolbarprobe/toolbarprobe.csproj -- <out-dir>

# Does a system action reach the machine, and what does it say back? Distinguishes carried out,
# refused, and NOTHING LISTENING AT ALL - which look identical from the technician's chair. It
# refuses to send reboot on purpose: a diagnostic should not restart somebody's machine because
# it was run with the wrong argument.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/sysactioncheck/sysactioncheck.csproj -- DESKTOP-OPHQIDH [lock]

# Which capture path is a REAL machine using, and what is it costing? Starts a session, subscribes
# the way the console does (waiting for MonitorsMsg, so a missing subscription shows up as "no
# tiles"), and measures what arrives: time to the first frame, frames and KB per second, tiles per
# frame, and a PNG of the composed picture. It is the only place stage 2.1's four open questions
# can be answered - the host as SYSTEM, the Winlogon desktop, a right picture rather than a fast
# one, and whether a refused duplication falls back AND SAYS SO in the Info tab.
#   --uac   then waits 45 s for you to raise a UAC prompt on that machine and dismiss it. Every
#           prompt costs an ACCESS_LOST and a rebuild; this is whether it comes back.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/capturecheck/capturecheck.csproj -- DESKTOP-OPHQIDH [--uac] [--seconds N]

# What does the screen pipeline COST? THIS machine alone - no server, no session, no customer
# machine. It drives the real capture path against a scene it paints itself, so two runs a week
# apart are looking at the same screen, and it reports fps, KB/s, tiles per frame, where the
# milliseconds went and CPU - for each capture source, under an idle screen, a scrolling document
# and a stand-in for video. It is the before-and-after stage 2 insists on, and it has already
# caught a ten-times bandwidth regression and a run that was measuring the wrong screen entirely.
#   --compare     puts both capture paths against the same frozen frame and reports the pixel
#                 difference; this is the FIRST thing to run on a customer machine, because a
#                 fast picture that is wrong is not an improvement.
#   --idlewatch   maps which tiles will not sit still on a screen that ought to be static, and
#                 writes a PNG of what was actually on it.
#   --live        measures the real desktop instead of the scene; use it once against a real film.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/codecbench/codecbench.csproj -- --source gdi,dxgi [--seconds N]

# Lists a folder on a customer machine and brings a file OFF it, driving the same wire path the
# Files tab uses. Drag OUT is not built (roadmap 1.3), so this is how a log or a screenshot is
# collected today. It prints the host's Error field rather than showing an empty folder, which is
# a distinction the first version got wrong and which sent the reader to the wrong place.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/fetchfile/fetchfile.csproj -- DESKTOP-OPHQIDH --list
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/fetchfile/fetchfile.csproj -- DESKTOP-OPHQIDH "C:\Users\Lenovo\Desktop\x.log" [--out DIR]

# Does a tenant get warned before its trial lapses? THIS machine alone: a throwaway database and
# a REAL minimal SMTP server on a local port that accepts a message and keeps it. It sends real
# mail over a real socket rather than stubbing the send, because the things most likely to be
# wrong are the addresses and the wording. Covers silence at 8 days, the notice reaching every
# admin and no technician, it not repeating hourly, and — the one a shortcut breaks — a mail
# failure NOT consuming the warning. SHOW_MAIL=1 prints what arrived.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/trialnoticecheck/trialnoticecheck.csproj

# Runs ANY PowerShell diagnostic on a machine through a session, finding the script next to
# itself or in tools/hostinfo. Warns if the script is not pure ASCII: PowerShell 5.1 reads a
# BOM-less file as ANSI and the host writes the script out without one.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/runscript/runscript.csproj -- DESKTOP-OPHQIDH clipboardprobe.ps1

# Drives the REAL DashboardForm, logs in for real, and prints the bounds of every control from
# the form down to the device ListView — maximised, restored, and on each monitor — with a
# screenshot of each. "The devices disappear" has several causes that look identical from the
# outside (empty list, list sized to nothing, list pushed off the parent); only the numbers tell
# them apart. It found a one-pixel-high list on the secondary monitor.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/dashprobe/dashprobe.csproj -- <out-dir>

# Proves the console closes to the TRAY rather than quitting, comes back, still alerts while
# hidden, and can still actually be exited. It presses the REAL X button (WM_SYSCOMMAND/SC_CLOSE),
# because Form.Close() produces a different CloseReason and would exercise the one path the
# handler deliberately ignores. Checks both failure directions: an accidental close must not kill
# the console, and Exit must still work — a window that hides from everything needs Task Manager.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/trayprobe/trayprobe.csproj

# Tests the whole-tree engine on THIS machine alone — no server, no session, no customer
# machine. Two seconds. Everything genuinely hard about copying folders is hard here rather
# than on the wire: empty folders, zero-byte files, duplicate names, and paths crafted to
# escape the destination. It caught four real path-traversal holes the day it was written.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/filesetcheck/filesetcheck.csproj

# Proves FILES AND FOLDERS over a real session, both ways, by checksum. Pushes a tree, has a
# SEPARATE PowerShell process on the customer machine hash everything that landed, pulls the
# tree back and compares with the originals, then checks the CF_HDROP file list on their
# clipboard. Covers empty folders, zero-byte files and non-ASCII names. Cleans up after itself.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/treecheck/treecheck.csproj -- DESKTOP-OPHQIDH [--keep]

# The console's half of moving files, on THIS machine alone — no server, no session, nothing
# installed anywhere, four seconds. The wire was already proven by treecheck and clipcheck; what
# had never been checked was what the CONSOLE does, which is where every remaining fault of
# 2026-09-15 turned out to live. The hard one is drag OUT, because a real drag is a Windows shell
# interaction rather than a message: CHECK 4 performs a REAL DoDragDrop with REAL mouse input into
# a REAL drop target and compares SHA-256 of what arrives, so the assertion is on what Windows
# delivered rather than on the file list we built. CHECK 5 runs the REAL SessionForm against a
# REAL websocket the harness answers as the customer's machine, and answers the first request with
# the error a machine at the logon screen gives, so the fallback is exercised rather than argued
# about. It writes a screenshot of the Files tab. --keep leaves the staging folders.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/dragoutcheck/dragoutcheck.csproj -- [--out DIR] [--keep]

# Does the customer's desktop shortcut carry the logo? It did not, on every machine installed so
# far. Renders the .ico the installer renders, checks the frames Explorer asks for at each view
# size are really there — read with PrivateExtractIcons, the API the SHELL uses, because
# System.Drawing will not return a 256 px frame and reports the next size down instead of saying
# so — then builds a shortcut through the same WScript.Shell COM object the installer uses, reads
# it back FROM DISK through a second object, and asks what icon it carries. No install, no machine.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/iconcheck/iconcheck.csproj -- [--out DIR]

# Proves clipboard text both ways — and, crucially, that it is the clipboard the USER has.
# After setting text it runs clipboardprobe.ps1 as a SEPARATE process on the machine and checks
# the length and hash it reports. A round trip through the host alone cannot tell a shared
# clipboard from a private one; another process seeing the text can. Restores what was on it.
dotnet run -c Release --project tools/clipcheck/clipcheck.csproj -- DESKTOP-OPHQIDH
```

Two traps already sprung, do not repeat them:

- Closing a pop-out window with `Form.Close()` is **not** the same path as the X button. The X
  sends `WM_SYSCOMMAND`/`SC_CLOSE` and produces `CloseReason.UserClosing`; `Close()` and a bare
  `WM_CLOSE` leave it `None`. Testing with `Close()` hid a real bug and made a wrong fix look right.
- A harness that ends the session it joined will close the technician's window out from under them.
  `hostinfo` now only ends sessions it started.

---

## 8. State of play

**Working and verified by eye or by harness:** unattended sessions; screen rendering (docked,
popped out, popped in, full screen); remote mouse and keyboard, including against elevated
windows; session chat in both directions; monitor list; script execution; ticket recording of
session events; the branded tray icon.

**Hearing the customer's machine — built and working 2026-09-13, see §18.** Loopback capture as
SYSTEM, streamed to the console and played there, with a Listen button and a level meter. Proven on
this laptop by `tools/audiolocal`, and confirmed working over a live session to DESKTOP-OPHQIDH
once a build was shipped to it.

**Fixed on 2026-09-09** — the lessons matter more than the fixes:

- *Session chat, inbound never arrived.* `RouteChat` fanned out to `/ws/tech` dashboards and the
  customer's `/ws/device`, but not to `/ws/session` **viewer** sockets, which is where
  `SessionForm` listens. Fixed in `TenantHub.RouteChat` and mirrored in `RemoteSupport.Server`.
- *Black screen.* Closing the pop-out window re-entered `TogglePopOut` from inside `FormClosing`,
  so the pop-in branch's `w.Close()` re-entered the same handler with `_popped` already null,
  took the **pop-out** branch, and built a second, empty, all-black window — then the outer call
  pulled the view back out of it. The same handler cancelled **every** `CloseReason`, so the
  owned pop-out window also blocked "Leave / End" from ever closing the session. Fixed by
  ignoring closes it must not intercept and deferring pop-in with `BeginInvoke`.
- *Remote control dead in attended sessions.* Not the console — it sent 1708 mouse messages and 24
  keystrokes. The customer's tray app was running **elevated**, because the elevated installer
  started it as a child, and it is the foreground window in an attended session. UIPI silently
  discarded everything. Fixed in the installer, and then properly by running the host as SYSTEM
  (§4).

**File transfer — proven on 2026-09-13, by checksum rather than by eye.**
`tools/filecheck` pushed a 3 MB file of random bytes to DESKTOP-OPHQIDH, listed the folder it
landed in, pulled it back and compared SHA-256. 10 of 10 checks passed: the bytes that came back
were the bytes that went out. It also landed in `C:\Users\Lenovo\Downloads` and **not** in
SYSTEM's profile, so `FileTransfer.DefaultDir` resolves the logged-on user correctly. Drag and
drop can now be built on top of this knowing the plumbing underneath it is sound.

**Clipboard text both ways — built 2026-09-13, not yet proven against a machine running the new
client.** `ClipboardAccess` in the host, a Clipboard tab in the session window, and `tools/clipcheck`
to prove it. Deliberately manual rather than syncing on focus change: automatic sync would copy
whatever the customer had — very often a password — onto the technician's machine unasked, and
overwrite whatever the technician had copied. The host is on **WinSta0**, measured, so this is the
user's real clipboard; unlike capture and injection the clipboard is per-**window-station**, not
per-desktop, so `DesktopFollower` does not come into it.

**Writing the clipboard needs a real window handle.** `OpenClipboard(NULL)` reads fine, but then
`EmptyClipboard` sets the owner to NULL and `SetClipboardData` **fails** — documented, silent, and
indistinguishable from a paste that never arrived. The host keeps a message-only window alive for
exactly this.

**Files and folders — built 2026-09-13. The engine is proven; the wire path is not.**
Copy and paste and drag-in now move whole trees. `FileSetTransfer` in Shared does the walking and
rebuilding for both ends; chunks reuse `BinKind.FileChunk` with an id of `<setId>#<entry index>`,
so the binary framing did not change. `tools/filesetcheck` proves the engine locally — 20 checks
including byte-for-byte hashes, empty folders, zero-byte files, non-ASCII names, collision
renaming and five hostile paths. **Proven over a real session on 2026-09-13**: `tools/treecheck`,
19 of 19 against DESKTOP-OPHQIDH — pushed a tree, had a separate PowerShell process on that
machine hash everything that landed, pulled it back and compared with the originals, and checked
the `CF_HDROP` file list on the customer's clipboard. It landed in `C:\Users\Lenovo\Downloads`,
not SYSTEM's profile. Clipboard text is proven too: `tools/clipcheck`, 7 of 7.

**A file on the clipboard is a list of PATHS, not content** (`CF_HDROP`). Pasting those across
machines would hand the far end paths to files that do not exist there, so the bytes always move
as a file set first and only then is the clipboard pointed at where they landed. That ordering is
what makes it a paste rather than a download.

**Validate a received path BEFORE rewriting it.** The collision-rename step turned `..\evil.txt`
into a legal-looking file name, which then passed every check below it; an absolute
`C:\Windows\Temp\x` went the same way because `Directory.Exists("C:")` is true and the rename duly
turned the drive letter into something harmless-looking. Four hostile paths were accepted until
`filesetcheck` caught it. The receiving side runs as **SYSTEM**, so this is full machine rights.
One bad entry now condemns the whole set.

**Dragging IN is proven end to end, 2026-09-13.** A folder dragged from the technician's desktop
onto the remote view arrived on `C:\Users\Lenovo\Desktop` with all three files identical by
SHA-256, in 280 ms. It was reported as "not working" only because it was invisible: the transfer
reported into a label inside the Clipboard tab, and a drag gives no other feedback. Transfers now
show on the session window's **status bar** with a progress bar, and stay up for twenty seconds
after finishing — a fast transfer is otherwise indistinguishable from one that never started.
A drop lands on the customer's **desktop**, requested with the `%DESKTOP%` sentinel that the host
resolves against the logged-on user (the technician's end cannot know that path, and must not
guess it, because the host runs as SYSTEM).

~~**Dragging OUT is not claimed.**~~ **Built 2026-09-15 — see §22.** It is a drag out of the Files
tab's list onto anything in Windows, and the difficulty was never WinForms: `DoDragDrop` hands the
far end paths, so the bytes have to be here first. It reuses paste's ordering rather than
inventing a second one.

**Not yet verified by eye:** the Tickets button in the console.

**Open, not reproduced:** "nothing worked after pop out" was reported once. Five measured runs had
working mouse, keyboard focus and rendering in every viewing mode, so it was most likely the same
UIPI problem seen from a different angle. The traces will name it if it recurs.

## 9. Product decisions already made (do not reopen)

- Windows-only clients. Built from scratch. Client-side consent before every connection.
- Up to 5 technicians per tenant; several technicians can join one session.
- A customer support request rings **all** signed-in technicians until one accepts.
- A centre-screen incoming-call popup, so a minimised console with sound off still gets noticed.
- Pricing: $49/month international, R500/month South Africa. PayFast + Stripe later; manual
  invoicing for now. 14-day trial that starts **only after owner approval**. Signup collects
  country and contact number. Per-company download link `/get/<slug>`.
- **Public signup is disabled** — Clint is testing privately with his own clients before reselling.
  Client installs are done over AnyDesk for now.
- Code signing is deferred.
- Roles: `tenant`, `billing`, `owner`. Reception/accounts sign in for billing and can see ticket
  history. **Anyone** can reassign a ticket, and the whole history follows it.
- Ticket categories: Walk In, Workshop, Call Outs, Remote Support.
  - Call Out: address plus appointment date/time.
  - Workshop: make/model, serial, fault description, accessories supplied, a password-protected
    flag and a password field.
- Clients are first-class records; tickets link to clients; the new-ticket form has a type-ahead so
  duplicates are not created.
- The device list shows processor type and generation, memory, disk usage and OS. Remote-support
  devices link to ticketing clients.

## 10. Hard-won gotchas

Re-learning any of these costs an afternoon.

**Protocol / server**
- `MonitorsMsg` and `SysInfoMsg` are announced once by the host. A viewer that attached later used
  to get nothing — screen, mouse and keyboard all appeared broken. Fixed by caching them on the
  session and replaying to each new viewer. Keep that.
- That replay lands the instant a viewer connects, and `MonitorsMsg` is the **only** thing that
  triggers the console's first `SubscribeMsg`. Losing it means no tiles, permanently. The console
  window handle does not exist until `Show()`, and `BeginInvoke` throws without one — measured
  margin on the LAN was 113 ms. The trace says `LOST inbound …` if it ever happens. The cheap
  hardening, not yet done: buffer inbound messages until `IsHandleCreated` and drain them from
  `OnHandleCreated`.
- Session chat must be routed to the **customer**, not to the host process, which ignores `ChatMsg`.
- ~~`SessionLink` does not reconnect.~~ **Fixed 2026-09-13 — see §19.** It retries for 120 s, and
  the server holds the session for 90 s. Anything written before that date that says a session
  cannot survive a dropped socket is out of date.
- Never `await` inside a `lock` (CS1996) — take the list under the lock, send outside it.

**Windows privilege** — see §4 for the full story.
- Input and capture fail silently when integrity levels or desktops are wrong. Always check
  `host-trace.log` before suspecting the protocol.
- Never start a user-facing app from an elevated installer with a plain `Start-Process`.

**Data**
- SQLite stores no timezone, so every `DateTime` needs a UTC value converter in `PlatformDb`. This
  was caught by an appointment showing the wrong time.
- **Data Protection keys are tied to the folder the app runs from unless you say otherwise.** It
  mixes an "application discriminator" into the key derivation, defaulting to the content root
  **path**, so the same `data/keys` produces different keys once the application moves and every
  stored password fails with *"the payload was invalid"* while the keys sit there looking perfect.
  `Program.cs` now calls `SetApplicationName("RemoteSupportPlatform")` to pin it. **Never change
  that string** — it invalidates everything already encrypted. Found on 2026-09-13 when the server
  could not read a password it had stored days earlier; measured by running one build from two
  paths against one key ring. Without it, the move to a Linux host would have silently lost every
  workshop device password and the tenant mail password.
- Use EF **migrations** (`Data/Migrations`, applied with `Database.MigrateAsync()`).
- Workshop device passwords are encrypted with ASP.NET Data Protection. **Back up `data/keys` and
  keep it private** — losing it loses every stored password. The portal reveals a password only
  behind a "Show" button.

**WinForms**
- A `Label` eats `&` unless `UseMnemonic = false`.
- A `Panel` wrapping a `TextBox` swallows Tab — set `TabStop = false` and handle `NextField()`.
- Dialogs must size with `ClientSize`, never `Size`.
- Among bottom-docked controls, the one added **first** sits highest.
- A `Resize` handler must never set its own control's `Height` — instant recursion.
- Do not touch controls before `HandleCreated`; start links from that event.
- F11 is handled locally by `ScreenView` and must not be forwarded to the remote machine.
- Never call `Close()` on a form from inside its own `FormClosing` handler — defer with
  `BeginInvoke`. And check `CloseReason`: cancelling a `FormOwnerClosing` close on an owned window
  cancels the owner's close too.

**Branding**
- Tenant branding ships `logo.jpg`, never an `app.ico`, so anything needing an icon must render
  one. `RemoteSupport.UI/BrandIcon.cs` does that (and still prefers a real `branding/app.ico` if
  one is ever supplied). The client tray used to fall back to `SystemIcons.Application`, which
  customers do not recognise.
- **An in-memory `Icon` cannot brand anything Windows draws on our behalf.** A shortcut's
  `IconLocation` is a PATH the shell reads long after our process has gone, so
  `BrandIcon.WriteIcoFile` renders a real multi-size `.ico` FILE and the installer points the
  shortcuts at it. **There is deliberately no `ApplicationIcon` in any csproj**: every reseller
  downloads the same binaries with their own logo beside them, so an icon compiled in at build
  time would put Anywhere IT's logo on somebody else's customers' desktops. Anything else that
  needs branding on disk should call `WriteIcoFile` rather than growing a second renderer.
- **`System.Drawing` will not return a 256 px icon frame**, in either PNG or DIB form — it hands
  back the next size down in silence. Read icons with `PrivateExtractIcons`, which is what the
  shell uses, or a perfectly good 256 frame looks missing. `tools/iconcheck` does.
- **A JPEG logo has no transparency**, so a rendered icon is the logo *including its background* —
  a black square, in Anywhere IT's case. That is not a fault in the renderer and cannot be fixed
  in one: supply `branding/logo.png` with an alpha channel, or a hand-made `branding/app.ico`,
  both of which the code already prefers.

**PowerShell**
- `$MyInvocation.MyCommand.Path` is null inside `param()` defaults — use `$PSScriptRoot`.
- `@(A + '\Programs', B)` concatenates the string with the *array* and yields one mangled path.
  Parenthesise each element. This broke the installer's shortcuts.
- `New-PSDrive` throws "Index was outside the bounds of the array" here; use a `WNetAddConnection2`
  P/Invoke with a qualified username.
- Test any diagnostic script locally before sending it to a customer machine.
- **A docked Fill control takes the whole shortfall when the window is short**, and it is usually
  the one that matters. The dashboard's calls (250px) and sessions (180px) cards are fixed and the
  devices card fills the rest, so on a 1360x768 secondary monitor the device list was measured at
  **910x1** — one pixel, holding eleven devices and showing none. Fixed cards now give way
  proportionally and the list keeps a floor. Anything docked `Fill` between fixed siblings needs
  the same treatment.
- **Maximising can make a window SHORTER.** A restored window may be taller than the screen and
  hang off the bottom; maximising clamps it to the working area. On that monitor maximising *lost*
  84px. "It breaks when I maximise" is therefore not evidence of a maximise-specific bug — it is
  usually evidence of a height the layout cannot survive, which the restored window was hiding.
- **Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads a BOM-less file as ANSI, and writes stdout in the console's OEM
  code page.** Both are silent, and together they turn `café` into `café` in either direction.
  `ScriptRunner` now writes the temp `.ps1` **with** a UTF-8 BOM and prepends one guarded line
  setting `[Console]::OutputEncoding` to UTF-8. Before that, a script listing a file called
  `Dané se rekening.pdf` showed nonsense in the Scripts tab and nothing reported a fault. Any
  diagnostic that compares names across the wire should base64 them rather than trust the
  encoding — `tools/treecheck` does, and that is why it can tell "the file did not arrive" apart
  from "the file arrived and I cannot read its name".
- **Attach every `WsConnection.OnMessage` handler before calling `RunAsync`.** The host's one-shot
  announcements — `ParticipantsMsg`, `MonitorsMsg`, `SysInfoMsg` — arrive within milliseconds of
  the viewer socket opening, and a handler registered after the pump has started misses them for
  good. This cost an hour on 2026-09-13: a harness reported "the host never attached" while 601
  `CursorMsg`s from that very host went past. Only the repeating messages were being seen.
- **A new session has no host for a second or two.** The hub relays a viewer's message with
  `s.Host?.Send(m)`, which is a silent no-op when the host has not connected yet, so anything sent
  immediately after `SessionReadyMsg` vanishes without a trace. Wait for evidence of the host
  before sending. `hostinfo` only gets away with it because its four-second cursor watch happens
  to cover the gap.
- **PowerShell binds methods against the runtime type of a COM wrapper, not the interface it was
  cast to.** Handing a COM interface back from `Add-Type` C# into script fails with "does not
  contain a method named …". Keep the whole COM walk inside C# and return strings.
- **`Marshal.ReleaseComObject` can throw**, and in a `finally` that loses the result you came for.
  In a diagnostic, release through a helper that swallows the exception.

**Web**
- The Web SDK ignores `None Update wwwroot`; use `Content Update`.
- Razor folder and page policies combine with **AND**, so a folder policy allowing two roles plus a
  narrower page policy is how admin pages get restricted.

## 14. Source control

`git init` was run on 2026-09-09; before that there was no undo. One commit, 164 files, ~1 MB.

**Deliberately not tracked** (see `.gitignore`, which explains each rule):

- Build output, `dist/` and `demo/` — about 1 GB of self-contained exes, all regenerable with
  `.\build.ps1`.
- `**/branding/brand.json` — it carries the **tenant key**, which authenticates devices to a
  tenant. `branding/brand.example.json` is committed instead and shows the shape. After a fresh
  clone, restore `brand.json` from the portal or from the example plus the real `serverUrl` and
  `tenantKey`.
- The SQLite database, uploaded logos, and `data/keys` (the Data Protection keys that encrypt
  stored workshop passwords). **Losing `data/keys` loses every stored password** — back it up
  somewhere private, but not in the repo.
- `tools/rs-credentials.json` — the portal login the diagnostic harnesses use. They previously had
  Clint's password hardcoded in all three; they now read `RS_EMAIL` / `RS_PASSWORD` from the
  environment, falling back to that file, and fail with a clear message if neither is present
  (`tools/Common/RsCredentials.cs`).

Do **not** add a bare `data/` rule to `.gitignore`: git on Windows is case-insensitive by default
and it would also swallow `src/RemoteSupport.Platform/Data/`, which is source.

There is no remote. Before adding one, re-check the ignore rules and rotate anything that has
leaked into a working copy.

## 15. Device identity across a reinstall — fixed 2026-09-09

**Was:** `DeviceIdentity` lives in `C:\ProgramData\RemoteSupport\device.json`, and
`Uninstall-Client.ps1` deletes that folder, so an uninstall/reinstall produced a **new `DeviceId`**
and a **second device row** — unlinked from its client, with the history stranded on the stale row.
DESKTOP-L2B85US accumulated four rows this way.

**Now:** devices report a hashed hardware fingerprint (`MachineFingerprint`, in Shared) — SMBIOS
UUID plus `MachineGuid` — in `HelloMsg.HardwareId`. When a machine presents an unknown `DeviceId`
but a fingerprint already on file, `PersistDeviceAsync` **adopts the existing row**: new DeviceId
and key, `ReinstallCount++`, `LastReinstallUtc` set, and the client link and history kept. The
devices page shows "reinstalled once, last 9 Sep" instead of a second machine.

Deliberately **not** keyed on machine name: two PCs in one company are often called the same thing
(`RECEPTION`, `SERVER`, a re-imaged fleet), and merging those would fuse two machines into one
record. Adoption needs **exactly one** fingerprint match; blank and known shared OEM/hypervisor
UUIDs are rejected.

Two things to remember:

- **Existing duplicates are not merged retroactively.** Fingerprints are recorded from each
  machine's next connection onwards. The rows already in the database stay as they are.
- **It only works once customer machines run the new client build.** The fingerprint comes from
  the endpoint.

`Uninstall-Client.ps1` also now copies `*.log` to `%ProgramData%\RemoteSupport-logs` before
deleting the folder, because it was destroying `host-trace.log` — the evidence for whatever was
being diagnosed. It still deletes `device.json`; the fingerprint is what makes that survivable.

## 17. The monthly health check, as of 2026-09-13

The toolkit at `C:\PCHealthCheck` is folded in. That project is **still separate and still
finished** — it was imported here at its v2.7, unmodified, in one commit so later changes show as
a clean diff, and its own repo was left alone. Its scope rules (no multi-tenancy, no web UI, no
database) were right for it and are reversed here on purpose.

Our copy lives in `healthcheck/`. Read `C:\PCHealthCheck\HANDOVER.md`'s **Traps** section before
editing any of that PowerShell; every one of them has already cost real time there, and two of
them recurred during this work.

### How it works

```
[customer machine]  monthly scheduled task, as SYSTEM
      asks the server which customer it belongs to
      maintenance (restore point first, or it skips)
      read-only health check
      builds the branded PDF with the Edge already on the machine
      uploads JSON + PDF          ---->   [server] stores it, shows it, emails it
```

**The machine holds no mail settings at all.** That was the decision taken before any code
(`docs/PLAN-HEALTHCHECK.md`): the standalone toolkit stores an SMTP password on every client
machine because it has no server, and this platform has one.

**Edge will not run as SYSTEM, so the server makes the PDF.** The plan had the machine build its
own, reasoning that every Windows machine has Edge and a Linux server does not. Half right: the
machine has Edge, but the monthly run is a scheduled task running as SYSTEM and Edge refuses to
start under that account. Measured on DESKTOP-OPHQIDH — **exit code 1002, no output at all,
identically for `--headless`, `--headless=new` and `--headless=old`, with and without
`--no-sandbox`**. The same machine prints a PDF perfectly when a logged-in administrator runs it,
so it is the account, not the browser, the flags or the machine.

So the endpoint sends whatever it managed to build, and `ReportPdfService` converts HTML to PDF on
the server before the mail goes out. When the server has no engine either, the HTML is sent as it
is — a complete, self-contained report — and the reason is recorded on the run. `Platform:PdfEngine`
points at a browser explicitly, which is how the Linux host will be told about its Chromium.

**A trap this leaves behind:** if the platform is ever run as a Windows *service*, it will be
SYSTEM too, and server-side conversion will fail exactly the same way. It works today because the
server runs as Clint. On Linux this does not arise.

| Piece | Where |
|---|---|
| Tenant settings | `/portal/healthcheck` — on/off, report address, day of month, maintenance or inspection only, and the tenant's own mailbox |
| Which machines | **Since 2026-09-28 (§50)**: a tick on the client plus a per-machine override; the agent service installs and removes it. The client installer no longer does. |
| Results | `/portal/healthchecks` — every run, its findings in the collector's wording, the PDF, and whether the mail actually went |
| Upload / context | `POST /api/healthcheck/report`, `GET /api/healthcheck/context`, authenticated by the machine's existing `DeviceId` + `DeviceKey` |
| Server side | `Services/HealthCheckService.cs`, `HealthCheckRun` in `PlatformDb` |
| Endpoint side | `healthcheck/src/*.ps1`, staged into the client payload by `build.ps1` |

### Things that will bite if forgotten

- **Two different addresses.** Reports are *delivered* to `HealthCheckEmailTo`; the report is
  *footed* with the tenant's `SupportEmail`, because a customer reading it needs somewhere to
  write. Clint hit this and reported it as a fault. The settings page now says so.
- **`Organisation` in the toolkit means the END CUSTOMER**, not the IT company. The installer
  cannot know it — a machine is linked to a client in the portal afterwards — so it writes the
  machine name as a placeholder and the monthly run replaces it from `/api/healthcheck/context`.
  Pass the **runtime** value to the report builder, not the one in `config.json`; naming the
  placeholder matched no records and silently produced no report at all.
- **Retries are driven by `.pending` markers, never by scanning the work folder.** A machine that
  had the standalone toolkit on it still holds that toolkit's results under a different
  organisation, and a sweep would post another organisation's data into this tenant.
  `DESKTOP-OPHQIDH` is exactly such a machine.
- **`SetApplicationName` must not change** — see §10. The tenant mail password depends on it.
- The report's colours were literals that happened to be Anywhere IT's own, so it looked correctly
  branded here and would have looked wrong on every reseller's first report. They come from the
  tenant now.

### Proven, and not

**Run for real:** the installer download with the toolkit inside it, a clean install on
DESKTOP-OPHQIDH with the task registered for 5 Oct 08:14, branding reaching `config.json`, a
read-only check on Clint's laptop, a branded PDF, the upload, the customer name resolved from the
device identity, the retry queue (broken connection, marker written, marker cleared on the next
run), the portal page, the PDF download and its access control — and on 2026-09-13 **a real email,
sent by the server through the real mailbox, arriving with the PDF attached**.

**Not yet:** a scheduled run firing on its own, unattended, as SYSTEM with nobody logged in. Every
part of it has been exercised by hand; Windows starting it has not. First real one is
**5 October 2026, 08:14** on DESKTOP-OPHQIDH. Also untested: a Windows Server (maintenance always
skips there, by design), a machine neglected for a year, and whether ESET objects to an unsigned
script running as SYSTEM.

## 18. Hearing the customer's machine, as of 2026-09-13

The technician presses **Listen** on the session toolbar and hears what that machine is playing.
`docs/NEXT-SESSION-AUDIO.md` is the brief and the reasoning; this is what was built and what was
measured.

### What was measured first, and what it bought

Nothing was designed until loopback capture had been proven with the host's own token, because
rendering a sound and capturing one are different permissions and different code paths — and Edge
refusing to render a PDF as SYSTEM (§17) is what that lesson cost last time.
`tools/hostinfo/audiolisten.ps1`, run through `audioprobe --listen`, on DESKTOP-OPHQIDH as
`NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM` in session 1:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Can SYSTEM open `IAudioClient::Initialize` with `AUDCLNT_STREAMFLAGS_LOOPBACK`? | **Yes.** Verified by a Goertzel filter against a tone the machine was playing, not by ear. |
| Does a **muted** endpoint still feed loopback? | **Yes, at full amplitude.** Loopback is taken *before* the endpoint's volume and mute are applied. Confirmed twice: on a muted DESKTOP-OPHQIDH, and on this laptop by muting, capturing, unmuting, capturing again — identical RMS to five decimals. |
| What arrives when nothing is playing? | **No packets at all**, not packets of zeroes. A loop that waits for a packet stalls forever and looks broken. |
| Mix format | 48 kHz stereo float32 on both machines. |

That last row of the fear list — "mute makes silence ambiguous" — turned out to be wrong in our
favour. The mute and volume are still shown next to the meter, precisely *because* they are the
first thing anyone blames for silence.

### How it works

- **`BinKind.Audio = 3`**, framed `[3][seq:u32][rate:u32][channels:u8][format:u8][pcm]`. The
  format travels **with** the data so a mid-session device change cannot arrive out of order with
  the samples it describes. **The hub needed no change at all**, as predicted.
- **`AudioCapture` (host)** — WASAPI loopback on the default render endpoint, on a dedicated
  thread like capture, cursor and input. Downmixed and resampled to **24 kHz mono 16-bit**: about
  48 KB/s against the 384 KB/s the device hands us, no library, no codec. It polls for the default
  device changing and reopens on `AUDCLNT_E_DEVICE_INVALIDATED`.
- **`AudioPlayer` (console)** — `waveOut`, a 280 ms jitter buffer, silence written to cover a gap
  rather than stopping the device, and drift absorbed by dropping the oldest packet when the queue
  runs past 600 ms.
- **The UI** — a Listen button on the toolbar, a level meter and the endpoint's device, mute and
  volume on the status bar. The meter is the point: it is the only evidence available to a
  technician who is not wearing headphones, and a feature with no visible feedback gets reported
  as broken (the drag-and-drop lesson, §8).

### Things the harnesses found that reading the code would not have

- **A misaligned struct read that changed between runs.** `WAVEFORMATEXTENSIBLE`'s SubFormat GUID
  is at offset **24**, not 26. The wrong offset produced a different GUID every run — which is
  what an unaligned read looks like, and is worth recognising on sight.
- **A broken reader that looks exactly like a silent machine.** With the format unrecognised, the
  first probe filled its sample array with zeroes and reported "300 packets, peak 0". Both the
  probe and `AudioCapture` now refuse a format they cannot decode, before capturing anything.
- **"The resampler is 1.1% slow" was an edge effect.** Running the same test for 20 s instead of 5
  left the same ~50 ms absolute shortfall. Measure at two lengths before believing a rate error.
- **The jitter buffer collapsed the moment playback began**, because all four `waveOut` buffers
  take a packet at once — a 200 ms prebuffer became one spare packet. It is now sized as buffers
  plus slack.
- **The player wrote silence too eagerly**, filling a freed buffer the instant the queue was empty
  even with 120 ms still playing in the driver. It now waits unless every buffer has come back.
  Starvation over eight seconds went 9 → 7 → 4, each step measured rather than assumed.
- **The Listen button half-covered the connection pill** at the default window width. There is no
  room for a fifth right-hand toolbar button at 1320 px, so the pill moved to the status bar.
  `viewprobe`'s screenshot is the only reason that was seen before it shipped.

### Proven, and not

**Proven:** capture, downmix, resampling, framing, parsing and playback, end to end on this
laptop, by `tools/audiolocal` — a 1 kHz tone played by the machine at itself and recovered from
the frames by a Goertzel filter. The session window's layout, by `viewprobe`, on real hardware.

**Proven on real hardware, 2026-09-13:** the wire. A build was shipped to DESKTOP-OPHQIDH and
Clint confirmed audio streaming working over a live session. So capture as SYSTEM, the new binary
frame, the hub relaying it untouched, and playback on the console are all done and working
against a real customer machine, not just on one laptop.

**A trap worth remembering**, now written into `ship-build.ps1`'s closing advice: a harness that
joins an EXISTING session is talking to the `Host.exe` that was running when that session started.
Straight after a ship that is the old binary, and the check reports "no audio arrived" — correctly,
about a host that has never heard of `AudioListenMsg`. End any open session first.

**What the first real `audiocheck --screen` run said, 2026-09-13:** PASS on the tone, 102 frames,
**zero sequence gaps**, peak 0.97, and 1 kHz energy three orders of magnitude above its
neighbours. The wire is good.

It also reported "−32.12% clock error", and that was the **harness lying**, not a fault:

- Zero sequence gaps means the host never *sent* the missing frames. Nothing was lost.
- `audiotone.ps1` built its wave in a 350,000-iteration PowerShell loop and took **seconds** to
  start playing. Loopback sends nothing at all while a machine is quiet, so that thinking time
  arrived as missing audio. It now tiles one 48-sample period at 48 kHz: 6 s of tone in 260 ms.
- `audiocheck` measured drift against the whole window instead of the span frames were arriving
  over. It now separates the two and says which is which.

**The lesson worth keeping:** a diagnostic that can report a fault the code does not have is
worse than no diagnostic, because it sends the next person to the wrong file. Both halves were
fixed the same day the number appeared.

### The bandwidth measurement, 2026-09-13 — the input to the Opus question

Measured with a **video playing** on DESKTOP-OPHQIDH, which is the case that matters:

| | |
|---|---|
| Audio, while flowing | **~47 KB/s** (24 kHz mono 16-bit plus 11 bytes of header per 40 ms frame — exactly what the design predicted) |
| Screen, video playing | **~1,513 KB/s** |
| Screen, desktop idle | **~0.3 KB/s** (only changed tiles go on the wire) |
| Clock drift over the span | **+0.10%** — normal, and absorbed by the console's queue |
| Sequence gaps | **zero**, through a socket carrying 1.5 MB/s of tiles |

**What that says about Opus.** Against a busy screen audio is ~3% of the traffic and a codec
would save nothing anybody notices. Against an *idle* screen audio is the entire cost: 47 KB/s
continuous, about 380 kbit/s, which is most of a typical South African ADSL uplink and would be
felt. So the honest answer is that it depends on the link, not on the screen — and the decision
belongs to Clint under the "nothing is bought in" rule. **Not decided, deliberately.**

That run also proved something worth more than the numbers: **zero sequence gaps while screen
tiles were using 1.5 MB/s of the same socket.** The worry in the brief — that a tile burst would
stall audio into an audible gap — did not happen.

**Still not measured:** drift over a twenty-minute session.

### Telling the customer, added and working 2026-09-13

A machine that can play music can carry a speakerphone call, and an unattended session can be
listened to with nobody in the room. The host reports `AudioStatusMsg` on the session socket,
which only technicians see, so **both hubs relay it to the customer's tray app on the device
connection** — the route chat already takes, and the only one that reaches a window the person at
the machine can see. Three places say it: the corner banner (amber, named, and it re-presents
itself at the moment listening starts even if it had been dismissed), the tray window's status
pill, and the chat log plus a balloon. It is cleared when the session ends, because the host dies
with the session and cannot send a closing "stopped".

**Confirmed working on DESKTOP-OPHQIDH after a ship, 2026-09-13.** Note that this one needs the
**tray app** replaced, not just `Host.exe` — a host-only update would leave the indicator silent
while everything else worked, which is the most misleading possible outcome for a disclosure
feature.

### The Sound tab — why a machine is silent, added 2026-09-13

Roadmap 3.1, folded in as the sixth side-panel tab. Streaming answers "is there sound"; this
answers "why is there none", which is the question a support call actually starts with, and it is
the half neither competitor offers.

- **`AudioDevicesRequestMsg` / `AudioDevicesMsg`** — the technician asks, the host answers with
  every playback and recording endpoint in every state, which of Windows' *three* defaults each
  one holds, volume, mute, the per-application mixer on the default device, and whether `Audiosrv`
  and `AudioEndpointBuilder` are running. Read on the host by `AudioDiagnostics` through the same
  MMDevice API the Windows sound page uses, so "what Windows thinks" is literally what is shown.
- **`AudioFindings` turns that into sentences** and is deliberately kept out of the window,
  because pure rules can be asked about machines that are a nuisance to arrange for real.
  `audiolocal --findings` runs ten of them — no devices, everything unplugged, no default, the
  defaults disagreeing, a muted app, a stopped service — and says pass or fail. **The healthy
  machine is checked the other way round**, that it produces *nothing*.
- The tab asks on first open rather than showing an empty box, and repeats the Listen button and
  meter so nobody has to go back to the toolbar.

### The PROPVARIANT bug, worth remembering

`PROPVARIANT` is **24 bytes on x64**. Declared `[StructLayout(LayoutKind.Explicit)]` with fields
at 0 and 8 it comes out **16**, and `IPropertyStore::GetValue` then writes **eight bytes past the
end of the caller's stack slot**.

What that looked like from the outside: the device's friendly name read perfectly, the adaptor
name came back empty every single time, and **adding a diagnostic print made it work** — because
that changed what was sitting next to the struct on the stack.

It was found by comparing against `audioprobe.ps1`, which prints the adaptor correctly on this
laptop: same wrong struct, getting away with it. All three declarations now say `Size = 24`, and
the value is released with `PropVariantClear` rather than leaking the string.

**A heisenbug that moves when you look at it should point at a struct size every time.**

### Shipping note

The Sound tab needs a **new host** on the customer machine — `AudioDevicesRequestMsg` did not
exist before this. Against an older host the tab will sit on "asking…" for ever. The listening
indicator needed the **tray app** replaced; this one needs `Host.exe`. After any ship, end any
open session on the machine before testing, or the harness joins a session still hosted by the
binary that was just replaced.

### The console window, as of 2026-09-13

**Closing the console hides it to the tray.** It stopped calls ringing and chat arriving, which is
never what an X button means; the customer's tray app has worked this way since the start. Exit is
on the tray menu and nowhere else. Anything arriving while hidden raises a balloon — a ringing call
names the caller and their machine. `tools/trayprobe` proves both failure directions, because they
are opposites: an accidental close must not kill the console, and Exit must still work.

**The session window's tabs are reachable in every viewing mode.** Two separate causes were behind
"I have to pop the screen back in before I can do anything":

- Full screen hid the side panel outright. The tabs now stay; a narrow strip on the panel's left
  edge folds them away when the whole monitor is wanted.
- **A pop-out window is owned by the session window, and Windows keeps an owned window above its
  owner, always.** On a single monitor the pop-out covered the tabs and nothing could raise them
  past it. The panel now travels into the pop-out window with the screen, and returns to the child
  index it came from — docking is resolved in z-order, so re-adding it at the end leaves it running
  full height behind the toolbar.

**Tabs wrap to two rows when the words do not fit.** Six tabs across a 337 px bar is 51 px each and
"Clipboard" does not fit at any readable size; shrinking only produced "Cli…" in smaller type.
`LayoutTabs` traces the bar width, row count and the font each button ended up with, because "the
tabs say Scri…" has several causes that look identical on screen.

## 19. Surviving a dropped socket, and the system-action buttons — 2026-09-13

Roadmap 1.4 and 1.5. `docs/NEXT-SESSION-RECONNECT.md` is the brief; this is what was built and
what was measured. Clint's three decisions are recorded first because they are choices, not
findings: **90 seconds** of grace, **the customer is told** while it lasts, and a failed reconnect
**leaves the window up with a Reconnect button**. Reboot holds for **five minutes**.

### The measurement that shaped it — do not lose this

The console announced a recovery that no code performed: `SessionLink` connected once and never
retried, while `SessionForm` set the pill to "○ reconnecting" on the very event that meant it had
given up. But a retry loop on its own could never have worked, and this is the part worth keeping:

> The server **ended the session** the moment the last viewer's socket closed, and closed the host
> with it. A retry would have dialled back into a session that no longer existed.

**A dropped Wi-Fi packet and a technician clicking "Leave / End" were the same event.** Everything
below follows from separating them.

### What the two halves do

**Server** (`TenantHub`, mirrored in `RemoteSupport.Server/Hub.cs` — both were changed):

- `BeginGrace` holds the session for 90 s when the last viewer's socket drops. The host keeps
  running, the session stays in `HubRegistry`, and a viewer that comes back rejoins the session it
  left. Overtaking is by a **`GraceToken` counter**, not by cancelling timers: a timer that fires
  holding a stale token has been overtaken and does nothing, which cannot race with a reconnect
  landing mid-tick.
- **`EndSessionMsg` is now handled on the viewer socket.** It was only ever handled on the
  technician's dashboard socket and **nothing in the solution ever sent it** — closing the session
  window was the only way a session ended, which is exactly why the two cases were
  indistinguishable. "Leave / End" sends it now, and a deliberate end still ends the session at
  once. With several technicians in a session it means "I am leaving"; the others keep it.
- A session that is **gone** answers a viewer with `SessionEndedMsg`, not a bare `ErrorMsg`. A
  retry loop has to tell *not yet* from *never again*, and an error reads as the first when it
  means the second.
- **`SessionStateMsg`** goes to the customer's tray app when a session starts being held, when the
  technician returns, when it ends — and **whenever a device connection appears**. That last one is
  the fix for BUGS #2; see below.

**Console** (`SessionLink`, `SessionForm`):

- Retries with backoff (1, 2, 3, 5, 5, 8 s) for **120 s** — deliberately longer than the server's
  90, because the server is what decides when a session is over and a client that gave up first
  would turn a recoverable drop into a lost session.
- **Every handler is attached before the pump, on every attempt.** This is the trap from §10 and it
  is central here: the replayed `MonitorsMsg` lands within milliseconds and is the only thing that
  triggers a first `SubscribeMsg`. A handler attached late leaves a reconnected viewer on a
  permanently black screen — **indistinguishable from a reconnect that failed**.
- **State is put back after a reconnect**, because the server replays the monitor *list* and
  nothing else: the selected monitor (with `On = true`, which forces a full frame), the quality,
  and **Listen**. Listening is a disclosure, so it is restored rather than quietly dropped — the
  customer's banner would otherwise be the only thing in the system that still knew.
- A failed reconnect **does not close the window**. It greys the view, says so, and offers
  Reconnect, which starts a *fresh* session on the same machine and re-attaches the window to it —
  the chat, the transfers and the script output survive. The pill says **"disconnected"**, never
  "reconnecting", when nothing is trying.
- `ScreenView.Stale` veils the picture and refuses input. **A frozen last frame is the most
  convincing lie a remote view can tell**, and clicks aimed at it land where the windows were a
  minute ago.

### The buttons (1.5)

One **System ▾** menu, not three buttons — there is no room for three, and grouping them is honest:
these are the things you do *to* a machine rather than with it.

- **The old Ctrl+Alt+Del button could never have worked.** It synthesised the three keystrokes with
  `KeyMsg`. Windows reserves the secure attention sequence and **discards a synthesised one in
  silence** — the same shape of failure as UIPI in §4. It goes through `SysActionMsg` now and the
  host calls **`SendSAS`** from `sas.dll`, which a SYSTEM process may do without the
  `SoftwareSASGeneration` policy. That is exactly how `SessionLauncher` starts the host. An
  attended-only host is not SYSTEM and is told so rather than failing quietly.
- `DoSysAction` had a bare `catch {}`, so **every failure looked like a success**. It answers with
  **`SysActionResultMsg`** now, always. A reboot Windows refused looks exactly like a reboot about
  to happen, and the window would have waited five minutes for a machine that was never going.
- **Reboot confirms first**, and the confirmation says whether the console can get back in:
  unattended, yes; attended-only, *"somebody has to be at it to accept"* — said up front rather
  than discovered by waiting.
- Reboot does **not** use the grace period. The machine is gone for minutes and the host dies with
  it, so the window holds, polls for the machine, and re-attaches to a **new** session.
- Reboot, lock and Ctrl+Alt+Del are all **logged to the ticket**, like a script run.

### BUGS #2 — closed, and why the diagnosis is trusted

The hypothesis in the bug was right. `DeviceLink` reconnects on its own and **nothing re-sent it
anything when it did**, so a tray app whose socket blinked never learned the session had ended and
went on saying "support in progress". It is reproduced deliberately by `tools/reconnectlocal`
CHECK 2 — the device socket is aborted mid-session and brought back — and the fix is the
`SessionStateMsg` sent to every device connection as it appears. See `docs/BUGS.md` for the
reproduction and the one caveat.

### Proven, and not

**Proven on this laptop, 17 of 17, by `tools/reconnectlocal`** — no customer machine, no live
server, nothing installed anywhere. It runs **its own platform on port 8099 against a throwaway
database in the temp folder** and pretends to be a customer machine: a device connection, a host
socket, tile frames, and viewer sockets killed with `Abort()` rather than closed. Clint's live
server on 8090 and his real database are never touched. Same argument as `tools/audiolocal`: the
thing being tested is session *lifetime*, and SYSTEM, desktops, capture and UIPI have nothing to
do with it.

It covers: the session surviving an aborted socket, the host staying alive, the viewer being let
back in, the monitor list being replayed, **tiles resuming** (counted before and after — "it
looked fine" is not the measurement), the customer being told, the device resync of BUGS #2,
Leave / End still being immediate, and **the hold expiring on its own** so a held session cannot
leak a host forever.

**Proven by `tools/toolbarprobe`, 6 of 6** — the session window's layout at 1280, 1320 and 1600 px
with overlap computed rather than eyeballed, plus screenshots of the reconnecting, disconnected and
restarting states. It found three real things before they shipped: the System menu overlapping
Refresh and Listen by up to 74 px at narrow widths, the quality slider sitting under the Control
checkbox (pre-existing), and the banner's text cut mid-word with no ellipsis to admit it.

**Proven on real hardware, 2026-09-13 — `tools/reconnectcheck`, 10 of 10 against DESKTOP-OPHQIDH.**
The viewer socket was killed with `Abort()` mid-session; the session survived, the same host
process was still alive and answering, the monitor list was replayed, and tiles resumed (135 before
the kill, 138 after). "Leave / End" was still refused instantly. With `--grace`: the server
announced the hold at 30 s and had cleaned the session up by 100 s on its own.

**So 1.4 is done on hardware.** It needed only the new *server* — the grace period is server-side
and the harness is the viewer, so it was confirmed before the customer machine had new binaries.

**Not proven yet — needs the new client binaries on DESKTOP-OPHQIDH:**

- **Ctrl+Alt+Del actually reaching the Winlogon desktop.** The reasoning is sound and the host
  already runs as SYSTEM, but `SendSAS` has never been called on a real machine here. Prove it,
  do not assume it.
- A real reboot, and the five-minute hold re-attaching when the agent brings a host back.
- The customer-side banner and pill during the grace window, seen on the machine.

### A refused machine is no longer silent — added 2026-09-13

Found while chasing a customer machine that had stopped connecting. Three separate faults, all
the same shape: a device turned away at `/ws/device` was invisible from **both** ends.

- **The server logged nothing** on any of the four refusal paths — no hello, no tenant key,
  unknown or inactive tenant, device key mismatch. All four log a warning now, naming the machine,
  the remote address and the reason.
- **`DeviceLink` had no `ErrorMsg` case at all.** The server sent the reason and closed the socket;
  the reason was received and dropped on the floor. There is an `OnServerError` event now, shown
  on the tray app's status pill, in its chat log and as a balloon, and logged by the agent, which
  has no window and was otherwise silent everywhere.
- **It retried every 3 seconds for ever.** A refusal is a decision, not a blip. It backs off to 30
  seconds after one — which matters most in exactly the case that hurts: a lapsed trial turns away
  every machine on the tenant at once, and each of them was dialling back twenty times a minute.

**Why it matters more than it looks.** `IsServiceEnabled` is `Active || (Trial && !expired)`, so
the day a tenant's 14-day trial lapses, every one of its customer machines goes quiet
simultaneously with nothing written anywhere. The message now distinguishes a lapsed trial from a
suspension and gives the date, because those have completely different fixes.

**Proven by `tools/reconnectlocal` CHECK 5, 20 of 20**: it suspends the throwaway tenant through
the CLI, reconnects the pretend machine, and checks both halves — that the machine is told in
words, and that the line appears in the server's own output naming the machine and the reason.
Suspending takes the identical branch a lapsed trial does.

### Traps found along the way

- **`ASPNETCORE_URLS` does not override `"Urls"` in `appsettings.json`.** The JSON provider is
  added after the environment one, so the file wins. `tools/reconnectlocal` passes `--urls` on the
  command line instead. This does not fail quietly: it tries to bind 8090 and collides with the
  live server.
- **A probe that checks whether a held session is alive by connecting a viewer REJOINS it**, which
  correctly cancels the hold — and aborting that probe starts a fresh ninety seconds. The grace
  test checked at 30 s with a viewer and then declared a leak at 100 s, because its own probe had
  moved the deadline to 120. **This bit twice, in two different tools** — it was found and fixed in
  `reconnectlocal`, written up here, and then hit again on the first real-hardware run of
  `reconnectcheck`, which still had it. If a third tool ever needs to ask "is this session still
  held", it must ask **without joining**:
  - `reconnectlocal` asks the **host socket**, which `EndSession` closes.
  - `reconnectcheck` cannot see that socket (it is on the customer's machine), so it watches the
    **technician dashboard** passively — `BeginGrace` broadcasts a `SessionReadyMsg` with
    `Held = true`, and `EndSession` broadcasts one with the host gone and the technicians cleared.
    Take a watermark of the queue at the abort first: `StartSession` broadcasts its own
    `SessionReadyMsg` before the host has connected, which is byte-for-byte the same shape as the
    one `EndSession` sends and otherwise reads as "it had already ended", every time.

  Same lesson as the clock-drift number in §18: a diagnostic that can report a fault the code does
  not have sends the next person to the wrong file. Both times the product was correct.
- **A docked WinForms `Label` did not wrap here.** The banner's second line was simply not drawn
  and the text was cut mid-word. The messages are written to fit one line, with `AutoEllipsis` as
  the backstop rather than the plan.
- The session window now has a **`MinimumSize`**. Below about 1280 px the toolbar cannot lay itself
  out and piles buttons on top of each other — silently, because an obscured button looks exactly
  like one that is not being pressed.
