## 20. Warning a tenant before its trial lapses — 2026-09-13

§19 made a lapsed trial *visible*; this stops it happening. `IsServiceEnabled` is
`Active || (Trial && !expired)`, so the moment a 14-day trial runs out **every one of that
company's customer machines is refused at the same instant**. Explaining that afterwards is not
the same as preventing it.

Clint's decisions, taken before any code: a **new platform mailbox**, notices at **7 days, 1 day
and on expiry**, sent to **every admin** on the tenant.

### The two halves, and why one of them does not need mail

- **A portal banner**, in `_Layout.cshtml` rather than on the dashboard, so it is on *every*
  portal page. Somebody signing in to work a ticket is exactly the person who never opens the
  dashboard. It shows inside the last week and after expiry, and **it works with no mailbox
  configured at all** — which is why the warning is not left to the email alone.
- **`TrialNoticeService`**, the **first `BackgroundService` in this codebase**. Nothing else on
  this server runs on a timer; copy this pattern rather than adding a second mechanism. It wakes
  hourly, and every pass is wrapped so a tenant that throws is skipped rather than stopping the
  loop.

### The platform mailbox is not a tenant's mailbox

`PlatformSettings` is a single row holding the address **the product** writes from. A tenant's own
SMTP already exists, but it is for writing to *their* customers (the monthly health check), and
using it here would mean a reseller's own mail server telling them their trial had ended — and
would simply not work for a new trial that has configured nothing. The password is encrypted with
Data Protection under its **own purpose string**, so a tenant protector cannot read it and vice
versa. It is still tied to `data/keys` and `SetApplicationName`; see §10.

Set it at **`/owner/mail`**, which also has a **Send test** button and a **Run the trial check
now** button. Mail that has never been tried is mail that does not work, and the first time these
settings matter is the moment a customer is lapsing. There are CLI equivalents too
(`platform-mail show|set|test`, `trial-notices`), because the Linux host will not have a browser
and a mailbox that can only be set through a web page is a mailbox that does not get set. **The
password comes from `RSP_SMTP_PASSWORD`, never an argument** — an argument ends up in shell
history and the process list.

### Decisions inside it that are easy to get wrong

- **A notice is recorded only when it was actually sent.** A mail failure leaves it unrecorded so
  the next pass retries. Marking it sent and moving on would let a mail outage silently eat the
  one warning that mattered — `trialnoticecheck` CHECK 5 exists to catch exactly that.
- **No mailbox configured is not a failed send.** It is reported once per pass, not once per
  tenant per hour, and nothing is marked — so configuring a mailbox later still delivers every
  notice that is due.
- **The wording names the consequence.** "Your trial is ending" gets filed; "every computer you
  installed it on will be refused, all at once" gets acted on. It also says plainly that nothing
  is deleted, because the first fear is data loss.
- Ordinary technicians are **not** written to. Admins are.

### The bug the harness found, which was really a disagreement

`TrialDaysLeft` used `Math.Floor`, and the portal's status pill had always used `Math.Ceiling`.
Two consequences, both caught by `tools/trialnoticecheck` and neither obvious by reading:

- a tenant with 7 days and 20 hours left was counted as **7**, so the seven-day warning went out a
  day early — **and disagreed with the number the portal was showing them at that same moment**;
- the last twelve hours counted as **0**, so the "your trial has ended" notice was sent while the
  trial was still running.

Everything that counts trial days now goes through `Tenant.TrialDaysLeft`, and `StatusText` uses
it too, so the email and the portal cannot drift apart again. **A number shown in two places that
differ by one is worse than no number**: it makes the reader distrust the whole notice.

### Proven

**`tools/trialnoticecheck`, 18 of 18, on this laptop.** Throwaway database in the temp folder,
and a **real SMTP server** — a minimal sink on a local port that accepts a message and keeps it.
It sends real mail over a real socket rather than stubbing the send, because the things most
likely to be wrong are the addresses and the wording, and a test that only asserted "it decided to
send" would pass just as happily with an unroutable From address.

It covers: silence at 8 days; the 7-day notice reaching **both** admins and not the technician;
the subject and body saying what actually happens; the notice **not** repeating on the next hourly
pass; the 1-day notice saying "tomorrow"; the on-expiry notice in the past tense; nothing after
all three; and a mail failure leaving the notice unrecorded and then delivering it once the
mailbox works again. `SHOW_MAIL=1` prints what arrived, for reading the prose, which no assertion
can judge.

**Not proven:** a real mailbox, a real internet SMTP server with TLS and a password, and the
hourly pass firing on its own overnight. Every part has been exercised by hand or by the sink;
Windows and a real mail provider have not been.

## 21. Testing the buttons for real — 2026-09-15

Everything §19 and §20 built went to a machine and was used. Four faults came back. All four were
measured before anything was changed, and **two of my own assumptions were wrong along the way** —
both recorded here, because the wrong ones cost more than the right ones saved.

### Ctrl+Alt+Del: three attempts, and the answer was a machine policy

| Attempt | What it did | Why it failed |
|---|---|---|
| Original | Synthesised Ctrl, Alt and Delete as `KeyMsg` | Windows **reserves** the sequence; a synthesised one is discarded in silence |
| Second | Host calls `SendSAS` as SYSTEM | `SendSAS` needs a **service**; the host is a process launched into session 1, which is not the same thing |
| Third | Agent (a real session-0 LocalSystem service) calls `SendSAS` | Correct — but still did nothing, because of the policy below |

**The cause is `SoftwareSASGeneration`, which defaults to 0 = none** — software SAS disabled for
everybody, services included. `SendSAS` then **returns successfully and does nothing**. That is why
it took three goes: the host reported "carried out", the agent reported "sent Ctrl+Alt+Del", and
both were telling the truth about a call with no effect.

`Install-Client.ps1` now sets it to **1 (services only)** when the unattended agent is installed,
and only when it is absent or 0, so an administrator who chose 2 or 3 is left alone.
`tools/hostinfo/enablesas.ps1` does the same for machines installed before that. **Confirmed
working by Clint** once the policy was set.

The routing stays: **Ctrl+Alt+Del goes to the AGENT, everything else to the host.** An
attended-only machine is told it needs the agent rather than being sent a request nothing can
carry out.

### Restart: it reconnected too early, which looked like not reconnecting at all

Read out of the session log rather than reasoned about:

```
08:58:43  restart sent
08:58:49  session ends — the host is going down
08:58:54  a NEW session starts   <- the poll, five seconds later
08:58:55  it dies
```

`shutdown /r /t 5` leaves the machine up and accepting connections for several seconds, and the
agent answers right until the service stops. So the poll succeeded against a machine already on
its way down, `ReattachAsync` cleared `_rebooting`, and the next failure took the ordinary dead
path and offered a Reconnect button. Two changes, because either alone leaves a gap: **leave the
machine alone for 30 s** before the first attempt, and **if a session re-attached during a restart
dies within 25 s, go back to waiting** rather than calling the restart a failure.

### The toolbar vanished in pop-out and full screen

The tabs had been fixed for this once (§18); the toolbar had not — so both modes lost the monitor
selector, the Control tick box and the System menu, the last of which is exactly what full screen
is for. It travels into the pop-out with the panel now, and stays in full screen along with the
status bar, which carries the connection pill.

**`toolbarprobe` passed every assertion while "Pop in" sat underneath "Leave / End"** with two
buttons off the end: the toolbar had been added to the pop-out *before* the side panel, so it only
got the width left beside it. Docking resolves from the highest child index down, so the toolbar
must be added **last**. Only the screenshot caught it, so the probe computes overlap per viewing
mode now as well as per width.

### The startup error on the customer's machine was Windows, not us

Clint could not get a file **off** the machine to show what the error was. The file was collected
with the new `tools/fetchfile`, and the screenshot turned out to be Windows' *Open File — Security
Warning: the publisher could not be verified*, naming `RemoteSupport.Client.exe`.

**All three installed exes carried `ZoneId=3`** — the mark Windows attaches to anything downloaded
and propagates to files extracted from a marked zip, which is exactly how the installer arrives.
The tray app is launched from the HKLM `Run` key, so that dialog appeared **at every logon** and
nothing started until somebody clicked Run. **On every customer machine installed from the portal.**

`Install-Client.ps1` now unblocks what it installs, and the health check scripts. 
`tools/hostinfo/unblockclient.ps1` fixes a machine already installed — run on DESKTOP-OPHQIDH,
5 marked files cleared. Code signing (stage 5) would fix the *Unknown Publisher* wording, but it
is the **mark** that raises the dialog at all, so this is needed whether or not we ever sign.

### Found while fetching that file, and NOT yet fixed

- **`%DESKTOP%` is only resolved for drag-in.** `HostEngine` translates the sentinel for
  `FileSetOfferMsg` and nowhere else, so `FileListRequestMsg`/`FilePullMsg` treat it as a
  **relative path** and resolve it against the host's working directory:
  `Could not find a part of the path 'C:\Program Files\Anywhere IT\Remote Support\%DESKTOP%'`.
- **The Files tab lists nothing when it is opened.** The path box starts empty and nothing sends a
  first `FileListRequestMsg`, so the tab is blank until something is typed. It *does* display
  errors (`[Error] …`), so a blank list is genuinely "nobody asked", not a swallowed failure.

Both are in `docs/BUGS.md` and both belong to the next piece of work,
`docs/NEXT-SESSION-FILES.md`.

### New tooling

| Tool | What it answers |
|---|---|
| `tools/sysactioncheck` | Does a system action reach the machine, and what does it say back? Distinguishes carried out, refused, and **nothing listening at all** — which look identical from the technician's chair. Refuses to send `reboot` on purpose. This is what roadmap 1.5 asked for and never got. |
| `tools/fetchfile` | Lists a folder on a customer machine and brings a file off it, driving the same wire path the Files tab uses. A harness that can do the job is also the measurement of whether the job is possible. |
| `tools/hostinfo/deployedprobe.ps1` | What is actually installed and running there, and **has the agent service been restarted since its binary changed** — a service whose exe is new but whose process is old behaves exactly like one never updated. |
| `tools/hostinfo/sasprobe.ps1` | Which `SendSAS` argument works, observed by watching the input desktop rather than by asking anybody to look. |
| `tools/hostinfo/hosttrace.ps1` | The host's own trace, its identity lines, and every system action ever attempted. |
| `tools/hostinfo/agentprobe.ps1` | The agent service's account and session — the thing `SendSAS` turns on. |
| `tools/hostinfo/enablesas.ps1` | Sets `SoftwareSASGeneration` on a machine installed before the installer did it. |
| `tools/hostinfo/motwprobe.ps1` / `unblockclient.ps1` | Finds and clears the downloaded-from-internet mark. |
| `tools/userpaste <machine>` | **The paste, asked as the customer.** Runs a real paste, then has the far machine ask the SHELL — from a task running as the logged-on user at Medium integrity — whether Explorer offers Paste, and invokes it. The only harness that stands where Explorer stands; everything before it read the clipboard back as SYSTEM and got a true answer to the wrong question (§39). |
| `tools/clipil` | The integrity boundary on its own, this laptop, no server needed: a file list written at Medium, read and pasted from a LOW child, and the reverse. Checks the mechanism behind §39 with no customer machine involved. |
| `tools/hostinfo/stationprobe.ps1` | Window station, desktop, clipboard sequence number, sessions, who owns explorer.exe, whether LogonUI is up. Where a clipboard question should start. |
| `tools/hostinfo/helperprobe.ps1` | What the `--put-files` helper did, and who owns or holds the clipboard right now. |

`ship-build.ps1` also learned two things that each cost a step: a server started from an **elevated**
terminal cannot be stopped from a normal one (the giveaway is an **empty** `ExecutablePath` and
`CommandLine` from `Win32_Process`), and the **technician console holds its own exe open**, so
`demo\technician` cannot be refreshed while it runs — checked up front now rather than after two
minutes of publishing, and the message says that closing its window is not enough because it hides
to the tray.

### The lesson worth keeping from all of it

**Three separate faults were each reported honestly as a success by the layer underneath.** The
host said a Ctrl+Alt+Del was carried out; the agent said the same; `fetchfile` showed an empty
folder where the host had actually returned an error it was not printing. In every case the code
was telling the truth about the wrong question. When something "does nothing", the next move is to
find the layer that would *notice* — an input desktop that should change, a session row that
should appear, an error field nobody reads — rather than the layer that reports.

## 22. Moving things between the machines, finished — 2026-09-15

Roadmap 1.3, widened. `docs/NEXT-SESSION-FILES.md` is the brief; this is what was built. The wire
was already proven and was not touched: `treecheck` 19 of 19, `clipcheck` 7 of 7, `filesetcheck`
20 checks. **Every gap that was left was in the console's UI or in one unresolved path on the
host**, exactly as the brief said, and no time was spent in `FileSetTransfer`.

Clint's three decisions are recorded first, because they are choices rather than findings:

- **The Files tab opens on the customer's desktop.** Their drives cannot fail but are never the
  folder anybody wants; their desktop is where the screenshot or the error log that started the
  call actually is.
- **A drag-out lands where it is dropped**, not always in Downloads — symmetric with drag-in,
  which already lands where the gesture pointed, and it is the only answer that lets a file go
  straight into an email or a ticket.
- **A file taken off a machine is LOGGED, not announced.** No banner, no balloon, no change to the
  status pill: a line in the tray app's chat log and a note on the ticket. Sound has a banner
  (§18) and files are not obviously different in kind, but a banner per file would interrupt the
  customer several times in a normal job, so it is auditable afterwards instead of intrusive
  during.

### The ordering problem, which is the only hard part of drag-out

`DoDragDrop` gives the drop target a **`CF_HDROP`: a list of PATHS, not bytes.** Explorer does not
ask us for content — it copies from the paths it was handed, the instant the button comes up. So
the files have to exist on the technician's machine *before the drop completes*, or the drop fails
with no error worth reading.

That is the same problem paste solved, so it takes the same route rather than a second one: the
bytes move first as a file set into a staging folder under `%TEMP%\RemoteSupport\drag`, and only
then is the shell handed those paths. Which means the fetch happens **inside the `ItemDrag`
handler, with the mouse button still down**, through a nested message pump — the drag has to begin
from inside that handler or Windows has no gesture left to carry. Three files took 280 ms on real
hardware, so ordinarily it is not felt. When it is, **the files are already here**: a drag whose
`DoDragDrop` returns `None` puts them on the clipboard and the status bar says so. Nothing
fetched is ever lost to a mistimed gesture.

**The drag starts in the Files tab's list, not on the picture of the remote desktop.** The console
knows what is selected in its own list; grabbing an icon on the remote screen would need the host
to hit-test its own desktop and report what is under the cursor, which is a separate piece of work
and is not what the job — getting a log, a screenshot or a backup off a machine — needs.

### `%DESKTOP%`, resolved once, where a path arrives

`HostPaths.Resolve`, called in `HostEngine`'s message switch for `FileListRequestMsg`,
`FilePullMsg`, `FileSetPullMsg`, `FileOfferMsg` and `FileSetOfferMsg` alike. **Resolving at each
use site is exactly how it came to be wired for one message out of five** (BUGS #6), and below
that line nothing else in the host has to know the sentinel exists. `FileSetTargets` is now
`RemotePaths`, with `%DOWNLOADS%` and `%DOCUMENTS%` as well. An unknown sentinel is passed through
**unchanged and traced**, never quietly turned into a relative path — that is the bug in miniature.

### A latent fault found on the way

`_pullOnToClipboard` was a field that was **set and never read**, so every tree that arrived went
onto the technician's clipboard whatever it had been fetched for, and two overlapping pulls shared
one answer. It is a per-set-id `PullIntent` now, which is what lets a drag land its bytes in its
own folder without touching a clipboard the technician is relying on.

### How it is proven — `tools/dragoutcheck`, 39 of 39

On this laptop alone: no server, no session, nothing installed anywhere, four seconds.

- **The drag, for real.** Everything about the staging folder and the `CF_HDROP` is asserted — one
  folder per drag, nothing outside it (`..\`, an absolute `C:\Windows\...`, a UNC path), one bad
  entry condemning the whole drag, a copy rather than a move, and a file still in flight refusing
  to be dragged at all. Then **CHECK 4 performs a real `DoDragDrop` with real `SendInput` mouse
  input into a real drop target and compares SHA-256 of what arrives.** That is the difference
  between "we built a file list" and "the drop worked", and it is the answer to "a real drag is a
  shell interaction, so how would you test it".
- **The Files tab, over a real socket.** CHECK 5 runs the **real `SessionForm`** against a
  websocket the harness answers as if it were the customer's machine, so what is asserted is the
  message that actually left the console. A flag the console set itself would have agreed with the
  bug. The harness answers the first request with the exact error a machine at the logon screen
  gives, so the fall back to the drives is exercised rather than reasoned about, and it checks the
  request happens **once per session** rather than on every click.
- **The sentinel**, by its properties rather than by asking the code what it thinks: fully
  qualified, ends in `\Desktop`, exists, and is not under `config\systemprofile`.

**It was verified to FAIL when the code is wrong, not merely to pass when it is right.** The
existence check, the tab's fallback and the sentinel resolution were each broken deliberately;
each was caught, and nothing else moved. A harness that has never been seen failing is an opinion.

**Found by the screenshot it writes, which no assertion would have caught:** the file list's fixed
columns totalled 390 px in a 337 px panel, so the Modified date was cut off and the list scrolled
sideways — on the one tab whose whole job is now to be readable the moment it opens. Same lesson
as the Listen button half-covering the connection pill (§18).

`toolbarprobe` 18 of 18 and `filesetcheck` 20 of 20 still pass.

### Shipped and run on DESKTOP-OPHQIDH — 2026-09-16

The ship happened. Five harnesses run from the laptop against the real machine, all passing:

| Harness | Result |
|---|---|
| `fetchfile --list` (no path) | `C:\Users\Lenovo\Desktop` listed, 7 items — **BUGS #6 closed** |
| `reconnectcheck` | 7 of 7 — tiles resumed after the socket was killed; a deliberate End still refused immediately |
| `clipcheck` | 7 of 7 — round trip byte-exact, and a separate process on that machine saw the same text on WinSta0 |
| `treecheck` | 19 of 19 — both ways, byte for byte, empty folder, zero-byte file and `café ümläut.txt` all survived |
| `audiocheck --screen` | the 1 kHz tone arrived: Goertzel 1000 Hz = 0.754 against 0.0004 either side, 0 sequence gaps |

**The drag out works on a real machine — confirmed by Clint, 2026-09-16.** A file dragged from the
Files tab onto his own desktop arrived and opened. That is roadmap 1.3's actual deliverable and the
one thing `tools/dragoutcheck` could only approximate here: the harness drives `SessionForm`
against a socket it answers itself, so it proves the ordering and the messages, but the drop itself
is Windows handing a `CF_HDROP` to Explorer and no harness performs that.

**The Files tab opens on the customer's desktop by itself — confirmed by Clint, 2026-09-16.**
Nothing typed, no Go pressed: the tab was opened and their desktop was listed. **BUGS #5 closed**,
and it is the same listing the drag out came off, so 1.3's two halves are proven together rather
than separately.

**The disclosure works too — confirmed by Clint, 2026-09-16.** The customer's tray app carried a
line naming the file taken, and the ticket for that session carried the same line. Both were the
last things checked on purpose, because they are the pair that fails silently: they need
`RemoteSupport.Client.exe` replaced and not merely `Host.exe`, and a host-only ship leaves the
disclosure quiet while everything else looks right — the trap the listening indicator sprang in
§18. It did not spring this time.

### Stage 1 is finished, and finished on hardware

Nothing in §22 is outstanding. Roadmap 1.3 is proven end to end on DESKTOP-OPHQIDH: the sentinel
resolves (BUGS #6), the Files tab opens on the customer's desktop unprompted (BUGS #5), a real drag
lands a real file on the technician's desktop and it opens, and the person whose machine it came
off is told — in their tray app and in the ticket.

**What that means for the harnesses.** `dragoutcheck` stays at 39 of 39 and stays useful, but it
never covered the two things that actually mattered to a customer: a `CF_HDROP` reaching Explorer,
and a human being told a file left their machine. Both needed a hand and a pair of eyes. Worth
remembering the next time a harness count is mistaken for proof — the harness measured what it
could reach, which is not the same as what the feature is for.

### Two things the 2026-09-16 run said in passing, neither a fault

**Their speakers are muted and at 31%, and the tone still arrived.** That is correct and worth
knowing before someone reports it as a bug: WASAPI loopback captures the render stream *before* the
endpoint's mute and volume are applied, so we hear what the machine is playing even when the person
in front of it cannot. It is also the exact fault `audioprobe` found on this machine in §18 — still
muted, still the reason a real "no sound" call would start.

**With an idle screen, audio is most of the traffic:** 47.1 KB/s of audio against 8.6 KB/s of
screen. §18 measured the other end of that range — 47 KB/s against 1,513 KB/s with video playing.
So the Opus question is not "is audio expensive"; it is "how often is the screen quiet while
someone is listening", and on an unattended machine being diagnosed the answer is "usually". That
strengthens the case for Opus more than the video-playing measurement did.

## 24. The capture path, and what measuring it changed — 2026-09-16

Stage 2.1 is done. `docs/NEXT-SESSION-CODEC.md` is the brief for the rest of the stage and carries
the detail; this is the state of the build.

**The stage's complaint was "our picture looks worse", and measuring it split that in two.**

- **Speed was the CAPTURE.** GDI `BitBlt` cost 43–115 ms a frame while JPEG cost 8. The product's
  12 fps was a fiction: the pipeline could not reach it on anything but an idle screen. That is
  fixed.
- **Bandwidth is the CODEC, and it is untouched.** A scrolling document costs **2.8 MB/s** — about
  22 Mbit/s of customer uplink, which no ADSL or LTE line here has. 2.1 did not move that number
  and could not have: the tiles and the JPEG are the same either way. **2.2 is the whole of what
  is left.**

### What is in the build now

`ScreenCapture` (GDI) and `DxgiCapture` (Desktop Duplication) both implement `IScreenSource`.
`HostEngine` tries the fast one and keeps the slow one, because duplication is refused on some
adapters, in some session states, and whenever another process already has the same output
duplicated — a running screen recorder is enough. Losing capture entirely is a worse fault than a
slow picture.

Two things about where and when, both of which cost thinking and neither of which is obvious:

- The source is chosen **on the capture thread**, not in the constructor. A duplication object is
  bound to the desktop of the thread that created it, and the capture thread is the one that
  follows the user between Default and Winlogon (§4).
- The fallback fires after **30 consecutive real faults**, not one. `ACCESS_LOST` is routine —
  every UAC prompt and every resolution change costs one and the capturer rebuilds itself — so
  giving up at the first sign of it would mean running GDI for the rest of any session in which the
  customer touched a prompt.

`src/RemoteSupport.Host/Dxgi.cs` is hand-rolled DXGI and D3D11 interop; nothing is bought in, so
COM objects are IntPtrs called through the vtable by slot. **Read its class comment before editing
it.** A wrong slot number does not throw — it calls a different method with the wrong arguments.

### Measured, 1920x1200, quality 55, 12 fps cap, both paths against the same scene

| condition | GDI | DXGI |
|---|---|---|
| idle | 64.2 ms/poll, 30% CPU | **0.3 ms, 0% CPU** |
| scroll, capped | 71.6 ms/frame, 46% CPU, 2817 KB/s | **21.3 ms, 16% CPU**, 2792 KB/s |
| scroll, ceiling | 14.9 fps | **45.1 fps** |
| video, capped | 89.1 ms/frame, 50% CPU, 2625 KB/s | **24.1 ms, 22% CPU**, 2618 KB/s |
| video, ceiling | 12.0 fps | **22.4 fps** |
| full frame on subscribe | 107 ms | **28 ms** |

Idle is the number that matters most for this business: unattended machines sit idle nearly all the
time, and that went from a third of a core to nothing.

### Three faults the bench caught, none of which looked like faults

- **Dirty rectangles are a superset of what changed.** A dirty rect says Windows *redrew* those
  pixels, not that they came out different, and an application that invalidates its whole window
  every frame — most of them — makes duplication report the whole window. Trusting them sent 150
  tiles a frame where 24 had changed. The rectangles now rule most of the screen out and the
  survivors are compared against the previous frame exactly.
- **A forced-full frame has to work on a screen that has not changed.** Duplication only hands over
  what moved, so a technician subscribing to an idle desktop would have waited for the screensaver.
  One GDI grab primes the buffer when the duplication is created.
- **The bench was measuring the wrong screen.** Its scene window lost the front to an always-on-top
  application, so an "idle" pass photographed a live editor and reported 100 KB/s of somebody
  else's animation. It now proves which window owns the middle of the monitor and marks any row it
  cannot vouch for.

### Proven on hardware — DESKTOP-OPHQIDH, 2026-09-16

`tools/capturecheck`, 11 of 11, against Windows 10 19045 with the agent hosting as SYSTEM:

- **Desktop Duplication runs as SYSTEM.** `Host running as: SYSTEM`, `Screen capture: DXGI Desktop
  Duplication`. First frame 149–249 ms after subscribing, across six runs.
- **The picture is right.** Four PNGs read by eye: legible file listings, the Start menu, correct
  colours and geometry.
- **It survives the Winlogon desktop.** Follows the user there, loses duplication, rebuilds,
  follows back — round trip 1.4 s, frames still arriving across it, never falling back to GDI.
- **The UAC prompt itself is captured, and legible.** "Do you want to allow this app to make
  changes to your device? Windows Command Processor." That is the protected-content question
  answered as well, and it is the one no harness on this laptop can reach: a host that is not
  SYSTEM gets a frozen picture there and no error whatsoever.
- **An idle machine sends nothing.** 0 KB/s over twelve seconds, repeatedly.

**Still not observed: the GDI fallback firing in the field.** Duplication has never been refused on
either machine, so that path is exercised only by the constructor's own failure route. It is the
one thing in 2.1 that has not been seen working outside the code.

### The bug this found, and how

**A forced-full frame demanded by a desktop switch was never sent**, and the only thing that showed
it was looking at the picture. Every check passed while `capture-winlogon.png` was a torn composite:
blocks of dimmed UAC desktop over blocks of the previous desktop, seconds stale, no error anywhere.

The switch sets `_forceFull`. The very next capture pass **reads and clears** that flag, then hits
`ACCESS_LOST`, drops the duplication and returns nothing — so the complete frame was spent on a pass
that sent none. Everything after was incremental against a buffer the viewer had never seen. The
quiet part: a UAC prompt sitting still is a **still screen**, so the rebuilt duplication had nothing
new to offer and correctly said nothing, leaving the stale half stale for as long as the prompt was
up.

Fixed in two places, because the flag can be lost two ways: a new duplication owes a whole frame in
its own right (`Output.NeedsWholeFrame`), and the host puts the demand back rather than spending it
on a pass that produced no tiles.

**Three times in this work a harness reported confidently on a question it was not able to answer** —
an idle screen read as a live one, a missing field read as "Default", and the last frame of a prompt
read as the prompt. Each was fixed by making the harness say what it could not see. That is the same
lesson as §21 and it is apparently worth relearning.

## 25. The codec — 2026-09-16

Stage 2.2. The half of stage 2 that 2.1 deliberately did not touch: **2.8 MB/s for a scrolling
document**, which is about 22 Mbit/s of customer uplink and is not a number any South African ADSL
or LTE line produces. Speed was the capture and 2.1 fixed it; bandwidth was always the codec.

> **SUPERSEDED 2026-09-17. The encoder works, and the conclusion this section reaches is wrong.**
>
> Everything below about *what was built* is still accurate. What is wrong is the finding it ends
> on — that this laptop's Quick Sync has no encode engine behind it. **It has.** The fault was two
> of our own constants: `MFT_MESSAGE_NOTIFY_END_OF_STREAM` (0x10000002) and
> `..._NOTIFY_START_OF_STREAM` (0x10000003) were **swapped** in `Mf.cs`, so `BeginStreaming()`
> started the stream and then told the encoder it had ENDED. Every encoder answered `S_OK` and
> then correctly never asked for a frame. Behind that sat a second fault: the first
> `ProcessOutput` returns `MF_E_TRANSFORM_STREAM_CHANGE` — how a hardware encoder settles its
> output type — and `H264Encoder.Encode` declared that flag and never read it.
>
> Both fixed. A whole 1920x1200 screen encodes to **10.9 KB** and decodes at **1.0 of 255**
> against the original; scrolling went **2785 → 198 KB/s** and CPU **12.7% → 1.0%**.
> `docs/NEXT-SESSION-CODEC.md` is the current record. **Do not re-derive the missing-silicon
> theory from the text below** — it was reasoned carefully from real evidence and it was still
> wrong, which is the most useful thing in this section.

**Built and compiling; the encoder is NOT yet proven on hardware, and this laptop cannot prove it.**
Read the last section here before trusting anything in the rest.

### What was built

A new project, `src/RemoteSupport.Media` (net8.0-windows), referenced by the host and the console.
Nothing bought in: Media Foundation is driven the same way `Dxgi.cs` drives DXGI, as IntPtrs called
through the vtable by slot, with every interface written out in header order so the count can be
re-derived rather than trusted.

| file | what it is |
|---|---|
| `Mf.cs` | the interop. Read the class comment before editing it. |
| `MfTransform.cs` | one transform, driven correctly whether it is synchronous or asynchronous. |
| `MediaDevice.cs` | the D3D11 device as Media Foundation will accept it: multithread-protected, behind a device manager. |
| `GpuColourConverter.cs` | BGRA to NV12 on the graphics card, for encoders that will not take a desktop frame as it comes. |
| `H264Encoder.cs` | the encoder, and the bitrate curve the quality slider drives. |
| `H264Decoder.cs` | the console's end. Software decoder on purpose. |
| `Nv12.cs` | NV12 to BGRA, with both YUV matrices. |
| `MediaInventory.cs` | what this machine actually has, unfiltered. |

**The frame never touches the CPU on the host.** `DxgiCapture.TryAcquireGpuFrame` keeps a second,
on-card copy of the screen (`Output.Video`) and copies the duplicated texture into it GPU to GPU.
That texture is wrapped as an MF sample in place. The staging texture and readback in the tile path
exist only because encoding a tile needs the bytes; re-introducing one here would give back most of
what 2.1 won.

**The device now asks for `D3D11_CREATE_DEVICE_VIDEO_SUPPORT`, and asks for it second.** A machine
that refuses it still gets the capture path 2.1 proved on hardware and simply cannot encode, which
is a negotiation the session already knows how to lose.

### The negotiation, and why it is a list

`SubscribeMsg.Codecs` carries what the console can decode, best first. Absent means JPEG tiles,
because absent means an older console. The host picks what it can produce and falls back — an old
console, the GDI capture path, no encoder, a device without video support, an encoder another
application is holding — and every one of those refusals ends with a sentence in the console's Info
tab: **"Video codec"** and **"Video codec fell back because"**. `BinKind.Video = 4` carries
`[monitor][flags][width][height][annex-B]`. The hub relays binary frames without inspecting them,
so **the server was not changed at all.**

Three things that are not obvious and each of which is a black screen if got wrong:

- **A decoder must start at a key frame.** Fed a predicted frame first it does not fail; it builds
  a picture from a reference frame it never saw, which is a slowly self-correcting smear that looks
  exactly like a bad link. `VideoFlags.KeyFrame` is on the wire and everything before the first one
  is dropped and counted.
- **"A packet was sent" is not "the forced full frame was honoured".** An encoder can answer a
  forced key frame with a predicted one. `SendVideo` returns whether a key frame actually went out,
  and the host puts the demand back if not — the same trap as §24, with a worse symptom.
- **Only the console knows whether it can decode what it asked for**, and it only finds out when the
  first frame arrives. `ScreenView.OnVideoUnavailable` makes it subscribe again without H.264.

### What is proven, and on what

**Proven on this laptop, and the picture was looked at:** `codecbench --mfpipe` takes a real
duplicated frame through the device manager, the GPU colour conversion and the NV12 conversion and
compares it to the screen — **0.5 of 255**, with correct primaries, no channel swap, correct
geometry. That exercises everything the encoder stands on: `MediaDevice`, `SetD3DManager`, media
type negotiation, `ProcessInput`/`ProcessOutput`, the texture wrapping, `IMF2DBuffer`, and
`Nv12.ToBgra`.

**Proven against a real machine over a real session:** `codeccheck` against DESKTOP-OPHQIDH, which
is still running a pre-2.2 host. It ignored the `Codecs` field exactly as an older build should,
sent JPEG tiles, and the new console composed the picture correctly. **Backward compatibility is
not a theory.**

**The colour matrix is measured, not assumed.** BT.709 scores 0.5 and BT.601 scores 3.9 at
1920x1200, agreeing with `Nv12.Is709`. That measurement was wrong the first time and the way it was
wrong is the point: the bench's text scene is black ink on white paper, which is grey, and **on grey
the two matrices produce identical pixels**. The check ran, compared both, got the same number to
one decimal place and reported a pass without having tested anything. `SceneKind.Colour` — still,
saturated, with a grey ramp as a control — is what made the two states distinguishable. That is the
fourth time in two stages that a harness has confidently reported on a question it could not answer.

### The category GUID, and a conclusion reached by luck

**The first version of `Mf.cs` had the video encoder category GUID wrong**, and the way it failed
is the whole reason this section exists.

`MFTEnumEx` given a category that does not exist **does not complain**. It returns `S_OK` and zero
transforms — which is byte for byte what a machine with no encoder returns. So the enumeration came
back empty under every combination of flags, and the conclusion written into this handover, the
roadmap and the commit message was that this laptop has no H.264 encoder at all. It was a confident,
thoroughly documented, well-evidenced conclusion, and the evidence was a typo.

What caught it was going to look at the registry for a different reason. Every registered category
is a subkey of `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Classes\MediaFoundation\Transforms\Categories`, named by its GUID
without braces, so the real ones can be READ rather than recalled:

```
video encoder   f79eac7d-e545-4387-bdee-d647d7bde42a     <- the right one
video decoder   d6c02d4b-6833-45b4-971a-05a4b04bab91     <- was already right
video processor 302ea3fc-aa5f-47f9-9f7a-c2188bb16302     <- was already right
```

The decoder and processor GUIDs were correct, which is exactly why they worked and why nothing
looked suspicious: two of the three categories enumerated perfectly. **One empty category among
several full ones should have been the question, and was not.**

With the GUID corrected, this laptop lists a dozen video encoders, including **Intel® Quick Sync
Video H.264 Encoder MFT** — hardware, asynchronous, and willing to take BGRA directly, which is the
best case the encoder was written for.

### What is NOT proven

**Neither D3D-aware encoder on this machine will actually encode**, in two different ways:

- **Intel Quick Sync Video H.264 Encoder MFT** activates, unlocks (verified by reading the attribute
  back), accepts the Direct3D device manager, accepts both media types, returns `S_OK` to
  `MFT_MESSAGE_NOTIFY_BEGIN_STREAMING` and `MFT_MESSAGE_NOTIFY_START_OF_STREAM` — and then **never
  raises a single event**. Twenty frames offered, twenty refused, `GetEvent` empty throughout.
- **Microsoft AVC DX12 Encoder** refuses the H.264 output type at 1920x1200 outright with `E_FAIL`.

The software `H264 Encoder MFT` is refused by us, correctly: it is not D3D-aware, so using it would
mean copying every frame back to the CPU, which is the cost stage 2.1 spent a session removing.

Two independent encoders declining in two different ways, on an Alder Lake-N part, is consistent
with **a GPU that has no H.264 encode engine while its driver registers the transform anyway**.
That is a guess, and it is written down as one.

**So the async pump is still unproven, and this machine cannot prove it.** An encoder that never
asks for input looks identical whether the silicon is absent or the event loop in `MfTransform` is
wrong, and nothing measurable here separates them. That is the single biggest open risk in 2.2, and
`MfTransform.Diagnostics` exists to answer it in one line on the first machine that has a working
encoder: if `events` is still 0 there, the pump is wrong; if `needInput` climbs and `haveOutput`
does not, the fault is downstream of it.

The silver lining is real though: **the fallback has now been exercised on hardware.** A machine
whose encoder enumerates and then does nothing is a state the design has to survive, and it does —
it falls back to JPEG tiles and says why.

### What the two machines actually have

`tools/hostinfo/codecprobe.ps1`, run through `runscript`, reads the Media Foundation transform
registry — no runtime needed on the far machine, nothing copied. Run it before assuming anything
about a machine's codec:

```
tools\runscript\bin\Release\net8.0\runscript.exe DESKTOP-OPHQIDH codecprobe.ps1
```

| | this laptop | DESKTOP-OPHQIDH |
|---|---|---|
| | Acer Aspire AL14-31P | Lenovo IdeaCentre K430 (MAHOBAY, BIOS 2013) |
| CPU | Intel i3-N300 (Alder Lake-N) | Intel i5-3330S (Ivy Bridge) |
| GPU | Intel UHD (integrated) | NVIDIA GeForce 615, driver 2018 |
| H.264 encoders | Quick Sync **and** software | **software only** |
| usable by 2.2 | neither — Quick Sync never asks for a frame | none — software is not D3D-aware |

**Neither machine can hardware-encode H.264, for two unrelated reasons.** Here it looks like
Alder Lake-N has no encode engine. On the K430 the GeForce 615 is Fermi-class and NVENC begins at
Kepler, and the i5-3330S's Quick Sync silicon is invisible to Windows — **no Intel display device is
present at all**, not even hidden or problem-flagged, so the iGPU is disabled in firmware because a
discrete card is fitted.

Keep it in proportion: that is a sample of two, and both are unusual. Most machines from Ivy Bridge
onward with a live Intel iGPU do have Quick Sync encode, so the field is very likely healthier than
this test estate. But it does mean **2.2 cannot be proven on either machine.**

**Giving the K430 its iGPU back was tried on 2026-09-16 and is a dead end.** Its BIOS has one
video option, `Video Setup`, fixed at `Auto` and not changeable — so the firmware takes the discrete
card whenever one is fitted and there is no override. The obvious answer, pulling the GeForce 615 so
that `Auto` falls to the iGPU, does not work either: **that machine has no onboard video outputs**,
so removing the card leaves it with no display at all. Both doors are shut; do not spend time
reopening them.

The other devices on the portal — `BILL-PC`, `DESKTOP-L2B85US`, `INPUT-PC`, `SPEC-PC`, `TICKET-PC` —
are demo dummies, not real machines, and are no use for this.

**So 2.2 waits on a machine that has not been seen yet.** `codecprobe.ps1` is the thing to run on
each candidate, and it needs nothing installed: it is plain PowerShell reading the registry, so on a
machine that is not on the portal, copy the one file and run it locally rather than deploying
anything.

```
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File codecprobe.ps1
```

**Run this next, on a machine whose encoder actually works:**

```
tools\codecbench\bin\Release\net8.0-windows\codecbench.exe --mfts
tools\codecbench\bin\Release\net8.0-windows\codecbench.exe --h264check
tools\codeccheck\bin\Release\net8.0-windows\codeccheck.exe DESKTOP-OPHQIDH --seconds 20
```

`--h264check` takes `--encoder <substring>` to pin one candidate, which is how the two failures
above were told apart. `MfTransform.Diagnostics` prints on failure and is the first thing to read.

The first says whether that machine has an encoder. The second encodes a frame, decodes it and
compares it to the screen — **run it before believing any byte count.** The third is the one the
roadmap's "done when" asks for: the same machine, the same screen, seconds apart, once with H.264
offered and once with only tiles, printed side by side. Both ends must be the new build; the host
lives in the client payload, so `build.ps1` then a reinstall on the far machine.

**And the figure to watch for is not the idle one.** `codeccheck` on an untouched machine reports
0 KB/s for both codecs and says so, because 2.1 already made an idle screen free. The comparison
only means anything while the screen is doing something.

## 26. The clipboard mirrors itself — 2026-09-18 (stage 3.5.1)

**Copy on either machine, paste on the other. No tab, no button, no toggle.** Text, files and
folders, by `Ctrl+C` / `Ctrl+V` and by right-click Copy and Paste, which are the same clipboard and
therefore the same code. The Clipboard tab is **deleted**, and with it `BuildClipboardPage`,
`SendClipboard`, the Auto-send toggle and the "Get theirs" button.

**What was actually missing was one watcher.** §8 and 2026-09-16 had already built most of this:
the console watches its own clipboard and pushes text to the customer, and a file set arriving from
a paste is already fetched and put on the technician's clipboard. But **nothing ever watched the
customer's clipboard** — `HostEngine` only answered a `ClipboardRequestMsg`. That is the whole
reason "Get theirs" was a button, and the whole reason copy and paste felt like a place to visit.

### How the watcher works, and why it is not the obvious thing

`ClipboardAccess` polls **`GetClipboardSequenceNumber`** every 250 ms rather than registering with
`AddClipboardFormatListener`. The listener is the documented way and it is the wrong one here:
`WM_CLIPBOARDUPDATE` is **posted to a window**, so it needs a message loop on the thread that owns
that window — and that thread is the one that must stay free to open the clipboard on demand
(reason 3 in the class header). A counter any thread may read has none of that. The cost is a
quarter-second of latency, which is invisible to a human who copies and then reaches for the other
machine.

**The echo guard is inside the class and invisible from outside.** Two ends watching one logical
clipboard is a loop: we write the technician's text, our own watcher sees a change 250 ms later,
sends it back as "the customer copied this", and the two ends trade one string until somebody gives
up. `Writing()` wraps both setters, holds the watcher off, and **re-reads the counter after the
write** so the change we just made is already accounted for.

### The bug `clipmirror` found on its first run — read this before touching the loop

`GetClipboardSequenceNumber` **returned 0 on the first call at process start**, the loop read that
as "this window station has no clipboard" and returned, and the watcher was dead for the life of
the host. Everything downstream still passed, because a watcher that never fires cannot echo
either — 11 of 13, with the two failures three checks apart.

Zero is **transient**, not permanent: the very next run read 48 immediately. And the case where it
is genuinely zero for a long time is the one that matters most — **the host starts as SYSTEM at
boot, before anybody has logged in**, and there is no interactive clipboard until somebody does.
Shipping the first version would have meant copy and paste silently never working on unattended
machines, which is most of them, on the customer's side only. It now waits for a window station
rather than giving up on one, and holds rather than firing if the counter drops back to zero under
it (a logoff).

### The two gates, which are the whole of the privacy answer

Clint's decision, 2026-09-18. §8 refused an automatic sync because the customer's clipboard is very
often a password. That objection is answered by **when** each direction is allowed to move, not by
making one of them manual:

- **Theirs reaches us only while a viewer is subscribed to the screen** —
  `HostEngine.OnCustomerClipboardChanged` checks `_subscribed`. Nobody looking, nothing leaves.
- **Ours reaches them only while the session window is in front** — unchanged since 2026-09-16.

So the password a customer copied at nine this morning never crosses, and the licence key they copy
while being helped does. **§8's "no automatic sync" is narrowed by this, not overturned.**

### The size rule, because a clipboard file list is paths

Copying files puts **paths** on a clipboard, so the bytes must be fetched before a paste can work
on the other machine — the decision has to be made ahead of time, with nobody to ask. Under
`FileSetLimits.AutoFetchBytes` (50 MB) the set moves silently and `Ctrl+V` works; over it, the
status bar says what is on offer and how big and **waits to be clicked**. Both directions measure
the tree with `FileSetSender.Plan` on the machine that holds the files, because only that machine
can. Fifty megabytes is a starting figure, not a measured one.

The proper answer with no threshold at all is a COM delayed-rendering data object
(`CFSTR_FILEDESCRIPTOR` / `CFSTR_FILECONTENTS`), which is how TeamViewer does it and is days of
interop. It is the right answer eventually and it was not the answer now.

### On the ticket, without burying it

Clipboard **text** is reported through `FileActivityMsg` with `Kind = "clip-text"` — the same route
that already carries transfers to the tray app's chat log and the ticket. **A count of characters,
never the characters.** It is coalesced per direction per quiet minute and flushed at session end:
a line per `Ctrl+C` would leave a ticket that is mostly clipboard and unreadable for it.

Clipboard **files** deliberately get no line of their own. The bytes move as an ordinary file set,
and that transfer already reports itself; a second line at the moment of the copy would
double-count every paste and leave the ticket disagreeing with itself.

### How it is proven

| | |
|---|---|
| `tools/clipmirror` | **13 of 13 on this laptop, no server or machine needed.** The watcher fires for another process and stays silent for its own writes, for text, files and folders — including an empty directory, the failure only a folder has. This is the one to run on any change to the watcher. |
| `tools/clipcheck` | **15 of 15 against DESKTOP-OPHQIDH, 2026-09-18.** Four new checks: nothing crosses while nobody is watching (the leak test, and it matters more than the rest put together), a copy arrives within 8 s while somebody is, a folder arrives as a file list with a size a separate process on that machine agrees with, and what we send them does not bounce back. |
| `tools/toolbarprobe` | 18 of 18 with five tabs instead of six. |
| `tools/dragoutcheck`, `tools/filesetcheck` | 39 of 39 and 26 of 26, unchanged. |

**PROVEN ON HARDWARE 2026-09-18: `clipcheck` 15 of 15 against DESKTOP-OPHQIDH**, mirror section
included. The leak test passed on a real machine — four seconds after a separate process on that
machine copied, with no viewer subscribed, nothing arrived. So did the push (within 8 s), the exact
text with its tab and non-ASCII characters, `Auto = true`, a folder arriving as a file list with a
size that machine's own PowerShell agrees with, and the echo guard holding. The wire half of the
mirror is no longer theory.

**What is still open, and it is now console-side rather than wire-side.**

- **The 50 MB threshold has never been crossed in a test, in either direction.** Everything
  measured so far is 3 KB against a 50 MB line, so the branch that has actually run is the one that
  fetches. The offer — status bar, click to fetch, click to send — has never been seen by anybody.
- **`clipcheck` is a viewer, not the console.** It proves the host speaks and what it says. It does
  NOT exercise `SessionForm`: the automatic fetch onto the technician's own clipboard after a
  customer copies files, and `SyncMyClipboard` pushing a copied file set the other way, have both
  only ever run locally. A real session driven from the real console is what closes that.
- **Nobody has performed the gesture by hand.** `Set-Clipboard` from a separate process on the
  customer's machine is the same clipboard write that right-click Copy performs, so the code path
  under test is the right one — but a human right-clicking a file on a real desktop and pressing
  Ctrl+V here is the thing being claimed, and it has not been watched.
