## 27. Copy and paste: a day spent, six real faults fixed, and it still does not work — 2026-09-18

> **SUPERSEDED ON 2026-09-21 BY §39, WHICH FOUND IT.** It was not the data on the clipboard; it
> was who owned it. **Explorer will not paste from a file list owned by a process above it**, and
> the host is SYSTEM. Everything below is still true as a record — the six faults were real and
> are still fixed — and the section is kept for two reasons: those six faults, and the reason the
> seventh was different. Every probe here read the clipboard back **as SYSTEM**, which is not who
> pastes; §39 asked the shell instead, as the user, and got the opposite answer from the same
> paths. **The "ding" below is still unexplained and still open.**

**Read this before touching stage 3.5.1.** It is not a record of a success. It is a record of what
was proven, what was fixed, and what is still unexplained, written so the next attempt starts where
this one stopped rather than where it began.

### What works, on Clint's own hardware

- **Text, both ways.** Copy on either machine, paste on the other. Proven by `clipcheck` 15 of 15
  against DESKTOP-OPHQIDH, including the leak test — nothing crosses while no technician is
  watching.
- **Files reaching the customer's clipboard.** `pasteprobe` on his machine reported three files
  staged in `C:\Users\Lenovo\AppData\Local\Temp\RemoteSupport\paste\...`, all three present on
  disk, and the host's own trace saying `clipboard: put 3 file(s) on the customer's clipboard`.

### What does not work

**Ctrl+V on the customer's machine.** With a correct `CF_HDROP` on their clipboard, pointing at
files that exist, set by a host running as SYSTEM in session 1 on WinSta0. Nobody has explained it.

### The six faults found and fixed — all real, none of them this one

Worth keeping because each is a genuine bug with a harness, and because the pattern matters more
than the list: every one was found by measurement, and every one looked like it would be the
answer.

1. **The paste race.** The console recorded "this transfer was a paste" in a callback queued after
   the last chunk. A small file was written and confirmed by the far machine first, so the handler
   decided it had been an ordinary send and never set their clipboard. **Smaller files failed more
   reliably**, which is the wrong way round for anything anybody would guess at. Recorded at offer
   time now. `pastecheck` reproduces it by answering from inside the binary handler.
2. **`%PASTE%` staging.** A paste delivered into the customer's Downloads, so pasting three files
   onto their desktop left three more in Downloads that nobody asked for. Staged under their temp
   now, the mirror of `DragOut.StagingRoot`.
3. **The hub dropped file chunks silently.** `ws.OnBinary += b => s.Host?.SendBinary(...)` threw
   away the return value; `WsConnection` refuses a frame when its queue is full and says so. A
   70 MB file lost twelve consecutive chunks. `BinaryRelay` waits for room on anything that must
   arrive. **This is the stage 2.3 floor fault in a second place.**
4. **The UI thread walked the copied tree twice.** Fixed once in `OfferMyFilesToCustomer` and left
   in `PushFileSet`, so the console still froze. Both off the UI thread now.
5. **A path-based guard refused every re-copy.** `_lastSentFiles` compared paths, and Explorer
   copying the same file twice produces the identical list — so the second copy did nothing, and so
   did every copy after it. **Testing with one file meant copy and paste worked once per session.**
   Keyed on `GetClipboardSequenceNumber` now, which is what tells a copy from an alt-tab. There
   were two of these, one behind the other.
6. **A pasted file list carried no drop effect.** The drag path has set Copy since 2026-09-15; the
   paste path set nothing, so a paste could MOVE the files out of a staging folder nobody opens.

### The "ding" — three theories, all disproved by the traces

The session window will not restore from the taskbar; clicking it beeps. Still unexplained.

- **A frozen UI thread.** Disproved: `UiWatchdog` is a heartbeat on the UI thread with a watcher
  thread that cannot be blocked by it, and it never fired. `Responding` was True.
- **A modal drag loop.** `DoDragDrop` was being entered with no mouse button held, which is a real
  fault and was fixed — but the trace from the build that reported the ding **contains no
  `drag-out` lines at all.** He was never dragging.
- **A disabled window.** `IsWindowEnabled` on the raw HWND, checked once a second, with
  `GetLastActivePopup` to name the dialog. Never fired either.

So the window is healthy, pumping, enabled, and processing input at the moment it is reported dead.
**The instrumentation is watching the wrong window, or the ding is not this window at all.** That is
where the next attempt should start: find out which window Windows is beeping about, before
theorising about why.

### What to do differently

Six hours went into this and the three worst detours share one shape: **a claim asserted from an
empty log rather than a measurement.** "Your console must be on another machine" came from reading
a trace before a session had opened it. Two freeze fixes came from reading code rather than
reproducing. `tools/console-state.ps1` and `tools/pasteprobe` exist now so those questions get
answered rather than guessed — **run them first.**

And the harnesses lied twice, because they take the real clipboard and Clint was using the machine.
They serialise on a named mutex now and skip rather than fail when they cannot win it. A harness
that cries wolf costs more than one that does not exist.

## 28. The side panel goes: every tool is its own window — 2026-09-18 (stage 3.5.4)

Clint, after the first attempt at 3.5.4 turned five tab buttons into one `Tools` dropdown and left
the panel exactly where it was:

> the whole idea is to get rid of the side bar on the right. listen should be added to the tools
> bar so that all tabs sit at the top instead of anything being on the side.

That is what is built now. The session window is the picture, a toolbar across the top, and the
status bar. Nothing on the right.

### What it is

`Tools ▾` sits on the top toolbar next to `System ▾`, and holds **Chat, Files, Scripts, Sound,
Info** — and, under a separator, **Listen**, which moved off the toolbar. Choosing a tool opens it
as **its own movable, resizable window** (`ToolWindow`), owned by the session window.

The numbers that make it worth doing: the panel was **400 px wide and was 400 px wide whether or
not anybody was using it**, in every viewing mode — so pop-out and full screen, the two modes that
exist to give the picture more room, gave it less. `toolbarprobe` now measures the opposite
directly: *1338 px of a 1338 px canvas*. A window costs nothing until it is opened, and can be put
on a second monitor, which is the thing a docked panel could never do.

### Three decisions worth keeping

**Every page is built at construction and parented into its window straight away, opened or not,
with its handle forced.** The chat log, the script output and the file listing are written to by
messages arriving off the socket whether or not anybody has opened anything, and a `RichTextBox`
with no window behind it silently drops what is appended to it. A tool built lazily on first open
would have lost everything said before it was opened — and it would have looked like a chat bug.

**Closing a tool hides it; it does not destroy it.** What is in these pages is the session's
history. `FormClosing` cancels only `CloseReason.UserClosing` — everything else (the session window
going, the app exiting, Windows shutting down) is let through, or `Leave / End` could never close.

**A tool window never takes the focus by itself.** `ToolWindow.ShowWithoutActivation` is true, and
`ShowTool(index, activate)` is the whole of the distinction: a technician choosing Chat from the
menu gets the focus, but a chat message arriving from the customer, or a file the customer's
machine could not write, brings its window up *behind* the keyboard. The technician may be typing
on the remote machine at that moment, and swallowing their keystrokes into a chat box would be a
worse fault than the one being reported.

### What this simplified

The pop-out no longer carries the panel with it. It had to before, because a pop-out window is
owned by the session window and Windows keeps an owned window above its owner always — so on one
monitor the pop-out buried the panel and the technician had to pop the screen back in before they
could do anything at all. A tool window is owned by the session window too, which makes it the
pop-out's **sibling** rather than something underneath it. `ToggleSidePanel`, `LayoutTabs`,
`_sideIndex`, `_sideCard`, `_sideToggle` and `SidePanelWidth` are all gone.

### How it is proved

`tools/toolbarprobe` — **37 of 37**, at 1280, 1320 and 1600 px and in all three viewing modes. The
checks that matter are about the *panel*, not the menu, because a tidy menu on a 400 px panel is
the half step that was already built once: `_side` no longer exists as a field, the screen host
spans the canvas, `Tools` is under `_toolbar`, Listen is on the menu and **not** on the toolbar,
nothing is open before anything is asked for, a chosen tool is a `Sizable` top-level window owned
by the session and out of the taskbar, closing it keeps it and its page, and a tool still opens
over a full-screen picture and beside a popped-out one.

`tools/dragoutcheck` — **43 of 43**, including the Files window opening on `%DESKTOP%` once per
session, and it photographs the Files *window* now rather than the session window, which after
this change would have been a picture of the remote desktop.

`tools/viewprobe` had not compiled since 222a8a5 gave `Theme.FromBranding` a required `surface`
parameter. Fixed in passing — a harness that does not build is a harness nobody runs.

**CONFIRMED ON THE REAL CONSOLE, 2026-09-18.** Clint ran `demo\technician` against a live session:
*"all seems to be working well."* That is the layout, the Tools menu, the tool windows and both
viewing modes, driven by hand rather than by a harness.

**Still open, and it needs a customer rather than a session.** Whether a chat window that comes up
*without* stealing focus is actually **noticed** while the technician is working on the remote
machine. Nobody has yet been chatted at mid-session. If it turns out to be too quiet, the answer
is a mark on the `Tools` button — not a window that grabs the keyboard, for the reason in the
third decision above.

### One thing this made easy that was not

`tools/ship-build.ps1 -OnlyTechnician`, added the same day. Clint tests through
`demo\technician` — *"i am and always being using the demo technician until the product is
finished"* — so a console change is not testable until that copy is refreshed, and it goes stale
silently. The full ship did refresh it, but also stopped the server, republished Host, Agent and
Client, rebuilt the installer payload and asked for a reinstall on the customer's machine, none of
which a console-only change needs.

The switch publishes the console, refreshes `demo\technician` and the portal's `technician.zip`,
and stops. Ninety seconds rather than five minutes, **and the server stays up**: the `Shared.dll`
lock that forces the stop is on the *platform's* output folder, and publishing the console writes
only to a staging folder under `TEMP`. A console change no longer costs a server restart and a
re-login.

Use the full ship whenever Host, Agent, Client or Shared changed — including when unsure. A stale
`Host.exe` presents as the feature being broken rather than as an old binary, which is §27's
half-day trap and the reason this script exists at all.

## 29. The chat window stays where it is put — 2026-09-18 (stage 3.5.5)

3.5.5 asked for both sides' chat windows to be movable and to remember where they were put. The
technician's half arrived with 3.5.4 — chat is a real window there now. This is the customer's
half, which was the one with an actual fault in it, plus position memory for both.

### The fault

`ChatPopup` was pinned to the bottom-right corner, and **re-pinned there on every message**:
`Present()` called `Reposition()` unconditionally. That is not a preference about where windows
go. The bottom-right of a Windows desktop is where icons are, so the popup could sit on top of
the very icon the customer had just been asked to double-click — and dragging it out of the way
was impossible anyway, because the window was borderless with nothing to drag it by. Even if it
had been movable, the next sentence the technician typed would have put it back.

### What it does now

**It can be dragged**, by the company name across its top — which is that window's title bar and
now says so with a move cursor — and by the window's own background, via `WM_NCHITTEST` returning
`HTCAPTION` for client points. The drag is handed to Windows (`ReleaseCapture` then
`WM_NCLBUTTONDOWN`/`HTCAPTION`) rather than tracked from `MouseMove`, which is what makes Aero
snap, the screen edges and Escape-cancels-the-drag all work without writing any of them.

**The message log and the reply box are deliberately NOT drag handles.** A customer selecting a
licence key out of what the technician typed is a thing that happens, and a log that moved the
window instead of selecting would be the kind of small maddening fault nobody reports and
everybody remembers. `tools/chatprobe` asserts both halves of that, from the popup's own list.

**It stays put.** `_placedByPerson` is the whole of the fix: once the customer has moved it,
`Reposition()` does nothing. Positions are remembered between runs in
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\RemoteSupport\windows.json` via the new `RemoteSupport.UI.WindowPlacement`, which
both sides use — the technician's tool windows remember their size as well as their place, per
tool rather than per customer machine.

**A remembered position that is no longer anywhere is refused.** `WindowPlacement.IsReachable`
wants a grabbable slice of the window's TOP edge on some screen, not one pixel of overlap: a
window showing only its bottom corner cannot be dragged back into view, so it is not reachable.
A laptop undocked, a projector unplugged and a resolution change all otherwise produce a window
nobody can see, click or close — which presents as chat having stopped working. When the screens
change under a window the customer HAS moved, it is nudged back into view rather than sent home
to the corner: throwing away where somebody put a window because they plugged in a projector is
this same fault arriving by another route.

### What the harness found that the screenshot could not

`tools/chatprobe` measures what overlaps what, the way `toolbarprobe` does for the console, and it
earned that on its first run: **the reply box overlapped the Send button by 7 px.** A single-line
`TextBox` takes the height its FONT needs and ignores the height it is docked into — 33 px at this
theme's body font, against the 26 it was given — so the top strip of Send typed into the box
instead of sending. On the window whose entire job is answering the technician. It is invisible in
a picture, because a text box drawn over a button looks exactly like a text box above one.

The fix asks the control (`_input.PreferredHeight`) rather than hard-coding 33, so a tenant with a
larger font gets a taller box instead of the fault coming back for them alone.

### How it is proved

`tools/chatprobe` — **23 of 23**, no server, no session, no customer machine. Default corner
placement with room for the session banner; every control inside the window's bounds; nothing
clickable covered; the drag handles and the two deliberate non-handles; a move recorded; **a
message no longer dragging it back to the corner**, which is the original fault stated as an
assertion; a new popup opening where the last one was left; and an off-screen position refused
with the window coming up somewhere visible instead.

It touches the real `windows.json`, because a fake one would prove nothing, so it copies it first
and puts it back in a `finally` — the harnesses that took the real clipboard while Clint was using
the machine (§27) are why that is not optional.

`toolbarprobe` 37 of 37 and `dragoutcheck` 43 of 43 still pass with the console reading remembered
placements.

**The drag gesture itself is a manual check and the probe says so** rather than pretending: Windows
runs a drag inside a modal loop that cannot be driven from the test process, so the probe proves
what a drag leaves behind, not the drag.

**CONFIRMED ON HARDWARE, 2026-09-18.** Clint, after a full ship and a reinstall of the client on
the customer's machine: *"it works."* That is the drag itself and the window staying put — the
two things the harness could only surround rather than perform, because Windows runs a drag
inside a modal loop the test process cannot drive.

Worth remembering for anything like it: this one needed a **full ship**, not `-OnlyTechnician`,
because it changes `RemoteSupport.Client` and the customer's machine has to get the new client.
A console-only change and a client change look identical from the chair and are not.

## 30. Two items, and a reason attached — 2026-09-18 (stages 3.5.6 and 3.5.7)

### 3.5.6 The tray menu is the two things a customer wants, and Exit

`Request Support`, `Chat with a Technician`, a separator, and `Exit`. It was four — Open, Request
Support, a separator, Exit — and `Open` is the one that went, because double-clicking the icon
already does it and is what people try first.

Chat opens the chat window itself, with the caret in the reply box, rather than opening the tray
window so the chat card inside it can be found. It is the one place a chat window is allowed to
take the focus (`ChatPopup.Open`), and the reason is that the person just clicked a menu item that
says chat: everywhere else the window arrives unbidden and must not swallow what they are typing.

**`Exit` stays, and the roadmap asking for exactly two items was wrong about it.** It was removed
first — nothing in the product depends on it, since `Install-Client.ps1` stops the process itself
before replacing the exe (line 79) and the HKLM `Run` key starts it again at the next logon — and
Clint put it back the same day. He is right: this app runs on somebody else's computer, and a
program that watches for support requests and cannot be closed from its own icon is the kind of
thing people uninstall rather than trust. Quitting it costs the customer nothing they cannot undo
by logging in again, and the alternative to a menu item is Task Manager.

`Open` going is why the double-click on the icon is now load-bearing rather than a convenience.

### 3.5.7 A request must say what is wrong

The dialog asked "What do you need help with? **(optional)**", so calls rang with nothing
attached — and the technician's alert had a "No description given." line to prove it. The
description is required now: at least three characters, refused in the dialog itself rather than
in a message box on top of it, and the complaint clears the moment they start typing.

The floor is three characters and not cleverer than that on purpose. Any rule strong enough to
reject "asdf" also rejects somebody in a hurry writing something true and short, and the person it
would obstruct is by definition already having a bad day. It exists to stop a keystroke dismissing
the question, not to grade the answer.

**On the technician's side the reason is now read first**: largest text, top of the alert, with the
caller's name and machine beneath it. It used to be third, in body text, under a name in 17 pt
bold — so the biggest thing on a support alert was the one fact that changes nothing about how you
answer it. The empty-description branch stays, reworded to "No description — ask what is wrong
(their client app is an old one)", because an old client on a customer's machine can still produce
one and a blank alert would be worse than an honest one.

### What building it turned up, which is the part worth reading

Three faults, each hiding the next, all in the same shape: **a size in pixels measured against a
font in points.**

1. **`AutoEllipsis` and wrapping are exclusive.** A Label with `AutoEllipsis` lays its text on ONE
   line and truncates, so "Sage will not open — it says the licence server cannot be found" became
   "Sage will not open — it says ..." and lost the half that says what to bring. Trimming is done
   by hand now (`FitIssue`), so the text wraps *and* admits when it was cut.

2. **Re-fitting from inside `Resize` broke the layout.** Setting a control's `Text` during its own
   Resize mutates it mid-layout, and the pass then never applies the dock: `_issue` kept the 100 px
   a Label is born with while its five siblings all measured 428. Everything downstream followed
   honestly from a width that was never real, so a whole description came out as "Sage…" — and the
   trimming took the blame for it.

3. **The alert had been clipping its own text on this machine all along.** Its label heights were
   pixel constants written against a 100% display; at Clint's 150% one line of 14 pt is 38 px, not
   the ~25 the constants assumed. Adding a multi-line description is only what made it visible.
   Every label now measures itself from its own font, with the same `TextFormatFlags` the Label
   renders with — measuring one way and drawing another is what cut "found" off the end with
   nothing to show it had been cut — and the alert grows to fit. Three lines of description,
   because two held about 56 characters and a real description is a sentence.

The same fault was in the new dialog hint, found the same way: it ran off the edge of the card and
stopped at "it is the first". It is sized from its font now, and the sentence is short enough to
fit anyway.

**The lesson for the next window in this codebase: do not write a control height as a number.**
Measure it from the font it will draw with. Two of these three were invisible on the developer's
own screen and would have been reported from a customer's.

### How it is proved

`tools/callprobe` — **25 of 25**, no server, no session, no customer machine. The dialog refuses
an empty description and a single character, says why inside itself, clears the complaint when
typing starts, accepts a real one and hands it out; the alert carries the reason as the topmost
and largest text with the name and machine still readable, shows a normal sentence whole, cuts a
very long one at a word with an ellipsis, keeps everything inside its own bounds, and still says
something useful when an old client sends nothing.

It prints the alert's real geometry on every run, and that is deliberate: every wrong turn above
came from a control whose actual size was not what the code assumed, and having the numbers on
screen is what turned each guess into a measurement.

**The tray menu is a manual check and the probe says so** rather than pretending — a `NotifyIcon`
menu needs a running client and a real tray. Three things to look at: Request Support, Chat with a
Technician, a separator and Exit, with no `Open`; `Chat with a Technician` opening the chat
*window* with the caret in the reply box; and a double-click on the icon still opening the tray
window.

`chatprobe` 23 of 23 and `toolbarprobe` 37 of 37 still pass.

**Not yet on hardware, and it needs a FULL ship** — both halves change `RemoteSupport.Client`,
and the alert change is in the console, so this is `ship-build.ps1` with no arguments plus a
client reinstall on the test machine.

## 31. Unattended access becomes a switch the customer holds — 2026-09-20

Clint, 2026-09-20: *"an unattended check box… by default the client installer should be attended,
then by checking the checkbox it switches to unattended, with a message saying that technicians
from the tenant can now access the machine unattended… This should follow through to the
technician dashboard."*

### What unattended used to mean, and why that was the problem

It meant one thing: **the `RemoteSupportAgent` service is connected.** The hub derived it from a
live `DeviceRole.Agent` socket and nothing else. The service was installed only by
`Install-Client-Unattended.bat`, so unattended access was a decision taken **once, at install
time, by whoever was holding the mouse** — and impossible to change afterwards without another
visit and another administrator password. The customer, whose computer it is, was never asked.

### What it means now

Two facts instead of one, and both must be true:

* **the capability** — an agent service is connected (`DeviceInfo.AgentOnline`);
* **the permission** — the person at the machine has allowed it (`Device.UnattendedEnabled`).

`DeviceInfo.Unattended` is now the AND of those, which is what the console's Access column has
always meant and can now actually deliver.

**The permission lives on the server.** That is the important decision here. A flag stored on the
machine being protected is one that machine can decide to believe; stored on the hub, it is
enforced at the point where a session is created — `StartSession` will not choose the agent
connection for a technician-initiated connect unless the device has allowed it. The client app
holds no authority at all, only a view of the server's answer.

**A call is not unattended access.** The rule is not "agent or client", it is *who asked*: if the
customer requested support they are sitting there, so the agent may host it — and it should,
because an agent-hosted session survives UAC and the logon screen. Only a technician connecting
out of the blue needs the permission. Getting this wrong in the obvious direction (block the
agent whenever the flag is off) would have quietly cost every attended machine its UAC capture.

**Only the client connection may change it.** The agent is the thing being permitted and must not
be able to permit itself; a technician cannot grant themselves access to a machine they are not
allowed into. `SetUnattendedAsync` refuses anything that is not `DeviceRole.Client` — one line,
and it is the whole security property.

### What the customer sees

A checkbox on the tray window and a matching item on the tray menu. Ticking it asks first, naming
the company: *"Technicians at Anywhere IT will be able to connect to this computer and control it
when nobody is sitting at it, without anybody here accepting first."* Unticking asks nothing —
withdrawing permission is always allowed to be easy. Both are written into the chat log, which is
this app's record of what has happened on the machine.

Under the box, one line that always says which of the four situations this machine is in: waiting
for the server, no agent service installed, off, or on and naming the company.

**The box shows the SERVER's answer, never its own last click.** A machine that was switched off
while the setting changed comes back telling the truth.

### What the technician sees

Nothing new to learn: the Access column already said `Unattended` / `Attended`, and the hub
already broadcast `DeviceUpdateMsg` when an agent connected or dropped. Ticking the box now
produces the same broadcast, so the console flips live. The portal's device list grows an
"unattended allowed" pill carrying who allowed it and when.

`ConnectDevice`'s refusal was the one thing that had to change: *"Device is offline"* was its only
answer and is now often the wrong one. A machine that is on, connected, and simply has not granted
unattended access is a different situation with a different fix, and a technician told "offline"
goes and checks the network instead of asking the customer to tick a box.

### The installer

**Every install now installs the agent service**, and `-Unattended` no longer means "install the
service" — it means "and tick the box for them". The service does nothing without permission, so
installing it is not the same as turning it on, and that separation is what makes the checkbox
possible at all: a tray app running as the logged-on user cannot install or start a service.

`-Unattended` leaves `HKLM\SOFTWARE\TheRemoteSupportProgram\UnattendedRequested`, which the tray
app turns into one `SetUnattendedMsg` the first time it connects, recording in the user's own
folder that it has done so. HKLM because a standard user must not be able to forge it; recorded
as done because otherwise a customer who turned it off would find it back on at every logon with
nothing on screen to explain why.

**Machines already installed attended have no agent service**, so their checkbox is disabled with
that written under it. They need a reinstall to gain the switch.

### How it is proved

`tools/unattendedcheck` — **32 of 32**, driving the real tray window against a real WebSocket
server speaking the real protocol, with no platform, no database and no customer machine. It
covers: the switch is off and unusable before the server answers; the app identifies itself as a
*client*; ticking asks first and **saying no sends nothing**; saying yes sends the request but the
server's answer is what the box ends up showing; the tray item and the window agree; both changes
are logged; unticking asks nothing; a change the customer did not make still reaches the box
without asking them to confirm somebody else's decision; a machine with no agent service says so
rather than offering a dead tick box; losing the server disables the switch; and everything fits
on the card it is drawn on — §30's rule, checked again, because this is the third control added
to a card whose height is a row of constants.

`MainForm.ConfirmUnattended` exists for the harness alone. The confirmation is a modal dialog,
which a test process cannot dismiss because it blocks the message loop the test is pumping —
without that seam the single most important behaviour here ("turning it on asks first, and not
confirming leaves it off") could only be checked by hand, which is how it would stop being
checked.

**The hub's half is not covered** and the probe says so. Three things to check against a real
server, the first two being the security:

* a technician connecting to a machine with unattended access off is refused, and told to ask the
  person at it to tick the box;
* that same machine still answers a call the customer makes themselves;
* the device list flips between Attended and Unattended live, with no refresh and no reconnect.

**Not yet on hardware.** It changes the client, the agent's installation, the hub and the
database, so it needs a full ship, a server restart to apply migration
`20260920071252_DeviceUnattendedSwitch`, and a client reinstall on the test machine.

## 32. Three things a screenshot found — 2026-09-20

Clint installed the build from §31 on a real machine and sent three pictures. All three were
right, and none of them was visible from here.

### Two "The publisher could not be verified" warnings before the installer even starts

The second one was ours. Every `.bat` in `deploy-client` re-launched **itself** elevated:

```
Start-Process -FilePath '%~f0' -Verb RunAs
```

A file downloaded from the internet carries a mark-of-the-web, and it is **ShellExecute** — what
a double-click does, and what `Start-Process` does by default — that stops and asks about it. So
the customer was asked twice: once for their double-click, and once for our re-launch of the very
same file.

They now elevate **`cmd.exe` with the batch file as an argument**. `cmd.exe` is a Windows binary
and carries no mark, and a batch file passed to `cmd /c` is *read* rather than shell-executed, so
nothing asks. Everything in the script still runs in the elevated window, including the "Done"
message and the pause — which is why this is `cmd /c <bat>` and not `powershell -File <ps1>`: the
latter also removes the warning, and also throws away the only feedback the customer gets.

The quoting was **proved rather than assumed**, from a path with a space in it, before it went in:
a launcher and a target batch file in `%TEMP%\rs quoting test\`, the exact line from the
installers, and the target writing its own path to a file. It arrives intact.

**The first warning cannot be removed without a code signature (roadmap stage 5)** — it is the
shell's, on our file, before any of our code can run. What removes it today is unblocking the zip
before extracting, which clears the mark from everything inside. That is now the *first* step in
`INSTALL - read me.txt` and a highlighted box at the top of the customer's download page, with the
reason given, because a customer who is not told meets a frightening dialog instead.

### Asking for support put two windows on screen

The tray menu's Request Support opened the tray window and then the request dialog on top of it,
so the window underneath existed only to show a button the customer had already pressed. It now
opens the dialog and nothing else, unowned and centred on the screen rather than on a window that
may not be there.

Two consequences had to be handled rather than ignored:

* **feedback.** "Requesting support… please keep this window open" was written for a window that
  is now usually absent. The line is shortened, and when the request came from the tray a balloon
  says it is ringing and that the icon will cancel it.
* **cancelling.** The tray item now follows the state — `Request Support` / `Cancel request` /
  `Support in progress` — because somebody who asked from the icon must be able to cancel from
  the icon.

### The unattended checkbox was on the request window

Clint: *"there should only ever be the unattended check box in the tray, not as part of the
request."* Right, and the reason is what that window is *for*: it is what somebody opens when they
want help now, and a permission that is set once and left for months competes with the button they
came to press.

The checkbox **object** still exists, unparented, and is still the single place the confirm /
send / put-it-back logic lives; the menu item drives it. Two copies of *this* decision is exactly
the bug worth avoiding. The sentence that used to sit under it — which is what tells somebody what
they have agreed to — is the menu item's tooltip, set after the text it mirrors rather than
before, which the first attempt got wrong.

### Proved

`unattendedcheck` **28 of 28**, now asserting that the switch is on the tray menu and **not** on
the window, and that the tooltip carries the current sentence. `callprobe` 25 of 25, with its
manual tray checklist updated: the new five-item menu, Request Support opening exactly one window,
and the item reading "Cancel request" while ringing.

Still not on hardware — this is the same ship as §31.

---

## 32. Contacts, and the console's two tabs — 2026-09-20 (stages 3.6.1 and 3.6.2)

The brief for the whole of stage 3.6 is `docs/NEXT-SESSION-DASHBOARD.md`. Read it before building
3.6.3 onwards; this section is what the first two stages actually turned into.

### 3.6.1 Contacts

A client was one row with one contact person in it, so the second person at a company had nowhere
to live. `Contact` now belongs to a `Client`; a `Device` hangs off either a contact (one person's
PC) or the client itself (a server, the PC at reception); `Ticket` carries a `ContactId` beside the
`ContactName` string it already had.

**`Ticket.ContactName` stays and is still written.** The link answers "who is this, now" and
follows a contact whose number changes. The string answers "whose job was this, then", and survives
the contact being archived or the machine reassigned. Same argument as `HealthCheckRun.ClientId`.

**The invariant SQLite cannot keep**: a machine's contact must belong to its client. It is a pair
of foreign keys where one side is nullable, so there is no constraint to write. It lives in
`ContactService.LinkDeviceAsync`, which is now the ONLY thing that may change a device's owner —
`Devices`, `Client` and the portal dashboard all route through it, and it refuses a mismatch rather
than picking a side. Writing `Device.ContactId` directly is how the two halves get to disagree.

**The migration copies, it does not move.** `Clients.ContactName` stays populated because the
client type-ahead still searches it. Devices are deliberately NOT pointed at the contact it
creates: one contact person was never a statement about who sits at which machine, and a company
with eight PCs would come out claiming all eight belong to whoever answered the phone. Tickets are
not backfilled either — matching free text to a contact by name is a guess written into a permanent
record.

**Linking a machine is one dropdown, not two.** Clients carry their people nested underneath, and
the posted value says which kind it is (`c:3` a company, `p:12` a person). A technician who has
picked "Bob at Zenith" has already said Zenith. Contacts are edited in place on the client page for
the same reason — a separate page to change a phone number is how phone numbers end up in somebody's
own notes instead.

`tools/contactcheck`, **34 of 34**, against the real model, the real migrations and the real service
on a throwaway database. It includes the replay case: run the data step twice, still one Bob.

### 3.6.2 The console's home screen

Two tabs — Attended and Unattended, each carrying its count — over a list of machines gathered under
the customer who owns them. First column is the owner (contact, else client, else whoever is signed
in at the machine, so it is never blank); machine second; a green or red dot at the left edge in
place of the Status column; the Access column gone, because it repeated the tab heading on every row.

`DeviceList` is a class of its own so `dashtabs` can ask it which tab a machine lands on without
reaching into a Form through reflection. **The tab is the customer's PERMISSION, not whether their
agent is up** (`UnattendedEnabled`, not `Unattended`): using the latter would move rows between tabs
as agents came and went, and a list that will not hold still cannot be clicked on.

Grouping uses `ListView`'s own groups rather than a hand-built tree — they collapse natively and
keep the keyboard behaviour. Folds are remembered per CUSTOMER NAME, not per group heading, because
the heading carries a machine count and changes underneath them.

### Three things the numbers passed and a picture did not

The harness was 47 of 47 before any of these were found. `dashtabs` writes a screenshot on every
run for exactly this reason.

1. **The column rules are not `GridLines`.** That property is off, and was off before this stage.
   The faint vertical lines Clint complained about come from the Explorer visual style that
   `NativeDark.Apply` puts on for the dark scrollbars — Explorer's own details view draws them, so
   ours did. Owner-drawn rows paint over them, so they only ever showed where nothing else was
   drawn: under the last row, and in the band a group heading sits in. `NativeDark.NoColumnRules`
   removes the style from the three dashboard lists. **The cost is real and visible**: that list
   goes back to the classic scrollbar and a square `[-]` collapse box instead of the modern chevron.

2. **Two empty cards were holding 430 px of a 900 px window** while the machine list — the thing the
   console is for — got four rows. An empty "Incoming calls" does not need a table with four
   headings and an Accept button; it needs one line saying nothing is waiting. The cards now shrink
   to a heading and a sentence and open to full size the moment something arrives, which is when the
   space is worth spending.

3. **`SectionTitle` had been clipping its own descenders on this machine all along.** `Height = 26`
   against Segoe UI 10.5 pt bold: one line of that is 28 px at Clint's 150%, so "Incoming calls"
   lost the tail of its g — in a control every card in the product uses. It is measured from its
   font now, and its dot is sized and centred from the same measurement.

   And then the fix caused the next one: the quiet line's card height computed the heading's height
   a SECOND way, the two disagreed by eight pixels, and "No calls waiting." was cut in half by the
   bottom of the card. It is added up from the real controls now. §30's lesson keeps being right,
   including while you are applying it.

`tools/dashtabs` — **47 of 47**, no server, no session, no customer machine. Half of it asks
`DeviceList` the rules directly; the other half opens the REAL `DashboardForm` and checks the
`ListView` actually built what the rules said, because the first version passed every rule while the
list rendered flat — `ShowGroups` had not been set.

**Not on hardware.** The console changed and nothing else did, so this ships with
`ship-build.ps1 -OnlyTechnician` — but 3.6.1 is a SERVER change with a migration
(`20260920083611_ContactsAndDeviceOwner`), so the platform needs a restart too.

### The classic scrollbar is a decision, not an oversight

Clint chose it, 2026-09-20, looking at the screenshot: **no column rules, and the classic
scrollbar and square `[-]` collapse box that come with losing the visual style.** The two cannot be
separated — they are the same `SetWindowTheme` call. The third option, drawing the customer rows
and chevrons by hand to get both, was offered and declined as not worth half a day.

So do not "tidy up" `NativeDark.NoColumnRules` or put the Explorer style back on those three lists
because the scrollbar looks dated. That is the trade, and it was made on purpose.

---

## 33. The portal learns who a person is — 2026-09-20 (stage 3.6.3)

The least visible stage in 3.6 and the one everything browser-side was waiting on.

**The portal used to resolve a COMPANY and nothing else.** `PortalPage` read a tenant from the
cookie, so every page was company-wide by construction, and `Login` turned technicians away with
"technicians use the desktop console". That was honest while only administrators could sign in —
and it meant "a technician sees only their own tickets" could not be written down, never mind
enforced.

`PortalIdentity` is now the one place that turns a person into a cookie and back: `technicianId`,
the `TenantRole`, and the home page each role lands on. Administrators stay `"tenant"` and billing
stays `"billing"` — every policy and page convention in `Program.cs` is written against those two
strings and renaming them buys nothing. `"technician"` is the new one, and `PortalUser` is the
folder policy. `/Portal/Billing` is narrowed back to `TenantOrBilling`: it is the ONLY page a
technician may not see that was not already admin-only.

A cookie issued before this stage has no role claim. `RoleOf` reads that as Admin, because until
this stage an administrator is the only thing that could hold one.

### The hand-off

The console's Tickets button opens the browser instead of `TicketsForm`, signed in as the person
already signed in to the console. The socket carrying the request is **already authenticated** —
that is the whole mechanism. The server mints a token, the console resolves it against the server
it is connected to, and `/portal/enter` trades it for a cookie.

- **Single use.** `Redeem` removes before it returns. Two browsers racing one link: one signs in.
- **One minute.** Long enough for a cold browser, short enough that a link read over a shoulder is
  worthless before it is finished being read.
- **In memory**, like `AuthService`'s console tokens. A restart kills every outstanding link, which
  is correct for something with a one-minute life.
- The URL lands in browser history, as every URL does. What is in it is spent by the time the page
  has rendered, which is why it is single-use and not merely short.

**The path is an allow-list, not a sanitiser.** It arrives from the console and ends in a redirect,
and "starts with a slash" does not keep out `//evil.example.com`, which a browser reads as another
host entirely. It is also corrected when the token is MINTED rather than when it is used, so there
is nothing to tamper with in between.

**The link the server sends is RELATIVE, on purpose.** The console resolves it against the server
it is already talking to rather than the server naming itself through `Platform:PublicUrl` — which
is unset on every development machine and stale on any production box the day a domain changes. The
address the console connected to is the one address known to work.

### Scoping came early, deliberately

`TicketService.VisibleTo` belongs to 3.6.4, but letting technicians reach `/portal/tickets` without
it would have shipped a hole. It is applied BEFORE any filter the page offers, so `filter=all` asks
within what somebody is allowed rather than instead of it, and a ticket out of scope looks exactly
like a ticket that does not exist. A technician sees their own work and the unassigned pool — the
pool half is the one deliberate hole, because a ticket nobody has been given must not be work
nobody knows about.

It compares on `Ticket.AssignedTo`, which has always been a display NAME. Changing that to an id is
a migration of every ticket in every tenant. Recorded because it is what breaks the day two people
share a display name.

**`TicketsForm` stays and still builds.** It goes when the browser queue has everything it had,
which is 3.6.4. Leaving a technician with no way to see a ticket at all would be a worse afternoon
than a cramped window.

### A gap from 3.6.1, found while wiring this

The hub loaded a device's contact only in `PersistDeviceAsync`, so a machine that had not
reconnected since the last server restart showed its CLIENT's name in the console's first column
instead of the person's — and would have gone on doing so until somebody rebooted it. The stored
unattended permission had the same gap. Both are loaded in the constructor now.

### How it is proved, and how to try it

`tools/handoffcheck` — **42 of 42**: the token cannot be redeemed twice, the allow-list refuses the
four things that get past a naive slash check, each role lands on its own home page, an old cookie
reads as an administrator, and a technician sees their own tickets and the pool and nothing of a
colleague's.

`tools/testtech` makes one account of each role in the same company, so the three answers to "what
am I allowed to see" can be compared in three browser windows. The password is GENERATED and
written to `data/test-accounts.txt` rather than printed, because passwords do not go in a chat
window (CLAUDE.md); that folder is under `bin/` and is gitignored. `--remove` takes them away. It
refuses to touch any address that is not `@testing.local`, so it can never reset a real
technician's password by being pointed at the wrong company.

**Not on hardware.** Server change plus console change, so it needs a full platform restart and
`ship-build.ps1 -OnlyTechnician`. No client reinstall.

## 34. Roles that are enforced rather than hidden — 2026-09-20 (stage 3.6.4)

### Nothing compares a role

`Services/Permissions.cs` holds the questions: `CanSeeAllTickets`, `CanChangeStatus`,
`CanAssignToAnyone`, `CanClaim`, `CanOpenTicket`, `CanComment`, `CanSeeWorkload`. Pages and
services ask those; none of them looks at a `TenantRole`.

That is not tidiness. Roadmap **3.6.8** makes a person hold a SET of roles — a one-man business is
owner, technician and office administrator at once, and "technician and office administrator but
not owner" cannot be said today at all. Every `role == TenantRole.Admin` scattered through the
pages would be a rewrite the day that lands; this way the answers change in one file and the union
of two roles is simply the OR of two answers. **Do not add a property to `Permissions` that returns
the role** — the point is that callers cannot see it.

### The boundary is in the service

`TicketService.UpdateAsync` gained an overload that takes the asker's role and drops what they may
not change. Not the page — a control that is not on the page is a courtesy to the person using it;
the rule is what runs when the form is posted anyway, from a stale tab, from the console, or by
hand.

A field they may not change is dropped **silently** rather than refused: the rest of what they sent
is legitimate, and rejecting the lot would lose a note they had just typed. The page then says what
actually happened — "Note added." rather than "Ticket updated." — so somebody who may not move a
status is never told they just did.

**The old overload stays and stays wide open.** Session and call handling call it, and they act as
the SERVER rather than as a person; role-limiting them would quietly stop tickets opening from
calls. `ticketscope` asserts that.

### Where the lines fall

| | Technician | Office administrator | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| See | own + the unassigned pool | everything | everything |
| Open a ticket | yes | yes — usually them | yes |
| Comment | yes | yes | yes |
| Status / priority | yes | **no** | yes |
| Assign to somebody | no | yes, any time | yes |
| Claim from the pool | yes, to themselves only | n/a | yes |
| Who has what | no | yes | yes |

Claiming and assigning are deliberately different questions. A technician picking up work nobody
has been given is not the same act as deciding what a colleague will do today.

### The console is not a second door

The hub carried ticket messages with no scope and no role at all, so everything above would have
been walkable around by using the console instead of the browser. `TenantHub.MayTouchTicketAsync`
now gates detail, update and note, `ListAsync` takes the role, and `UpdateAsync` is called with it.
A permission enforced only in a Razor page is a permission with a door standing open beside it.

### /portal/workload

Every technician, what they are carrying, busiest first, and the unassigned pool **on the same
page**. The pool is there and not elsewhere because a ticket nobody has been given is the thing
most likely to be forgotten, and a board that shows six people's work and hides the work nobody has
reads as "everything is in hand".

Work assigned to somebody no longer on the technician list — they left, or were renamed — gets its
own row rather than vanishing. Open work disappearing off a board is the worst way for a board to
be wrong.

### TicketsForm

**Nothing opens it any more.** It is kept, unreachable and still building, until this stage is
proved on real hardware: if the hand-off misbehaves on a machine that is not this one, the fallback
is one line rather than a revert. **Delete it once the browser queue is proved, and delete the
hub's ticket message handling with it.** It is not a way around the rules in the meantime — the hub
scopes and role-checks every message it would send.

### How it is proved

`tools/ticketscope` — **26 of 26**, every check through `TicketService` and `Permissions`, none
through a page. If a check passes and a page still shows the control, that is cosmetic; if a check
fails, the rule does not exist however the page looks.

`contactcheck` 34 of 34, `dashtabs` 47 of 47 and `handoffcheck` 42 of 42 still pass.

**Not on hardware.** Server and console, so a full platform restart and
`ship-build.ps1 -OnlyTechnician`. No client reinstall. `tools/testtech` makes one account of each
role for comparing the three side by side.

---

## 35. Three photos in and three out — 2026-09-20 (stage 3.6.5)

Three photographs of a workshop machine as it arrived before it can be booked in, and three of it
finished before the job can be closed. The point is the argument that does not happen six weeks
later about a scratch on a lid, so what matters is that they cannot be skipped.

### The gates are in the service

`TicketPhotoService.CheckBookInAsync` and `CheckCloseAsync`. The counters on the booking form and
in the console dialog are manners; the rule is what runs when the form is posted anyway — from a
stale tab, from the console, or by hand. **A rule that lives in markup is not evidence of
anything.**

The close gate is wired into `TicketService.UpdateAsync`, which is the single place every status
change passes through, so the browser and the console and anything added later all meet it. A
refused close sets `LastBlockedReason` and drops only the STATUS: the note typed in the same form
still saves. Losing what somebody just typed is a worse failure than the refusal.

**Only Resolved and Closed are gated.** A technician can say "in progress" on a machine with no
photos at all — it is still on the bench.

**Only Workshop.** A remote support ticket has no machine to photograph. `photogate` checks all
four categories rather than trusting the one.

### TicketPhoto.TicketId is nullable, and that is the awkward part

Three photos are required to CREATE a ticket, so they exist before there is a ticket to hang them
on. They are staged against a `StageId` (one per booking form) and a `StagedBy`, and attached in
the same breath that writes the ticket. Two people booking machines in at one counter cannot take
each other's photographs, which `photogate` asserts.

Anything still staged after a day was an abandoned form; `SweepStagedAsync` clears it. Without that
every abandoned booking leaves three photographs on disk for ever.

### The file's NAME is not evidence

`SniffType` reads the leading bytes and decides. The upload folder is served back to browsers, so
accepting "totally-a-photo.jpg" on the strength of its extension is how an image upload becomes a
way to host a script on your own domain. JPEG, PNG, WEBP and HEIC, 12 MB each — a phone photo is
2–5 MB, which leaves room for a real camera without letting somebody put a video on a ticket.

### One endpoint, two callers

`POST /api/portal/photos` takes the portal cookie OR the console's bearer token, because Clint
asked for **both** ways of booking a workshop machine in. One endpoint rather than two, so the
gates cannot drift apart.

The photos go over HTTP and never over the websocket: three 5 MB images on the control socket
would block it, and that is the same socket a customer's call rings on. The console uploads as the
pictures are picked rather than when OK is pressed, so a slow set does not look like a frozen
dialog at the counter.

### The console got its New Ticket back

`NewTicketDialog` was only reachable from `TicketsForm`, which nothing has opened since 3.6.3 — so
the console had quietly lost the ability to raise a job at all. There is a **New ticket** button on
the dashboard header now, beside Tickets.

### How it is proved

`tools/photogate` — **36 of 36**, every check through the services and none through a page.
Including: a text file called `.jpg` is refused; two photos are not three; not even the owner can
close a workshop job without them; a refused close still applies the rest of the update; a remote
support ticket closes with none; and deleting a photo takes its file with it.

`contactcheck` 34, `dashtabs` 47, `handoffcheck` 42 and `ticketscope` 26 all still pass.

**Not on hardware.** Server and console, migration `WorkshopPhotos`, so a full platform restart and
`ship-build.ps1 -OnlyTechnician`. No client reinstall. Photos live in `data/ticketphotos/<tenant>/`,
which is a NEW folder to remember when the platform is deployed or backed up.

## 36. One session, one ticket — 2026-09-20 (stages 3.6.6 and 3.6.7)

The stage that **undoes behaviour that was deliberate**, which is why it is worth reading before
touching any of it.

### What changed, and why it was right before

`ActiveForDeviceAsync` reused a device's newest open ticket with **no time limit**, and
`OpenTicketForCallAsync` added a note rather than opening a second ticket. Both were correct when
a ticket meant *this machine has an open problem*. Since 3.6.6 a ticket means *this was a piece of
work somebody did*, so:

- **Every remote session gets its own ticket and its own number.** A hundred sessions to one
  machine in a day is a hundred tickets. It is supposed to look like a lot — that is what a hundred
  sessions is.
- The only exception is `TicketService.ReuseWindow`, **30 minutes**, measured from the device's
  last ticket's `CreatedUtc`. It absorbs a dropped connection and a customer double-clicking
  Request Support, and nothing else.
- A closed or resolved ticket is never reused however recent.

**The thing most likely to happen to this code is somebody quietly widening that window back**
because the queue looks busy. `ticketpersession` is what stops that.

### A reason, or no session

A technician starting an unattended session is asked why, and the answer becomes the ticket's
description AND its subject — so the queue reads as work rather than as "Remote session on
DESKTOP-2N6FVGT" a hundred times. It is the other half of 3.5.7: a customer has had to say what is
wrong since then.

**The reason travels WITH `ConnectDeviceMsg`.** The ticket is written on the server the moment the
session starts, so a reason sent in a second message would be racing the thing it describes.
`TenantHub.ConnectDevice` refuses a connect without one — the console asks first, so reaching there
without a reason is an old console or somebody driving the socket by hand.

Three characters, matching the customer's dialog and for the same argument: any rule strong enough
to reject "asdf" also rejects somebody in a hurry writing something true and short.

**A session from a CALL carries no technician reason.** The customer already said what was wrong,
and asking the technician to say it again would replace their words with a guess.

**The reconnect path does not re-prompt.** `StartSessionOnAsync` — the Reconnect button and a
machine coming back from a restart — sends the ORIGINAL reason again from `_reasons`, because a
dialog appearing in the middle of a reboot loop would be asked over and over for something nobody
has changed their mind about. Inside 30 minutes the server reuses the ticket anyway.

### A ticket can be part of another ticket (3.6.7)

`Ticket.ParentTicketId`. **One level, and this is the rule that matters**: a child may not be a
parent, a parent with children may not become a child, and nothing may be its own parent. Two
levels would mean a tree, and a tree means somebody deciding where in it a job belongs at the end
of a long day. `SetParentAsync` is the only thing that writes it and refuses all three.

- The parent lists its children and totals **its own time plus theirs**. That total is the job's
  time, and it is what gets billed.
- Each child keeps its own number, description and time. Destroying that would undo 3.6.6.
- **A parent with an open child cannot be closed** — otherwise "the job is finished" and "somebody
  is still working on it" are both true at once.
- **Closing a parent does NOT close its children.** Each is the record of a session somebody
  worked. The foreign key is `SetNull` for the same reason: deleting a parent must not take its
  children's records with it.
- What the page offers as a parent is recent work on the SAME MACHINE, because that is what a link
  is in practice — yesterday's session on the PC you are on again today.

### The queue had to change with it

`/portal/tickets` groups by customer, busiest first, strays last, each block collapsible and
carrying its own total. A flat list of a hundred rows is unreadable, and an unreadable queue would
make the whole change look like a mistake rather than like time being tracked. A parent shows `+n`
for the sessions under it; a child says "part of a job".

### How it is proved

`tools/ticketpersession` — **28 of 28**. The window is tested by AGEING rows rather than by waiting
thirty minutes, which is the only honest way to check a rule about elapsed time in under a second.
It also asserts that the console's three-character floor and the server's are the same number, by
referencing `ReasonDialog.MinLength` rather than hard-coding 3 — the two drifting apart is exactly
the sort of thing that goes unnoticed.

`contactcheck` 34, `dashtabs` 47, `handoffcheck` 42, `ticketscope` 26 and `photogate` 36 all still
pass.

**STAGE 3.6 IS COMPLETE, and none of it is on hardware.** Server and console, two migrations
(`WorkshopPhotos`, `TicketParent`), so a full platform restart and `ship-build.ps1 -OnlyTechnician`.
No client reinstall anywhere in 3.6.

## 37. The New ticket dialog, rebuilt — 2026-09-20

Clint, with a screenshot: *"The layout is really bad on the console, let's fix this nicely. We have
to go wider and bigger."*

### It was worse than it looked, and it explains the photo report

The dialog was **one 592 px column of absolutely positioned controls** stepped along with `y += 40`
constants, inside a card declared 1180 px tall, inside a scroller, in a window fixed at 640x720.

At 150% one line of the body font is **28 px**, not the ~18 those constants assumed. Every row was
short by about ten pixels, the error accumulated down the form, and by the time the layout reached
the category panel it was **past the bottom of the window**. So choosing Workshop appeared to do
nothing — and that is why "I opened a new workshop ticket and it did not ask for photos" was
reported as a missing feature. **The feature was there. It was off-screen.** §30, a fourth time, and
the first time it cost a false bug report rather than a clipped word.

### What it is now

- **Two columns.** The job on the left, what the CATEGORY needs on the right. The right column is
  the part that changes, so putting it beside the form rather than below it means it is on screen
  the instant it appears.
- **Flow layout, not coordinates.** Nothing is positioned by hand. A hidden control takes no space
  in a `FlowLayoutPanel`, so the client-match list stops leaving an 84 px hole when there is nothing
  to match — the empty gap in Clint's screenshot — and the password box closes its own gap.
- **Sized to its contents and clamped to the screen**, and sized for the TALLEST category by
  showing each panel and measuring it, so the window does not jump about as somebody changes the
  category.
- **Resizable**, with a floor that can never exceed the working area.
- The right column always says something. `_noExtras` explains that remote support and walk-ins need
  nothing more, because an empty half-window reads as a fault.

640x720 with 1180 px inside it became **1092x941 with everything visible**.

### `tools/ticketformprobe` — 52 of 52

It caught a real fault on its first run, before any human looked: the window came out **560 px wide
with a 1030 px card in it**, the entire right column outside the frame. The cause is worth
remembering — **a `Dock = Top` control with `AutoSize` reports its PARENT's width**, so reading
`card.Width` back to size the form returned the width of an empty panel. The width is computed from
the columns now.

It opens the real dialog, switches through all four categories, and checks every field that should
be visible is inside the window and that no other category's fields are showing. It also covers
`ReasonDialog`, which stands in front of every unattended session and had never been looked at.

**Visible means visible ALL THE WAY UP.** A control on a hidden parent reports `Visible == true` for
itself, which is exactly how the old category panel looked present in code while being absent on
screen. And a hidden control has not been laid out, so measuring one proves nothing — the probe
shows the complaint label first and measures it where it will really be.

**Nothing in the suite could have caught the original fault.** `photogate` proved the RULE and the
rule was right. Only geometry catches geometry, and only a picture says whether it looks like
anything — so the probe writes one per category on every run.

**Console only.** `ship-build.ps1 -OnlyTechnician`, no server restart, no client reinstall.

## 38. Nobody is locked into somebody else's light or dark — 2026-09-20 (stage 3.6.9)

Clint: *"a switch on every portal allowing to switch between dark and light mode so that users of
the product are not locked into the owner/supervisor preferences."*

### It was more than a switch

`site.css` had **one palette** and `color-scheme: dark`. There was nothing to switch TO. The light
block is the stage; the switch took ten lines.

**Dark stays the default.** Every existing tenant and every signed-out visitor sees exactly what
they saw yesterday. Only somebody who asks for light gets it.

**The two purples swap roles.** On the dark ground `--grape` is the LIFTED purple for text and
`--fill` the deep one for filled buttons. On white that is backwards — the lifted `#a78bfa` manages
about 2.2:1 on white — so text takes the deep purple, and hover goes DARKER where on dark it went
lighter.

### The half that was nearly missed

The light block on its own was not enough. A dozen rules raised a surface with a wash of **white**,
which is how you lift something off a dark ground and is invisible on a light one — `rgba(255, 255,
255, .05)` and friends, plus a sticky header hard-coded to `rgba(11, 16, 22, .88)` that would have
stayed near-black on a white page. They are tokens now (`--lift`, `--lift-hi`, `--edge`, `--glow-1`,
`--glow-2`, `--top-bg`, `--sh-hover`), and both palettes define all of them.

### One setting, on the person, for both surfaces

`Technician.Appearance` — "light", "dark", or empty to follow the company.

- **One setting, not one per surface.** Somebody who prefers a dark screen prefers it in both
  places; two dropdowns would be two decisions where nobody has two preferences.
- **On the PERSON, not the machine.** A technician who sets it at their desk finds it already set on
  the workshop PC. A cookie or `localStorage` would have made it a property of the browser, which is
  the lock-in this stage exists to remove.
- **The company's `TechnicianTheme` stays** and is still the fallback; what changed is that it is no
  longer the last word. **`ClientTheme` is untouched, deliberately** — how an IT company presents
  itself to its customers is branding, not the preference of the person at the desk.

### How each surface gets it

**Portal**: carried in the cookie as a claim, so the layout paints the right palette on the first
render with no database read per page — and **re-issued by `/portal/appearance`**, because a claim
that is not re-issued means the switch appears to do nothing until the next sign-in.

**Console**: returned by `/api/login`, applied in `Program.Main` through the existing
`Theme.Override` — after sign-in, before the first window, because it is only known once we know who
signed in and every form takes its Theme at construction. `RSP_THEME` still beats both; somebody who
set it is asking to see one palette regardless of whose account they used.

**The console's login dialog is drawn in the COMPANY's theme, unavoidably** — nobody has said who
they are yet. One window, once.

### `tools/themecheck` — 40 of 40

Arithmetic, not opinion. It reads `site.css`, compares the two token sets, and computes real WCAG
contrast for every pair that carries text.

The two failures it exists to catch are both invisible to whoever wrote the palette: **a token
forgotten** in the light block keeps its dark value, so somewhere there is white text on white; and
**a colour too pale**, because the dark ground forgives a light purple and white does not.

Everything passes AA in both palettes. The tightest is the light warning colour at 5.0:1.

It also asserts that no bare `rgba(255,255,255,…)` or dark-ground colour is left loose in the rules
— that is the "half that was nearly missed" above, turned into a check so it cannot come back.

**Migration `TechnicianAppearance`. Server AND console**, so a platform restart and
`ship-build.ps1 -OnlyTechnician`. No client reinstall — the customer's app is untouched by design.

## 33. "The unattended box in the tray is greyed out" — 2026-09-20

Clint reinstalled the client from §31 and the tray item was dead. It was a race I put in the day
before, and it is worth writing down because of the *shape* of it rather than the fix.

### What it was

In `TenantHub`'s device-connect path, the hello block ends with

```csharp
_ = PersistDeviceAsync(hello, isNew);     // reads the stored permission and tells the device
```

and the connection is added to `_deviceConns` **fifteen lines later**. `PersistDeviceAsync` calls
`TellDeviceItsUnattendedState`, which looks up the machine's client connection in that list.
Against a local SQLite file the persist finishes in a millisecond or two — comfortably before the
connection is registered — so it looked for somebody to tell, found nobody, and sent nothing.

The tray app then waits for a message that was never coming. Its switch stays disabled, because
it will not offer a tick it cannot deliver, and it stays that way for the life of the session.

**A race whose fast path loses every single time is not a race anybody catches by running it
once.** It is not intermittent, it is not timing-dependent in practice, and it looks exactly like
a feature that was never wired up.

### The fix

The state is sent from the connect path itself, right after the connection is registered and
beside the `SessionStateMsg` that was already being sent there. `PersistDeviceAsync` still sends
too, as the correction once the stored value has actually been read — the connect-time send can
only be as right as whatever is in memory at that moment.

### Why nothing here caught it

`unattendedcheck` drives the tray app against a **stand-in** server, and its own output says, in
as many words, that the hub's half is not covered. The bug lived precisely in the gap the harness
admitted to. An honest note about what is untested is worth having; it is not a substitute for
testing it.

So `tools/unattendedwire` now exists and does the thing that was missing: it **starts a platform
of its own** — own port, own empty database in the temp folder, own tenant, via the `create-tenant`
CLI — and talks to it as a real device over a real socket. The live server on 8090 and its
database are untouched, which matters because this has to be runnable while Clint is working.

**It was proved to catch the bug before being trusted**: with the fix commented out it fails with
*"nothing arrived in ten seconds — the switch would be greyed out for ever"*, which is Clint's
report in the harness's own words. With the fix in, 7 of 7. A regression test that has never
failed is a claim, not a test.

It also covers two things no stand-in could: the permission **survives a reconnect** (the machine
disconnects and comes back and the hub still says on), and **an agent cannot grant itself access**
— it sends `SetUnattendedMsg{On=true}`, the hub ignores it because the role is wrong, and a
client connection for the same device confirms it is still off.

### And the second fault it exposed

Clint could not tell *which* of the three reasons the item was greyed for, because **a disabled
menu item shows no tooltip** — Windows does not raise the hover — and the explanation had been
moved into exactly that tooltip in §32. So while the switch is unusable the reason is now in the
item's own **text**: "Allow unattended access — not set up on this computer", "— not connected to
the server", "— waiting for the server". Longer than a menu item wants to be, and the right
trade: a grey line that says nothing is the thing being fixed.

`unattendedcheck` is 30 of 30 with that asserted both ways — the reason present while disabled,
and gone once it is usable.

### What Clint needs to do

**Restart the platform.** The fix is server-side; the tray app on the customer's machine needs
nothing. The switch comes alive within a second or two of the tray app's next reconnect.

The client-side improvement (a greyed item saying why) does need a ship, but it is only worth
having if the first thing does not work.

### CONFIRMED ON HARDWARE — 2026-09-20

Clint, after the platform restart: *"the unattended switch works."* The tray item comes alive on
the real machine and the permission is the customer's to give.

That is the first hardware confirmation of anything in §31, and it carries the §31 build with it:
the switch, the five-item tray menu and the mandatory request description were all in the same
ship. What has **not** been watched by eye is the far end — the console's Access column flipping
live while somebody ticks the box — and the §33 fix is precisely about the message that drives it,
so it is very likely right and is still worth one look during the next session.

---

## 34. Devices is everybody's, and the console can link one — 2026-09-20

Clint, 2026-09-20: *"devices should be an option that everybody has, otherwise it's only the
owner/supervisor that can link them to a client or contact. This should also be a console
feature."*

### Why it was wrong before

`/portal/devices` was on the `Tenant` page policy, with Devices in the owner's nav and in nobody
else's. So saying which customer a machine belongs to was the owner's job alone.

That is the wrong person. **Until a machine is linked, its tickets never reach a client page** —
the portal's own Devices page says so at the top, and puts the unlinked machines in a bucket
first for that reason. An unlinked machine is a hole in the records, and the person who notices
it is whoever is looking at the list: a technician, in the console, about to connect to it. Making
them fetch the owner to tidy a record is how the strays pile up.

**Nothing is disclosed that the same person could not already see.** Every role reaches
`/portal/clients`, and a technician has always seen every machine in the console's own device
list. This closes the gap between those two facts rather than opening anything.

### The question, not the role

`Permissions.CanLinkDevices(role) => true`, and both surfaces ask it. It is deliberately a
question in the 3.6.8 shape rather than a widened role comparison — when roles become tick boxes
the answer changes in one place and every caller keeps working.

### Three changes, and one of them is the one that mattered

1. **The page policy.** `/Portal/Devices` came out of the admin-only list in `Program.cs` and
   falls through to the folder's `PortalUser`. The nav gained Devices for the office
   administrator and the technician.
2. **`DeviceLinkMsg`**, technician to server. The hub checks `CanLinkDevices`, writes through
   `ContactService.LinkDeviceAsync` and nowhere else, then calls the same `RefreshDeviceOwner`
   the portal calls. One write path and one broadcast path, so the two surfaces cannot drift.
3. **`LinkDeviceDialog`** in the console, off a right-click on the machine list.

**`ClientInfo` now carries its `Contacts`**, and `ClientSearchMsg` gained a `Take` that defaults
to 12. The type-ahead's cap of 12 is right while somebody types a name they know; it is wrong for
an owner picker, because somebody looking at a stray machine often does not know whose it is and
needs to read down the list. The picker asks for 500.

### One list, not two

A company and a person at that company are the same decision, so they are rows in one list rather
than a client dropdown that enables a contact dropdown. Picking "Bob at Zenith" has said
everything. It is the reasoning the portal's single owner picker was already built on, so the two
surfaces behave alike, and it is Clint's standing rule that one control beats two.

The console sends **only the contact id** when a person is chosen; the server fills the company
in. If it did not, the machine would vanish from every group in the list — `DeviceList.Build`
gathers by client. That is asserted rather than assumed.

### The right-click had to be advertised

A right-click menu nobody is told about is a feature nobody finds. The section title now reads
**"Machines  (double-click to connect, right-click for more)"**, which is the pattern the
double-click hint already set.

The menu selects the row under the pointer before it opens. Without that, right-clicking one
machine and choosing Link would have relabelled whichever machine happened to be selected
before — the worst kind of wrong, because it looks like it worked.

### `tools/devicelink` — 19 of 19

It **starts a platform of its own** — own port, own empty database in the temp folder, own tenant
and one account of each role via `add-tech` — and drives real technician websockets against it.
The live server on 8090 is not touched, so it runs while Clint is working.

That shape is §33's lesson applied: asserting `CanLinkDevices` in-process would prove the RULE
says yes while saying nothing about whether the SOCKET honours it, and the last bug lived exactly
in a gap of that kind.

**It was proved to catch the fault before being trusted.** With `/Portal/Devices` put back on the
admin-only policy it drops to 15 of 19. Getting there found a real weakness in the harness: the
first version checked the HTTP status, and a refused page **redirects to the sign-in form, which
is followed, and arrives as a cheerful 200** — so it passed against the old policy. It asks for
the page's own `<h1>Customer machines</h1>` now. A check that cannot fail is not a check.

### A finding worth keeping: the office administrator has no console at all

The harness first reported that the office administrator could not sign in. That is correct and
deliberate — `/api/login` refuses `TenantRole.Billing` outright, because their seat has no remote
access (`docs/PRICING.md`: seven seats, one of them an office administrator who cannot connect to
a machine). The check was wrong, not the product.

It is now asserted **positively**: the office administrator is refused a console sign-in, and gets
Devices in the portal instead. A harness that silently skips a role proves nothing about it, and
the day somebody widens `/api/login` this will say so.

`handoffcheck` 42, `ticketscope` 26, `contactcheck` 34, `photogate` 36, `dashtabs` 47 and
`ticketpersession` 28 all still pass.

**Not on hardware.** Server and console, **no migration**, so a platform restart and
`ship-build.ps1 -OnlyTechnician`. No client reinstall.
