## 65. Office chat — 2026-09-30 (roadmap 3.8.1)

Clint: *"everybody at the office is able to chat with each other so that when you chat and do either
the @ or select the person it pops up a chat window in the browser or something similar where
internal chatting can take place."* His answers: **one to one, and one group — Everyone**;
**@mentions in ticket comments stay ticket comments**; **the browser shows a notification**.

### How it works

- **`StaffChatService`** is the one place the rules live: who may be written to (every ENABLED
  person of the company, the office administrator included — the one person with no console), what
  a conversation is (a pair, or Everyone), what is unread (somebody else's message after the last one
  you have seen), and what an @ means (`Mentions`: "@Sue Tech" in any case, not "@Sue Technician").
  Tables `StaffMessages` and `StaffChatReads` (migration `StaffChat`). Customers are never in it —
  their chat is `ChatLine`, per machine, untouched. **Sending counts as reading**: a reply is written
  below what it answers.
- **Its two events** (`Sent`, `ReadChanged`) are how the portal and the console hear each other:
  `HubRegistry` sends them to the right hub, which sends a message only to the consoles it concerns
  (`Involves`) and pushes each of them their counts (`StaffChatOverviewMsg`).
- **The portal** (`wwwroot/chat.js`, loaded by `_Layout` on every portal page for staff): a Chat
  button in the corner with the unread count; the list (Everyone, then whoever spoke last); *type @
  or a name, then Enter*; up to three windows docked beside it, which come back after moving to
  another page (sessionStorage). A message TO you, or an Everyone message naming you, **pops its
  window open without taking the keyboard**; the rest of Everyone only counts. In the Everyone box,
  typing @ offers the names. A browser notification when the tab is not in front — permission is
  asked the first time the Chat button is clicked, because a browser only asks after a click.
  Live delivery is **server-sent events** (`/api/portal/chat/stream`, a comment every 20 s); reads
  and writes are `/api/portal/chat…`, and **a write needs the `X-Chat: 1` header** as well as the
  cookie, which a page on another site cannot add.
- **The console** (`StaffChatForm`): an *Office chat* button beside Tickets with the count (red when
  anything is unread). The window is made at sign-in and kept hidden, so it can pop up; it pops up
  without activating (`ShowWithoutActivation`) and flashes the taskbar; closing it hides it. While
  somebody is typing to one person, a message from another does not take the conversation away.

### What building it found

- **A popped window showed only the newest message** (walked in the browser). The message that
  opened it was drawn before the window's history arrived and set its last id, so the history was
  all skipped as already shown. Live messages now wait while a window loads.
- **On a short screen the windows ran up over the page header** (the screenshot). They are capped
  at the screen's height.
- **"Sam Supervisor (1)" drew as "Sam Supervisor…"** in the console (the probe's picture) — the count
  was part of the name. It is its own pill now.
- `PeopleAsync` sorted before `Distinct`, and SQL is free to drop that order.
- A harness platform needs **`RSP_Urls`**, not only `ASPNETCORE_URLS`: the platform's settings file
  names its own port, and only the `RSP_` value wins over it.

### How it was proved

| | |
|---|---|
| `tools/chatcheck` (new) | **51 of 51**. The service: who may be written to (the disabled, a stranger, yourself refused; a name in any case stored as the company spells it), conversations never mixed, unread including "a reply reads it", reading backwards changes nothing, the @ rule. **The wire, on a platform of its own**: a console → a portal page's event stream, live, and back; a third console hears NOTHING of a private conversation; a portal write without its header refused; a refused send says why; Everyone naming Tom tells Tom and not the others; reading in the portal clears the count and tells the page. **50 of 51 with the hub sending every message to every console.** |
| `tools/staffchatprobe` (new) | **18 of 18**, the real console window with messages handed in where the socket delivers them: hidden until needed, pops up on a message to them without taking the keyboard, not on an Everyone message that does not name them, does on one that does, keeps the conversation being typed in, ignores a stale history, shows a refusal and clears it, and fits (§30). Pictures every run. |
| `tools/chatsay` (new) | signs in as one person's console on a TEST platform and says one thing — for watching a page receive it. |
| the portal, walked | on a `workflowdemo` platform as Sue: the list, `@Bo` + Enter opening Bob, a message sent; then (by `chatsay`) Bob's reply landing in the open window, Sam's popping a window of its own, an Everyone message only counting, an Everyone message naming Sue popping Everyone with its whole history, the @ names offered in the Everyone box, the windows coming back after a reload, and the counts clearing once the page was in view. |

**Not on hardware**: the browser notification (it needs a person to allow it), and two people on
two machines. **Platform restart (migration `StaffChat`) and `-OnlyTechnician`.** `TEST-3.6.md`
section AF, checks 206–213.

## 66. Support in the browser — 2026-09-30 (roadmap 3.8.2)

Clint: *"potential clients to be able to get remote support via a browser. So they click on a link,
put in their contact details, and request a support call online and it rings through to the
technicians the same way the app works. this would also be a good way for them to test the I.T
company's services before downloading the actual app."* **What a browser cannot do, and he
accepted it: move the pointer or type.** A page can only SHOW the screen, with the person's
permission. His answers: worth building; **switched off and on, with hours of the company's own**
(longer than office hours if they like); **a browser caller becomes a Contact and a ticket**.

### How it works

- **Settings: Portal → Browser support** (`/portal/websupport`, owner and supervisors). On/off, hours
  per weekday — a closing time before the opening time runs past midnight and belongs to the day it
  started — and an IANA time zone, so it works the same on Linux. `WebSupportHours` is the ONE reader
  of `Tenant.WebSupportHours` (migration `WebSupport`). **Off by default.** The page shows the link to
  give customers and whether it is open now.
- **The public page `/help/{slug}`**: off → says so; outside its hours → the hours and the company's
  phone and email; open → the form (name; company optional; a phone OR an email; what is wrong). A
  hidden field a person never fills in (a robot is thanked and nothing rings), **five requests an hour
  per address per company** (`HelpModel.Allow`), and at most **ten browser callers per company** at once
  (`TenantHub.MaxWebCallers`). The download page `/get/{slug}` now offers *"Can't install it? Get help
  in your browser instead"* while it is open — the reason Clint thought of it.
- **A browser caller is a pretend device, `web-…`, never saved and never in the machine list**
  (`TenantHub.Web.cs`). The handful of lookups — its name, its "client" socket (`DeviceConns`,
  `RouteChat`), the session's host (`StartSession`, only when they RANG), its client
  (`ClientForDeviceAsync`) — ask that file too, and everything else is the tray app's own path: the
  ring, accepting, the relay, the ticket's story, ending. Its ticket carries the web id as its
  device, so `ActiveForDeviceAsync` finds it for the session and the chat exactly as for a machine.
- **Contact and ticket**: found by email or phone if the company knows them (their existing name and
  client are used); otherwise the company they named, or their own name, is made a client (reused if
  it exists) with them as its contact. A Remote support ticket from a call, their words as the
  subject, their details in it.
- **The page (`wwwroot/help.js`)** has two sockets: `/ws/web` (ring, who answered, chat, the
  handover) and `/ws/session?role=host` — **the support app's host protocol, spoken by the page**. It
  announces one monitor, and on a subscribe sends **H.264 from the browser's own encoder (WebCodecs)
  in the host's binary layout** — so the console's existing decoder shows it — or JPEG pictures in
  the tile layout on a browser with no encoder. Frames come from `MediaStreamTrackProcessor` where
  there is one (Chrome, Edge): **a background tab's timers are slowed to a crawl, and the customer is
  looking at whatever they are showing**. SPS/PPS are put in front of a key frame if the encoder
  keeps them in its description; a key frame every 4 s; frames skipped before encoding when the
  socket is behind. Stopping and sharing again keeps the session.
- **The console**: `SessionInfo.ViewOnly`. `SessionForm.ApplyViewOnly` turns control off and hides
  it, the System menu, Files, Scripts, Sound and Listen, sends no clipboard, and says why in a banner.
  Chat, Info and recording work.

### What building it found

- **Every form post was refused, as "too long".** With nullable references on, ASP.NET treats a
  non-nullable `string` as REQUIRED, and the hidden field is always empty and Company optional. The
  harness's first post found it; a person would have met it on their first try. The bound fields are
  `string?` now.
- **"A Workshop Demo IT technician"** — the article, again (the download page learned it first).
- A settings form: a tick box's hidden "false" must come AFTER it (the binder takes the first
  value), and a disabled box is not posted, so a gap stops an indexed list binding.
- The page drew "Chat below." over the sharing prompt, because the handover arrives before the
  "accepted" update.

### How it was proved

| | |
|---|---|
| `tools/websupportcheck` (new) | **64 of 64**. The rules: the default hours, past midnight, a time zone, off, words, round trip; the per-address hour. **The wire, on a platform of its own, the browser spoken as RAW JSON exactly as help.js writes it**: off, unknown, closed (hours and phone, no form); each refusal of the form; the hidden field (thanked, nothing rings); the ring with who, from where and what; a wrong or reused token refused; the ticket, the new client and contact; not in the machine list; chat both ways with the page's claimed name ignored; answered → a VIEW ONLY session, the page told who and handed the session; the announcement arriving as a monitor, the subscribe reaching the page, a video frame and a JPEG tile byte for byte; the end, and the ticket's story; a page closed while ringing cancels on every console; the same person again found by email; the sixth request of the hour refused; the download page's link. **63 of 64 with the session not marked view only.** |
| `websupportcheck --browser` | **a REAL browser** (the desktop app's own, Chrome 152 underneath) filled the form, a canvas of known colours was shared through the page's own path: **62 of 62 H.264 frames decoded by the console's own decoder** (Microsoft H264 Video Decoder MFT), 1280 × 720, the middle pixel the blue that was painted, and the picture looked at. |
| `tools/viewonlyprobe` (new) | **12 of 12**: the REAL session window built view only — no control, no Control tick, no System menu, no Files/Scripts/Sound/Listen, Chat, Info and recording kept, a banner saying why (shortened after its picture showed it cut off) — and a normal session exactly as it was. |
| the portal, walked | the settings page saving hours (Saturday added), the form, the ringing page. |

**Not on hardware**: a real `getDisplayMedia` picker (the browser asks the person which screen —
automation cannot click it; the canvas takes the same path after it), Firefox and Safari, a phone
(no screen sharing there at all — the page says so), and a technician's real console window showing
it. **Platform restart (migration `WebSupport`) and `-OnlyTechnician`** — then Browser support must
be switched on for Anywhere IT. Behind Caddy the sockets are `wss://`, which the page works out
itself. `TEST-3.6.md` section AG, checks 214–222.

## 67. Talking to the customer — 2026-09-30 (roadmap 3.3)

Clint: *"lets work on the mic feature. this will be great if it can work on the app and the online
view only. Ideally mic chat should work both ways if a client has a mic installed."* His three
answers, the same day: **the customer allows their microphone every session, and never in an
unattended session**; **an open microphone with a Mute button**, not push-to-talk; **recordings stay
picture only**. `docs/NEXT-SESSION-VOICE.md` is the brief, with the measurements.

### Measured first (`tools/hostinfo/micprobe.ps1`, through `runscript`)

As SYSTEM on DESKTOP-OPHQIDH and DESKTOP-2N6FVGT (both **Windows 10** 19045): the microphone opens
with real audio, Windows' echo canceller (the Voice Capture DSP, `CLSID_CWMAudioAEC`) runs, and
process loopback activates. **No helper as the person is needed.** Still unmeasured: **Windows 11 as
SYSTEM**, and a person whose "Let desktop apps access your microphone" is Deny (the host reads that
and refuses rather than overriding it — `MicPrivacy`).

### How it works

- **`BinKind.Voice = 6`**, the audio layout (`Bin.Voice`), **16 kHz mono PCM16, 20 ms frames**
  (`VoiceWire`) — what the echo canceller produces; ~32 KB/s each way. Droppable, like screen frames.
- **Messages**: `VoiceTalkMsg` (technician → host; the HUB stamps the name), `VoiceStateMsg` (host →
  technicians AND the tray app: `Call`, `Technicians`, `Mic` ∈ `VoiceMic` = off/asking/on/declined/
  unavailable/unattended, `Detail`), `VoiceMicAnswerMsg` (tray app → hub → host).
- **`RemoteSupport.Media`** holds both ends' engine: **`EchoCancelledMic`** (the DSP in system mode,
  its own MTA thread) and **`PcmPlayer`** — Listen's player moved here with its timings as
  parameters; `VoicePlayer` is 20 ms × 4 + 2 spare (120 ms) on the **communications** device, and
  the console's `AudioPlayer` keeps Listen's exact 40 ms × 4 + 3 and 600 ms.
- **Host: `VoiceCall`.** Talk opens the player, then asks. Only `VoiceMicAnswerMsg` opens the mic;
  `ParticipantsMsg` takes a vanished technician out of the call (and ends it with the last one), so
  a microphone can never stay open for nobody. While a call is on, **Listen switches to process
  loopback EXCLUDING the host** (`AudioCapture.ExcludeSelf`) so the technician does not hear their
  own voice come back; only then, because EXCLUDE takes the whole process tree and a test-tone script
  is a child of the host.
- **Hub** (`TenantHub`): stamps and logs Talk; `PassOnVoiceState` turns "asking" into "unattended"
  in an unattended session, relays to the tray app, writes the ticket when the MIC changes; the
  answer is taken **only from the CLIENT connection** and **never in an unattended session**; and a
  **viewer's `VoiceMicAnswerMsg` is dropped** (see below). A tray app that reconnects mid-call is
  re-sent the state (`NotifyDeviceSessionState`). `LogToSessionTicketAsync` waits up to 5 s for the
  session's ticket.
- **Tray app**: the banner's voice row — the one place it has buttons — measured from its fonts;
  `MainForm.ShowVoice` and a balloon; every change in the chat log.
- **Console**: Tools → *Talk to the customer* / *Stop talking*; a status-bar pill that mutes with a
  click (muting stops the frames, not the microphone, so the canceller keeps learning); a line for
  the customer's microphone. `SessionForm` is `partial` now — `SessionForm.Voice.cs`.
- **Browser** (`help.js`, `Help.cshtml`): the page's host socket opens **at the answer**, not at
  sharing — the only way a Talk can reach it, and what lets a PHONE talk. `getUserMedia` with the
  browser's own echoCancellation, an AudioWorklet, resampled to 16 kHz in the page; the technician's
  voice scheduled into an AudioContext 120 ms ahead. The buttons are also the click a browser needs
  before it will play sound.

### What building it found

- **A technician could open the customer's microphone.** The hub passes everything on a viewer
  socket to the host, so a `VoiceMicAnswerMsg` from a console opened the mic — attended or not.
  `voicewire`'s first run: *"the microphone opened"*. The viewer socket now drops it, logged.
- **The echo canceller delivers NOTHING until a render stream is open** — S_FALSE for ever. The
  voice player starts first and plays silence for the whole call, or the mic goes dead between
  sentences.
- **`ProcessOutput`'s array must be `LPArray`**: as a SAFEARRAY (the COM default) the DSP read
  garbage and PowerShell died with no message; only .NET 8 said "SafeArrayMarshaler".
- **Process loopback must be used on an MTA thread** (E_NOINTERFACE on STA), and a COM callable
  wrapper needs PUBLIC types — `AudioInterop` is public now for its completion handler.
- **A steady test tone is eaten by noise suppression** (this laptop's Realtek driver, and the DSP):
  the probes use 250 ms pulses. This laptop's driver also cancels its own speakers before we see
  them, so its echo figure means nothing — a desktop with a webcam mic will differ.
- **"Started talking" was lost** when Talk came in the moment before the session's ticket was
  attached — hence `LogToSessionTicketAsync`.
- **In the page**: an `Int16Array` cannot start at byte 11 (the header), so the first capture sent
  nothing; and `endVoice` asked "was there a call?" after emptying the list, so Talk-off was never
  reported. Both found by `websupportcheck --browser-voice`.
- The console's microphone line docked at the window's edge, ahead of its pill (a later-added
  control docks further out), and was cut off — `viewonlyprobe`'s picture.

### How it was proved

| | |
|---|---|
| `micprobe.ps1` | mic, DSP, process loopback: this laptop by hand; **as SYSTEM on both Windows 10 machines** |
| `tools/voicelocal` (new) | 4 of 4 — the player and the echo-cancelled mic in .NET 8: 200 frames in 4.01 s, player never starved |
| `tools/voicewire` (new) | **37 of 37** over a real hub with the HOST's own `VoiceCall` behind a hand-written host socket: the name stamped; the tray app asked; the technician's voice played (60 of 60); agent and technician answers refused; yes → 50 frames/s of 16 kHz mono; a reconnecting tray app re-told; no → silence; a vanished technician ends the call; unattended → told, never asked, a yes refused, 0 frames; the ticket lines. **33 of 37 before the fixes; 34 of 37 with the unattended guard removed (the mic OPENED, 68 frames of the room reached the technician)** |
| `audiolocal --exclude-self` | Listen during a call: 126 frames, our own tone at 0.00000; the ordinary mode still 0.36 |

## 68. Readable customer names, customers first, the username remembered — 2026-09-30

Three small things technicians asked for, the same day.

### The customer headings in the console's device list

*"In dark mode on the console, the client names are hardly readable, they are black. Lets make it the
same as the dashboard."* They were black — `dashtabs` read them off the screen before anything was
changed. They are the ListView's own GROUP headings, and Windows draws those: not `ForeColor`, not the
owner-draw events (rows only), not `LVGROUPMETRICS` (ignored). The list does send a custom-draw
notification per heading, marked `LVCDI_GROUP`, and **`UI/GroupHeaders.cs`** answers it ahead of
WinForms and draws the heading whole: the name in `SurfaceAltText` — the colour of the column
headings just above, the portal's lifted signature (`--grape`) — the machine count muted, a
`CardBorder` hairline, and the fold chevron. Folding stays the list's own; the chevron is drawn on
the list's fold button, found by asking the list (`LVM_HITTEST`, `LVHT_EX_GROUP_COLLAPSE`).

Three things that were wrong on the way, each seen in a picture rather than a number:

- **`NMHDR` must be NESTED in the custom-draw struct**, not written out flat — on 64-bit it pads to
  24 bytes, and flat, every field after `code` read four bytes early (every stage came out 0).
- **A heading arrives at `CDDS_PREPAINT` with `dwItemType == LVCDI_GROUP`**, not at item-prepaint.
- **The list's group positions are not `ListView.Groups`' positions**: WinForms keeps a hidden default
  group at the list's index 0, and the first working run wrote every customer's name over the heading
  below it. Everything is asked of the list by group ID (`LVM_GETGROUPINFO`, which fails with -1,
  not 0 — 0 is a real id).

Also: machines over 90% disk were a fixed `#991B1B`, as unreadable as the headings; now `BadText`.

`dashtabs` **84 of 84** (79 before; its new heading checks fail on the old code): the signature colour is
on the first heading in both palettes, nothing in a dark heading is darker than the list, and **a
REAL click where the chevron is drawn folds the customer** — a posted `WM_LBUTTONDOWN` is not a click:
the list hit-tests where the cursor really is, and it selected the customer's machines instead. So
the harness moves the mouse for a moment and puts it back.

### The portal's Devices page puts the unlinked machines LAST

As the console always has (`DeviceList.Build`). The count of unlinked machines stays in the stats row
at the top. `devicelink` **20 of 20** (19 with the old page).

### The console remembers the last username

`Technician/LastSignIn.cs`: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\RemoteSupport\signin.json`, **per Windows user and per
server** (a harness platform never offers the live account's name), written **only after a sign-in
that worked**. The password is never stored. With a name filled in, the cursor starts in Password.
`tools/signincheck` (new) **12 of 12** against a platform of its own and a file of its own; **7 of 12**
on the old form, whose last failure is the complaint word for word: *"Enter your username and
password."*

**Platform restart (no migration) and `-OnlyTechnician`.** `TEST-3.6.md` section AI, checks 233–237.

## 69. A download link for technicians, and a way to sign out — 2026-09-30

### /tech/{slug}

Clint: *"There should be a technician download link, much like the client download link so that we
dont have to run around with usb sticks every time."* The console WAS downloadable
(`/downloads/{slug}/technician.zip`), but only from a button inside the portal, and the route let in
only the `tenant` role — supervisors and the owner. A technician could not fetch their own tool.

`Pages/Tech.cshtml` is the technicians' `/get`: the company's banner, and **a sign-in form on the page
itself** (the console's email and password), because unlike the customers' app this one should only
reach somebody with an account — so the link can be pasted anywhere. Signing in there gives the same
portal cookie as the login form. Then the button and the steps: Unblock, unzip into a folder that
stays, run it, pin it; updating is unzip-over. Who may have it is **`Permissions.CanDownloadConsole`**
— a seat, or a supervisor/owner (who hand it out); an office administrator alone is told why not,
since `/api/login` would refuse them anyway. The route asks the same question, and only for the
cookie's OWN company. Another company's account is refused on the page. **"not you?"** signs out back
to the page: `/logout` takes `back`, but only a local `/tech/` path, so it is not an open redirect.
The portal's Downloads page gives the link with a Copy button.

On the way: `Downloads.cshtml`'s `else` became literal text once a `</p>` sat between it and its
`if`. `techdownload` checks for stray Razor on that page.

(`RSP_Platform__TechnicianPayloadDir`); **19 of 22** with the old download rule.

### Sign out in the console

*"There is also no logout for technicians. closing the console simply minimizes it."* The X going
to the tray is deliberate and stays (`BuildTray`: calls and chat must keep arriving). What was
missing was a VISIBLE way out: Exit existed only on the tray icon's right-click menu. Now **Sign out**
is the right-most button in the header and on the tray menu beside Exit, and the tray balloon says
"sign out or exit". It asks first only if a session window is open (`OpenSessionWindows`), then
closes like Exit, and **`Program` starts the console again as a fresh process** at the sign-in
window, username filled in (§68). A new process rather than a new window, so every session, tool
window, socket and hidden form of the person who left goes with them. The old process then
`Environment.Exit`s, so a lingering thread cannot keep it — still signed in — beside the new one.

## 70. Website chat — 2026-09-30 (roadmap 3.8.3)

Clint: *"a chat windows for a tenants website. This would allow them to install it on their own
website and when one chats in it is goes through to every logged in technician including supervisors
and office administrators. this would be a great way for someone to answer questions immediately and
guide them to the support page."* He thought it could not be done yet; only GOING LIVE cannot — the
platform is on the office network until stage 4. His answers: **the first reply takes it**; **name and
an email or phone** first, and they become a Contact; **nobody signed in or outside the hours → a
message, which becomes a General ticket**; build it now.

### How it works

- **One line on the company's website**: `<script src="https://<platform>/webchat/<slug>.js" async>`
  (Portal → **Website chat**, with Copy and **Try it** — `/webchat/{slug}/try`, a sample website with
  the bubble on it). `wwwroot/webchat-embed.js` draws a round button in the company's colour and, when
  clicked, OUR frame `/webchat/{slug}/frame` in an iframe — so everything the visitor does is on our
  origin; the only thing another site ever asks us is the public state (`GET /api/webchat/{slug}`, CORS
  `*`: off / open / message). Switched off, or a lapsed trial: no bubble at all. On a phone (< 480 px)
  the frame is the whole screen. The embed script is served through `WebRootFileProvider`, NOT
  `WebRootPath`, which on a build is a copy and went on serving the old script (found in the browser).
- **The frame** (`Pages/WebChatFrame.cshtml`, `wwwroot/webchat.js`): the start form (name, email OR
  phone, question, a hidden robot field), the chat, or the leave-a-message form. `{id, token}` in the
  frame's localStorage, so moving to another page of their site carries the SAME chat on. Links a
  technician sends are made clickable as text nodes plus `<a>` for http(s) only. The visitor socket is
  `/ws/webchat` — **plain JSON, not the console protocol** (`Hub/WebChatVisitor.cs`): it hears only its
  own chat, and speaks as the name given at the start, never one the page claims.
- **`WebChatService`** holds every rule: `ModeFor` (off / open while in the chat's hours AND somebody
  signed in / message), `Check` (a name, an email or a phone, a question), start, leave a message (a
  **General** ticket, source Chat, in their words, with a note), say, **claim by one conditional
  update** (`AnsweredBy == ""`, so two people replying at once cannot both take it — and since 2026-10-15 it
  can be **handed over**, §145), end (by staff,
  "visitor", or "idle"), and the minute-by-minute **`WebChatSweep`** that ends a chat whose visitor has
  gone and that has been quiet 30 minutes. 20 open chats per company; **10 per address per hour** (its
  own limit — browser support's 5 ran out inside the harness, and a customer's office is one address).
  Tables `WebChats` (secret kept only as SHA-256) and `WebChatLines`; tenant columns `WebChatEnabled`,
  `WebChatHours`, `WebChatTimeZone` — `WebSupportHours.IsChatOpen` is the same rule as browser support's.
- **`StaffPresence`**: who is signed in right now — a console (the hub) or an open portal page (its chat
  stream). "Nobody signed in" is a fact the server knows, not a guess. The office administrator counts
  while a portal page is open, which is when they can answer.
- **`Services/Visitors`**: browser support's "a visitor becomes a Contact" moved out of the hub so both
  use ONE rule — and it was wrong: phones were compared as text, so `0825551234` did not find the
  contact `082 555 1234`. Now by digits, and the last nine when both have that many.
- Saving **Browser support** tells every console too, so its link button comes and goes at once.
- **The office**: every change and line goes to every console of the company (HubRegistry →
  `PushWebChat`) and to every portal page (`webchat` / `webline` events on the chat stream).
  **Console**: a *Website chat* button beside Office chat, shown only while the company has it on,
  counting who is waiting (red); `WebChatForm` pops up WITHOUT taking the keyboard for a new visitor,
  then only for whoever answers (or everybody while nobody has); buttons *App link*, *Browser support
  link* (only while browser support is on) and *End chat*; a tray balloon while the console is hidden.
  **Portal**: the Chat corner lists *Website visitors* above the office, the corner button turns amber
  — *Website visitor 1* — and a window pops open, with the same buttons. The portal page also lists the
  last 50 chats and messages with their transcripts; settings are the owner's and supervisors'.

### What building it found

- **`?page=` is Razor Pages' own route value** — the frame's `page` parameter arrived as
  "/WebChatFrame", so every visitor would have seemed to be on that page. It is `from` now.
- The visitor's own "state" arrived BEFORE its "hello"; hello is sent first now.
- The console window's three buttons did not fit at its smallest (the probe's picture): shorter words
  with tooltips, and **the minimum width is measured from the buttons** (§30). The list cut "Vic
  Visitor" to "Vic Vi…" beside its state; the name has its own line now.
- The frame's header promised "a reply within a minute" above "nobody is available" (walked).
- A frame that was full-screen once stayed full-screen after the window widened (walked).

### How it was proved

| | |
|---|---|
| `tools/webchatcheck` (new) | **80 of 80.** The service in-process: the details rules, off / message / open (another company's staff do not count; outside the hours is message), the sweep (not while the visitor's page is open; idle once gone). **The wire, on a platform of its own**, the visitor as raw JSON: the script with its company in it, the state answering any website, no chat with nobody there, a left message → a General ticket and a Contact, **the same phone typed two ways is one contact**; signing in turns it to open; the robot; a chat reaching BOTH consoles and the office administrator's portal page and NOT another company; the secret hashed; a wrong secret or another chat's number shown nothing; the visitor's claimed name ignored; **the first reply takes it** and a second person joins without taking it; a portal write without X-Chat refused; the app link from the portal; leaving and coming back to all of it; ending (by staff, by the visitor), nothing said after; settings refused to the office administrator; browser support switched on and every console given its link at once; switched off by a supervisor with every console told; the frame and Try it; the hour's limit; nobody left → message. **76 of 79 with the claim unconditional** (before the browser support check was added). |
| `tools/webchatprobe` (new) | **32 of 32**, the REAL dashboard and window, messages handed in where the socket delivers them — light, and dark (`RSP_THEME=dark`). |
| the browser, walked | a throwaway platform (port 8095): the settings page switched on; Try it; the bubble; a chat started; it popped up in the portal, amber, waiting; a reply and the app link; the visitor saw both and who; another page of the site carried it on; ended; with nobody signed in, the message form (after the wording fix) and a ticket #1 on the General route; the history on the page; a phone's full-screen frame and its close. |
| regressions | `websupportcheck` 64 (it uses `Visitors` now), `chatcheck` 51, `dashtabs` 98. |

**Not tried**: a REAL website on another address (the frame's storage is then third-party — kept per
site by Chrome, Edge and Safari, but unwatched), a real phone, a console on another PC, and **an https
website against this http server** — a browser blocks that, which is one more reason it waits for
hosting. **Platform restart (migration `WebsiteChat`) and `-OnlyTechnician`**; then switch it on at
Portal → Website chat. `TEST-3.6.md` section AK, checks 244–251.

## 71. One downloadable .exe instead of the zip — 2026-09-30 (roadmap stage 5)

Clint: *"Will these still be zip files once the digital signing is in place. It would be much
better if every download was an exe. it would be way more professional."* Then: *"would creating
one exe affect the digital signing in any way? limits etc?"* — it does not (docs/CODE-SIGNING.md,
"One .exe for every company"): no limit on a hardware token, and one identical file is the ONLY way
every company's download can carry a signature, because the key never leaves the YubiKey.

### How it works

- **The download is the customer app itself**, `RemoteSupport.Client.exe`, with the host, the agent
  service, the install scripts and the health check toolkit **packed inside it** as the embedded
  resource `client-payload.zip` (`ClientPayload`). **161 MB, against about 173 MB for the zip.**
  Every company's customers get the SAME file.
- **`/download/{slug}`** serves it named **`{slug}-support.exe`**; **`/download/{slug}/brand.json`** is
  what the zip's `branding\brand.json` held (no more public than the zip was). A Razor page
  (`Pages/Download.cshtml.cs`), so `Program.cs` was not touched. Offered only when the payload folder
  holds **`client-exe.packed`** — an ordinary client could "get help now" but never install.
- **A copy with no `branding\brand.json` beside it is a downloaded one** (`Launcher.IsDownloadedCopy`).
  It works out whose it is (`DownloadIdentity`): **the address the browser recorded beside the
  download** (`Zone.Identifier`, `HostUrl=…/download/{slug}` — the company AND the server, and it
  survives a rename), then **its file name**, then **the last company used on this PC**, then it
  **asks** for the company's code. It fetches the branding into
  `%LOCALAPPDATA%\RemoteSupport\download\{slug}` (the copy from last time will do offline), and shows
  **`LauncherForm`: Get help now, or Install** (with *Also let them connect when I am away*, unticked).
- **Get help now** unpacks only the host beside that folder (`HostSpawner.Directory`) and runs the tray
  app as before. **Install** unpacks everything into a temp folder shaped exactly like the old
  unzipped download — this .exe, the host, the agent, the scripts, the company's `branding\` — and
  runs **the same `Install-Client.ps1`** elevated, the Windows prompt its only question, its words to
  `install.log`. The single-instance mutex is only LOOKED AT by a downloaded copy, never held, or the
  installed tray app the script starts would quietly exit.
- **`tools/Pack-ClientExe.ps1`** makes it, and **the order is the point**: sign the inside (skipping
  anything already validly signed), pack, publish the client with the pack and the server's address
  (`client-defaults.json`, from `PublicUrl`) embedded, **sign the outside last**, drop it in the
  payload folder with the marker. `build.ps1` and `tools/ship-build.ps1` (new step **4b**) both run it.
  The signing functions moved from `build.ps1` into **`tools/Signing.ps1`** for both to use —
  unchanged, except that its `signtool` search regex (`'\x64\'`) is now `'\x64\'`.
- **The download page** offers the .exe with *Open it and choose Get help now or Install*; the zip
  becomes *"Installing it on many PCs at once? The zip for IT staff"*, and its Unblock-and-unzip
  instructions show only while the zip is the download.

### What building it found

- **Copying a file on Windows carries its Zone.Identifier with it** — the harness's first run: its
  "second copy with no recorded address" still had one. Real downloads are unaffected; the harness
  writes its copies fresh.
- **The tick box's words were cut off at "…when I"** (an AutoSize tick box never wraps), and once
  given room, **its second line sat under the Install button** (the layout measured it as one line).
  Both from the harness's picture; it now checks the wrapped text fits and that nothing in a card
  overlaps anything else.

### How it was proved

| | |
|---|---|
| `tools/oneexecheck` (new) | **52 of 52**. The rules: file names (a browser's " (2)", capitals, `setup.exe`), Zone.Identifier (Edge/Chrome's, a LAN port, somebody else's file, none). **A REAL .exe packed by `Pack-ClientExe.ps1`** for a platform of its own: served as `acme-it-support.exe`, byte for byte the packed file; its brand.json; unknown, not-yet-approved and anything else refused; the download page's button and the IT-staff zip link, and the old page back without the marker. **The downloaded .exe itself**, marked as a browser marks it, driven through `--identify`, `--unpack` and `--stage-install` with a cache of the harness's own: whose it is and WHY (the address; the name; the last company; refusing when there is nothing to go on), the branding fetched, the host, agent, scripts and health check toolkit **byte for byte**, none of its own branding, and the Install folder with this .exe and the company's key. The window: both choices, words that fit, one line of buttons, nothing overlapping, and the *installed* and *cannot install* versions. |

**Not on hardware, and not run here**: the elevated install itself — it would install on this PC. It
runs the same `Install-Client.ps1` the zip always did, from a folder shaped the same. Chrome's and
Edge's own download warnings for an unsigned .exe are expected until the certificate (stage 5).
**Needs a full ship** (`tools\ship-build.ps1`, whose new step 4b makes the .exe) — no platform
restart and no migration. `TEST-3.6.md` section AL, checks 252–258.

## 72. Signing in safely, before go-live — 2026-10-01

Clint: *"The key created by the system seems easily hackable. Can we have something like 256 bit or
higher encryption? … I am very concerned for someone hacking into a tenant database, or technician
username or either the technician or client apps."* Then, to the recommendations: *"yes, lets go
according to your recommendations."*

### What was measured first

- **The tenant key is not the weak point, and is not a secret.** 24 bytes from
  `RandomNumberGenerator` (192 bits), and `/download/{slug}/brand.json` hands it to anybody, because
  every customer's install needs it. It is an ADDRESS — "this machine belongs to Anywhere IT" — and
  it lets a machine ask for help, never lets anybody in. Making it longer changes nothing. Do not
  "fix" it.
- **The encryption is TLS.** Caddy (GO-LIVE.md) gives TLS 1.3 with post-quantum key exchange.
  **Measured on the live server, 2026-10-01: TLS 1.3, `X25519MLKEM768`, `TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256`,
  a Let's Encrypt certificate renewed by Caddy.** Not AES-256 as first said here: Go's TLS (Caddy)
  picks AES-128-GCM on hardware with AES instructions, and TLS 1.3 suites cannot be configured in
  Go. AES-128 has no practical attack; the part that needed future-proofing — the key exchange —
  is the post-quantum one. Stored secrets were already AES-256 (Data Protection), passwords a
  one-way PBKDF2 hash. No app turns certificate checking off; none should.
- **What actually guarded every customer machine was a technician's password**: unattended access
  plus scripts as SYSTEM means one stolen password is every machine of that company. And it had
  four faults: (1) **removing somebody, or changing their password, signed nothing out** — the
  console's token lived until the server restarted and the portal cookie renewed itself for as long
  as it was used; (2) **nothing stopped guessing** — no lockout, no second factor; (3) **behind
  Caddy every caller was 127.0.0.1** — no `UseForwardedHeaders`, so one busy hour of website chat
  would have refused every visitor, and no per-address limit could mean anything; (4) **every app
  turned `http://` into `ws://` and connected** — one wrong `PublicUrl` and passwords, screens and
  keystrokes would cross the internet in the clear, silently. And the owner portal was one shared key.

### What it is now

- **Two-factor sign-in, everybody.** Password, then six digits from an authenticator app (RFC 6238,
  `Shared/Totp.cs` — SHA-1/6/30 s is the only setting every app honours; inside HMAC, SHA-1 is fine).
  Nobody set up → the next sign-in shows a **QR code** (drawn on the server, `QrImage`, QRCoder —
  the one library brought in, MIT), and they cannot get in without finishing it. **Each 30-second
  step is accepted once, ever** (`TotpLastStep`). **Ten recovery codes**, each good once, shown once,
  stored as SHA-256. Supervisors: **Reset two-factor** and **Sign out** on the People page (the
  owner's row by the owner only). CLI: `reset-2fa`, `signout`. Three steps on the wire:
  `/api/login`, `/api/login/code`, `/api/login/enrol`; every non-token answer is a 401 whose `error`
  an OLD console shows as it stands ("update your console") and whose `step` a new one acts on.
  `/api/login` also takes `code` in the same request — that is what the harnesses do.
- **The security stamp** (`Technician.SecurityStamp`). Every token and portal cookie carries it; a
  password, boxes or two-factor change, a removal or Sign out changes it. **The console is closed at
  once** (`AuthService.SignedOut` → `TenantHub.SignOutTechnician`, `SignedOutMsg`; a session they
  were alone in ends now), **the portal on its next page** (`OnValidatePrincipal`, cached 15 s). A
  change from the **command line** runs in another process, so a **15 s sweep** finds it. The
  migration gives everybody a fresh stamp, so **every cookie from before signs out once**, and the
  next sign-in is the one that sets up the authenticator.
- **Tokens expire after 12 hours unused** (`Security:TokenIdleHours`). A running console pings every
  15 s (`Touch`), so it never expires; a token copied off a closed laptop does. A console whose token
  is refused (401 — the server restarted, or it was signed out) **goes back to its sign-in window**
  instead of redialling for ever (`TechLink.OnSignedOut`, `DashboardForm.SignedOutByServer`).
- **Guessing stops** (`SignInGuard`): five failures on an account → refused 15 minutes, even with the
  right password; thirty from one address → that address refused. In memory, deliberately.
- **A sign-in from a network never used before is mailed to the person** (platform mailbox, when
  there is one). The first sign-in after this arrived is only recorded, or go-live would mail everybody.
- **The real caller behind Caddy**: `UseForwardedHeaders` (X-Forwarded-For/-Proto, trusted from
  loopback only — Caddy overwrites whatever a client sends). Cookies `Secure` over https, **HSTS**,
  `nosniff`, a referrer policy, and **no framing** (`X-Frame-Options`, `frame-ancestors`) **except
  `/webchat`**, whose whole job is to sit in a frame on the company's website. No full CSP: the
  pages carry inline script, and a policy that breaks a page is worse than none.
- **Never unencrypted across the internet** (`Shared/SecureTransport.cs`): plain http/ws only to a
  private address (loopback, 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16, 100.64/10, link-local, a bare machine name,
  .local/.lan/.test/.internal). The device socket, host, viewer, console and launcher all ask it,
  so the office server at 192.168.1.115 works exactly as before. The server warns at start if
  `PublicUrl` is plain http on a public address, if the admin key is short, and if two-factor is off.
- **The platform owner**: admin key, then a code (`OwnerTwoFactor`). Whoever first signs in with the
  key sets the authenticator up; `reset-owner-2fa` on the server clears it. The owner's cookie stamp
  is a hash of the key and the stored secret, so changing either signs every owner browser out.
  Owner pages now send a signed-out visitor to `/owner/login`, not the companies' form.
- **The server itself** (`go-live.sh` step 6, `remotesupport-platform.service`): security updates
  install themselves; fail2ban on SSH; **SSH passwords off only if a key is already there** (never
  otherwise — that is how you lock yourself out); the program root-owned and read-only to its
  service, `data/` the service's alone (`700`); systemd fencing (`NoNewPrivileges`, `PrivateTmp`,
  `ProtectSystem=full`, `ProtectHome`…); and **a nightly AES-256 backup** of `data/` (gpg, and
  SQLite's own `.backup` so a write cannot tear it) into `/var/backups/rsp`, 14 days kept. **Its
  passphrase is `/etc/rsp-backup-key` — copy it off the server**, or the backups cannot be opened.

### The traps

- **`Security:RequireTwoFactor` is a harness switch.** Every harness with a platform of its own sets
  `RSP_Security__RequireTwoFactor=false` (19 of them, one line each). It must never be off on a
  server a customer can reach; the server says so in its log at start.
- **Harnesses against the live server now need the code.** `tools/rs-credentials.json` takes a
  `"totpSecret"` — the key printed under the QR code when the account was set up — and
  `RsCredentials.Code()` computes the code with the server's own arithmetic. Without it they get
  `step: "code"` and stop.
- **Every platform restart signs every console out** (tokens are in memory — that was always so;
  what is new is that the console SAYS so and goes to its sign-in window, rather than sitting empty).
  Persisting tokens would trade that annoyance for a table of live credentials; not done.
- **The per-address count is only as good as the forwarded address.** With `UseForwardedHeaders`
  taken out, `securitycheck` showed the thirty test failures locking out 127.0.0.1 — which behind
  Caddy is everybody.
- **A role change signs the person out** (their stamp moves). It used to take effect only at their
  next sign-in, so a box UNticked left them able to do it until then.
- **`go-live.sh`'s hardening and the systemd fencing have not run on a real Ubuntu server** — this
  laptop is Windows. `bash -n` passes. Watch step 6's output, and a health-check PDF, the first time.

### Left for soon after (agreed order, not built)

*Items 1 and 2 are BUILT, 2026-10-07 — §111. Item 4 is BUILT the same day — §112.*

1. **A machine can be taken over by its hardware fingerprint.** Anybody with the (public) tenant key
   and a machine's `HardwareId` can present it as a "reinstall" and take over that machine's row —
   unattended permission included (`TenantHub.PersistDeviceAsync`, the candidates block). A
   technician would then connect to the wrong PC, clipboard and all. Fix: a takeover clears
   `UnattendedEnabled` until the customer ticks it again, and the console marks the row reinstalled.
2. **PBKDF2 at 600,000 rounds** (now 120,000), upgraded at each person's next sign-in.
3. **Code signing** (stage 5, `CODE-SIGNING.md`).
4. **End-to-end encryption of sessions** — ECDH between console and host, AES-256-GCM, the server
   relaying ciphertext only. Protects against a compromised server or hosting company.
5. **An outside penetration test** before selling widely; and an off-box copy of the backups.

### How it was proved

| | |
|---|---|
| `tools/securitycheck` (new) | **63 of 63**, against a platform of its own with two-factor ON. The transport rule (14 addresses); the code arithmetic against **RFC 6238's own published values**; set-up (401 not a token, a real PNG QR code, the hand-typed key, the old-console sentence, a wrong first code, ten recovery codes); each code once, the next accepted, recovery codes once and forgiving of case and dashes; a token opens the console socket and a made-up one is a 401; **People page Sign out closes a live console in ~100 ms**; **`set-password` from the command line closes it via the sweep in ~8 s, and the portal cookie lands on the sign-in form**; Remove closes a console in ~40 ms; Reset two-factor means set up again and the old recovery codes are gone; the headers, HSTS through `X-Forwarded-Proto`, website chat's frame still frameable; five wrong passwords lock the account; **thirty from one forwarded address lock that address and not the same account from elsewhere**; the owner's key → QR → code → `/owner`, and `reset-owner-2fa` signing the owner out. **With the forwarded headers, the stamp check and the hub's sign-out taken out it drops to 54** — each one caught. |
| the self-contained harnesses | **all 22 re-run, every count as before**: appearancecheck 14, handoffcheck 45, rolecheck 72, signincheck 12, techdownload 22, devicelink 20, ticketwire 31, unattendedwire 13, chatcheck 51, mentionwire 9, webchatcheck 80, websupportcheck 64, healthcheckwire 52, trayexit 16, voicewire 37, sessionextras 26, photomany 21, clipledger 20, oneexecheck 52, trialnoticecheck 18, reconnectlocal 20. (Those that load the platform in-process need `-c Debug` while the live server holds the Release build.) The live-server harnesses were updated to send the code but not run — they need `"totpSecret"` first. |

**Not on hardware.** Needs a **platform restart (migration `TwoFactorSignIn`)** — which signs
everybody out once, on purpose — and a **full ship** (`tools\ship-build.ps1`): the console's new
sign-in, and the plaintext refusal in the client, host and agent. Existing installs keep working
meanwhile (192.168.1.115 is private). On the live server, `go-live.sh` again for step 6.
`TEST-3.6.md` section AM, checks 259–268.

## 73. People choose their own passwords — invitations, resets, Forgot password — 2026-10-01

Clint, setting up the live server: *"when setting up users, will it send each one a link for their
download and request them to change their password? I think this is an important feature."* It did
not. The supervisor typed a password for the new person on the People page and passed it on by
hand; nobody could change their own (a supervisor could, by typing one — so a supervisor knew
everybody's); and "Forgot password?" said *contact support*. Built the same day, before anybody but
Clint is on the live server.

### What it does

- **Add a person = name, email, boxes. No password.** `AddTechnicianAsync(…, password: null, …)`
  makes a row with no password (`Technician.AwaitingSetup`), which nothing can sign in to, and
  `AccountLinks.IssueAsync` mails an **invitation**: from the platform mailbox **in the company's
  name**, replies to the company's **support address**, **no copy to the owner's NoticeCopyTo**
  (a password link is one person's), a **one-use link good for 72 hours**, and — with a seat — the
  console download link (`/tech/{slug}`). The People page shows *Invited — not set up* and
  **Resend invitation** (the old link stops working).
- **The link** (`/account/setup?t=…`, `Pages/Account/Setup`): choose a password (twice; the one rule
  is `Passwords.Problem` — 8+, not the email), then **on the same page, through the same steps as
  signing in (`WebSignIn`)**, the authenticator QR code, then the recovery codes once, then the
  console download for a seat or their portal home. **Opening the link spends nothing — only the
  POST that sets the password does** (mail filters such as Safe Links open every link first; a
  link spent by a GET would arrive used). Spent by ONE conditional update, so the same link posted
  twice sets one password.
- **Send reset link** on the People page replaces typing a password for somebody (2 hours; the
  current password works until it is used; the owner's row by the owner only). Somebody who never
  finished their invitation gets the invitation again instead.
- **Forgot password?** (`/forgot`, linked from the sign-in page, `/tech/{slug}` and the console's
  sign-in window): the same answer whether or not the address has an account; **3 an hour per
  address, 10 per caller**; the new password **still needs the code** afterwards.
- **Setting a password from a link moves the security stamp** — a reset signs out every console and
  browser signed in with the old one (§72).
- **My account** (`/portal/account`, in every portal menu): change your own password — the current
  one, the new one twice, **and a code**, so an unattended open browser cannot lock its owner out.
  Every other console and browser is signed out; this one stays in (cookie re-issued with the new stamp).
- **The command line**: `invite <slug> <email> ["Name"] [--owner] [--admin] …` — how each company's
  first owner is added once signups are closed. `add-tech` with a password is kept for the very
  first owner of the platform's own company. When the mail cannot go (no platform mailbox, or the
  server refused it) the supervisor — or the command line — is **shown the link once to pass on**.

### What building it found

- **The command line never sees the live address.** `PublicUrl` reached the SERVICE through
  systemd's environment, and `appsettings.json` ships with the office LAN address — so an `invite`
  typed on the server would have mailed a link to `192.168.1.115`. `go-live.sh` now writes
  `/opt/rsp/appsettings.live.json` (`PublicUrl`, `SignupsEnabled`; nothing secret), which every run
  of the program reads, the environment still winning.
- **The harness's own fault, twice, worth knowing for the next one:** Razor writes a line break
  inside `<pre>` as `&#xA;` (a browser shows it; a regex does not), and `/tech/{slug}` has no
  download button on a platform with no console payload — assert "signed in, not asked to sign in".

### How it was proved

| | |
|---|---|
| `tools/invitecheck` (new) | **51 of 51**, against a platform of its own with two-factor ON and **a real SMTP server inside the harness** that the platform mails to, so every message is read as it would arrive: From in the company's name, Reply-To the support address, **one envelope recipient** (the owner's copy address is configured and absent), the setup link and, for a seat, the console link. Invited cannot sign in; the link opened twice still works; mismatched and short passwords refused without spending it; the right one → QR → ten recovery codes → the download page, signed in; used once only; resend kills the old link; Forgot answers the same for a stranger and sends nothing; a real reset needs the code and **signs out a live console**; three Forgot mails an hour, not five; Send reset link names who asked; My account refuses a wrong password and a wrong code, keeps this browser in and signs the console out; with the mail server unreachable the supervisor is shown a working link; `invite` on the command line mails one at the public address. **With the owner's copy put back and the stamp left alone on a reset it drops to 49** — exactly those two. |
| the harnesses it could touch | re-run, every count as before: `securitycheck` 63, `techdownload` 22, `signincheck` 12, `appearancecheck` 14, `handoffcheck` 45, `rolecheck` 72. |

**Needs a platform deploy (migration `AccountInvitations`) and `-OnlyTechnician`** for the console's
Forgot link. On the live server: `Publish-Platform.ps1` again (it writes `appsettings.live.json`).
**The platform mailbox must be set (Owner → Mail) or every invitation falls back to the hand-on
link.** `TEST-3.6.md` section AN, checks 269–276.

## 74. The installer window closes; the console downloads as one .exe too — 2026-10-01

### The customers' .exe would not close after installing

Clint: *"The exe installer does not close when you click on close or when you click on the X."* In
`LauncherForm.InstallAsync` a **good** install `return`ed before `_busy = false`, and
`OnFormClosing` refuses every close while `_busy` (rightly — not while the installer runs). So after
every successful install, Close and the X were refused for ever. A failed install was fine, which is
why nobody had seen it: `oneexecheck` drew the window but never ran an install through it. `_busy`
is cleared in a `finally` now; Close does only that (it used to be a SECOND click handler beside
`InstallAsync`). The installer is `LauncherForm.Installer`, so the harness stands in for it.
`oneexecheck` **61 of 61** (9 new: the X before anything, Close and the X after a good install, the
installer not run twice, after a declined prompt, the X refused WHILE installing and allowed after);
**58 with the old line back** — exactly the three closes after a good install. Full ship.

### The technician console as one .exe

Clint: *"the technician console still downloads as a zip, that should be an exe as well."* As the
customers' (§71), and for the same reason: **one file for every company**, so it can be signed.
The console was already one .exe; what made it a zip was the company's `branding\` beside it.

- **`/downloads/{slug}/technician.exe`**, behind the same rule as the zip (`MayDownloadConsole` in
  `Program.cs`, one rule for both), served as **`{slug}-console.exe`**. `/tech/{slug}` and the
  portal's Downloads page offer it once the payload holds **`console-exe.ready`**; without the
  marker (an older console, which would start pointed at nobody) they offer the zip as before.
- **A console with no `branding\brand.json` beside it is a downloaded one**
  (`ConsoleDownload.IsDownloadedCopy`). It learns whose it is like the customers' .exe —
  `DownloadIdentity`, **moved to Shared**, with the console's own address
  (`/downloads/{slug}/technician.exe`) and name (`-console.exe`), never confused with the customers'
  — then the last company, then it asks (`AskCompanyDialog`, moved to UI, with the console's own
  question). It fetches `/download/{slug}/brand.json` and the logo, and **sets itself up for this
  Windows user**: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\RemoteSupport\Console\{slug}\`, no administrator, a Start
  menu and a desktop shortcut (*{Company} technician console*), then starts that copy and exits.
  That is the zip's unblock-unzip-run-pin, done for them. **The copied .exe has its
  Zone.Identifier removed** — copying carries it (§71), and Windows would warn at every start.
- **Updating = download and open the new one.** While the old console is open the copy is a
  sharing violation, and it says to Exit first and changes nothing. The same file twice is no copy.
- **The fallback server is embedded at publish** (`console-defaults.json`, the `ConsoleDefaults`
  property): `build.ps1` uses `-PublicUrl` (so `Publish-Platform.ps1`'s live build names the live
  server), `ship-build.ps1` the platform's `appsettings.json` (the office). Both write the marker.
- Existing zip installs are untouched: they have `branding\` beside them.

`tools/consoleexecheck` (new) **31 of 31**: the rules; **a REAL single-file console published as
the build scripts do**, served by a platform of its own (401 signed out; the page's .exe button and
words; the file byte for byte as `consoleexe-console.exe`; the zip again without the marker); that
file written as a browser leaves it and driven through `--set-up` with `RSP_CONSOLE_HOME` and
`RSP_CONSOLE_SHORTCUTS` in the harness's own folder (never this PC's desktop) — whose it is and why
(address; name + embedded server; last company; refusal; a file from the CUSTOMERS' link refused),
itself and the company's branding in place, no Zone.Identifier, the shortcut's target, the update
refused while open and done once closed; **the copy it set up opening the sign-in window in the
company's name; and the real double-click (no switches) setting up, starting that copy, exiting.**
**30 of 31 with the Zone.Identifier line out.** `techdownload` 22, `oneexecheck` 61. `ship-build
-OnlyTechnician` run: the marker is written and `demo\technician` still has its branding.

**Platform restart (no migration) and `-OnlyTechnician`** for the office; for the live server,
`deploy\Publish-Platform.ps1` (it runs `build.ps1 -Platform -PublicUrl`). The launcher fix needs a
full ship. `TEST-3.6.md` section AP, checks 278–283.

## 75. Picking a client by typing, the portal on a phone, and the code once a week — 2026-10-02

Clint, before uploading: three things.

### 1. A client is found by typing, everywhere one is picked

*"when linking a client, it brings a dropdown of all clients and one has to scroll through the list
… there should be a search bar that works the same as client search so that when typing the client
it automatically narrows."* Three places picked a client from a list: the Dashboard's *Link to*
(a `<select>` of every client), the Devices page's owner (a `<select>` of every client with its
people under it), and a ticket's Details (a browser `<datalist>` — a different control in every
browser, and a poor one on a phone). All three are now **`wwwroot/clientpick.js`**: a box that asks
`/api/portal/clients` — **`ClientService.SearchAsync`, the Clients page's own matching** (name,
contact, phone, email, any case) — as you type, 150 ms after the last key. Nothing typed is the
whole list, alphabetically (so a stray machine can still be read down). Modes: `id` (Dashboard),
`owner` (Devices — each company with its people; **typing a PERSON's name brings their company**,
`ClientService.PickAsync`), `name` (Details, which the server matches by name as before). Arrow keys,
Enter (the highlighted row, or the only one), Escape. **Half-typed and not picked is refused, not
sent as "nobody"** ("Pick one from the list."); emptied is nobody / unlink. The console's own dialog
already narrowed as you type (`LinkDeviceDialog`). `/api/portal/clients` keeps its old answer unless
`take` or `people` is asked for. `Ticket.ClientNames` (the datalist's query) is gone.
`tools/workflowdemo` now makes 16 clients, three people and four machines (three unlinked).

Walked in the browser as Sue and as Sam: "zen" → Zenith with Thandi and Pieter under it, picked,
Set → *linked to Thandi Mokoena at Zenith Accounting*; "bay" + Enter → Bayside Dental, linked on the
ticket; "harb" not picked → refused; picked → linked, gone from the Dashboard's unlinked list.

### 2. The portal on a phone

*"If a technician logs into the dashboard via their cellphone, tickets and workflows must work
flawlessly almost as if they are working from an app."* **Measured first at 375 × 812**, as Sue:
the **sticky header was ~245 px — a quarter of the screen on every page, all the way down**; the
ticket list was an **853 px table** swiped sideways, and its filter filled the whole first screen;
Clients, a client's page and Devices had tables of 600–1000 px; **every field was under 16 px, so an
iPhone zooms the page on each tap** (32 on one ticket); the Chat button sat over the content. The
ticket page itself already fitted, its step forms worked, and photos take `image/*` (the camera).

Now, below 700 px only (`site.css`, "the portal on a phone"; nothing changes above it — checked at
1280):
- **One line of header**: the brand and a **Menu** button (the "waiting on you" count rides on it);
  the links fold behind it as 50 px rows (`_Layout.cshtml`, `.menu-btn`, `.top.open`).
- **The ticket list is cards**, one per job, **tapped anywhere to open** (the Open link stretched
  over the card): number and subject, status and stage, then category, who, machine, opened, time.
  The filter keeps Show, Search and Apply; **Dates** folds the dates away (open if one is set). The
  three totals boxes are hidden on a phone (`.tstats`).
- **Every other list becomes cards** of label / value lines: **`wwwroot/phone.js`** labels each cell
  with its column (`data-label`) and wraps its contents in `.cell-v`, for tables whose first row is
  all headings (`no-cards` opts out; a label/value table like `tk-facts` is left alone). **Anything
  that swaps a table in after load must call `phoneTables.label()`** — the Clients search does.
- **Fields at 16 px** (no zoom), allowed to shrink in a row (`min-width: 0`); 16 px gutters; smaller
  cards; room under the page for the Chat button.
- **The ticket page** (`_Timeline.cshtml`'s own style block, `@@media`): the next steps as
  full-width buttons, the tabs one swipeable row, the comment box above Post, the booking's facts
  label over value.

Found on the way and fixed: `Menu@if (…)` printed literally (Razor reads `x@if` as an email
address); the brand wrapping onto four lines; the search box squeezed by its own inline `flex:1`;
pills breaking into single letters inside flex cells; a two-line label running into the next row;
the picker's list 21 px off the screen; the Clients search's Clear button pushed off the edge.
**Measured after, on 14 pages** (the list, all, eight tickets at every stage with every step form
open, New ticket, Clients and a search, two client pages, Devices, My account, Website chat): no
horizontal scroll, nothing past the edge, no field under 16 px.

### 3. The two-factor code once a week

*"sign in requires two factor authentication on every sign in. can we change that to require
authentication every 7 days?"* After a code (or a recovery code, or setting up), the server gives
the browser or console a **trust token**: `AuthService.IssueTrust` — the person's id and **security
stamp**, sealed by the server's Data Protection keys (`RemoteSupport.TrustedDevice.v1`,
time-limited) and **dated to run out after `Security:TwoFactorTrustDays` (7; 0 = every time)**.
With it **the password alone signs in; the password is always asked.** Signing in on trust does
**not** renew it, so the code comes back seven days after it was last typed. Anything that changes
the stamp voids every token at once: a password change, Reset two-factor, Sign out on the People
page, removal, a change of boxes. Tokens survive a platform restart (the keys are in `data/keys`).
- **Browser**: the `rsp_trust` cookie (HttpOnly, Secure over https, SameSite=Lax), **one token per
  person, up to five**, so two people on one office PC are each asked once a week
  (`WebSignIn.KeepTrust`, `AuthService.TrustOwner`). The sign-in page, `/tech/{slug}` and account
  set-up all go through `WebSignIn`, which now takes the `HttpContext`.
- **Console**: `/api/login` takes `trust` and answers with a new one after a code;
  **`TrustedSignIn`** keeps it in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\RemoteSupport\trust.json`, per server and username,
  **sealed with DPAPI to the Windows user** — useless copied anywhere else.
- The code screens say *"This browser/PC then asks only for your password for the next 7 days"* —
  written as 7; change the words if the setting ever changes.
- The platform owner's sign-in (`/owner`, admin key + code) is unchanged: every time.

`securitycheck` **75 of 75** (12 new; its platform trusts for 43 s so running out can be watched):
a code gives a token; with it the password alone; not renewed by use; a wrong password still
refused; a token altered at all ignored; one person's token useless for another; the browser cookie,
signing out and back in on it with the password alone, any other browser still asked; **Sign out on
the People page voids it** (3 s after issue, so not expiry); after 45 s it has run out. **74 with the
stamp comparison taken out** — exactly the Sign out check. `signincheck` **20** (8 new: the console's
store — per person and server, any case, sealed on disk, a damaged file is no trust, an empty token
forgets). Re-run unchanged: `devicelink` 20, `invitecheck` 51, `techdownload` 22, `dashtabs` 98,
`handoffcheck` 45.

**Platform deploy (no migration) and `-OnlyTechnician`** (the console's half of the 7 days).
`TEST-3.6.md` section AQ, checks 284–292.
