## 117. Several owners — 2026-10-08

Clint, on being told the code still allowed one owner: *"Lets make this change."* His earlier words
set the price: *"If more than one owner is selected, this must be considered a seat taken even if no
extra roles are assigned"* — which §116's `Pricing.SeatsFor` already counted.

### What it is now

- **The Owner box is a tick box like the others**, in Add a person and on every row — **shown only to
  an owner**. A supervisor sees owners' rows read-only, as before, and no Owner box anywhere.
- **Only an owner** makes somebody an owner, changes an owner's row, or removes an owner
  (`TenantService.OnlyAnOwner`; `RemoveTechnicianAsync` takes `asker` now). Resetting an owner's
  password or two-factor, or signing one out, was already owners-only (`CanChangeOwner`).
- **A company always keeps one owner** (`TenantService.LastOwner`, `IsLastOwner`): the last owner's
  Owner box is drawn locked on, has no Remove, and the service refuses both — the command line too.
- **Price**: the first owner-only login is free, every other is a seat, so adding a second owner-only
  login is a price question like any other seat, and counts toward the ten. The add form's help line
  says which (`FreeOwnerTaken`).
- **Handing over (`set-owner`, command line)** gives the new owner the box and makes EVERY other owner a
  supervisor; the seats are counted over all of them (`Pricing.SeatsAfter`, and `LimitProblem` /
  `RiseIf` overloads that take counts). To add an owner beside the others, tick the box.
- Wording: "Only an owner can agree to a higher price", "only an owner can agree to that".

Nothing else assumed one owner: the 16 `IsOwner` uses were all the People page and `TenantService`, and
trial notices already go to every owner and supervisor. **The command line's `list-techs` still prints
"(the owner alone is free)"** — `Program.cs` had another session's work in it, so it was left.

### How it was proved

| | |
|---|---|
| `rolecheck` | **84 of 84** (was 74; its "only ever one owner" section rewritten). A supervisor refused at adding, making, changing and removing an owner; the last owner never unticked or removed, the command line included; a second owner-only login priced R800 → R1,100 and added once agreed; an owner stepping down while others remain; an owner removing another; handing over demoting every other owner and recording the seat. **With the five owner guards out: 30 of 47, then a throw.** |
| `seatcheck` | **78 of 78** (was 72): the owner's page offers the Owner box and locks the only owner's; a supervisor's page has none; an owner adds a second owner from the page, who takes a seat (8), and then neither is locked and the other has Remove. |

**Not on hardware.** **`Publish-Platform.ps1`** only (no migration). `TEST-3.6.md` section CG, 551–555.

## 118. PostgreSQL, step 1: the platform can run on it — 2026-10-08

Clint, after §115: *"we should move to PostgreSQL before anything else, then do the testing as this is going
to be a requirement anyway."* Agreed, with the local load test (BUGS #11) as the before-measurement and one
xneelo run afterwards. Five steps: **1 the code (this)**, 2 the harnesses on PostgreSQL, 3 the local load
test again, 4 the live switch (PostgreSQL on the same xneelo server — data stays in South Africa, the
privacy policy unchanged — a data copy, `pg_dump` backups), 5 the xneelo load test.

**Step 4 also takes the backups OFF the server (Clint, 2026-10-08: "yes, lets do that").** Today `go-live.sh`'s
nightly `/usr/local/sbin/rsp-backup` (02:30, `/etc/cron.d/rsp-backup`, AES-256, 14 days in `/var/backups/rsp`,
plus one before every deploy kept 60) writes them to the SAME server's disk: a lost server takes them with it.
No xneelo product is involved and it costs nothing. The plan: a nightly copy pulled down to the office share
(the WD My Cloud), still encrypted, so data stays in South Africa as the privacy policy promises, with the
passphrase (`/etc/rsp-backup-key`) in Clint's password manager and NEVER beside the copies. To settle when it
is built: which office machine is on at night to do the pulling, and a key of its own on the server that can
fetch the newest backup and nothing else. xneelo volume snapshots (about R1.20/GB a month, taken by hand as
far as was seen) were the paid alternative. (BUILT the same day, ahead of step 4: §120.)

**Step 4 also moves the data OFF the system disk (Clint, 2026-10-08: "yes add it").** Today photos, recordings,
knowledge-base pictures, health-check reports, the key ring and the database share the server's one 40 GB disk
with Ubuntu: a full disk stops everything, the database included, and recordings are what will fill it. Two
xneelo **Volumes** (block storage, attached to the instance; about R1.20/GB a month standard, R1.80 premium):
- **`rsp-files`, standard, 50 GB to start** (about R60): mounted at `/opt/rsp/data`, so the platform's paths and
  code do not change. Holds everything in data/ — and the backups (below).
- **`rsp-db`, premium NVMe, 20 GB** (about R36): PostgreSQL's data directory.
Mounted by UUID with `nofail` in /etc/fstab so a reboot brings them back; either can be enlarged later in the
panel. Done in the SAME quiet window as the PostgreSQL switch — one interruption, not two.
**The backups must change with it:** `rsp-backup` tars ALL of data/ every night and keeps 14 on the system
disk, which recordings alone would fill. So: backups kept on `rsp-files`, not the system disk; recordings left
OUT of the nightly full copy and backed up ONCE each when made (a recording never changes); the office copy
(§120) then stays a sensible size. Clint creates and attaches the two volumes in the panel; one script does
the rest.

**What the live server actually is (`deploy/Get-ServerReport.ps1`, 2026-10-08 15:35)** — read-only, prints no secret:
**4 vCPU (AMD EPYC Genoa), 7.8 GB memory (under 1 GB used), no swap** — bigger than GO-LIVE.md's 2/4. System disk
`vda` **20 GB, but its root partition is only 9 GB** (4.7 used, 4.0 free; Clint enlarged the boot volume from 10 to 20 GB, which Ubuntu has not taken up yet — grow it
with `growpart /dev/vda 1` + `resize2fs`, online, in step 4). **A second disk `vdb`, 50 GB, is attached and was
never formatted or mounted** — it IS `rsp-files` (Clint, same day: created for this, standard), blank on purpose: step 4 formats it; only `rsp-db`
then needs creating. data/ 40 MB (1 company, 5 machines, 63 tickets); backups 27 files, 443 MB on the 9 GB root
(14 nightly + one per deploy, 60 days). Updates wait on a reboot. Ports 22/80/443 only; fail2ban, unattended
upgrades, Caddy, Chrome all running.
**The database disk (Clint, same day):** the 20 GB disk was the system disk enlarged, not a database disk. Offered
PostgreSQL on the system disk (simpler, free, about 14 GB free once grown), Clint chose its OWN disk: `rsp-db`,
20 GB premium, to be created and attached; step 4 formats it and puts PostgreSQL's data directory on it.
**All three attached and confirmed by the report at 15:50:** `rsp-server` = `vda` 20 GB (system; root still 9 GB),
`rsp-files` = `vdb` 50 GB blank, `rsp-db` = `vdc` 20 GB blank. **The step 4 script must NOT trust `vdb`/`vdc`** —
those names can change across a reboot: it finds each disk by its size, refuses one that is not blank, and
mounts by filesystem UUID (`nofail`) once formatted.

**SQLite stays the default until step 4.** `ConnectionStrings:Postgres` (on a server
`RSP_ConnectionStrings__Postgres`) switches the platform to PostgreSQL; without it nothing changes, so the
live server and every other session carry on as they were. The rest of the program still only sees a
`PlatformDb`.

- **`Data/PgPlatformDb.cs`**: `PgPlatformDb : PlatformDb` exists for ONE reason — EF finds migrations by
  context TYPE, and PostgreSQL needs its own set (`Data/PgMigrations`). `PlatformDbFactory` hands them out
  as `PlatformDb`; `PgPlatformDbDesignTime` lets `dotnet ef` make one with no server. `PlatformDb` is no
  longer sealed (a protected constructor for the subclass). The start-up line says
  `DB: PostgreSQL host/database`, never the password.
- **`dotnet ef` now needs `--context`**: `--context PlatformDb` for a SQLite migration as before.
  **Until step 4 the PostgreSQL set is ONE migration, `PgInitial`, made again from the model** (no
  PostgreSQL database anywhere holds data yet): delete `Data/PgMigrations`, then
  `dotnet ef migrations add PgInitial --context PgPlatformDb --output-dir Data/PgMigrations`. **Never pass
  `--namespace`** — it put the snapshot in a stray `RemoteSupport/Platform/...` folder.
- Nothing else needed changing, and that was checked: no raw SQL, no SQLite types or error codes, no
  `DateTimeOffset`, and every text comparison already lowercases both sides (24 places), which means the
  same on both. Every `DateTime` already goes through the UTC converter — what Npgsql insists on. The
  script is 38 tables, 74 indexes, dates as `timestamp with time zone`, ids `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS
  IDENTITY` (so a data copy can keep them; the sequences must be moved past them after).
- **`tools/pgcheck`**: part 1 always — both migration sets match the model (`has-pending-model-changes`;
  **0 of 2 with an index added and no migration, 2 of 2 without**). Part 2 with a PostgreSQL: a fresh
  database, the command line, sign-in, a machine, a session that writes its ticket, UTC read back, the
  case rule, a restart that applies nothing twice; the database dropped after (`--keep`).
- **`tools/Setup-TestPostgres.ps1`** (once, after installing PostgreSQL 16 on this PC): the administrator
  password in a Windows box, never in chat; makes `rsp_test` (CREATEDB and nothing else) with a random
  password in `tools/rs-postgres.txt`, git-ignored. **`tools/Common/TestPostgres.cs`** gives a harness a
  database of its own and drops it.

SQLite proved unchanged: `watchcheck` 57 of 57, `loadtest local` comfortable. **`pgcheck` 19 of 19 on PostgreSQL 16.15**
(installed on this PC 2026-10-08), its test databases dropped after. Its first restart check read EF's
log, which the platform keeps at Warning, so it could not fail: it reads `__EFMigrationsHistory` now.

## 119. PostgreSQL, step 2: every harness runs on either database — 2026-10-08

**`RSP_TEST_DB=postgres`** puts a harness on PostgreSQL; without it, SQLite exactly as before. **61 of 61
harnesses pass on SQLite and 61 of 61 on PostgreSQL** (`tools/Run-DbHarnesses.ps1 [-Postgres] [-Only a,b]`,
one at a time — two platform builds at once trip over each other; logs and `results.md` in `tools/dbruns/`,
git-ignored). Left out: the two demos (servers until stopped), `loadtest` (its own `local` mode, which follows
`RSP_TEST_DB` too — step 3), `pgcheck` (PostgreSQL only), and the tools that work on a real database
(`backfill-clients`, `testtech`).

**`tools/Common/HarnessDb*.cs`**, three files so a harness includes what it uses:
- `HarnessDb.cs` (Npgsql only, every harness that starts a platform): `HarnessDb.Use(env, dataDir)` beside
  every `RSP_Platform__DataDirectory` (a fresh database per SQLite FILE — `For(dataDir)` is its
  `platform.db`; a restart gets the same one; dropped at exit, `RSP_TEST_KEEP=1` keeps; a killed run's are swept
  the next day, never today's — another session may be mid-run). **`HarnessDb.Portable(sql)`** quotes every
  PascalCase word and turns `$x` into `@x`, leaving text in quotes alone — both databases accept the result.
  **Booleans are not translated**: `CAST(x AS INTEGER)` reads 0/1 on both (PostgreSQL says `True`).
- `HarnessDb.Ef.cs` (harnesses with the platform project): `UseHarnessDb(...)` in place of `UseSqlite(...)`;
  **`HarnessDb.MigrateAsync(db)` in place of `db.Database.MigrateAsync()`** — a `PlatformDb` on Npgsql would
  apply SQLite's migrations; `ResetSequencesAsync` moves every id counter past ids a harness chose itself (an
  identity column does not notice them — step 4's data copy needs the same); `SqliteUpgradePart(what)`.
- `HarnessDb.Sql.cs`: `HarnessDb.Connect(...)` in place of `new SqliteConnection(...)`, `cmd.With(name, v)`.

**Seven harnesses test an UPGRADE of an older SQLite database** (seed rows as they stood, migrate, check the
backfill): `calloutcheck`, `clockcheck`, `contactcheck`, `quotecheck`, `rolecheck`, `seatcheck`,
`workflowcheck`. On PostgreSQL there is no older migration to stand at, so that part is skipped and SAID, and
the harness seeds what the upgrade LEAVES (`Seed.Tenant`, through today's model; the roles, regions, seats,
contacts the checks prove) — every other section runs. **`Seed.OldTenant` writes through the model on
PostgreSQL by itself**, for harnesses that only want a company (`deliverycheck`, `machinescheck`).

What PostgreSQL found, all in the HARNESSES — no product code changed:
- **Time precision.** PostgreSQL keeps a microsecond; .NET and SQLite a tenth of one. `calloutcheck` held
  `DateTime.UtcNow + 3 days` in memory and asked to reschedule to it: not equal to what was stored, so the
  "already booked for then" rule did not fire (4 failures). It reads the stored time back now. **The product's
  one exact time comparison (`TicketService.Workflow`, reschedule) only ever sees a time from a date-and-time
  box**, which has no fractions; every other is before/after/is-set.
- **A Windows Forms harness deadlocks on `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()`** (`signincheck` hung for its full 20
  minutes): the database is made and dropped on a pool thread now (`Task.Run`).
- Two harnesses end "N passed, F failed", not "N of M passed" — the runner reads both.
- **Windows PowerShell 5.1 reads a .ps1 with no byte-order mark as Windows-1252**, so an em dash inside a
  string became a curly quote and the script would not parse. Every new .ps1 here is plain ASCII.

**And one product fault (2026-10-08, after the run above).** The final PostgreSQL run had `clipledger` at 18 of
20, three times running, while SQLite passed 20. A clipboard line sent the moment a session opened was
**dropped without a word**: the hub looked up the session's ticket in `_sessionTickets` once, and the ticket
is written as the session starts — a few milliseconds later on PostgreSQL, so it lost every time; on a busy
SQLite server it could too. The FileActivity path now waits for the ticket as script lines always did
(`LogToSessionTicketAsync`, up to 5 s; not on the free version, which has none). `clipledger` 20 of 20 on
both (18 of 20 on PostgreSQL before), `freecheck` 45 and `sessionextras` 35 on both. **Final: 61 of 61 on
each database.** A platform deploy carries it.

## 120. The backups leave the server: a nightly copy to the office — 2026-10-08

Clint: the nightly backup made by `go-live.sh` (§72) sat on the server's own disk — no xneelo product, no
cost, and lost with the server. He chose a copy to the office share (WD My Cloud, `\192.168.1.33\anywhereit`),
pulled by an office Windows PC that can open the share, the office having a fixed address; built now rather
than with step 4 of §118, since it does not depend on PostgreSQL. **`deploy/backup/README.md` is the set-up**:
`Install-BackupPull.ps1` on the office PC, `Enable-OffsiteBackup.ps1` on Clint's laptop in the office, then
`Install-BackupPull.ps1 -Finish`.

- **On the server: the account `rspcopy`**, its one key in `authorized_keys` as
  `from="<office>",command="/usr/local/sbin/rsp-backup-serve",restrict` — whatever is asked, the gatekeeper
  runs: `list` (name, size, SHA-256 of each nightly `rsp-YYYYMMDD.tar.gz.gpg`) or `get <exact name>`; anything
  else is refused (exit 2), a missing one is 3. It reads `/var/backups/rsp` as the group `rspcopy` (setgid
  2750, files 640); the files stay AES-256, `/etc/rsp-backup-key` stays root's.
- **`go-live.sh` keeps it working**: the nightly script it writes chmods the folder 700 every night, which
  would lock the copy out again — now group-aware when `rspcopy` exists, root-only (as before) when not.
  `enable-offsite.sh` brings the ALREADY-installed script to the same lines (tested on the exact script live
  has, from the committed template: identical lines, and running it twice adds nothing).
- **On the office PC: `Pull-Backup.ps1`**, a scheduled task at 04:00 (catches up if the PC was off; runs with
  nobody signed in, so Windows keeps the account's password). It refuses a server whose key does not match
  the fingerprint Clint's laptop read over its trusted connection (`server-fingerprint.txt` on the share),
  fetches the newest backup it lacks as raw bytes (**PowerShell's own `>` would turn the file into text**),
  keeps it only if size and SHA-256 match the server's, prunes by the date in the NAME past 60 days, and says
  WARNING when the newest is not today's after 03:00 (the server's own backup stopped).
- **Proved on this PC against the real gatekeeper** (an ssh stand-in that runs `rsp-backup-serve.sh`): first
  copy byte-identical; a second run "already have"; a 99-day-old copy pruned and a 10-day one kept; a
  damaged transfer refused and not kept; the server's backups stopped → WARNING (which found the first rule
  too lax: it waited two days). Hostile asks — `../etc/passwd`, a before-update file, `rm -rf /` — refused.
  **Not proved: the real server and the real office PC**; that is the README's three steps.

## 121. PostgreSQL, step 3: the load test again — and BUGS #11 was never the database — 2026-10-08

The same rush as §115 (`loadtest local --companies 100 --machines 50 --ramp 30`: 5,000 machines in 30 s, `/health`
timed by curl from outside), each database, before and after:

| | connect, median / 95% | failed / dropped |
|---|---|---|
| SQLite, before | 6.7 s / 14.6 s | 0 / 174 |
| PostgreSQL, first try | a 30 s freeze | 13,219 refused / 4,481 |
| PostgreSQL, pool capped at 40 | 239 ms / 7.8 s (after a 30 s freeze) | 7,649 refused / 39 |
| **PostgreSQL, hub loaded once and async** | **3 ms / 59 ms** | **0 / 0** |
| SQLite, hub fix in | 8.9 s / 22.8 s | 15 / 682 |

1. **PostgreSQL's connections must be capped** (`PgPlatformDb.Prepare`, 40 unless the connection string names a
   number): Npgsql's pool and PostgreSQL's `max_connections` are both 100, so the rush was REFUSED connections
   ("remaining connection slots are reserved…") and each refusal dropped a machine.
2. **BUGS #11 was loading cold company hubs** — proved with `loadtest local --warm` (one machine per company
   first): warm, 3 ms. `HubRegistry.GetAsync` loads each company's hub ONCE (`Lazy<Task<…>>`) through
   `TenantHub.CreateAsync` (the constructor's queries, now async and private); `/ws/device`, `/ws/tech`,
   `/ws/session`, `/ws/web` await it; `Loaded()` for events that must never load one; `Get()` stays for the
   portal pages (a lookup once loaded). BUGS #11 has the whole account.
3. **SQLite still stalls with that fixed** — its driver's "async" is synchronous — which is the measured case for
   the move.
`loadtest`'s VERDICT now counts the rush (connect 95% over 2 s; drops over 1%), not only the calm after it — it
said "comfortably" for every run above. **61 of 61 harnesses on each database with all of this in.** The heavier
run with sessions is still to come. **A platform deploy carries the hub fix and the cap** (the cap only matters on
PostgreSQL).

**The heavier runs (same day), all on this one laptop playing server and load at once:**
- 2,000 machines over 60 s, 100 technicians, **100 sessions** at 200 KB/s: PostgreSQL — connect 3 ms, session start
  3 ms, first picture 2 ms (95% 4 ms), 99% relayed; SQLite — the same machines and 99%, but session start 14 ms and
  first picture 95% within 173 ms. At 33 machines a second there is no storm; both cope.
- **PostgreSQL, the storm AND 300 sessions** (5,000 machines in 30 s, 200 technicians, 58.6 MB/s of picture):
  connect 2 ms (95% 45), session start 3 ms, **first picture 1 ms, 300 of 300, 100% relayed**, nothing failed or
  dropped; the server's processor peaked at 27%, its memory at about 700 MB (roughly 100 KB a connection).
- The first try showed 27 of 300 sessions with no picture — **the TOOL**: it asked for the picture the moment
  the session was ready, before the host had connected, and the hub had nobody to give it to. The real console
  asks when the screen list (`MonitorsMsg`) arrives, which the server replays to a viewer that came after the
  host (SessionForm) — so the tool does that now.
**Step 3 is done.** The real ceiling — bandwidth, a real network, TLS through Caddy — is step 5, on xneelo.

## 122. Five faults from internal testing: offline, reconnecting, parent jobs, unlinking, the request — 2026-10-09

Clint's list, his answers in brackets: (1) no unlinking in the console or portal [ticket from its parent job, AND
machine from a client]; (2) a screenshot when a client requests support, and a subject line apart from the
description, because a long description made a mess of the tickets [ticked, with a preview]; (3) machines still
online in the console when they are off; (4) reconnecting inside the 30 minutes asks for a reason every time [count
the 30 minutes from the END of the last session]; (5) a parent ticket closes with its child open, "closing both"
[the child stays open after linking, closed on its own; the parent waits for it with a pop-up naming it].

### 3. Online when off — the server never noticed a silent machine

A machine switched off at the wall, asleep or off its network never closes its socket. .NET 8's
`KeepAliveInterval` only SENDS pongs; it never asks for an answer, so the server waited on the operating system to
give up on TCP — about a quarter of an hour on Linux. Every app has pinged every 15 s since the first commit and
nothing ever listened for the silence. **`WsConnection.DropWhenSilent`** aborts a connection that has pinged and then
sent nothing for `Platform:SilenceSeconds` (45 — three missed pings), on `/ws/device` and `/ws/tech`; the hub logs
*"went silent — switched off, asleep or off its network"*. **Only a connection that has pinged is held to it**: the
harnesses' pretend machines never ping, and a free installer's one-off connection lasts 45 s at most, so nothing
that does not promise to ping is ever cut off. `tools/silentoffline` 13 (8 with the two lines out — and one of those
5 was a session STARTED on a machine that was off).

### 4. Reconnecting — the console asks the server first, and the window moved

The console asked "why" on every Connect, before it could know whether the server was about to reuse a ticket.
Now **`ConnectSelectedDevice` sends no reason first** (with a password typed earlier this run, if any). The hub
(`ConnectWithoutReasonAsync`) asks `TicketService.ActiveForDeviceAsync`: a ticket to carry on → the session simply
starts on it; none → **`ErrorMsg.NeedsReason`** and the console opens the usual window. With an unattended password
the order matters: no ticket → the reason first (one window asks both, as before); a ticket → the password ALONE
(`_continuing` in `DashboardForm` tells the window not to ask a reason), and **`ErrorMsg.NoPasswordGiven`** stops the
first ask showing in red as if it were wrong. A technician whose password the server remembers is asked nothing.

**`ActiveForDeviceAsync` counts the 30 minutes from the END of the ticket's last session** (or its opening if it
has none). Read its comment before touching it: still 30 minutes, still only a ticket nobody has decided on — the
window MOVED, it did not widen — and **a session with no end recorded counts from its START**, never as still
going (a server stopped under it would otherwise keep a ticket open for ever). `ticketpersession` 37 (34 with the
old rule), `tools/reasonwire` (new) 20 (3 of 9 with the hub's old refusal).

### 5. "Closing both" — linking closed the child

Nothing ever closed children with a parent, and the guard (§36, and §48's fix for routes) stood. **`Link to parent
ticket` went straight to Closed** (§48, Clint's choice then), so the child was closed the moment it was linked, and
the parent then closed freely. Clint chose the other way: **linking files it and leaves it where it is**
(`"@stay"`), to be finished and closed on its own; once filed it is not offered Link again (`Offered`).
**`TicketService.ClosesJob(action, ticket)`** is the one rule for "this step finishes the job" (a Done stage,
Abandoned excepted — `TargetOf` resolves `@close` and friends), used by `ActAsync`'s refusal AND sent to the console
as `StageActionInfo.ClosesJob`, so the pop-up and the server never disagree (a workshop's *Payment received* with
the machine still here goes to Awaiting collection, not Done, and is not stopped). **`Shared/JobParts.Refusal`** is
the one wording: *"This job cannot be closed yet: #11 Mapped drives… is part of it and still open. Close it
first."* — the server's refusal, the portal's `alert` (`TicketModel.RefusalFor`, `data-refuse`) and the console's
`MessageBox` (`TicketsForm.Press`). `routecheck` 61 (54 with linking closing the child).

### 1. Unlinking

- **A ticket from its job**: neither the portal's routed ticket page (`_Timeline`) nor the console's ticket window
  showed a parent or children at all — only the retired classic page did. Both now show **Part of: #N … (stage)
  [Not part of it]** and **Part of this job — N still open, and this job cannot be closed until they are: …**,
  each a link. The console's needs `TicketDetail.Parent`/`Children` (`TicketService.JobOfAsync`, filled for every
  ticket, routed or not) and a new **`TicketSetParentMsg`** (0 = out), which the hub hands to the same
  `SetParentAsync` the portal uses. `ticketwindowprobe` 188.
- **A machine from a client**: it always could — Link's window has "Not linked to anybody" as its first row, and
  the portal's owner box emptied — which nobody found. Console right-click: **Unlink from {customer}…** (and Link
  reads *Change the customer…* on a linked machine); portal Devices: an **Unlink** button beside Set.

Walked in the browser on `workflowdemo` (port 8196): #11 linked under #10 stayed at Remote session with *Not part of
it*; Done on #10 popped up the refusal and sent nothing; the form forced through was refused by the server in the
same words; Not part of it put Link back; Unlink on Devices unlinked ZEN-PC-07.

### 2. Request Support: a subject, a description, and a picture of their screen

The one box was the ticket's subject whole, so a paragraph became a paragraph in the queue. The tray app's
`RequestDialog` now asks **Your name / What do you need help with? A few words** (one line, required, 3 to
`SupportRequest.SubjectMax` = 80 characters) **/ Tell us more (optional)** and, when a picture could be taken,
**Include a picture of my screen** — TICKED, with the picture itself under the tick (Clint's answer), so nobody sends
what they have not seen. **`Client/ScreenSnap`** takes it BEFORE the window opens (the tray window, if up, goes
transparent for 150 ms): every monitor as one picture, no wider than 1920, JPEG 80 — 164 KB of two monitors here.
A screen that cannot be read (locked, secure desktop) gives no picture and no tick; it never stops a request.

`RequestCallMsg` gains `Details` and `Screenshot`; **the hub keeps the picture and rings every console with only
`CallInfo.HasScreenshot`** (a 323-byte ring for a 27 KB picture). **`Shared/SupportRequest.Words`** is the one rule
for the subject: an OLDER tray app's single box becomes its first line, cut to 80 with "…", and ALL of it the
description — so old installs stop making a mess too, and nothing anybody wrote is lost. The ticket's description is
the description (or the subject when there is none, as "Fault reported" always showed). The picture is a
**`PhotoKind.Screenshot`** (3; an int column, no migration — uploads can only name before/after/part) on the ticket;
asking again inside the 30 minutes notes *"Customer requested support again: {subject}"* and adds its picture; one
that is not an image is refused by `TicketPhotoService` and SAID in the story. Shown in the "how it started" card
(portal: *Their screen — when they asked for help*, each opens full size; console: **🖼 See their screen**, opening
`/portal/photo/{id}` — `PortalHandoffService.SafePath` allows exactly that, digits only).

`callprobe` 50 (it caught the tick's words cut off by the picture beside it — now above it), `tools/requestwire`
(new) 20 (10 of 19 with the hub's old handling: no description, no picture, the paragraph as the subject). Walked in
the browser on requestwire's database. **A FULL ship and a client reinstall** — the tray app changed; the server
alone tidies old installs' subjects.

**Deploying all of §122**: `Publish-Platform.ps1` (no migration) and re-download the console for 1, 3, 4 and 5; a
FULL ship and client reinstall for 2. `TEST-3.6.md` section CH, 556–571.

## 123. Updating the client from a ticket — 2026-10-09

Clint: *"If someone posts a comment, there should be an option to update client. The client then gets the original
fault as per the ticket description with the comment whoever has posted, but not the entire string of the ticket. If
a client replies, it should come back into the same ticket. A lot of comments would be for internal purposes only ...
The email would include the name of the person that made the comment."* His answers, the same day: **both** a tick
box when posting and *Email to the client* on a comment already posted; **the ticket's contact by default**,
changeable to another of the client's people or an address typed in; **every email is the fault plus THAT one
comment**, never the comments sent before; the address is **Tickets by email's**, and **signup asks for it** too; and
a reply **flags the people on the ticket until they open it**.

### What it is

- **The tick box** — *Also email this to the client*, under the comment box, **unticked by default**, in the story page,
  the classic page's Update form (§61: both layouts) and the console. Ticked, it shows who it goes to (a dropdown of
  the client's people the server offered, and *Another address…* with a box) and says what goes and from where.
- **Email to the client…** under every comment that may be sent (`ClientUpdateService.Sendable`: typed comments only —
  never an automatic line, a step's form, a Work done entry or the customer's own reply). After a send it reads
  *Email it again…*.
- **The marker** under a comment: *✉ Emailed to jane@acme.co.za by Tess Tech, 9 Oct 14:02*, or *⚠ Not emailed to …:
  why*. One row per send (`TicketClientUpdate`, kept whether it went or not). `ClientUpdateService.Marker` is the one
  wording; the console gets the same strings in `TicketNoteInfo.Emailed`.
- **The email**: subject `[Ticket #N] subject`; *Hello {name}*, *"{author} has an update on ticket #N — subject"*, the
  comment, *Your original request* with `Ticket.Description` (cut at 4,000 characters, left out if empty), *To reply,
  simply reply to this email*. Text and HTML, the logo inline (`cid:`), the company's accent colour **only if it is
  `#rrggbb`**; every typed word HTML-encoded. Sent exactly as the auto-reply is — `TicketIntake.SendAsCompanyAsync`
  (factored out of the auto-reply): their own server as support@, else ours in their name with Reply-To support@.
  **Not** marked `Auto-Submitted` — a person wrote it. Message-ID `rsp.{tenant}.{number}.…` (`TicketIntake.NewMessageId`),
  In-Reply-To the last message of the ticket's thread, ours or theirs.
- **The reply** comes back the way §79's does, with two changes in `TicketIntake.ProcessAsync`: it is **also accepted
  from any address an update from this ticket went to** (a typed address is not on file, and would otherwise have
  opened a stranger's ticket), and it is written by **`TicketService.AddCustomerReplyAsync`** — `TicketNote.FromCustomer`,
  and a `TicketMention` for everybody on the ticket plus whoever sent the last update. That reuses the @mention badge
  (*waiting on you*, portal and console) and the *Waiting on my reply* filter. **A customer's flag clears when that
  person OPENS the ticket** (`SeenCustomerRepliesAsync`, called AFTER the page or console has read the flags so the
  banner still shows once) — or comments on it. A colleague's @mention still clears only by replying. The console gets
  them in `TicketDetail.RepliedBy`, kept out of `AskedBy`, which older consoles word as "asked you something".
- **Offered only when Tickets by email works** (`ClientUpdateService.Ready`: switched on, an address, and mailbox
  reading or a CONFIRMED forward) — an update the client cannot answer would be a dead end. Otherwise the comment box
  says why: owner/supervisor get *set up Tickets by email first* with the link; anybody else *ask the owner or a
  supervisor*. Who may send: `Permissions.CanEmailClient` — everybody who may comment.
- **Signup** (full version only) asks *Ticket email address (optional)*: saved as a `TicketIntakeSettings` row,
  switched OFF, so Tickets by email opens with it filled in. Its password is never asked at signup. The next-steps card
  says to set it up; the Tickets by email page explains the updates.

### The rules that matter

- **A bad address posts nothing.** `ClientUpdateService.CheckAsync` runs BEFORE the comment is written (portal comment,
  classic Update, console `TicketNoteAddMsg.EmailTo`); refused, the words come back into the box, ticked. Otherwise a
  comment would be posted and not emailed, and posting it again to fix the address would duplicate it.
- **Back by a GET**: after a send the portal redirects to `?sent={noteId}`, which says how it went from the stored row —
  a refresh cannot post and email twice.
- **Nothing of the ticket goes but the fault and the one comment.** Not other comments, not the story, not who else is
  on it. The harness checks the internal comment and the earlier update are absent from every email.

### Found on the way: `dotnet ef --context PlatformDb` made a POSTGRESQL migration

The first SQLite migration since the split (§118) went into `Data/PgMigrations` against Npgsql, twice — even with
`--context RemoteSupport.Platform.Data.PlatformDb`. EF accepted the design-time factory for `PgPlatformDb` as one for
`PlatformDb` (a subclass IS one). Measured: `dotnet ef dbcontext info --context PlatformDb` said *Type: PgPlatformDb,
Provider: Npgsql*. Fixed by **`PlatformDbDesignTime`** (in `Data/PgPlatformDb.cs`), a SQLite factory for `PlatformDb`
itself; the documented commands now work as written. **After making a SQLite migration, check its Designer says
`[DbContext(typeof(PlatformDb))]`.** Remaking `PgInitial` needs a build first — `--no-build` finds the deleted one in
the old assembly.

### Where it lives

`Services/ClientUpdates.cs` (`ClientUpdateService`: every rule, the offer, the email, the marker).
`TicketService.Mentions.cs` (`AddCustomerReplyAsync`, `SeenCustomerRepliesAsync`). `TicketIntake.cs`
(`SendAsCompanyAsync`, `NewMessageId`, the reply's sender rule). Data: `TicketClientUpdate`, `TicketNote.FromCustomer`
(migration `ClientUpdates`; `PgInitial` remade). Portal: `_EmailClient`, `_EmailTo`, `_NoteEmail` partials,
`Ticket.cshtml.cs` (`OnPostComment`, `OnPostEmailNote`, `OnPostUpdate`). Hub: `TicketEmailNoteMsg`,
`TicketNoteAddMsg.EmailTo`, `ClientUpdateInfo`; `HubRegistry.ClientUpdates`. Console: `TicketsForm.CommentBox`,
`AddressChooser`, `NoteEmail`.

### How it is proved

| | |
|---|---|
| `tools/clientupdatecheck` | **91 of 91**. A real platform with the fake IMAP and SMTP servers from `mailintakecheck`. ## 124. Job types in colour, and the portal's menu as tabs — 2026-10-09

Clint, before publishing §123: *"Can we make the categories when creating a new ticket more pronounced on the dashboard
and console ... We have already had instances where a wrong ticket category has been selected because it is not
pronounced enough"*, and *"all the tabs at the top are mostly just text that one clicks on. Can we make these rounded
buttons"*. His answers: the portal's main menu (not a ticket's own tabs); the suggested colours; the console's dropdown
replaced by the same buttons.

- **One colour per job type, one list**: `TicketSummary.CategoryColors` (Shared), by VALUE — General slate, Remote
  support blue, Walk in green, Workshop orange, Call out purple, Recurring task teal. `Fill` carries white words (5:1 or
  better) and is the outline on a light ground; `OnDark` the outline on a dark one.
