## 125. PostgreSQL, step 4: the live switch, built — and waiting for its rehearsal — 2026-10-09

The brief was `docs/NEXT-SESSION-POSTGRES-SWITCH.md`; every decision in it stood (three disks, backups on `rsp-files`,
PostgreSQL on the same server, one command each way). **Built and proved on this PC as far as a PC can; the rest is
the rehearsal on a throwaway xneelo server — `deploy/postgres/README.md`, click by click. The live server is still on
SQLite and nothing here has touched it.**

**1. The data copy — `RemoteSupport.Platform copy-to-postgres --from <platform.db> --to "<conn>" [--verify-only]`**
(`Services/PostgresCopy.cs`, from the draft, which is retired). Four changes from the draft, each found by reading it
against the code:
- **It runs BEFORE the platform is built** (top of `Program.cs`), not beside `seed-loadtest`: building the platform
  migrates the SQLite file — a write to the file the switch promises never to touch — and would make the "behind on
  migrations" refusal unreachable.
- It **refuses a model it cannot carry faithfully** (a column with no C# property, two types in one table, an owned
  type): the copy and its check both read properties, so such a column would be lost AND the check would agree.
- It **refuses text holding a NUL**, naming table, column and row: SQLite stores one, PostgreSQL cannot.
- Lists stored in a column are compared by contents (the draft hashed their type name — always "same").

And one found by running it: **PostgreSQL counts microseconds from 2000-01-01 and Npgsql drops a tenth of one TOWARD
that date** — down after 2000, UP before (`1999-12-31 23:59:59.9999999` is stored as `2000-01-01`). The check's
canonical time is truncated the same way (`ToPgMicrosecond`); with the draft's rule, 37 of 39 tables read DIFFERENT.
A difference names its first row and column — for text only the position, never the words (password hashes).
**`tools/pgcopycheck` 42 of 42**: (A) every one of the 39 tables filled with awkward values — sub-microsecond and
pre-2000 times, `DateTime.MinValue`/`MaxValue`, extremes, empty text, emoji, a parent ticket; (B) a scratch copy of the
local test server's own `platform.db` (3,709 rows), first REFUSED for being a migration behind; (C) the load-test
seed, a COPIED person signing in. Each: OK; the SQLite file's SHA-256 unchanged even after the platform ran on the copy;
counts and highest ids equal by plain SQL; a second copy refused; new rows not colliding; the platform up on it. (D)
damage — a character, a microsecond, a lost parent, a missing row — each DIFFERENT in its table alone, and the id
counter left unmoved makes adding a company fail. (E) a NUL refused, nothing copied. 26 of 34 with the old time rule.

**2. `go-live.sh` survives the switch.** **The drop-in `remotesupport-platform.service.d/postgres.conf` is THE sign
that a server is on PostgreSQL**: written only by the switch, removed only by the way back, never by go-live — which
reads its connection string into `appsettings.live.json` on every deploy (the command line never sees systemd).
The nightly backup is a file now, **`deploy/rsp-backup.sh`** (go-live refuses to run without it; `build.ps1` ships it):
`pg_dump` when the drop-in is there, SQLite's `.backup` when not; data/ WITHOUT recordings; **each finished recording
(`*.mp4`, never `*.part`) encrypted once, on its own, into `/var/backups/rsp/recordings/`**, its copy removed once the
recording is gone and the copy is 60 days old; written under a hidden name and renamed, so the office pull never sees
half a file; **it stops if `/var/backups/rsp` is in fstab and not mounted** (or a dead disk would fill the system
disk). Recordings' copies are NOT in the office pull — they stay on `rsp-files`. **`tools/backupcheck` 30 of 30**, in
Git Bash against the test PostgreSQL — a PostgreSQL backup RESTORED into an empty database is the SQLite original row by
row (`--verify-only`), id counters included; the office gatekeeper (`rsp-backup-serve.sh`) lists the new file and no
recording. 28/28/29 with three faults put back.

**`PgInitial` is FROZEN (`20261009072435`)**: once a server holds data in PostgreSQL, a PgInitial made again has a new
id, and that server would try to create every table again and refuse to start. **Every model change now needs TWO
migrations, the same name in each: `--context PlatformDb`, and `--context PgPlatformDb --output-dir
Data/PgMigrations`.** `pgcheck` 20 checks that (18 with a remade one).

**3. The switch — `Switch-ToPostgres.ps1 -Server … [-FilesGB 50 -DbGB 20]`** sends `switch-to-postgres.sh` over ssh
(written to a file first, so nothing it runs can read the rest of it as input), runs `--check`, asks for SWITCH, runs
`--go`, and saves everything in `deploy\reports\`. In order: the root partition grown (growpart, resize2fs); **the two
disks found by SIZE and BLANKNESS, never by name** — no filesystem, partition table, partition, mount or blkid
signature, and an empty first megabyte; a disk already labelled `rsp-files`/`rsp-db` (an earlier run) used, never
formatted; anything ambiguous refused — then ext4 with labels, **fstab by UUID with `nofail`, each entry's note on its
own line above it** (fstab promises comments only on lines of their own); PostgreSQL 16 installed AFTER `rsp-db` is at
`/var/lib/postgresql`, role and database `rsp`, **peer sign-in over the socket — no password exists — and no TCP at
all** (`listen_addresses = ''`, which is also how the script proves `conf.d/rsp.conf` was read); a database called
`rsp` already there is RENAMED, never dropped. Then the platform stops: a backup kept as `before-switch-*` (never
pruned); `/opt/rsp/data` and `/var/backups/rsp` copied to `rsp-files`, every name/size/mode/owner compared, then
**bind-mounted back at the same paths** (originals kept in `/var/lib/rsp-before-disks`); the drop-in `disks.conf`
(`RequiresMountsFor=/opt/rsp/data` — on an empty data/ the platform would start a new key ring); `copy-to-postgres`
must say OK; the drop-in and `appsettings.live.json`; `/health` and the start-up line must say PostgreSQL; counts side
by side; the nightly backup once. **Any failure after the stop starts the platform again on SQLite.**

**4. The way back — `Switch-BackToSqlite.ps1`**: `--check` runs `--verify-only` and lists the tables that changed
since the switch (what going back loses; "cannot compare" if a deploy has since changed the model — going back still
works); then a backup (`before-way-back-*`), the database RENAMED, the drop-in and connection string out, started on
the frozen SQLite file. The disks stay. `Get-DatabaseStatus.ps1` is a read-only report for either state.
**`tools/switchcheck` 51 of 51**: every script plain ASCII (PowerShell 5.1 pipes them as ASCII) and parsing in bash
and PowerShell 5.1; the `.dll` test for copy-to-postgres; the disk choice against 14 layouts with stand-in
`lsblk`/`blkid` — the live one, names swapped by a reboot, decimal sizes, a filesystem, partitions, a mount, a dirty
first megabyte, a hidden signature, two alike, an earlier run's disks, a volume never attached (the 20 GB system disk
is never taken), equal sizes, the rehearsal's — and the fstab functions lifted out of the script. 29/29/23/49 with four
faults put back. **NOT provable here: mkfs, mount, apt, systemd, the switch and the way back themselves.**

**5. The rehearsal — `deploy/postgres/README.md`.** A throwaway `rsp-rehearsal` with 10 GB and 20 GB volumes (6 GB was planned; both came out 10 and the switch rightly refused),
deployed by `Publish-Platform.ps1 -Domain rehearsal.theremotesupportprogram.com`, then **`Copy-LiveToRehearsal.ps1`**:
live's newest nightly is decrypted on live and encrypted again with a one-time passphrase this PC holds only in memory
(the gpg 2.4 chain checked here; the live backup passphrase never leaves live); and **before the platform starts on the
copy, the rehearsal server's outgoing connections are blocked except DNS, time and the web, and PROVED blocked against
a real mail server** — the platform's only outbound traffic is mail (SMTP for reports, notices, client updates and
auto-replies; IMAP for tickets by email), and the copy holds real companies' settings. Then Step A rehearsed, the
switch, a write, a deploy after it, a reboot, the way back, and the switch again. Delete the instance AND its volumes
afterwards. **Then the live day: Step A (`Publish-Platform.ps1`, no `-SkipBuild` — the rehearsal's build is in
dist\), Step B (`Switch-ToPostgres.ps1 -Server 154.65.110.136`) at a quiet time, the waiting reboot, the status.**
Still to build: retiring the SQLite fallback a week later.

**THE REHEARSAL PASSED, 2026-10-09, on xneelo (`rsp-rehearsal`, 154.65.105.235, Ubuntu 24.04.4, 2 vCPU / 3.9 GB,
boot 10 GB, volumes 10 and 20 GB), with a copy of live (1 company, 887 clients, 66 tickets, 2,538 rows) — all twelve
steps, logs in `deploy\reports\`.** The switch: down **8 seconds** (11:29:32 → 11:29:40 UTC), every table "same";
new writes went only to PostgreSQL while the SQLite file stayed at its stop time; a deploy after it kept PostgreSQL
(and backed up with `pg_dump`); a **reboot** brought both disks, the bind mounts, PostgreSQL and the platform back
by themselves; the way back listed exactly the two tables written (Tickets, TicketNotes), renamed the database, and
was down 7 seconds; the second switch took the earlier-run path everywhere (nothing formatted or installed, data
already in place, a fresh `rsp`), down 7 seconds. What the rehearsal found, none of it in the switch itself:
- **xneelo's smallest volume is 10 GB**, so the planned 6 GB came out the same size as the files volume — the
  switch would have refused (two alike). The rehearsal uses 10 and 20.
- **The panel offered Ubuntu 26.04**; the switch's check refused it (live is 24.04). README says 24.04 now.
- **Security group `default` drops 80/443** — the rehearsal needs live's groups (README fixed).
- **Detach/attach SWAPPED `vdb` and `vdc`** on the first instance, and on the final one the boot disk was the SAME
  size as the files volume — both handled by size-and-blankness exactly as designed ("vda … left alone").
- Cosmetic, fixed: the status report cut its DB line at "platform", drew the disk tree in UTF-8 PowerShell garbled,
  and the check counted data already on rsp-files as "to move" (the last one changed AFTER the rehearsal; it is in
  the look-only half).
**Not rehearsed: growing the root partition** — every rehearsal boot disk was already full; live's (20 GB disk, 9 GB
root) will. growpart + resize2fs online is the standard Ubuntu way, and a failure there stops before the platform does.

**LIVE IS ON POSTGRESQL — 2026-10-09, 11:56 UTC.** Clint, on hearing the rehearsal had passed: *"I want everything to
be live now and all updates and fixes from here on in to go there."* Step A (`Publish-Platform.ps1`, carrying §122–§125)
then the switch, the same afternoon: `vda` (21 GB, the system disk, the same size as rsp-db) left alone; rsp-files =
`vdb` 53 GB, rsp-db = `vdc` 21 GB; the root partition was already 19 GB of 20 (Ubuntu had grown it at a boot, so
growpart had nothing to do — still never exercised); data 41 MB and backups 584 MB (33 files) moved; PostgreSQL 16.15,
shared_buffers 992 MB; **down 11 seconds** (11:55:52 → 11:56:03); all 39 tables, 2,538 rows, "same"; tonight's backup a
`pg_dump`. Log `deploy\reports\switch-154.65.110.136-20261009-135409.log`. Kept until the fallback is retired:
`/opt/rsp/data/platform.db`, `/var/lib/rsp-before-disks`, `before-switch-20261009-115529.tar.gz.gpg`.
**Then the reboot Ubuntu had been waiting for (11:57 UTC): both disks, the bind mounts, PostgreSQL and the platform
came back by themselves on the live server too** — `Get-DatabaseStatus.ps1`: PostgreSQL, `/health` 200, root 4.7 of
19 GB, rsp-files 656 MB of 49 GB, rsp-db 50 MB of 20 GB.

## 126. PostgreSQL, step 5: the xneelo load test — the tooling, proved on this PC; the run itself to follow — 2026-10-12

The brief was `docs/NEXT-SESSION-LOADTEST.md`. The question: how many companies of up to 10 technicians one cell
(one server like live: platform + Caddy + PostgreSQL, `rsp-files` and `rsp-db`) carries before the next is needed.

**The profile — Clint, 2026-10-12, not to be re-asked:** 10 technicians all signed in all day; 500 machines, each with
its tray app AND its agent (1,000 sockets); **10 sessions at once** (he chose the worst case over the brief's 3) at
200 KB/s; and **a measured restart storm** rather than an assumed margin. So one company is about 1,030 connections
and 2 MB/s of picture in AND out. Steps are by company count: `Run-LoadStep.ps1 -Companies 5 / 10 / 20 / 40 / 80`.

**The gaps closed (all in `deploy/loadtest/` and `tools/loadtest`; the README is the click-by-click):**
1. **The load server is on PostgreSQL like live.** `Prepare-LoadServer.ps1`: Publish-Platform, then the SAME
   `Switch-ToPostgres.ps1` live used (`-FilesGB 10 -DbGB 20`, asks for SWITCH) unless the `postgres.conf` drop-in is
   already there, then it REFUSES to seed unless the drop-in exists, the platform's start-up line says
   `DB: PostgreSQL`, and the seed itself prints `Database: PostgreSQL` (new line in `LoadTestSeed`). Seeds 200
   companies of 10 by default; `-People` over 10 refused. Slow statements (over 250 ms) logged, load server only.
2. **Companies of 10 people.** `tools/loadtest`: `--sessions-each N` (per company), `--techs` passed through by
   Start-LoadRun/Run-LoadStep (it used to sign in ONE person per company — the steps never passed it), refuses
   `--companies` beyond the seed (it used to run fewer, silently) and `--techs` beyond a company's people.
3. **The server's readings** (`rsp-loadstats.sh`, rewritten): platform / Caddy / PostgreSQL processor and memory,
   the machine's busy AND steal, free memory and swap, network in/out, connections on 443, **Caddy's connections to
   the platform (`upstream`, `upstream_tw`) and `ports_left`**, PostgreSQL's active/idle (against the pool of 40 and
   `max_connections`), lock waits, longest query, commits a second and slow statements, and the database disk's
   read/write MB/s and busy %. A header says cores, memory, database and port range. **`tools/loadstatscheck` 40 of
   40** (Git Bash): a pretend /proc with two readings and stand-in systemctl/ss/psql/findmnt, every column worked by
   hand; a server not on PostgreSQL; two faults put back (the old network reading missed a counter run into its
   interface's name — `ens3:53428800`; steal left out); and every script ASCII, parsing in PowerShell 5.1, with no
   double quote in what goes to ssh. It caught a real one at once: `"-People $People:"` would not parse.
4. **The load boxes.** VERDICT now also blames the BOX for its own memory (under 10% free) or its own ports
   (`Cannot assign requested address`); Run-LoadStep refuses a step needing over ~60,000 sockets a box; a third box
   is optional (`Save-Addresses.ps1`). A 502 from Caddy is named as such.
5. Live refused everywhere it was; `Restart-LoadServer.ps1` (new, the storm's one command) refuses it too.

**The storm (`--storm`, `Run-LoadStep -Storm` + `Restart-LoadServer.ps1`; local mode restarts its own platform).**
Two things the tool had wrong about the real apps: **`DeviceLink` retries every 3 s, fixed** (the tool waited 5–15
s — gentler than reality), and **console sign-ins live in the server's MEMORY** (`AuthService._tokens`), so every
restart — every deploy — signs every technician out (`TechLink`: *"the server was restarted… Please sign in
again"*). The tool now does both: machines every 3 s, consoles every 3 s and, on a 401, signing in again after up to
`--resign` seconds; then the sessions again. It prints a separate STORM summary and verdict; the hold's verdict is
computed before the restart, so its drops never count against the hold. Machines also send `HardwareId` and a
network card, as `DeviceLink` does.

**Proved locally, on PostgreSQL** (`RSP_TEST_DB=postgres loadtest local --companies 5 --machines 500 --agents --techs
10 --sessions-each 10 --ramp 60 --hold 60 --storm --storm-hold 60 --resign 15`): hold — 2,500 machines + 2,500 agents,
50 technicians, 50 sessions; connect 2 ms (95% 57), sign-in 315 ms (600,000 rounds), first picture 2 ms, **100%
relayed**, nothing failed. Storm — platform back in 4 s; **all 5,000 sockets back in 13 s**; 50 of 50 consoles signed
out, signed in again, all back in 24 s; **50 of 50 sessions again**, 100% relayed. **Seen in it: one database read took
3.4 s (95%) while the 5,000 hellos queued for the pool of 40, clear in ~10 s** — the figure to watch on xneelo. And a
real, older fault: **`duplicate key … IX_Devices_TenantId_DeviceId`** — a new machine's tray app and agent hello at
once and both insert its row (a real first install does the same); thought harmless (the row exists) — **it was not, and is fixed: §127** —
a race. **Rerun with that fix (same command): the server logged nothing at all**; hold the same (connect 95% 5 ms, 100%
relayed); storm all 5,000 sockets back in 13 s, consoles 26 s, 50 of 50 sessions, 99%; the worst database read about 1 s
(3.4 s before) — but **one `/health` reading of 2.3 s** during the reconnect rush (92 ms the first time): a short
whole-server stall of BUGS #11's shape, on a laptop also playing the load. Read the xneelo storm's `/health` line for it.
This PC cannot go bigger: Windows allows ~16,000 connections to one address.

**Predicted before the run, to be confirmed by it: Caddy reaches the platform on `127.0.0.1:8090`, and Linux gives
one destination only the 32768–60999 port range — about 28,000 connections.** At this profile that is a ceiling
near **28 companies**, whatever the processor does — and it applies to live today. The watch's `upstream` and
`ports_left` columns will show it; `Prepare-LoadServer.ps1 -SkipInstall -WidePorts` (load server only) widens it to
~64,000 to see the next limit. If it is confirmed, the real fix is Kestrel on a Unix socket behind Caddy
(`reverse_proxy unix//…`), which has no port limit — not built.

### The xneelo run, 2026-10-12/13 — THE ANSWER

`rsp-loadtest` 154.65.109.142: **`s-g-4cpu-8gb` as live** (4 vCPU, 7,940 MB, no swap), Ubuntu 24.04, live's security
groups (`default` + `allow-http`); `rsp-loadtest-files` 10 GB standard, `rsp-loadtest-db` 20 GB premium; switched by
`Switch-ToPostgres.ps1` (vda left alone, vdb/vdc by size, all 39 tables same, PostgreSQL 16.15, shared_buffers 992 MB);
200 companies × 10 seeded INTO PostgreSQL (`Get-DatabaseStatus`: Tenants 200, Technicians 2,000). Load boxes
`rsp-load-1` 154.65.103.197 and `rsp-load-2` 154.65.104.68, 2 vCPU / 3.9 GB, never the limit (busiest 49%, ≥1.7 GB
free). Results in `deploy\loadtest\out\results\` (not in git). Ramp 300 s, sign-in 120 s, sessions 300 s, hold 600 s.

| Companies | Caddy→platform conns at hold | Machine CPU hold (peak) | Free memory hold (worst) | Platform / Caddy RSS | Net each way | PG conns peak | Machine connect p95 | First picture p95 | VERDICT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 5,152 | 16% | 5,960 MB | 0.8 / 0.6 GB | 10.4 MB/s | ≤7 | 34 / 25 ms | 8 / 14 ms | comfortable |
| 10 | 10,301 | 25% (28) | 4,900 (4,362) | 1.4 / 1.05 GB | 20.8 | 21 | 32 / 21 | 4 / 4 | comfortable |
| 20 | 20,602 | 32% (40) | 2,500 (1,039) | 2.6 / 2.1 GB (platform 4.05 at sign-in) | 42 | 40 | 33 / 23 | 5 / 4 | comfortable |
| 25 | 25,752 | 39% (48) | 1,300 (704) | 3.0 / 2.8 GB (platform 4.35 at sign-in) | 53 | 40 | 33 / 25 | 4 / 4 | comfortable |
| **30, live's ports** | **28,234 = all** | **100%** (Caddy ~92%) | 800 (641) | 3.0 / 3.3 GB | — | — | — | — | **BENT** |
| 30, `-WidePorts` | 30,903 | 40% (46) | 800 (702) | 3.2 / 3.1 GB | 64 | 40 | 29 / 19 | 7 / 7 | comfortable |
| **35, `-WidePorts`** | — | — | **159 MB** | platform **OOM-killed at 4.35 GB** | — | — | — | — | **BENT** |
| 20 + restart (live's ports) | back to 20,602 | **97% for ~45 s** | **524 MB**, 1,050 after | 2.3 / **3.98 GB kept** | 42 | **40 of 40**, 9,000 commits/s | storm below | 5 / 4 | passed |

Steady state, each company cost ~1,030 connections, ~210–240 MB, ~1.8% processor, 2.1 MB/s each way; PostgreSQL
never mattered (1–4 connections, a few commits a second, no statement over 250 ms, lock waits 0) except while machines
ARRIVE (≈40 connections, 300–900 commits/s; 9,000/s in the storm).

**1. The first limit: Caddy's ports to `127.0.0.1:8090`, at ~27 companies (28,232 ÷ ~1,030) — exactly as predicted,
and it fails TOTALLY.** At 30 companies with live's settings: 185,000 machine connects answered 502, **all 300
technicians' sign-ins refused (502)** — every HTTP request needs a port too, so the portal and console die with it —
and Caddy spinning on the refusals took the machine to 100%; `/health` up to 10.5 s. **Live has the same ceiling.**
BUGS #12. The fix: Kestrel on a Unix socket, `reverse_proxy unix//…` — no ports at all. Not built. (`-WidePorts`,
1024–65535, moved it to ~62 companies on the load server; that is a stopgap, not the fix.)

**2. Then memory, between 30 and 35 companies (~33).** With the ports out of the way, 30 carried with 10% free; at 35
free memory hit 159 MB while machines were still arriving and **the kernel's OOM killer killed the platform**
(`Out of memory: Killed process … (RemoteSupport.P) … anon-rss:4352004kB`, 13:36:30); systemd restarted it in 9 s.
Caddy holds ~100 KB per connection and gives nothing back; .NET adapts (the platform peaked LOWER at 30 than at 25 —
it collects harder when memory is short) but its sign-in peak (every console's 500-machine StateMsg) is the spike.
**No swap**, so running out is a kill, not a slowdown. Processor at 30 was only 40%: CPU is not the steady-state limit.
(Box 1's 6,272 machines that never came back after that kill were the TOOL — all its pretend machines shared one
HttpMessageInvoker, which jammed after thousands of 502s while its own separate `/health` probe answered in 2 ms; each
link now opens its own connection, as a real machine does, `27ddf0a`.)

**3. The restart storm at 20 companies passed — but it is the tightest moment.** `Restart-LoadServer.ps1` under full
load: all 5,000 machines + agents per box back in **26 s and 48 s**, every console signed in again (all 200 told their
sign-in had ended) within **70–73 s**, **200 of 200 sessions reopened**, 100% relayed after. But reconnects took a
**median 11.7 s** (95% 22–29 s) where the 3-s retry allows ~2: the machine sat at **88–97% for ~45 s**, PostgreSQL's
pool was **at its cap of 40** with 4,000–9,000 commits/s, `/health` up to **4.25 s** (BUGS #11's shape, now from load
rather than a stall), and free memory fell to **524 MB**. **Caddy grew from 2.18 to 3.98 GB during the storm and kept
it** (1,050 MB free afterwards against 2,280 before) — whether a second deploy grows it again is NOT measured; it is the
first thing to watch on live after deploys once it is busy.

**THE NUMBER: 18 companies of this profile per cell** (two-thirds of the ~27 where it bends, and under the 20 the
restart only just carried). **Plan the second cell when the first reaches 12.** The profile is the worst case the seat
limit allows (10 technicians all signed in, 500 machines each with an agent, 10 sessions at once) — real companies are
mostly smaller, so a real cell holds more companies; count CONNECTIONS (~1,030 per such company) not companies:
**~18,500 connections per cell on this flavor.**

**Bigger flavor or second cell?** A bigger flavor ALONE buys nothing — the port ceiling is the same on any size. In
order: (1) the Unix-socket fix (small; live needs it anyway); (2) then a bigger flavor helps directly, because memory
and the storm's processor are the next limits — roughly linear, so 8 vCPU / 16 GB should carry ~2× (≈ 35–40 companies
of this profile) — **an estimate from these measurements, not measured**; (3) a second cell when that fills (its code
needs are below the brief's "Not in scope"). Also worth doing before a cell is busy: raise the pool from 40 for the
storm (max_connections is 100), and decide on swap (a slow server beats a killed one) — neither measured yet.

Found on the way and fixed: the server watch's PostgreSQL processor (summed living processes, read negative — now its
systemd slice), the watch saved as UTF-16 by Windows PowerShell's Tee-Object, the second passphrase at the end of a run
(the results stayed on the boxes; `Get-LoadResults.ps1`), and the shared connection pool above. `loadstatscheck` 44.

### The port fix, built and proved the same day (BUGS #12, `39d6498`)

**Caddy reaches the platform through a Unix socket, `/run/rsp/platform.sock`; the port 127.0.0.1:8090 stays for the
checks run on the server itself** (go-live, the switch, the status report, the backup — a handful of connections).
systemd makes `/run/rsp` (`RuntimeDirectory=rsp`, 0750) at every start and removes it at every stop, so no stale socket;
once listening the platform lets its own group in (`UnixSocket.OpenToGroup`, 0660), and **`caddy` joins group `rsp`**
before Caddy restarts (supplementary groups are read at start). go-live's step 7 asks the socket **as caddy** — the
socket existing is not enough. **Read `UnixSocket.TrustCaddy` before touching forwarded headers**: a connection through
a socket has NO remote address, and ASP.NET then takes the first forwarder as given — right only because nothing but
Caddy can open the socket; were the header lost, every caller would be "?", one address for the sign-in guard's
30-per-address lock. `tools/unixsockcheck` 16 (11 with the old go-live back) holds that, with the platform's own
settings; `securitycheck` 76. Kestrel will not take a socket from `Urls` on Windows, so the socket itself is proved only
on Linux — by go-live's line and by the load test. The server watch has a `socket_conns` column.

**Proved on xneelo, 30 companies on live's DEFAULT port range** (the load that locked everybody out): both boxes
comfortable — 15,000 machines + agents, 300 technicians, 300 sessions, 100% relayed, first picture within 6 ms,
`/health` worst 204 ms; **0 connections over TCP, 30,902 through the socket, all 28,232 ports left**; 39% processor;
free memory ~700 MB at the hold (428 at worst). **So the limit is now memory (~33 companies), and a bigger flavor DOES
buy more.** The cell stays at 18 on `s-g-4cpu-8gb` — the restart at 20 is the tight moment and the fix does not change
it. **NOT YET ON LIVE** — a `Publish-Platform.ps1` deploy carries it; read step 7's socket line.

## 127. A new machine's two hellos at once: one row, both halves kept, the wait opens after both — 2026-10-12

§126's load test logged **`duplicate key … IX_Devices_TenantId_DeviceId`** and called it harmless. **It was not.** A
first install starts the tray app and the agent together under one device id; each hello runs
`TenantHub.PersistDeviceAsync`, both found no row, both added one, and the second save failed. Measured by
**`tools/firsthello`** (new: N new machines, each machine's two hellos sent in the same instant; the tray app ticks
unattended on its first state and sets a password once told the tick is on, as `FreeSetup` does):

- **The losing hello's details were never stored** — the tray app's user name or the agent's network cards (Wake-on-LAN),
  whichever lost: 35 of 40 machines on PostgreSQL.
- **And the wait for the stored record (`WhenRecordReadAsync`, §111) opened too early.** Both hellos shared ONE gate,
  and the loser's `finally` opened it before the winner had put the stored record into the live one; a password set
  next was then undone in the live record by the winner's older copy — **6 of 40 machines "unattended, no password"**
  until something else told the truth. The same fault §111 closed for one hello, back for two.

**A retry on the duplicate key (the obvious fix, and the one the task suggested) made it WORSE: 37 of 40** — the second
hello no longer failed, so its stale copy of the record always landed after the wait had opened. The fix is
**`RecordGate`**: one machine's hellos are stored IN TURN (`PersistInTurnAsync`; the second finds the row the first
wrote — no duplicate, no EF error in the log), and the wait counts them, opening after the LAST
(`Pending`; each `PersistDeviceAsync` gives its share back once, `Read()`). A hello that waits says so in the log
(*"waits for its other half's hello to be stored"*), which is also how the harness knows the race was hit.

**On SQLite the two hellos never meet** — a local file answers in under a millisecond — so the harness passed against
the fault there. `Testing:PersistDeviceGapMs` (harness only, never in production; like §50's `PersistDeviceDelayMs`
but BETWEEN the lookup and the save, where this race lives) holds the gap open: 200 ms in `firsthello`.

`firsthello` **9 of 9 on SQLite and on PostgreSQL** (and 100 machines on PostgreSQL). With the faults put back:
in-turn out → 6 of 9 on both (40 of 40 saves fail — SQLite error 19 / PostgreSQL 23505, as the load test saw); the wait
opened by the first → 5 / 6 of 9 (38–39 of 40 lose the password from the live record); both out (the old code) → 6
of 9. **No model change, no migration. `Publish-Platform.ps1` carries it; no ship.**

---

## 128. Damage reports, files and photos on comments, going back a stage, boxes that grow — 2026-10-13

Clint: *"in the workshop section, where we have Not repairable, Invoice inspection fee, there Should also be a Not
Repairable, Damage report needed. This should then have an option for comments, and an option to upload the damage
report, which can be mailed directly from there to the client. It then goes to to be invoiced etc. Secondly, all the
comments boxes in the ticketing system need to automatically expand when putting in a new line ... Thirdly, we should
have an option to go back at every stage."* Then: *"an option to upload files or photos on all comments ... This should
also be able to be emailed."* His answers: **every recommendation**, and the boxes were two lines in the portal, three in
the console; *up to 15 lines would be good*.

### What it is

- **Boxes that grow.** Portal: `wwwroot/autogrow.js` (every portal page) — every textarea from the height its page
  gave it to 15 lines, then a scroll bar; `data-autogrow="off"` opts out (the knowledge base editor). A box filled by
  script calls `autogrow(box)` (the timeline's `mention()`). Console: `InputBox.GrowWithText(maxLines = 15)`
  (`RemoteSupport.UI/Controls.cs`), counted by `EM_GETLINECOUNT` so a wrapped line counts as a line — on the comment
  box, every tall step field, the recurring cancel box and New ticket's description.
- **Files and photos on a comment** — `TicketAttachment` (table `TicketAttachments`, files in `data/ticketfiles/{tenant}`),
  every rule `Services/TicketAttachmentService.cs`. Each file goes up ON ITS OWN as it is picked (`POST
  /api/portal/attachments`, photos made smaller first by `photos.js` / `PhotoShrink`, §62) and is held LOOSE on the
  ticket by whoever picked it; posting names the ids and `ClaimAsync` hands over only loose ones, on THAT ticket,
  picked by THAT person. A comment may be files alone. Loose files a day old are cleared the next time that person
  picks one. Kinds are an ALLOW-list by extension (pictures, PDF, Office, text, zip, short video; 20 MB each); only
  pictures and PDFs — told by their BYTES — open in the browser (`GET /portal/attachment/{id}`, `nosniff`); anything
  else downloads. A browser's upload must send `X-Attach: 1` (the console signs with its bearer token instead).
  Portal: `_Attach` (the picker, both layouts), `_NoteFiles` (under each entry), `wwwroot/attach.js`. Console:
  `TicketsForm.FilePicker` / `NoteFiles`, `TechLink.UploadAttachmentsAsync`; `TicketNoteAddMsg.AttachmentIds`,
  `TicketNoteInfo.Attachments`.
- **Emailing them.** A comment's files go with it as attachments (`ClientUpdateService.SendAsync`); `Sendable(n,
  hasFiles)` lets a comment of files alone go, saying *"The files are attached."* Files over **15 MB together** are
  refused BEFORE anything is posted (`CheckWithFilesAsync`), words and files kept — as a bad address always was.
- **Not repairable — Damage report needed** (`Workflow.DamageReport`, label `Workflow.DamageReportLabel`): from Not
  repairable only (not after a rejected quote — his answer 4), fields **Comments (optional), Files (required),
  Minutes, Amount, EmailClient**, Outcome `damage-report`, to *To be invoiced*. Comments are written FIRST in the
  step; **`ClientUpdateService.Words` is the part the client reads — cut before "Time spent:"**, so the time, the amount
  and *"taken off — in the billing queue"* never leave. The email box is TICKED by default; the caller (portal
  `OnPostAct`, hub `ActOnTicketAsync`) checks the address and size first, then `ActAsync`, then `SendStepAsync`. Not set
  up: the form says so and the step can still be recorded. The step may be emailed again from the story.
- **Going back a stage** — `TicketService.Back.cs`. Every step that MOVES the job now writes `TicketNote.Before`: a
  `StepSnapshot` (JSON) of every route field as it was (stage, lane, status, StageReturn, Repairable, Outcome,
  WorkedBy, time, amounts, invoice and payment, the quote's suppliers, DNI/abandon reasons, collection, AssignedTo,
  ClosedUtc). **Back** (`GoBackKey = "go-back"`, one field: Reason) undoes the newest move not yet gone back over —
  only when it is the move that brought the job HERE — puts every field back from the snapshot, marks that step
  `UndoneUtc`/`UndoneBy`, and writes a `WentBack` entry *"Back to {stage}"* with the reason, what it undid, and any
  warning. Pressed again it goes one step further. It is an ordinary step: `ActionsFor(t, role, me, back)` offers it
  when the caller passes `BackStepAsync`'s answer (a null keeps every older caller and harness as it was), and
  `ActAsync` presses it — so older consoles draw and send it with no change.
  - **Who** (`MayGoBack`): supervisors and the owner; whoever made the step; the people on the job (AssignedTo or
    WorkedBy) who may change status; the office on its own stages. **A closed job: supervisor or owner only.**
  - **Never**: from Booked in (nothing to undo), across *Needs workshop work* / *Needs to be booked in* (the category
    changed), or at *Waiting on customer* (Back to work is that button already).
  - **Warned, not refused** (`WarningAsync`, shown above the form and written into the entry): reopening a closed job,
    an invoice number recorded, a payment taken, a machine collected or delivered, the quote request or quote already
    sent, the step already emailed to the client. **A step written before today has no snapshot**: Back moves the stage
    only and says so.
  - **Whose desk afterwards**: back to the office or a supervisor — nobody; back to the bench from one of those — who
    it was with before the step; on the bench already — whoever is on it now (a colleague who joined since is not
    taken off by somebody else's mistake).
  - The crumb's "came from" skips undone and Back entries. Portal: the story fades and strikes through an undone step
    (`.tk-undone`); the Back button is plain, not accent, with ↶. Console the same (`TicketNoteInfo.Undone`,
    `WentBack`, `StageActionInfo.Warning`).

### The rules that matter

- **Snapshots, not inverse steps.** Undoing by reversing each step's arithmetic (a delivery ADDS time) would be a
  second copy of `ActAsync` to keep in step for ever. A step that moves the job and does not write `Before` cannot be
  gone back over properly — **any new path that moves a stage must write it** (`ActAsync` and `SendForDeliveryAsync` do).
- **A loose file is the picker's alone.** Never let a comment claim by id without the person and the ticket.
- **The damage report's comments go first.** Anything added to that step's body above "Time spent:" will be emailed.

### Found on the way

`ticketwire`'s recurring-cancel check failed one run in two on PostgreSQL: a refused step comes back as a notice AND
the ticket again a moment later, and the harness cleared its queue after the notice — so the refusal's ticket was read
as the answer to the next step. Opening a ticket now asks whether Back is offered, one more read, which widened the
gap. The harness now takes that ticket first. **A harness that clears its queue after a notice must first take the
ticket the same answer sends.**

### How it is proved

| | |
|---|---|
| `tools/ticketstepcheck` (new) | **124 of 124**, both databases. In-process: what may go up, sniffing, the email's words for a damage report and for photos alone, the snapshot round trip; the damage report offered, refused without its report, refused with a colleague's file, recorded with time and amount, its report on the step and the colleague's left loose; Back by its maker and by the office, refused to a technician not on the job and without a reason, every field put back, the step marked, the entry written, one step further each time, nowhere from Booked in; an invoice warned of and cleared; a closed job reopened by the owner only; Waiting on customer, a call out turned workshop, an old step with no snapshot; a comment of photos alone, a posted file not claimable twice, 18 MB too large to email. On a platform with fake IMAP and SMTP: the X-Attach header, a program refused, another person's ticket 404; the form (comments, report, time, amount, email ticked to the contact); submitted — ONE email, "has sent the damage report", comments and fault, NOT time or amount, the PDF attached byte for byte; a refusal keeping comments, time, amount and the picked file; a PDF inline, a .docx downloaded with nosniff, a hidden ticket's file 404; photos alone emailed; too large refused unposted; Back in the portal with the "emailed already" warning, faded step, honest crumb; the console's files, undone marks, Back, a damage report emailed from it, Back from it, a photo comment from it. **120 of 124 with two guards out** (the snapshot restore, the X-Attach check). |
| `ticketwindowprobe` | **231** (24 new): Back plain with ↶, file buttons, a photo comment, *Email it again…* on the damage report, the undone line, the ↶ entry, *Attach files or photos…*, Back's warning and its button, the comment box growing at 8 lines, stopping at 15 with a scroll bar, back to its height emptied; the damage report's form, ticked email, *"Attach the damage report."*; pictures `files-and-back.png`, `going-back.png`, `damage-report.png`. |
| unchanged | `ticketwire` 43 (one expectation now includes Back to Repairable; the race above fixed), `workflowcheck`, `calloutcheck`, `routecheck`, `deliverycheck`, `machinescheck`, `recurringcheck`, `clientupdatecheck` 91, `photogate`, `mentioncheck`, `ticketformprobe` 140, `pgcheck` 20 (both migration sets match). Walked in the browser on a `workflowdemo` platform: the inspection box growing to six lines, Damage report needed with a picked PDF, Back with its reason, the faded step and the ↶ entry, the crumb, phone width with no sideways scroll, no console errors. |

**Not on hardware.** `TEST-3.6.md` section CL, 588–599. **`Publish-Platform.ps1` (migration `CommentFilesAndGoingBack`,
both sets), then re-download the console.** No client reinstall. `data/ticketfiles` is inside `data/`, so the nightly
backup takes it — at up to 20 MB a file it will grow the nightly file faster than photos did; watch it.

## 129. The customer's name remembered; a picture of what is actually open — 2026-10-13

Clint: *"the app should remember the client name, they should not need to put it in every time they request support.
It should default to the last name entered. Secondly ... When doing a screenshot, it does it of the desktop only. If a
client has explorer open with a folder list for example, it does not screenshot that."*

### The name

It was only ever held in `MainForm._contactName`, starting as the Windows username, so every restart and logon lost
it. **`Client/LastContact.cs`** keeps it in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\RemoteSupport\contact.json` — per Windows user, beside
`windows.json` and `sounds.json` (the tray app runs as the person, so two people on one machine each get their own).
Written only from a request that was SENT (`ToggleRequest`, after `ShowDialog` says OK), never blank; a missing or
damaged file is the Windows username, as before. The chat's name is the same field, so it follows.

### The picture — measured before anything changed

The capture was NOT the fault: run with an Explorer window up, `CopyFromScreen` takes it whole (and the tray app is
per-monitor DPI aware, so nothing is cropped). What it cannot take is a window that is not on the screen — and **the
installer puts the app's shortcut on the DESKTOP**, so the usual way in is Show desktop / Win+D, then double-click:
which minimises exactly the window the customer wants help with. The picture showed the desktop faithfully.

Restoring their windows for them was rejected: it cannot tell a window Show desktop hid from one they minimised on
purpose, and it rearranges the screen of somebody already having a bad day. Instead:

- **`ScreenSnap.OnlyDesktop`** — at the capture, is any program showing? `ProgramsShowing()`: the windows the taskbar
  would show — visible, not minimised, not CLOAKED (`DWMWA_CLOAKED`: suspended Store apps and other virtual desktops'
  windows are "visible"), not tool windows, not owned, titled, not ours, not `Progman`/`WorkerW`/the taskbars. A wrong
  answer only changes a sentence, so an error counts as "showing".
- **The request window says so**: beside the preview, in the warning colour, *"Only your desktop is showing. Open what
  you need help with, then take a new picture."*
- **Take a new picture**, a button under those words (shown whenever the picture is ticked). The request window and the
  tray window go to **Opacity 0, not Hide** — hiding a modal window ends its `ShowDialog`, and an alpha-0 layered
  window lets clicks through to what is under it. **`Client/PictureBar.cs`**: one line top centre of that screen,
  TopMost, not in the taskbar (that is where they are about to click), *"Bring up what you want us to see, then press
  Take the picture."* — no countdown. It closes before `ScreenSnap.Take(...)`, which waits the 150 ms frame for our
  windows to leave. Cancel keeps the picture there was. `RequestDialog` now takes the `ScreenSnap` itself and hands
  back `Screenshot` (the JPEG, or null); pictures it takes are its own to dispose.
- `ScreenSnap.Take(params Form?[])` hides any number of our windows now; **`Take(null)` is a null ARRAY**, guarded.

Found on the way, both by `callprobe` and both of a kind the handover already warns of: the row's height was measured
in the plain font while the desktop note is BOLD (button off the bottom of the row), and the layout read
`retake.Visible` back — false before the window is shown (§109). It asks the tick now.

`callprobe` **66 of 66** (the name: missing / remembered and trimmed / blank not saved / damaged file / the window opens
with it; the picture: the desktop note, the button beside the picture and fitting, the bar out of the way and top
centre with its words whole, a NEW picture after Take, Cancel keeps the old, unticked sends nothing). The desktop-only
case is made by reflection — minimising every window for real would do it to whoever runs the harness — so **the real
Win+D path is a hardware check**. `Publish-Platform.ps1` (no migration), then a client reinstall; `TEST-3.6.md` section
CM, 600–605.

## 130. Editing a ticket, sorting tickets by date, and the Unassigned tile that opened an empty list — 2026-10-13

Clint: *"Tickets, Subjects (names), scheduled appointment times, category etc cannot be edited and needs to be fixed and
we need the ability to sort tickets by date."* His answers: **subject, appointment, category and description**; a category
change **starts the new route at its first stage**; **anybody who can see the ticket**; a **Sort box**. And, the same day:
*"On the dashboard it shows 6 unassigned, but when you click on unassigned, it shows nothing."*

### Edit the ticket

- **Every rule is `TicketService.EditAsync`** (`Services/TicketService.Edit.cs`), with a `TicketEdit` (a null field is left
  alone; `AppointmentGiven` says whether the appointment was sent, because null there is "no appointment"). Checked in full
  before anything is written. Who: whoever the caller already let see the ticket (`VisibleTo` / `MayTouchTicketAsync`) —
  office administrators included. One story entry per save, `FormTitle` **Details changed** or **Category changed**, each
  change with what it was; a changed description keeps its old words there. `MovedTo` empty: it is not a step.
- **Subject**: required, `SubjectMax` 200. **Description**: may be emptied. **Appointment**: to the minute; a time gone is
  refused; may be taken away; not on a closed job. **Category**: not on a closed job; never TO Recurring (set up on its own
  page); unknown numbers refused, not guessed. The route restarts at `Workflow.FirstFor` with `StageReturn`, `Outcome`,
  `Repairable` cleared — money and work recorded stay. **To Workshop needs what a booking needs**: somebody on it
  (`CheckBookIn`) and three photos in — so **`/api/portal/photos` now takes arrival photos on any OPEN ticket**. Out of the
  billing queue raises `BillingChanged`.
- **Back never crosses a category change**: `LastStepAsync` refuses any step older than a `CategoryChangedTitle` entry (the
  empty `MovedTo` usually stops it first).
- **Portal**: `_EditTicket.cshtml`, on both ticket pages (the story's Details tab, first; the plain page's right column), and
  *✎ Edit* beside the title. The type as the coloured `.cat-pick` of New ticket; choosing another says where it starts again
  and, for Workshop, what it needs (with its own photo picker, `teUpload`). **`OnPostEditAsync` reads `subject` and
  `description` from `Request.Form`**: model binding makes an empty box null, which is "leave it alone" — an emptied subject
  was answered "Nothing changed" and a description could never be emptied. Refused, what was typed comes back (`Edit*`).
- **Console**: `TicketEditMsg` (`ticket_edit`), `TenantHub.EditTicketAsync`, `TechLink.EditTicket`; `TicketsForm.EditCard`,
  first on Details and above History on a plain ticket, *✎ Edit the ticket* under the title. Typed values live in `_drafts`
  as `edit:…` (a type click redraws), cleared only when the save's notice has no error (`_editPending`). *No appointment*
  hides the date and time (greyed, the time box still looked live).

### Sort by date

`Shared/TicketSort.cs` is the one list: Last updated (the old order, and what empty or unknown means), Newest first, Oldest
first, Appointment soonest (none last). **The server sorts, before the take** — `TicketService.Sorted`, used by `ListAsync`
and the portal list; sorting what arrived would sort the wrong 500. Portal: *Sort by* beside Show — **Customer** (the grouped
view it always had, the default) or a date order, which is ONE list with a Client column and the date it is sorted by;
remembered in the browser (`rsp_ticket_sort`, `/portal`). Console: *Sort:* under the search, a date column whose heading
follows it, remembered per Windows user (`TicketSortChoice`, `ticketsort.txt`); `TicketListRequestMsg.Sort` and an echo in
`TicketListMsg.Sort` (an older server echoes nothing, and is believed).

### The Unassigned tile

The dashboard counted **every open ticket with no name on it**; the list it opens shows **the bench's pool**. A job in the
billing queue or with a supervisor has no name either — a billing step takes the technician off — so the tile said 6 and the
list showed nothing. **The tile now asks the list's rule** (`AssignedTo` empty AND `Lane` Bench). With the old line back,
`ticketeditcheck` reads *tile 3, list 1*.

`ticketeditcheck` (new) **60 of 60 on SQLite and on PostgreSQL** (56 with the dashboard line and the empty-box binding back);
`ticketwindowprobe` 247 (from 231), and ticketwire 43, ticketstepcheck 124, workflowcheck 100, routecheck 61, calloutcheck 68,
dashtabs 133 unchanged. Walked in the browser (`tools/workflowdemo`, launch entry `platform-ticketedit`): a call out made
General with a new subject, the story entry, Oldest first on desktop and phone. **`Publish-Platform.ps1` (no migration), then
re-download the console**; no client reinstall. `TEST-3.6.md` section CN, 606–615.

## 131. Back un-collected a machine collected after the step it undid — 2026-10-13

Clint: *"If one selects Payment received — close ticket it takes one back to awaiting payment ... if one previously asked it
to go back a step ... it seems to get stuck in a loop"* (and then: *"it seems to be user error"* — perhaps, but this was
real). Reproduced in-process: invoiced → **Machine collected** (not a step — no snapshot) → **Back** over Client invoiced →
the step's `StepSnapshot` put back `CollectedUtc = null`, because the machine had not been collected when that step was
taken. Re-invoiced, **Payment received** then went to *Awaiting collection* (`@close` thinks the machine is still here), whose
Close is refused as not collected, and the button beside it is *Back to Invoiced — awaiting payment*: the loop. **Back now
puts the collection fields back only when the step undone IS the machine leaving** (`UndoesHandover`: the Delivered step),
and its warning says so only then. **The rule for any future snapshot field: restore it only if the undone step is what
changes it** — a side action taken after the step (collection, here) is not that step's to take back. `ticketstepcheck` 129
(126 with the old restore — the last check reads *awaiting-collection*). A ticket already caught by it: press *Machine
collected* (its photos are already there), then *Close ticket*. `Publish-Platform.ps1`, no migration; `TEST-3.6.md` check 616.

## 132. Platform admins: named people with levels, a log, and a suspension that takes effect — 2026-10-13

Stage A of the control dashboard (`docs/NEXT-SESSION-CONTROL.md` — Clint's nine answers, all *"go with your
recommendations"*; **do not re-ask them**). `/owner` was one shared admin key and an authenticator. Now:

- **`PlatformAdmin`** (migration `PlatformAdmins`, both databases): name, email, **`AdminLevel`** — Viewer (sees, changes
  nothing), Manager (companies: approve, reject, status, seats, billing, country, waiting list, email their owners), Full
  (also Viewer/Manager admins and the platform's mail; servers in stage B), Owner (also Full admins and Owners). **Every
  rule is `Services/PlatformAdmins.cs`** (`MayManage`, `MayRun`, `MayGrant`, `MayTouch`); pages only ask it. **An Owner is
  never changed or removed from the pages, not even by another Owner** — `remove-admin` on the command line can; nobody
  changes or removes themselves.
- **Set up from a mailed link** (`/owner/setup`, 72 h): password, then QR, then the first code — **saved together only
  then**, so an abandoned set-up leaves nothing. Opening the link spends nothing. *New set-up link* is the one control for a
  lost link, phone or password: it clears both and moves the stamp.
- **Sign-in** at `/owner/login`: email, password, code; the browser is then trusted 7 days (`rsp_owner_trust`, path
  `/owner`, bound to the admin's stamp). The cookie carries `rsp:admin` and `rsp:admin-level`; `OnValidatePrincipal` checks
  a named admin against **their own stamp** (`PlatformAdmins.StampAsync`, 15 s cache, cleared by any change in-process) — a
  level change or removal signs them out at once. **The admin key still works** (*Use the admin key instead*; the only
  form while no admin exists) and is an Owner named *Platform owner (admin key)* — it is how the first Owner is added
  (or `add-admin <email> "<Name>" owner`).
- **`AdminLogEntry`**: every change, sign-in and email, by NAME (outlives the admin), with the server's name
  (`Platform:ServerName`, else the public address's host). `/owner/log`, every level.
- **`Services/AdminCompanies.cs` is the one path for changing a company** — the owner pages now, another server's dashboard
  in stage B. A Viewer is refused there, not just shown no button.

**Found on the way, and fixed: *Suspended* did not take effect.** The Tenants page always said *"Suspended blocks logins and
devices immediately"*; it blocked only the NEXT sign-in and the NEXT connect. An open console, a connected machine, a
running session and an open portal page all carried on. Now, when a company can no longer use the service:
`TenantHub.TurnAway` ends its sessions, tells and closes its consoles (`SignedOutMsg`) and its machine connections
(`ErrorMsg`); `AuthService.SignOutCompany` voids its console tokens and the portal cookie cache; and the token sweep and
`CookieCheckAsync` now ask the company's status too (`Serviceable`), so a change made on the command line is felt within
15 s. Machines come back by themselves and are refused at the door until it is active, then let in with nothing done at
the machine. **Suspended emails the company's owners** (or its support address if it has none), and so does being made
active again (`AdminCompanies.Suspended` / `Restored`). A side effect worth knowing: a company whose **trial runs out** is
now signed out within 15 s as well, where before only its next sign-in was refused.

The Tenants page also shows each company's owners (*Email the owners* → `/owner/email`, from our mailbox, signed with the
admin's name, Reply-To the admin) and its people with how many are ticked Technician.

`tools/admincheck` **75 of 75 on SQLite and on PostgreSQL** (two-factor on, its own mail server, a fake machine). With
guards out: the Viewer check, the admin stamp check and the turn-away each fail their checks (72 of 75 with the turn-away
out — the console and machine stay connected). `securitycheck` 76, `onesignin` 42, `trialnoticecheck` 18, `pgcheck` 20.
Walked in the browser (set-up link → QR → Tenants and Admins). **`Publish-Platform.ps1` (migration `PlatformAdmins`)**, then
sign in with the admin key once and add yourself as an Owner on Admins. No ship, no console re-download. `TEST-3.6.md`
section CO, 617–624.

## 134. PayFast, stage A: the account, the checkout, the notices — 2026-10-13

Stage A of `docs/NEXT-SESSION-PAYFAST.md` (roadmap 4.8). Clint's PayFast account is verified; its **Recurring Billing**
page holds the notify URL `https://theremotesupportprogram.com/api/payfast/notify` and the IP whitelist `154.65.110.136`
(the live server — **move it if the server moves**). PayFast's general "ITN" switch stays OFF: every checkout carries its
own `notify_url`, which overrides it (PayFast's docs, read 2026-10-13). His sandbox has a passphrase.

- **`Services/PayfastWire.cs`** — PayFast's rules as pure functions. **Three signatures, three rules**: the checkout's is
  the non-blank fields TRIMMED in PayFast's DOCUMENTED order (`CheckoutOrder`; `CheckoutFields` puts them in it whatever
  order they were given, and refuses a field PayFast does not list); a notice's is every field AS POSTED — blanks
  included, nothing trimmed — in the order it ARRIVED, up to `signature`; the API's is headers + body + passphrase sorted
  ALPHABETICALLY, blanks out, `testing` out. All MD5 of PHP's `urlencode` (`Encode`: `-_.` kept, space `+`, `%XX` upper
  case — not `WebUtility.UrlEncode`). The checkout takes RAND (`500.00`), the API CENTS. PayFast's published address
  ranges are `PayfastRanges`.
- **`Services/PayfastService.cs`** — the account (`PlatformSettings.Payfast*`; key and passphrase encrypted with their own
  Data Protection purpose; **sandbox or live is stored WITH the keys** and only ever changed with them — the brief's
  `Payfast:Sandbox` setting became this); `BeginAsync` makes a `PayfastSubscription` (awaiting its card, our random
  `Reference` as `m_payment_id`, `Sandbox` fixed at creation) and the signed checkout; `HandleNoticeAsync`; the API
  (`PingAsync`, `FetchAsync`, `UpdateAmountAsync`, `CancelAsync`). **A notice is believed only from PayFast's addresses**
  (ranges, or what its four host names resolve to, cached 10 min — `RemoteIpAddress` after the forwarded headers, so
  behind Caddy it is PayFast's), **rightly signed, for our merchant id, confirmed `VALID` by PayFast's
  `/eng/query/validate`, for a subscription of ours with its own token, sandbox matching sandbox.** Failing any of those it
  is logged and kept in memory for the owner's page — **never stored**, so nobody can fill a table by posting at us.
  Passing them it is a `PayfastPayment`, unique on (`PfPaymentId`, `Status`) — a cancellation may carry a payment's id —
  and a second copy, even arriving at the same moment, is "already recorded". **The first payment must be what the
  checkout asked** (R0.00 for a trial) or it is stored NOT applied with the reason; a renewal for another amount is applied
  and the difference written on it (the money is real). COMPLETE → Active, token kept, next charge date from
  `billing_date`; CANCELLED → Cancelled, and a later COMPLETE does not bring it back. **200 to everything decided; 503
  only when PayFast's confirmation could not be reached or the database failed**, so PayFast sends it again. The
  `Applied` event is what stages B–D will listen to; nothing acts on a company yet.
- **`POST /api/payfast/notify`** (Program.cs) reads the body RAW — the signature is over the order — 64 KB at most.
- **`/owner/payfast`** (menu: PayFast): the account (SANDBOX / LIVE pill, merchant, "stored"), *Test PayFast's API*,
  every subscription and payment, the notices refused since the server started. **A sandbox test checkout** (Full admin
  or Owner, sandbox only): defaults R0 now, R5.00 monthly from tomorrow, twice — so a real charge arrives the next day. Its form
  has `action=` written out, so **no antiforgery token** — one more field would fall outside PayFast's signature.
- **Command line**: `payfast show | test | set --merchant-id N --sandbox|--live` (key from `RSP_PAYFAST_KEY`, passphrase
  from `RSP_PAYFAST_PASSPHRASE`; `set` pings the API at once). **`deploy\Set-PayfastKeys.ps1`** puts an account on the
  live server: two `Get-Credential` windows, the secrets down ssh's standard input into exported variables and `sudo -u
  rsp -E` — never an argument (the server's process list) or a file. `-Live` asks you to type LIVE.
- Migrations **`Payfast`** in BOTH sets (SQLite and `PgPlatformDb`); `PayfastSandbox` defaults to **true** in both, so the
  existing settings row can never start out live.
- **`tools\Save-PayfastSandbox.ps1`** stores Clint's SANDBOX account on this PC (Export-Clixml, DPAPI, git-ignored
  `tools/payfast-sandbox.xml`) for the harness's real-sandbox section.

**Found while building:** PayFast's published public test merchant (10000100 / `jt7NOE43FZPn`) is refused by the real
sandbox with "Generated signature does not match" for even the simplest payment, with or without that passphrase — it is
shared by every developer and its passphrase has evidently been changed. Do not chase a signature fault from it; test with
Clint's own sandbox (`Save-PayfastSandbox.ps1`).

**Found against Clint's real sandbox:** (1) **PayFast refuses any subscription more often than monthly** — *"The frequency
must be at least 3"* — though its documentation lists daily and weekly. `BeginAsync` refuses 1 and 2 itself now, and the
test checkout is monthly. (2) PayFast also refuses a recurring amount under R5.00 with its own message before it looks at
the signature, so a tampered-amount test must stay above R5. (3) The live API's ping answers `"PayFast API"`, even with
`?testing=true`; the docs' `"API V1"` is the sandbox's word. (4) **A harness that signs in with the admin key twice must
wait for the next 30-second code**: the owner's last code step is stored and a code is good once — the platform is right
to refuse, and payfastcheck's second platform failed one run in two until it waited.

`tools/payfastcheck` **56 of 56 on SQLite, 55 of 55 on PostgreSQL** (one check reads the SQLite file) — a real platform, a
fake PayFast (confirmation and API) in the harness, every signature worked out in the harness separately from the
platform's code; **42 of 50 with the address check taken out**. With `tools/payfast-sandbox.xml` present it also runs
against PayFast's REAL sandbox with Clint's account: the API accepts the right passphrase and refuses a wrong one, **the
platform's own checkout is ACCEPTED** (PayFast answers 302 to its payment page) and the same checkout with its amount changed
is refused *"Generated signature does not match"*. `pgcheck` 20. **`Publish-Platform.ps1` (migration `Payfast`), then
`deploy\Set-PayfastKeys.ps1` with the sandbox account.** No ship, no console re-download. `TEST-3.6.md` section CQ, 631–638.

**On the live server the same day (checks 631–637), and the fault it found.** Clint's sandbox checkout reached the live
server end to end: PayFast's notice from `144.126.193.139`, believed, R0.00 recorded, the subscription Active with the
next day's charge date; `Notices refused` empty. **Then he cancelled one in the sandbox dashboard, and the notice was
REFUSED: "PayFast did not confirm it (INVALID)".** Address, signature and merchant all passed — PayFast's own confirmation
(`/eng/query/validate`) answers INVALID to a cancellation, which carries the id of the payment that started the
subscription with its status changed. **A cancellation is now confirmed by asking PayFast's API** (`StateAsync` →
`GET /subscriptions/{token}/fetch`, `status_text`): CANCELLED there → recorded; anything else → refused ("PayFast's API
says the subscription is ACTIVE" — so a forged cancellation, even a rightly-signed one, cannot end a customer's service);
PayFast unreachable → 503. Payments are still confirmed only by the confirmation. And **Check with PayFast** on each
subscription with a token (Full admin / Owner, `CheckAsync`) asks the same API and puts ours right — for the one refused
here, and for any notice that never came; stage D's daily sweep will do the same for every subscription.
`payfastcheck` **64 of 64 on SQLite, 63 of 63 on PostgreSQL**; the fake PayFast now answers INVALID to every cancellation as
the real one does and has the fetch endpoint; **60 of 64 with the API check taken out**. Also learnt: an abandoned checkout
(no card) leaves nothing at PayFast — PayFast lists only subscriptions whose card went through.

## 135. PayFast, stage B: choosing the full version and paying, switched on by PayFast — 2026-10-13

Stage B of `docs/NEXT-SESSION-PAYFAST.md`. Clint's answers: card at signup, nothing charged for 14 days; a full-version
company switches on by itself once PayFast confirms the card; the free version is still approved by hand.

- **`Services/CompanyBilling.cs`** is every rule. `Refusal(t, account)`: card payment only for a billed, full-version,
  SOUTH AFRICAN company (PayFast is rand only) on a server with a PayFast account — anybody else goes the old way.
  `StartAsync` makes the checkout: R0.00 now, `Pricing.BillFor` for the people in seats from **`FirstChargeDate`** — 14
  days from signing up, the end of a running trial, or tomorrow, always the company's own date — monthly until cancelled,
  the owner's name and email. **It listens to PayFast** (`PayfastService.Listen`, now AWAITED before PayFast is answered, so
  the company is on by the time anybody looks): the first COMPLETE of a `signup`, `card` or `upgrade` subscription makes the
  company Active **through `AdminCompanies.SetStatusAsync`**, logged as *PayFast*, and its owners get *"your account is
  ready"* (a sign-in link, nothing charged until the date, the monthly amount). Suspended, closed or rejected companies are
  left alone (stage D).
- **Signup** (`Pages/Signup`): a full-version South African signup, made, goes to step **`pay`** — the checkout posted to
  PayFast at once. Elsewhere, or with no PayFast account, it waits for approval as before. **`/signup/paid?ref=`**
  (`SignupPaid`) is where PayFast sends them back: it asks **`GET /api/payfast/checkout/{ref}`** (the state only —
  waiting, ready, stopped — by 80 random bits) every 3 s and changes by itself; with `cancelled=1` it says the card was not
  added and offers it again — a NEW checkout for the same company, while it still waits for one. `PayfastService.BeginAsync`
  now takes `{ref}` in the return addresses.
- **Approvals**: such a signup is marked *Waiting for the card at PayFast* with no Approve (`CompanyRow.CardAtPayfast`), and
  **`AdminCompanies.ApproveAsync` refuses it** — a person must not switch on a company that has not paid.
- **Found and fixed: approval never emailed anybody**, though the signup page has always said *"We'll email you as soon as
  your account is approved"*. `ApproveAsync` now sends *"your account is approved"* with the sign-in address
  (`AdminCompanies.Approved`).
- **Billing**: a company paying by card sees the amount, the next charge and *Change the card* (PayFast's update link); one
  that could pay by card and does not, *Add your card* — **the owner only** (`Permissions.CanAcceptPrice`; an office

  accepts; abandoned there, the company is on its 14-day trial as before. **Trial reminders** in South Africa tell the owner
  to add the card on Billing. **A lapsed trial still cannot sign in** (AuthService) — so it cannot reach Billing; the new
  flow takes the card first, and only an upgrade abandoned at PayFast and then left 14 days ends up there.
- **The preview** (`Services/SitePreview.cs`, `/owner/preview`, any admin, logged): gives THIS browser a Data Protection
  cookie `rsp_preview` for 30 days; **go-live.sh's `@holding` matcher now skips a request carrying it** (`not header Cookie
  *rsp_preview=*`), and `SitePreview.SignupsOn` opens signup to it. Caddy only sees that the cookie is there; the platform
  checks it made it. Index, Features, Pricing and the layout ask `SignupsOn` instead of reading the setting.
- **Pricing**: *"Your card at signup — nothing is charged for 14 days"*, *"by card. No VAT is charged"* (it said *VAT
  excluded*, against the terms), and *"by credit or debit card through PayFast, and can cancel any time"*. The seat
  calculator and the free version's card on the page are stage E.

**For stage D:** South Africa's terms (2026-10-08) say service may be suspended when a payment is **more than 14 days late**

## 136. PayFast, stage C: the amount kept true, payments listed, our receipt — 2026-10-14

Stage C of `docs/NEXT-SESSION-PAYFAST.md`. Clint (2026-10-14): *"go with 14 days"* for stage D's grace — recorded in the
brief.

- **`CompanyBilling.SyncAmountAsync(tenantId)`** is the one rule: what the company owes now (`OwedCents` =
  `Pricing.BillFor` for the people in seats, in cents) against what PayFast has (`PayfastSubscription.AmountCents`);
  different → `PATCH /subscriptions/{token}/update` with `amount` in CENTS, from the NEXT charge (the run date is never
  touched — the terms say a change shows on the next bill). One company at a time (a semaphore each), so two changes cannot
  send two amounts out of order. Accepted → the amount moves, `AmountChangedUtc`, and the admin log says *"Monthly amount
  R500 → R800 from the next charge"* by PayFast. Refused or unreachable → **`AmountProblem`** says why; Billing shows *"Your
  price is now R… and PayFast has not yet taken the new amount — we keep trying"*, the owner's PayFast page shows it on the
  subscription.
- **When it runs:** `TenantService.PeopleChanged(tenantId)` (new — raised when a person is added, and by `Changed`, i.e.
  boxes changed, removed, disabled) → at once, not awaited. **`PayfastSweep`** (hosted, every
  `Platform:PayfastSweepSeconds`, an hour; first pass within a minute of starting) → `SyncAllAsync` over every active card
  subscription on this server's account: retries, and changes made on the command line (another process). Stage D adds the
  missing-payment checks to the same sweep.
- **Our receipt** (`CompanyBilling.Receipt`): every COMPLETE that took money (not the R0.00 card check, not a test) mails the
  owners — the amount, the date in the company's zone, PayFast's reference, the next charge, *"No VAT is charged: we are
  not registered for VAT"*. Plain ASCII on purpose (§135). **Billing lists the payments** (`PaymentsAsync`: applied,
  COMPLETE, above R0).
- Migration **`PayfastAmounts`** in both sets (`AmountChangedUtc`, `AmountProblem`).
- Not done here, on purpose: `NotBilled` switched on for a company paying by card leaves its subscription alone (the sweep
  skips it) — cancelling it is a person's decision, stage D's Cancel.

## 137. PayFast, stage D: a payment that did not come, 14 days' grace, and cancelling — 2026-10-14

Stage D of `docs/NEXT-SESSION-PAYFAST.md`. Clint, 2026-10-14: *"go with 14 days"* — South Africa's terms say service may be
suspended when a payment is **more than 14 days late**, so the brief's 7 days was against them. Every rule is
**`Services/CompanyBilling.Late.cs`** (`CompanyBilling` is `partial` now).

- **Lateness is an ABSENCE** (PayFast sends nothing for a failed renewal): the charge date a subscription waits for
  (`Due` = `NextRunDate`, else `BillingDate`) passed by a day or more, with no COMPLETE payment above R0 since the start of
  that day in the company's zone. **Before calling it late the API is asked** (`PayfastService.LookAsync` — `StateAsync` plus
  `run_date`): a `run_date` past the due date means PayFast was paid and only its notice was lost — `NextRunDate` moves,
  logged *"PayFast had moved on to … — its notice for … never came"*; CANCELLED means it ended there.
- **The steps** (`LateStage`): a day late → *"your payment did not go through"*; 7 → *"…a week late"*; 13 → *"your service
  will be suspended on …"*; **more than 14 → suspended** through `AdminCompanies.SetStatusAsync`, which now takes the email
  to send instead of its own (`notice`), so the owners get ONE email saying why. Only the step earned is sent, once
  (`LateDue`, `LateNotices`). Every one carries **PayFast's change-the-card link** — it works for a company that cannot sign
  in. Billing shows *"The payment due on … has not come through"*.
- **The payment comes** (`PaidAsync`, on any COMPLETE above R0): lateness cleared; **a suspension WE made**
  (`SuspendedUtc`) is lifted with *"payment received - your service is back"*. **An admin's suspension stays** — the
  harness proves it.
- **Cancelling:** Billing → *Cancel the subscription* (owner only, a tick box) → **PayFast first** (`PUT …/cancel`) → ours
  Cancelled → **`MarkEndingAsync`**: the service runs to **the day BEFORE the charge it was waiting for** (a month paid on
  the 14th runs to the 13th; a trial ends the day before its first charge; a charge that never came means it already
  ended), `EndsOn`, logged, the owners emailed — unless that day is already past. A CANCELLED notice (cancelled at PayFast),
  *Check with PayFast*, or the sweep finding one go through the same method. **`CloseEndedAsync`**: past `EndsOn` → the
  company is **Closed** and told *"your service has ended"* (nothing deleted). **A new card before then is first charged on
  the date the old one would have been** (`ResumeDateAsync`) — nothing paid twice — and nothing closes.
- **`PayfastSweep`** now runs `LatePassAsync` after the amounts. **All companies** shows each company's card
  (`CompanyRow.Payment`, `PaymentWords`: *Card*, *Card, unpaid since … (suspended)*, *Cancelled, ends …*).
- Emails ASCII (§135). Migration **`PayfastLateAndEnd`** in both sets (`LateDue`, `LateNotices`, `SuspendedUtc`, `EndsOn`,
  `EndedUtc`).
- **Not built:** a company suspended for payment cannot sign in to add a NEW card — the emails' change-the-card link is its
  way back; PayFast retries with the new card. If PayFast has LOCKED the subscription after its retries, an admin
  reactivates it in PayFast's dashboard (or *Check with PayFast* once it is paid).

`tools/signuppaycheck` **70 of 70** (stage D added: five companies whose charge was 1, 7, 15 and 3 days ago — that last one
"moved on" at PayFast — and one that ends): reminders 1 and 2 only as earned, suspended with ONE email, All companies and
the log, paid → restored, an admin's suspension kept, Cancel needs the tick and tells PayFast (signed) first, the last day,
one email even when PayFast's notice follows, a new card charged from the old date, an ended company closed and told.
`TEST-3.6.md` section CT, 652–658. **`Publish-Platform.ps1` (migration `PayfastLateAndEnd`).**

## 140. The website in light and dark, screenshots of the real windows, the cookie line — 2026-10-14

Clint, after looking at the preview: *"Is it possible that we can have it switch between light and dark mode like our product
does and can we add some screenshots so that people can get a good look and feel about what the product is about?"* — and then,
mid-build: *"We also need the privacy policy line about cookies."*

- **Light and dark on the public site.** The stylesheet already had the portal's light palette (§38); the public pages simply
  never chose it. Now an inline script in `_Layout`'s head — public section only, BEFORE the stylesheet, so nothing flashes —
  picks the visitor's own choice (`localStorage` `rsp-theme`, never sent anywhere), else their computer's setting
  (`prefers-color-scheme`), else dark as before. `#siteTheme` in the menu is the portal's switch (`.theme-toggle`, the same
  "☀ Light mode" / "☾ Dark mode" words), hidden until the script gives it its words. **`.theme-toggle[hidden]`** is new: the
  class's `inline-flex` beat the `hidden` attribute (the sound button had the same latent fault). The public menu's gap is 16px
  (it wrapped the switch at 20). `--text` in the footer headings was an undefined token; it is `--ink`.
- **Screenshots of the real windows: `tools/siteshots` (new).** Like `lookprobe`, it opens the console's and the customer's real
  windows with no server and hands them what the server would send — but to be PUBLISHED, so **every name is made up**: the IT
  company *Coastline IT* (the product's purple, a logo drawn in code), its customers, their machines, and **Jane Smith's screen
  inside the session window is drawn in code** (a mail program asking for her password) — never a capture of a real screen. Seven
  windows, each in light and dark, into `wwwroot/shots`: console, session (JPEG — its wallpaper is 400 KB as PNG), workshop ticket,
  Performance, Request support, Allow, the tray app. It reads them off the SCREEN, so it takes the screen for a minute: leave the
  mouse alone. Three things it has to do that `lookprobe` did not: set each window's size AFTER it is shown (Windows scales it
  first), move the pointer away (a tooltip was in the picture), and set the "connected" state LAST — a link that cannot reach a
  server keeps saying so (the tray app's needed its `OnConnectedChanged` emptied).
- **On the pages.** `SitePages.Shots` lists each picture with its real size (sizes in the page, so nothing jumps as it loads);
  `_Shot.cshtml` draws the dark and the light picture, both lazy — the hidden one is never fetched — and the stylesheet shows the
  one the page is in. A click opens it full size (`#shotView`, a `<dialog>`; without a script the link opens the picture). The
  home page's hero is now the real console with the tray app in front of its corner (the drawn window is gone, and its CSS), and a
  **See it for yourself** tour of five tabs; Remote support has the session, the customer's three windows and Performance;
  Ticketing has the ticket.
- **Found by the pictures, in the CONSOLE: the machine list's columns were pixel numbers** that did not grow with Windows'
  display scaling — at 150% "HV-FRONTDESK" read "HV-FRONT…" and "16 GB" read "16…". Now each is measured from a long sample in
  the list's font, and **`FitDeviceColumns`** shares the room when the window is too narrow — the first version let them run past
  the list's edge, the list scrolled sideways and the customer's fold chevron went out of sight (`dashtabs` 131 of 133 found it).
- **The cookie line.** `Terms/privacy-ZA.txt` said "no cookies" — true of the holding page, not of the real site. It now names
  the only cookies the site sets (signed in; the weekly sign-in code and signed-out-elsewhere notice; form protection), no

  policy now carries its date, as its last section promised. `Terms.Version` 2026-10-14; `landing-legal` re-run, so the holding
  page carries it too. Strictly necessary cookies need no banner under POPIA, so there is none.
