## 141. Everything moves to .NET 10 — 2026-10-14

Clint asked whether macOS Catalina would do for the Mac side, then: *"yes, start the move to .net10. How will this affect windows
10 machines?"* **.NET 8 leaves Microsoft's support on 10 November 2026**, and a Mac host (roadmap stage 6) would be built on .NET
10 anyway — which supports **macOS 14 and later**, so Catalina is out (it is also unpatched since 2022 and lacks ScreenCaptureKit).
Built on the branch **`dotnet10`** (its own worktree, `.claude\worktrees\dotnet10`) so master kept shipping until it was proven.

- **What changed.** Every project `net8.0` → `net10.0` (`-windows` kept); EF Core, `Microsoft.Data.Sqlite`, the Hosting packages
  → **10.0.13**; Npgsql and its EF provider → **10.0.3**; the scripts' and harnesses' `bin\Release\net8.0` paths → `net10.0`.
  `System.Drawing.Common` is gone from the host (part of .NET now — NU1510). **`System.Security.Cryptography.Pkcs` 10.0.13 is
  named in the platform** because MimeKit (under MailKit) asks for 10.0.0, which has two advisories (GHSA-846f-f764-76mx high,
  GHSA-2fmv-rv2c-59x7). Both servers load their certificate with `X509CertificateLoader.LoadPkcs12FromFile` (SYSLIB0057).
- **WFO1000 is off for the whole solution** (`Directory.Build.props`). From .NET 9 it is an ERROR that every public property of
  a control says how the Visual Studio designer saves it — 19 of them in `RemoteSupport.UI`. Nothing here uses the designer:
  every window is built in code, and the 68 `*.Designer.cs` files are EF migrations. If a designer is ever brought in, turn it
  back on.
- **No code change was needed for EF Core 10** — the risk was its refusal to migrate when the model and the snapshots disagree
  (from EF 9). `pgcheck` part 1 says both sets still match the model.
- **Nothing installs .NET on a customer's machine.** Every Windows program is published self-contained (`build.ps1`,
  `Pack-ClientExe.ps1`), and so is the Linux platform; the live server's Ubuntu 24.04 is on .NET 10's list.
- **Windows 10.** .NET 10 runs on Windows 10 22H2 (both test machines are 19045). But **Microsoft's list for .NET 10 names only
  the Windows 10 editions Microsoft still supports — Enterprise LTSC 2016/2019/2021 and IoT** — because Windows 10 itself left
  support in October 2025. Home and Pro 22H2 work; a .NET fault that appeared ONLY there would not be fixed by Microsoft. Staying
  on .NET 8 would have been worse: no fixes on any Windows after November.
- **The local platform's data moves.** It lives beside the program (`AppContext.BaseDirectory` + `data`), so on this laptop it
  was `src\RemoteSupport.Platform\bin\Release\net8.0\data` and is now `...\net10.0\data` — copied once at the merge. The live
  server is untouched by this: its data folder is configured to its own disk (§125).
- **A new worktree lacks the git-ignored files** the harnesses read: `tools\rs-postgres.txt` (without it `pgcheck` skips part 2
  and `-Postgres` runs fail), `branding\brand.json` (without it `iconcheck` finds no logo), `tools\rs-credentials.json`
  (`trayprobe` and the live-server harnesses). Copy them in; they stay ignored.
- **Building now needs the .NET 10 SDK** on any PC that builds (`winget install --id Microsoft.DotNet.SDK.10 --exact`); it sits
  beside the 8 SDK. `dotnet-ef` was already 10.0.11.
- **Found on the way, not .NET 10:** `seatcheck` crashed on master too — its upgrade part read the old companies through
  today's model, and §139 added `Tenant.ReviewAskAfterUtc`. It reads them by SQL now (§59's rule).

**Proven.** The solution and all 146 harness projects build with no errors. **Database harnesses 74 of 74 on SQLite and 74 of
74 on PostgreSQL**; `pgcheck` 20 of 20. Without a far machine: `lookprobe` 346, `fitprobe` 324, `ticketwindowprobe` 247,
`ticketformprobe` 140, `dashtabs` 133, `watchprobe` 68, `callprobe` 66, `toolbarprobe` 53, `soundcheck` 52, `e2ecore` 48,
`dragoutcheck` 43, `unattendedcheck` 40, `themecheck` 40, `filesetcheck` 35, `webchatprobe` 32, **`iconcheck` 24** (the private
`Form.s_defaultIcon` that `BrandIcon` reaches into is still there), `chatprobe` 24, `noticeprobe` 21, `dragoffcheck` 21,
`staffchatprobe` 18, `viewonlyprobe` 18, `legalcheck` 16, `privacyprobe` 14, `dragselcheck` 11, `recordcheck` 11, `voicelocal` 4,
`audiolocal` PASS. **`codecbench --source h264`: Quick Sync, scrolling 202 KB/s at 1.2% CPU** (§25 measured 198 KB/s, 1.0%), a
still screen sends nothing.

**On hardware, 2026-10-14, after the deploy:** both Windows 10 test machines, still on the .NET 8 apps, connected to the .NET 10 server and worked (check 677) — Clint: *"still working properly."* **And on 2026-10-15 the NEW apps on Windows 10, checks 678–683, all passed** — Clint: *"i have done 678, 679, and 680-683 all working"*: the console re-downloaded, the client reinstalled on DESKTOP-OPHQIDH, a session with the hardware encoder, Ctrl+Alt+Del and a UAC prompt with the host surviving, copy and paste both ways, Files, Processes and Chat. **THE MOVE TO .NET 10 IS PROVEN ON HARDWARE.** Still unrun: the harnesses that need one or the live server (`codeccheck`,
`capturecheck`, `clipcheck`, `sysactioncheck`, `trayprobe`), `shortcutcheck` (presses real keys) and the two elevated checks.
**`Publish-Platform.ps1` (no migration), then re-download the console and reinstall the client.** `TEST-3.6.md` section CX,
677–683.

## 142. A blurry picture that never sharpens: key frames a minute apart, a still screen sharpened — 2026-10-15

Internal testing, Clint, on DESKTOP-STD8M9C (Windows 10, 1366x768, Quick Sync *with a GPU colour conversion*, §99): *"the
graphics are very pixilated when connecting and then slowly starts to render correctly, but is never clear."*

**Measured first.** The console's trace (`\\localhost\C$\Users\Clint\AppData\Local\TheRemoteSupportProgram\technician-trace.log` —
read from Claude's sandbox, `%LOCALAPPDATA%` is a copy that stops early) had a 72 KB key frame, a SECOND key frame of 11.8 KB ten milliseconds later,
then 286-byte frames. The live server cannot be reached by a harness from here (`rs-credentials.json` names Clint and has no
`totpSecret`; §82 would sign his console out), so it was measured on this laptop's Quick Sync forced through the same colour
conversion (`--nv12`) — **new: `codecbench --sharp`** (one still page, the console's own decoder, PSNR against an exact GDI copy,
brightness and colour apart; `--twokeys`, `--gop N`, `--scene desk|idle|colour`). The `Desk` scene is new too: 12-pixel Segoe UI
with ClearType, coloured text, a search box with a blinking cursor and a window that opens — Consolas on white flattered it.

**Three causes, all in the H.264 path's constant bit rate.**
1. **The automatic key frame every 24 frames** (`CODECAPI_AVEncMPVGOPSize = Fps * 2`, "two seconds" but counted in FRAMES, which
   come only when the screen changes) is starved by the bit rate and throws the sharpened picture away: **46.9 dB → 36.1 dB** at
   the key frame, below the FIRST picture the technician saw. That is "never clear".
2. **Nothing sharpens a still screen.** After a change, Desktop Duplication hands over nothing, the encoder is never called, and
   the soft picture stays. That is "slowly starts to render": it sharpens only as unrelated small changes trickle in.
3. **The second key frame at connect** is the encryption setting arriving (`E2eModeMsg` → `_forceFull`, HostEngine) just after the
   first, and it gets what the first left of the budget (52 KB of 134 here; 11.8 of 72 on STD8M9C). Not changed — 1 and 2 repair it.

Colour stays at quarter detail (4:2:0, 35.7 dB at every step) — that is H.264 Main, and not part of this fix. The console also
draws a 1366x768 screen into a 1711x962 area with smoothing, which softens any picture; also not changed.

**The fix.**
- **`H264Encoder.KeyFrameSeconds` = 60** (was 2): a steady climb to 48.4 dB, 16% fewer bytes.
- **`Host/StillRefiner.cs`, THE rule for sharpening a still screen**: for **2 s** after a forced picture or a change covering
  **1%** of the screen or more, `SendVideo` encodes the unchanged screen again (`TryAcquireGpuFrame(…, true)`), never while more
  than a quarter of `LinkController.BackOffBytes` is queued. **A blinking cursor must not re-arm it** — a few dozen pixels every
  530 ms would keep it running on an idle screen for ever; a small change's one frame has the whole frame budget anyway. **Its frames
  are not changes**: `_passRefined` makes the link controller see 0, or every still screen would put it on the video ladder.
  Info tab: *Frames sent to sharpen a still screen*.
- **How much changed comes from Windows: `DxgiCapture.LastVideoChange`**, from the move and dirty rectangles — no readback.
- **The server asks for a picture when it drops one: `KeyFrameRequestMsg`.** Key frames a minute apart would leave a viewer whose
  frame the hub DROPPED (`WsConnection`: a viewer more than 2 MB behind) with a broken picture for up to a minute — the old 2 s
  floor had been hiding it. The relay in `TenantHub` (host binary → viewers) now asks the host when a VIDEO frame is dropped
  (`BinaryRelay.LossNeedsKeyFrame`, by `BinKind.Of`, so a sealed one counts), at most once a second per session
  (`AskHostForKeyFrame`, `KeyFrameRequestEveryMs`). It is on the clear list (`SessionSeal.ClearTypes` and `e2e.js` — only the hub
  knows of the drop) and carries nothing; the host sets `_forceFull`; the browser-support page (`help.js`) sets `needKey`; an older
  host ignores it.

**A fault found on the way, since 2026-09-16: `DXGI_OUTDUPL_FRAME_INFO` was read wrongly.** Its BOOLs were C# `bool`s, and
`AcquireNextFrame` is handed a raw POINTER to the struct, where `MarshalAs` does nothing and a `bool` is one byte — so every field
after `AccumulatedFrames` was misplaced, and `TotalMetadataBufferSize` was really `PointerShapeBufferSize`, nearly always 0. They are
`int`s now. Nothing visible broke because `LastPresentTime` and `AccumulatedFrames` come first. **The tile path therefore never used
the dirty rectangles** — it compared every tile on every frame, correctly but more slowly than stage 2.1 intended — and
`DxgiCapture.UseRectsForTiles = false` KEEPS it that way: switching on a shortcut that has never run, whose failure is a stale
rectangle, is its own change, with `codecbench --compare`.

**Proven.**
- `codecbench --hostloop` (new): twenty seconds of a session — connect with the double key frame, a blinking cursor, a window at
  8 s — through the host's own parts, old host then new, scored against the screen with the cursor left out. **5 of 5 at quality
  55** (3 s after connecting: 48.3 dB against 43.4; clean by 2 s; sharpening ends 2 s after the window; 74 frames against 40, about
  twice the bytes over the 20 s) **and 5 of 5 at 35**, STD8M9C's squeezed budget (45.9 against 39.3 at 3 s; the old host is knocked
  back from 45.5 to 41.4 by its key frame at 14 s; on that budget 2 s of sharpening gets most of the way and the cursor's own frames
  the rest, clean by about 8 s). The old host fails it, as it must.
- **`tools/sharpwire` (new) 9 of 9: the REAL `RemoteSupport.Host.exe`**, built from the checkout, on this PC, against a platform of
  its own, decoded as the console does: H.264; a still screen sends nothing; a window opening → 17–18 frames in 0.3–2 s, then
  none; the picture 49.2 dB against the screen; a blinking cursor 7 frames in 4 s; a moving picture 0 unrequested key frames;
  a viewer with a 4 KB receive buffer that never reads → key frames at the healthy viewer 1.05 s apart. (Loopback's own buffers
  swallowed ~17 s of picture before the hub's 2 MB limit until the slow viewer's buffer was made small.) **It covers the screen
  for ~40 s: leave the mouse alone.** A viewer with no end-to-end hello must subscribe AFTER the hub's grace: a sealing host
  refuses clear content, a subscription included.
- **`tools/keyframewire` (new) 12 of 12 (11 with the hub's request out)**: video dropped to a slow viewer asks; tiles do not; one
  a second (gaps 994–1001 ms); the healthy viewer goes on.
- Unchanged and passing: `codecbench --tail` and `--tail --nv12` PASS, `--h264check` PASS, `--adapt` 13, `e2ecore` 48 (the two clear
  lists match), `e2ewire` 31, `websupportcheck` 64, `guestcheck` 33, `viewonlyprobe` 18.

**Not on hardware.** **`Publish-Platform.ps1` (no migration) FIRST** — a new host on an old server has nobody to ask it for a
picture — **then reinstall the client** on DESKTOP-STD8M9C (and the other test machines). No console re-download. `TEST-3.6.md`
section CY, 684–690.

## 143. Two machines at once, at most, and copy on one, paste on the other — 2026-10-15

Clint: *"one can do concurrent connections if one moves one session to a second monitor … it works great. Can we limit it to
a maximum of two concurrent sessions and can we get copy and paste to work between them."* For remote workers, and for files
between two office machines.

**Copy and paste between them already worked, through this PC.** Measured in the code before anything was built: nothing links
the two machines. A copy on machine A lands on the technician's clipboard (text at once; files fetched into
`Downloads\Remote Support\<machine> <time>` and put on the clipboard), and `OnActivated` sends the clipboard into whichever session
window is clicked next (§26, §39, §40). Nothing new was needed for that — **`tools/twosessions` (new) proves it** with two real
`SessionForm`s at once, each against its own loopback "customer machine": text both ways, files both ways byte for byte, neither
machine sent its own copy back.

**The one gap was timing.** A's files are on the clipboard only once they have ARRIVED, and A empties the clipboard the moment the
copy is announced (§54, so a paste cannot give stale files). Click into B before they land and B saw nothing to send, sent nothing,
and **said nothing** — so Ctrl+V on B pasted B's own old clipboard. Now **`SessionForm.Between.cs`**: every session window is in
`s_openWindows`; a window's clipboard-bound fetch is `_clipFetchSet` (set in `PullFileSet` when `thenOnMyClipboard` and no
`into`); `SyncMyClipboard` asks `WaitingForAnotherWindowsCopy` FIRST, and while another window is fetching (or has a too-big offer
waiting for a click) it says so on the status bar — *"files copied on A are still arriving — don't paste on B yet; they come here
the moment they land"* — and sends nothing. When the fetch ends, the waiting window is told (`ClipboardFetchEnded` →
`OtherWindowsCopyEnded`): landed and still in front → sent at once; landed and not in front → *"click back into this window"*;
failed, refused, timed out or A's window closed → *"did not arrive, so nothing was sent"*. **A fetch with no sign of life for
30 s stops counting** (`ClipFetchStallMs`, refreshed by the offer and every chunk) — a stalled transfer must never leave B
refusing to send anything for ever. **The rule of WHEN a copy reaches a customer is unchanged: only the window in front.**

**The limit: two machines per technician — `Shared/SessionLimit.cs`, one number and one wording for both ends.** What counts is
a MACHINE: going back to one already open (Reconnect, a restart, a dropped socket, Connect again) is never refused.
- **The console** (`DashboardForm.OverSessionLimit`) counts its open session windows plus sessions waiting for somebody to accept
  (`_waits`), and refuses BEFORE it asks — Connect, Accept call (list and pop-up), Join session, Watch an outsider, Connect with a
  code — so a third machine's person is never prompted and no ticket is opened. Join on a session already open brings its window
  forward rather than opening a second.
- **The hub** (`Hub/TenantHub.SessionLimit.cs`) refuses the same in `ConnectDevice`, `AcceptCall` (before the call is marked
  taken, so it keeps ringing for a colleague) and at the viewer socket (`SessionEndedMsg` with the words). It counts sessions on
  OTHER machines where this technician has a viewer socket NOW — `Session.ViewerIds`, new beside `Viewers`. **Not** sessions
  waiting with nobody in them: one can outlive the console that would close it, and a stuck one would lock the technician out
  until a restart. Not visitors from another company: their own console counts.

**Proven.** `tools/sessionlimitwire` (new) **18 of 18** against a platform of its own (8 of 18 with the hub's rule switched off);
`tools/twosessions` (new) **27 of 27** (23 with the wait switched off — B shows a stale message and says nothing of the copy on its
way). It uses the real clipboard and the clipboard harness mutex, and tries to bring B's window to the front — leave the mouse
alone; when Windows refuses it the foreground it checks the "click back" path instead and says so. Unchanged and passing:
`pullcheck` 11, `pastecheck` 17, `reasonwire` 20, `consentwire` 34, `unattendedpw` 65, `outsidervisit` 65, `ticketpersession` 37.

**Host to host is BUILT the same day — §144.** Clint asked (same day) whether files could go straight between the two machines
rather than through this PC. Truly direct needs a listening port on SYSTEM hosts and the same network; through the server, host to
host, works anywhere and keeps both the technician's line and PC out of it — but end-to-end encryption is per session (§112), so it
needs its own handshake between the two machines' identities. Through-the-PC stays as the fallback.

**Not on hardware.** `Publish-Platform.ps1` (no migration), then re-download the console. No client reinstall. `TEST-3.6.md`
section CZ, 691–697.

## 144. Copy on one machine, paste on the other — straight between them, never through the technician's PC — 2026-10-15

Clint, after §143: *"Is it possible to build the copy and paste to work directly between both machines that are open instead so
that it doesnt go through the technician PC?"* The design and his six answers (all *"go with your recommendations"*) are
`docs/NEXT-SESSION-HOST2HOST.md`. **Through the server, host to host** — truly direct needs a listening port on SYSTEM hosts and
one network, and would fail for the remote workers he asked about.

### What it is

- **The gesture is unchanged**: Ctrl+C on A, click into B's window, Ctrl+V on B. With TWO windows open and both machines able
  (`HostCan.Bridge`, a word in the host's `SysInfoMsg`) and keyed end to end, A's copied files are **held**, not fetched — A's
  status bar says *"click into B's window and paste, or click here to bring them to this PC"* (answer 1). Clicking into B asks the
  hub to **bridge** the two sessions for that one copy (`BridgeAskMsg`, on B's socket, clear). **Nothing reaches B before the click
  into B** — customer A's files are never put on customer B's disk before anybody chose B (§26's rule).
- **The hub's yes is the ask sent back**; only then does the console make a 32-byte key for this copy and hand it to each machine
  **inside its own sealed session** (`BridgeKeyMsg`, NEVER on the clear list; `SessionLink.SendSealed` refuses to send it unsealed).
  A refusal is `BridgeEndMsg.Refused`, and nobody was given a key, so no host waits for a partner that is not coming.
- **`Shared/BridgeSeal.cs`**: the frame `[8][idLen][id][sender][counter][ct+tag]` — the bridge id clear (the hub routes by it and can
  read nothing else), AES-256-GCM, sender 1 / receiver 2, each end refusing its OWN number (a server bouncing frames back), anything
  not newer, another copy's id or key. Inside: a message, or a whole file-chunk frame. `BinKind.Bridge` (8) is must-arrive in
  `WsConnection` and `BinaryRelay`.
- **The console vouches for the pairing** rather than A and B checking each other's identities: each would need the other's key
  from somebody, and the only candidates are that same console (which already pinned both, §112) or the server we hide from.
- **The host (`HostEngine.Bridge.cs`)**: refuses a key unless its session is sealing — in a sealed session clear content is dropped
  before it gets there; in a clear one nothing bridges. The RECEIVER empties its clipboard at once (a too-early Ctrl+V pastes
  nothing, never its own old files — §54 on the other machine), says ready, **chooses its own staging folder whatever the sender
  says**, acknowledges every 1 MB, and on the last byte puts the files on the person's clipboard AS THEM (§39) before saying so. The
  SENDER waits for ready, offers, streams within **8 MB of the last acknowledgement** — so a slow B never makes the hub hold A's
  socket, which would freeze A's picture — and reports only once B says they landed. Frames that beat the key are kept briefly
  (`_bridgeEarly`): the two keys travel down two different sessions.
- **The hub (`TenantHub.Bridge.cs`) — `BridgeProblem` is THE rule**: the same technician with a viewer socket in BOTH sessions now
  (`ViewerIds`); never an outsider's visit, a guest or browser support; both hosts connected and allowed; **both sessions sealed**
  (`E2eSealed`); both hosts able; under `MaxBytes`; one copy into a machine at a time (a newer one replaces it). It ends a bridge when
  a host or the console says so, either session ends, the technician leaves either one (`BridgesLost`), or nothing moves for 35 s, and
  tells both hosts and the technician's windows. Viewers may never send a bridge frame; a host's never reach a viewer.
- **The record (answer 3)**: each host reports with `FileActivityMsg.BridgeId`; the hub fills `OtherMachine` — **never believed from
  a host** — for the ticket and the technicians only. The tray app says *"straight to another computer"*: it may be another
  customer's. *"Sue copied … from this computer straight to DESKTOP-B."* on A's ticket, *"… straight from DESKTOP-A"* on B's.
- **Answers 4–6**: the 50 MB rule is kept (over it, B's status bar offers *"click here to send it straight to B"*); the free version
  too (`FreePlan.MaySend`); an older host, a session not sealed, a refusal or **a server that does not answer in 10 s** → through
  this PC by itself, B waiting for it as in §143 (`SendThroughThisPc`); **a copy that fails half-way OFFERS the PC** — never doubles
  the traffic unasked. A window closing with files held for it: they come to this PC as with one window (`OtherWindowGone`).
- Text still goes through this PC (it is tiny and wanted here too). The console's half is `SessionForm.Bridge.cs`, asked FIRST by
  `SyncMyClipboard` (`TakeOtherWindowsCopyStraight`); a copy is "the newest" by this PC's clipboard sequence number, as everywhere.

### How it is proved

| | |
|---|---|
| `tools/bridgewire` (new) | **34 of 34**, a platform of its own (port 8187), **two REAL hosts** built from the checkout, the REAL `SessionLink`. The seal alone (no plaintext; replay, altered, reflected, another copy, another key refused); a copy A → B of a file, a folder with a file in a folder, an empty folder and 3 MB — **byte for byte, on B's clipboard, in B's own staging**; progress sealed; both windows told; the technicians' lines name the other machine, the tray app's says "another computer"; both tickets; the files' words in neither the database nor the server's log. Refused: another technician without A open, a session gone clear (an old viewer in it), over 5 GB, an older host. A key sent CLEAR by somebody in the session moves nothing. B's window closed part-way through 600 MB: A told why, A's line says it did not go, B's half-copy removed. |
| …with guards out | **31 of 34** with the hub's same-technician and sealed-session checks and the receiver's own-folder rule taken out (the files landed in the technician's Downloads — the harness host runs as the user); **33 of 34** with the half-copy removal out (alone: with the folder rule also out, the half-copy went to Downloads and hid it). **The host's refusal of an unsealed key is a second line no harness can isolate**: in a sealed session the connection drops clear content before it gets there, and in a clear one the hub refuses the bridge. |
| `tools/twosessions` (extended) | **53 of 53** (was 27). Two real `SessionForm`s onto fake NEW hosts (end-to-end encrypted, able): held not fetched; the ask; **no key before the yes**; one key, arriving sealed (the fakes refuse clear content); statuses; nothing through this PC; an alt-tab asks nothing; refused → through this PC unasked; failed half-way → offered, nothing fetched until the click; the 50 MB offer; "bring them to this PC"; a silent server → this PC after 10 s. **Its first 27 checks run on hosts that cannot bridge, so they are the proof that older hosts behave exactly as before.** |
| re-run | `e2ecore` 48 (the clear lists still match, `e2e.js` included), `e2ewire` 31, `sessionlimitwire` 18, `outsidervisit` 65, `freecheck` 45, `clipledger` 20, `pullcheck` 11, `pastecheck` 17. |

**Not proved:** the two machines being different PCs (both hosts ran on this one), the host as SYSTEM writing the receiver's
clipboard through the person helper (§39's path — the harness host runs as the user and writes directly), and **a slow B never
freezing A's picture** — the window is built for it and nothing measures it. **Not on hardware.** `Publish-Platform.ps1` (no
migration), console re-download, and a **FULL ship and client reinstall** — until a machine has the new host, its copies go through
the PC as before. `TEST-3.6.md` section DA, 698–706.

## 145. Handing a website chat over — 2026-10-15

Clint is putting the bubble on Anywhere I.T's own website for live testing and asked whether a website chat can be
**transferred, or a second person added**. Adding was always there — anybody signed in can type into any chat (§70). Transfer
was not: the first reply took a chat for good (`WebChatService.SayAsync`, one conditional update), and since §109 only the
person answering hears the ding for the visitor's lines — so a chat left with a colleague was **silent for them**.

### What it is

- **Hand over…** in the console's Website chat window (beside End chat) and in the portal's Chat corner window (a tool button
  that opens a *To* row with the people and *Hand over*). Pressed, it asks the server who is signed in now (console:
  `WebChatPeopleRequestMsg` → `WebChatPeopleMsg`; portal: `GET /api/portal/webchats/people`) and offers everybody **except the
  one who has it**; nobody else → *"Nobody else is signed in right now."*
- **Every rule is `WebChatService.HandOverAsync(tenant, chat, from, fromRole, to)`**: the person answering, a supervisor or the
  owner (`Permissions.CanHandOverAnyWebChat` — ask it, never a role), or **anybody while nobody has answered** (to a named person,
  themselves included — that simply takes it). The target must be **signed in at THIS company now** (`StaffPresence.Names`), so a
  chat never goes to an empty chair or another company. **The move is one conditional update on the answerer it read**
  (`AnsweredBy == current && not ended`): two hand-overs at once, or a hand-over and a first reply, cannot both win — the loser
  is told *"Somebody else has just changed who is answering this chat — have another look."* Refusals come back to the console as
  a `WebChatLineMsg` with `Error`, to the portal as a 400 with `error`.
- **The visitor is told** by a line from nobody — *"Sue Tech has taken over this chat."*, or *"Sue Tech will be chatting with
  you."* when nobody had answered. **A note is a `WebChatLine` with no name** (`FromVisitor` false, `Name` ""); every person's line
  has a name, so no migration. `WebChatLineInfo.Note` carries it; the frame, the portal window, the console and the history page
  draw it as a muted note with no "Name:" before it. Kept with the transcript.
- **The dings move with the chat** because every ding rule already keys on `AnsweredBy` (`WebChatForm.TakeLine`, `chat.js`'s
  `webline`), and `Changed` is raised **before** the note so every screen knows who has it first. New: the person it is handed TO
  is brought it — the window pops (without the keyboard), one ding, a tray balloon in the console / a notification in the portal.
  They tell that from their own move by **`WebChatInfo.HandedOverBy`**, set only on the hand-over's update and never stored: a
  first reply, or taking one yourself, is not news. An unanswered chat given away stops ringing for everybody (it is no longer
  waiting).
- `WebChatListMsg.MayHandOverAny` (so the list now goes to each console separately) and the portal's `mayHandOverAny` only HIDE a
  button the server would refuse.
- **`Testing:WebChatHandOverGapMs`** holds the gap between reading who has it and moving it, for `webchatcheck` only (as
  `Testing:PersistDeviceGapMs` does for `firsthello`): on a local database the calls otherwise never meet. Never set in production.

### How it is proved

| | |
|---|---|
| `tools/webchatcheck` (extended) | **127 of 127** (was 80), on SQLite AND PostgreSQL. In-process: anybody may give an unanswered chat; once it is Tom's a colleague or a technician is refused; to the one who has it, to a stranger, to a real colleague not signed in, to **another company's** person signed in there, to nobody — refused, and none moved it; the answerer hands it on; **a supervisor moves somebody else's**; the notes kept; an ended chat refused; **four hand-overs at once, ten rounds: exactly one wins every time, one note per move**; a hand-over that looked before Tom's first reply landed is refused and Tom keeps it. On the wire: `MayHandOverAny` for the supervisor only; who could take it (console and portal agree; not Otto, not the absent Abe); Tom → Sue reaches every console (with `HandedOverBy`), the portal stream and the visitor (state AND the note line, `note: true`); Tom cannot take it back, nor Olive from the portal, nor without X-Chat; Sue cannot give it to Otto, to Abe, or a chat that is not there; Sam moves it; Olive hands it on from the portal; **Sam's console and Sam's portal page at the same instant: one move, the other told**; an unanswered chat given away by the office administrator, the visitor told *"will be chatting with you"*, nobody waiting any more. |
| …with guards out | **122 of 127** with the condition on the answerer taken out of the update (every race check fails: 0 of 10 clean, 20 extra notes); **119 of 127** without the who-may check; **118 of 127** without the signed-in check. |
| `tools/webchatprobe` (extended) | **46 of 46** (was 32), the REAL window: no Hand over on a colleague's chat for a technician, there on an unanswered one and their own (beside End chat), there for a supervisor on anybody's; the menu is the people offered minus whoever has it, "(you)" marked; another chat's answer opens nothing; nobody else → said; the note drawn without a name; handed to them → pops on it without the keyboard; taking one themselves pops nothing; **four buttons on one row at the smallest size** (the minimum width is measured from them, §30). |
| `tools/soundcheck` (extended) | **60 of 60** (was 52): giving my chat away plays nothing and its note does not ding; that visitor no longer dings for me; a colleague's chat handed TO me dings once, then its visitor's lines ding for me; a waiting one given to a colleague stops ringing with no ding for me, then on to me dings; taking one myself does not. |
| walked in the browser | a throwaway platform (`workflowdemo`, `.claude/launch.json` "platform-handover", port 8205), Sam (supervisor) on `localhost`, Sue (technician) on `127.0.0.1`, the visitor's frame in a third tab, every `play()` recorded. Waiting → both rang; Sue gave it to Sam (offered: Sam, "Sue Tech (you)") → both rings stopped, **Sam one ding**, Sue saw "Sam Supervisor is answering" and lost her button, the visitor saw *"Sam Supervisor will be chatting with you."*; Sam handed it to Sue → **Sue one ding**, the note on all three; the visitor wrote → **Sue dinged, Sam did not**; the history page shows both notes in place; alone, Hand over says nobody else is signed in. Found: the *Hand over* button in the To row lost its accent to `.chat-tools button` — fixed. |
| re-run | `chatcheck` 51, `dashtabs` 133, `lookprobe` 348. |

**Not on hardware**, and the console not tried against a live server. No migration. **`Publish-Platform.ps1`, then the console
re-downloaded** (an old console still works: it simply has no button, and draws a note as a line with an empty name).
`TEST-3.6.md` section DB, 707–713.

## 146. Pilot companies, and an owner login that oversees but does not work tickets — 2026-10-15

Clint has a deal with two pilot IT companies: *"they each get 5 user license for free and have to pay for every extra user"*,
signed up from *"a link, that opens a free 5user tenant with the option to create extra seats, and then they just fill in their
details from there"* — and then *"the pilot side should be free forever for the 5 free seats"*. Before that he checked what the
free owner login may do: *"only ... setup the tenant and have an overview of all tickets and import and view clients and
machines. They should not be able to edit or work on the tickets or be able to do technician work"* — and *"yes, allow comments"*.

### The owner-only login (commit `c983ca2`)

It was NOT so: the console refused it (no seat), but in the portal `Permissions.Supervises` made Owner a supervisor for tickets —
moving any stage, editing, assigning, invoicing and closing. A company could have run its office through the one free login.

- **`Permissions.CanWorkTickets(role)` = any paid box** (Technician, Supervisor, Office administrator). Every ticket-WORK question now
  asks it through `SupervisesWork` (supervisor, or owner WITH a paid box): status, assigning, taking, passing on, opening, step in,
  billing queue, closing, approving, **emailing the client** (`CanEmailClient`), **answering a website chat** (`CanAnswerWebChat` —
  also who counts as here to answer, `StaffPresence`, so a visitor never waits for an owner-only login), handing one over, and
  being told of billing. **Unchanged for it:** running the company, seeing every ticket and the workload, clients and import,
  machines, items and suppliers (setting the company up), the knowledge base, **commenting and @mentioning**.
- **The second lock, `Pages/Portal/TicketWorkAttribute`**, asked by `PortalPage.OnPageHandlerExecutionAsync` before any handler on a
  marked page runs. **An allow-list**: the ticket page allows `Get`, `Comment`, `Update` (the classic page's comment box —
  `UpdateAsync` already drops status, priority and people for a login that may not change them) and `Eml` (reading a quote request
  already sent); New ticket and a recurring task's page allow nothing. **A handler added later is refused to an owner-only login
  until somebody decides it is not ticket work** — add its name to the attribute only then. A refused page goes to the ticket
  list; a refused post is a 403 with `Permissions.OwnerOnlyRefusal`. The services refuse too (`ActAsync`, `EditAsync`,
  `MayGoBack`, work done, `ClientUpdates`), and `/api/portal/photos` and the website-chat posts refuse it.
- The buttons are hidden for it (`PortalPage.WorksTickets`): New ticket (tickets, dashboard, client page), New recurring task, Edit
  the ticket, the client box, people and priority, Not part of it / File it under, photos, Email to the client, Add the sender as a
  contact. `chat.js` reads `mayAnswer`: website chats are shown, never rung, no reply box.
- **Ticking any other box beside Owner gives everything back — and takes a seat**, which is the rule it always was. The terms say
  so now (core section 2, version **2026-10-15**, `landing-legal` re-run).
- **A company with only owner-only logins and technicians has nobody to close a ticket** (a technician never closes, §44). That
  is the deal: the owner who wants to close ticks Office administrator or Supervisor, and takes a seat.

### Pilot companies

- **`Tenant.Pilot`**: `Pricing.BillFor` charges the package **R0** for as long as the company keeps its account; each seat beyond
  five is the region's extra-seat price (R300), **agreed by the owner first exactly as for everybody** (`RiseIf`: R0 → R300) and
  recorded as a `SeatAgreement`; ten seats at most. `Bill.Pilot`, `PackagePrice`, and `Sum` says the five are free; `PriceLabel`
  reads *"Pilot · R300 / month (we invoice)"* on All companies — **that is what to invoice**.
- **Extra seats are INVOICED, not carded** (`CompanyBilling.Refusal`). Considered and rejected: PayFast cannot hold a subscription
  of R0, and a pilot spends most months owing R0 — the card route would cancel and re-add a card each time somebody came or went,
  and the late-payment sweep (§137) would read a R0 month as unpaid and suspend a company that owed nothing. If card payment for
  pilots is wanted later, it is PayFast **tokenization** (charge ad hoc), not the subscription.
- **The link, `Services/PilotService.cs`** — every rule. Made at **Owner → Pilots** (`/owner/pilots`, Manager or above) or
  `pilot-link "<company>" [email]` on the command line. **Once, for 30 days, only its SHA-256 kept** — the link is shown once,
  to be sent by hand. Cancel stops it. It opens **`/pilot/{token}`** — its own address because `/signup` is behind the holding page
  on the live server and closed while signups are; the link works through both.
- **`/pilot/{token}`** (`Pages/Pilot.cshtml`): South Africa's terms with **`Terms/pilot.txt`** ahead of section 1
  (`Terms.ForPilot`: five free for as long as they are a customer, a price change does not touch it, extra seats invoiced monthly
  in arrears, pay within 14 days), ticked; then the company form, filled in with the company and email the link was made for. The
  person signing up is **Owner / Supervisor** — a seat, one of the five. `TenantService.SignupAsync(…, PilotToken)` makes it
  **Active at once — no trial, no approval, no card** — and **spends the link in the same transaction by a conditional update**
  (`UsedUtc == null && not cancelled && in date`); the loser of a race is rolled back. The terms are kept word for word.
- An existing company agreed a pilot afterwards: `set-brand <slug> pilot true` (and `status Active` if it was on a trial).

### How it is proved

| | |
|---|---|
| `tools/rolecheck` (extended) | **105 of 105** (was 84): the owner-only login runs the company, sees everything, imports, sets up items and suppliers, comments — and works no ticket in any lane, even one with its own name on it; edits no quote lines; goes back on no step it wrote; is not told of billing; ticking any other box gives it back; nobody who works tickets lost anything; the page lock refuses every handler but its allowed four, **including one named "SomethingAddedNextMonth"**. **92 of 105 with `CanWorkTickets` answering true.** |
| `tools/pilotcheck` (new) | **38 of 38 on SQLite AND PostgreSQL.** A real platform with **signups OFF**: the link from the command line, kept as a fingerprint; a link we never made, a cancelled one, an expired one refused; the pilot terms first with their own fingerprint (the ordinary terms' is refused); the form filled in; the company Active at once, a pilot, no trial, the pilot terms word for word, the link spent; the link again refused and a form posted to it makes nothing; **four sign-ups at once on one link make ONE company**; the price R0 / R300 / R900; invoiced, not carded. Then over HTTP: an owner-only login opens the ticket with the comment box and none of the work, its comment posts, an edit and a stage button are **403 before they run**, New ticket sends it to the list, the list has no New ticket; Owner / Supervisor still edits. **37 of 38 with the spend-once condition taken out (4 companies from one link); 35 of 38 with the page lock off.** |
| re-run | `workflowcheck` (its owner is Owner / Supervisor now), `billingwire` (owner-only is never told of billing), and 18 more ticket harnesses: 20 of 20 on SQLite; `pgcheck` 20, `legalcheck` 16. |

**Not on hardware.** **Before deploying, look at Anywhere I.T's People page: anybody who shows only *Owner* and works tickets
needs Supervisor ticked too** (Anywhere I.T is not billed, so no price is asked). Then **`Publish-Platform.ps1` (migration
`PilotCompanies`)** — no ship, no console re-download (an owner-only login never reaches the console). Then Owner → Pilots → make
the two links. `TEST-3.6.md` section DC, 714–722.

**On the live server, 2026-10-16: every tick of the terms answered HTTP 500.** Read with the new
`deploy\Get-ServerErrors.ps1` (the live log, link codes and keys blanked — only Clint's PC has the SSH key): a
`NullReferenceException` in `PilotModel.OnPostTermsAsync`. The links were made **without an email**, so the form posted an
EMPTY Email box, binding made it null (§130's trap again), and `Email.Length` threw. `pilotcheck` never made a link without an
email. Now every box goes through `PilotModel.Tidy()` first; `pilotcheck` **42 of 42 on both databases** (39 of 42 before the
fix — the new checks answered 500 exactly as live did). **A link that failed this way was never spent: once deployed, the
same link works.**

## 147. Real version numbers — auto-update, stage A — 2026-10-16

Clint, the day after signing went live: *"One of the most important things now that the digital key is in place is auto
updates. This needs to be in place for all features, health check, technician console, client app etc."* The brief is
`docs/NEXT-SESSION-AUTOUPDATE.md` (his decisions: silent on customer machines, the rollout ours alone). **Stage A is what
everything after it compares: until today every app said 1.0.0** (`Directory.Build.props`), so no two builds could be told
apart, and the hub threw away the `HelloMsg.Version` every machine has always sent.

- **The rule is `Shared/AppVersion.cs`.** A build's version is the moment it was built, in UTC: **`2026.10.16.1432`** is 14:32 UTC
  on 16 October 2026 (09:05 is `905` — the time is one number). It only goes up, needs no counter kept anywhere, reads as a
  date, and every part fits Windows' 65534. **`1.0.0.0` means "built any other way"** — `dotnet run`, a harness, and every
  install made before today — and is older than any stamped build; a blank (a half that never said) is older still.
  `Compare`, `Oldest` (a machine's version is the OLDER of its agent's and tray app's: the older is what still needs updating),
  `Label` (the stamp; `1.0 (old)`; `—`), `IsStamped`, `BuiltUtc`.
- **`tools\BuildVersion.ps1`** makes it (`New-BuildVersion [chosen]`, `VersionArgs`, `Get-StagedVersion`) for **`build.ps1`**
  (every publish, the Linux server, the platform, the packed .exe, ISCC's `/DAppVersion`), **`tools\ship-build.ps1`** and
  **`tools\Pack-ClientExe.ps1`** (told by build.ps1; otherwise it reads the staged host's file version, so the tray app is never
  stamped apart from the host and agent it carries). **`build.ps1 -Version 2026.10.16.1500`** stamps a chosen one — for the
  N / N+1 builds the auto-update hardware test needs.
- **Pass all of `VersionArgs`, never `-p:Version` alone.** `Directory.Build.props` pins `AssemblyVersion` and `FileVersion`
  as well, so Version alone changes nothing the apps read — `versioncheck`'s first run found exactly that.
- **The platform's version IS the apps' version**: one build.ps1 run stamps the platform and the payloads it serves alike, so
  the server knows what it hands out by knowing itself (`AppVersion.Current`). Stage C's release manifest will make that
  explicit; until then, a platform built apart from its payloads would claim the wrong version.
- **Stored per half**: `Device.AgentVersion`, `Device.ClientVersion` (migration **`AppVersions`**, both databases), carried on
  `DeviceInfo` and loaded at start, so a machine that is OFF still shows what it runs. A Helper hello (a session's host) is not
  the machine and changes neither. **The free installer's one-off hello (`FreeSetup`) now sends a blank version on purpose**:
  the hub keeps a Client hello's version as the tray app's, and a free machine has no tray app — the installer's would have
  sat there for ever, older than the updated agent.
- **Shown:** the console's machine list has a **Version** column (last, measured like the others) and the main window's title
  ends *"· version 2026.10.16.1432"* (left off a development build). The portal's Devices page has a **Version** column, **amber
  when older than the server's apps** (`DevicesModel.Behind` — never on an unstamped server, never for a machine that has not
  said), its tooltip each half by name. **`/owner`'s server cards** say *"Apps version X · N machines on it · M older (the oldest
  …)"* from `ServerReport.AppVersion` and `MachineVersions` (counted by each machine's older half, newest first; a server older
  than this sends neither and the line is left out).
- **What it will look like live:** every machine installed so far says **1.0 (old)**, amber on the portal — honestly, since
  every one of them needs the last reinstall the brief describes. Only a machine reinstalled from a stamped build shows a date.

**Proof.** `tools/versioncheck` **27 of 27 on both databases**: the rules; BuildVersion.ps1's output and refusals, read from
the script itself; each build script uses it; a platform **built with VersionArgs** reporting `2026.10.16.1200`; each half
stored apart, live and in the row, a newer hello replacing an older, the installer's blank clearing, the dashboard's counts,
the Devices page's column, amber and tooltip, and both halves still there after a restart. **20 of 27 with the hub's two
storing lines out.** It builds its stamped platform in a configuration of its own (`-c Versioned`, `bin\Versioned`) so the
Debug and Release outputs other harnesses use are never stamped. A real single-file publish of the agent with VersionArgs
reads `2026.10.16.1201` in its file properties and back through `Get-StagedVersion`. `dashtabs` 133, `fitprobe` 324,
`lookprobe` 348, `freeportal` 32, `devicelink` 20, `pgcheck` 20.

**To deploy:** `Publish-Platform.ps1` (migration `AppVersions`), then re-download the console. No client reinstall is needed
for the versions to appear; a machine shows a stamped one once it is reinstalled from a build made after this. `TEST-3.6.md`
section DD, 723–727.

## 148. Auto-update, stages B to F — every app keeps itself current — 2026-10-16

Clint: *"lets finish all the stages before i deploy."* The brief is `docs/NEXT-SESSION-AUTOUPDATE.md`; stage A (version
numbers) is §147. **Built in full and committed stage by stage; none of it has run on a real machine yet** — the parts that
need a signed, stamped build (our signature accepted, a real service swapped and restarted, a real rollback) are
`TEST-3.6.md` section DE. Decided by Clint: **silent on customer machines; the rollout is ours alone.**

### B. Only our signed, newer files install — `Shared/UpdateTrust.cs` (commit `73b323c`)

- `WinVerifyTrust` called by hand, revocation checked (a machine that cannot check does not update, and says why), and
  **the signer read from the verification's own state** (`WTHelperProvDataFromStateData` → signer chain → leaf), so a
  script's signature — a comment block no certificate loader reads — is checked exactly like a program's.
- The signer must be **O=The Remote Support Program (Pty) Ltd, C=ZA, read as FIELDS** of the subject — never a substring,
  never one thumbprint (the free second certificate of November 2027 must keep working).
- `Accept`: also a STAMPED build, NEWER than what is installed, and — when given — exactly the version offered. **A
  compromised server can never push an older, genuinely signed build.**
- **No test mode.** The runner takes its checks as functions so a harness can hand over fakes in code; nothing at run
  time — no setting, no file, no message — can change them.
- `tools/updatetrust` 8 of 8 with REAL files: our program and our script pass; Microsoft's `dotnet.exe` (valid, trusted, not
  us), one changed byte, one changed word in a script, an unsigned file, and **a certificate made on this PC with our name
  in it** are all refused. Its newer / same / older / offered-as checks run once `dist\` holds a signed STAMPED build (it
  prints NOTE until then) — run it again after the next signed build.

### C. The release, rings and Pause — `Services/UpdateService.cs`, `UpdateSweep.cs`, `Hub/TenantHub.Update.cs` (`4fc77c9`)

- **The release is what this server hands out**: the packed customer app (the tray app with host, agent and scripts inside
  — ONE signed file, 132 MB) and the console, at **`/update/client.exe`** and **`/update/console.exe`**, public like the
  downloads, with range requests. Its version is the server's own; **an unstamped server offers nothing, ever.** (The brief
  had separate files and a plain tray app; one packed file turned out smaller than the three apart, and is what is signed.)
- **Rings** (`UpdateService.RingOf`): 0 our own company (`Tenant.NotBilled`), 1 the pilots, 2 everybody (free included). A
  release starts at 0. **`/owner/updates`** (any admin sees; a Full admin or Owner acts): Offer it to the pilots / to
  everybody, Pause / Resume — on any server, through `ControlServers.Dispatch` (`update-ring`, `update-pause`,
  `update-resume`; a Manager is refused). Each server's rollout is in its `ServerReport.Update`.
- **A rollback pauses it by itself** (2% of machines offered it, and at least one — with few machines, the first) and emails
  every Full admin and Owner.
- **`UpdateSweep`** offers to at most `Updates:PerMinute` (20) machines a minute, every `Updates:SweepSeconds` (30) —
  only AGENTS that said **`DeviceCan.Update`**, only in open rings, never one already on it, never one that rolled back or
  refused this version (`_gaveUp`, reloaded from the history at start), and again after 6 h if still behind. The sweep
  also refreshes each hub's ring from the database (a company marked not billed or pilot later).
- Consoles: **`StateMsg.ConsoleUpdate`** (`ConsoleOfferNow` returns nothing until `WarmAsync` has read the rollout and hashed
  the files, so a sign-in never waits on hashing) and **`/update/console.json?slug=`** for the check before sign-in.
- **Only an agent's `UpdateReportMsg` is taken** — a tray app's is ignored. History: `DeviceUpdateEvent`; the rollout:
  `UpdateRollout`; `Device.SelfUpdates`. Migration **`AutoUpdate`** (both databases).
- `tools/updatewire` **33 of 33 on SQLite and PostgreSQL** (31 with the never-again and agent-only guards out), against a
  platform BUILT as a release, three companies in three rings, a restart, and `/owner/updates` drawn after an admin-key
  sign-in.

### D. The machine updates itself — `Shared/UpdateSwap.cs`, `UpdateRunner.cs`, `Agent/AgentUpdate.cs` (`6c6bc12`)

- **Only the real service says `DeviceCan.Update`** (`WindowsServiceHelpers.IsWindowsService()`): an agent run by hand is
  never offered one.
- **`UpdateRunner`**: a random wait (90 s at most); download from the machine's OWN server only (an offer naming any other
  host is refused), carried on after a break, retried at 1, 5 and 15 minutes (ESET, BUGS 9); size and hash; **`Accept` on
  the packed app BEFORE it is run** to unpack itself (`--unpack`), then on every file it lays down; one refusal → nothing
  installed, *Refused* reported, the version remembered in `update\state.json`; *Ready*; waits until **no session host for
  10 minutes** (`AgentService.NobodyConnected`, which forgets a host that died); *Installing*; starts the NEW agent with
  **`--apply-update <install> <unpacked> <version>`**.
- **`UpdateSwap`**: Windows lets a running program be RENAMED but not overwritten — each replaced file goes to `*.old` and
  the new one is copied in; **only the release's own files** (`TopFiles` + `healthcheck\*.ps1`), never `branding\`,
  `device.json`, `config.json` or a script the release does not carry; what it does is written to `update\applied.json`
  BEFORE it is done, so `RollBack` undoes it even half-done.
- **`UpdateApplier`** (the apply process, outside the service): stop the service through the SCM, swap, start it, and
  **keep it only if the new agent writes `update\healthy-<version>`** — which it does after **20 s connected** with the swap's
  record naming its own version. Otherwise (5 minutes): stop it, every file back, the old agent started, the version
  remembered. Whichever agent runs next reports the result (`update\result.json`, taken once). Log: `update\apply.log`.
- **The tray app** checks once a minute whether the file in its place is newer and restarts into it on the branding rules
  (no session, nobody ringing, no window). **Measured: a program renamed while running still names its ORIGINAL path**, so
  `Environment.ProcessPath` starts the new file.
- **The health check follows by itself**: its scripts in the install folder change, and `HealthCheckKeeper` already
  reinstalls an installed toolkit older than them (keeping the mail settings).
- `tools/updateapply` **36 of 36**: the swap against a running program, the machine's own files untouched, rollback byte for
  byte, a half-done swap undone, a path outside refused, the runner against a local server (resume, bad hash, refusals,
  never again, waits for idle, another server, older versions), the applier both ways, and the REAL checks refusing an
  unsigned release before running it.

### E. The console updates itself — `Technician/ConsoleUpdate.cs` (`dcf3bd2`)

- **Only an INSTALLED console** (`ConsoleDownload`'s folder, with its branding) — never a developer build, `demo\`, or a
  guest copy. **Before the sign-in window** it asks `/update/console.json`; newer → *"Updating the console to version …"*,
  downloaded beside it, `Accept`ed, then the NEW copy runs **`--install-update <installed exe> <old pid>`**: waits for the
  old one to close, renames it aside, copies itself in, starts it, and **keeps it only once it reaches its sign-in window**
  (`update\started-<version>`, written by `SayStarted`) within a minute — else the old one goes back and the version is
  remembered. `update\installing` stops the new console's tidy-up from deleting what a rollback needs.
- While running: **"Update ready"** in the header (first of the right-hand buttons when shown) → the same fresh start as
  Sign out, asked first, warned when it would end a session.
- `tools/consoleupdate` **14 of 14 with two REAL published consoles** (N and N+1): N refuses an unsigned N+1 before running it
  and remembers; N+1's `--install-update` takes N's place, keeps N aside until its sign-in window is up, then N's copy is
  tidied away at the next start. **Its rollback (a new console that never reaches its sign-in window) is unharnessed.**

### F. The one update by hand — `Shared/UpdateByHand.cs` (`9ca197f`)

- Every machine installed before today has an agent that cannot take an update. **Not a reinstall** (a new machine id —
  the office would have to confirm every machine again, §111 — and a Windows prompt at the machine): **Scripts → Update
  this machine** fills in a PowerShell script, shown before it runs, that downloads the release from the company's own
  server, checks the signature of it and of every file inside it (`Get-AuthenticodeSignature` — on a DOWNLOADED file, not a
  copy of a Windows file, so the catalog trap does not apply), and starts the new agent's `--apply-update` — the same swap
  and the same rollback. The session drops for a moment while the service restarts.
- Shown: the portal's Devices page counts them (*"N machines were installed before automatic updates…"*) and marks each
  *update by hand once*; the console's row tooltip says how; `/owner/updates` has *Need a reinstall* per ring.
- `tools/updatebyhand` **9 of 9**: valid Windows PowerShell; run for real against an unsigned file, Microsoft's, and our own
  with one byte changed — each REFUSED before anything is unpacked. **It never runs a passing case: that would install onto
  this PC's own support software.** `versioncheck` 28.

### To deploy, and what happens then

1. **A signed deploy**: `Publish-Platform.ps1` with the YubiKey (migrations `AppVersions` and `AutoUpdate`). It stamps
   everything; `/owner/updates` shows the release offered to **our own company only**.
2. **Every console once by hand**: re-download it (the old consoles have none of this). From then on they update
   themselves.
3. **Every machine once by hand**: connect → Tools → Scripts → *Update this machine* → Run (or a reinstall). Until then
   nothing is offered to it — it never said `DeviceCan.Update`.
4. From the NEXT deploy on, our own machines update themselves within minutes of it (when idle); move it on to the pilots,
   then everybody, from `/owner/updates`. **Do not move it on until our own have come through it.**

### Found while reviewing, fixed the same day

- **Every release's 130 MB download stayed on the machine for ever.** `UpdateRunner.ClearOldReleases` at the agent's start
  removes every `update\<version>` not newer than what runs — never while a swap's record is there (`updateapply` 39, with the offline case below).
- **A revocation check that could not be MADE was a refusal for ever.** A machine offline from Sectigo for a moment, or behind
  a firewall that blocks it, would have given up on that version permanently. `UpdateTrust.Verdict.TryLater` (only
  `CERT_E_REVOCATION_FAILURE` and `CRYPT_E_REVOCATION_OFFLINE`) makes it a *Failed*, tried again — in the agent and the
  console. A revoked certificate is still refused.

### Known gaps, not built

- **A reboot during the five-minute wait** leaves the swap with nobody to roll it back: the new agent starts at boot, and if
  it cannot connect, nothing puts the old one back. The window is the few minutes after an install, when nobody is
  connected; a visit or a reinstall fixes it.
- **The console's rollback** (a new copy that never reaches its sign-in window) is unharnessed.
- **The Updates page shows the history of THIS server's machines only**; another server's is on its own page.

## 149. The Allow prompt comes to the front — 2026-10-16

Clint: *"when connecting to a machine in attended access, the allow is behind other open screens, it should pop up to the
front, otherwise clients may miss it."*

**Measured first, with `tools/consentfront` (new).** It shows the host's REAL prompt through `ConsentPrompt.Ask` (by
reflection) from a process that is not the foreground one, as the host never is, and reads it back from where the customer
stands: `WindowFromPoint` at its middle and four corners, the foreground window, the always-on-top bit, and what lies above it
in the z-order. Its stand-ins for the customer's other programs are a second copy of itself (`--blocker`).

**What it found: Windows takes the always-on-top mark OFF.** The prompt has had `TopMost = true` since it was written. When
the person has just clicked into another program, the prompt's `WS_EX_TOPMOST` was already gone the first time it could be read
(0 ms, sampled every 5 ms) and the window sat behind the one they had clicked — 0 of 5 points visible. With an always-on-top
window in front instead, the mark stayed. No owner window was involved (`GW_OWNER` was none in every case). Only the
foreground program may put things in front of it; a background program's topmost window is demoted. The old
`Activate(); BringToFront()` on `Shown` did nothing for the same reason. **Old code: 8 of 12.**

**The fix, `RemoteSupport.UI/ComeForward.cs`:**
- `Now(form)` on `Shown`: join the foreground window's input for a moment (`AttachThreadInput`), which is what lets
  `SetForegroundWindow` through; take the foreground; then `SetWindowPos(HWND_TOPMOST)` again. If Windows still refuses, the
  taskbar button flashes until it is looked at (`FlashWindowEx`, `FLASHW_TIMERNOFG`).
- `StayOnTop(form)` on every tick of the prompt's one-second countdown: back above an always-on-top window that another program
  opens WHILE the question waits (a reminder, a call), with `SWP_NOACTIVATE` — it never takes the keyboard back from what they
  are typing in.

`consentfront` **15 of 15**: (1) this desktop as it is, (2) an ordinary window just clicked over the middle — the mark is OFF at
0 ms and back on by 16–31 ms, (3) an always-on-top window over the middle, (4) an always-on-top window opened while the question
waits. **14 of 15 with `StayOnTop` out** (case 4, 0 of 5 visible). It skips Windows' own notifications (`ShellExperienceHost`),
which sit above everything by design — one arrived during a run and covered a corner.

**Not proved: the prompt as SYSTEM.** On a customer machine the host is SYSTEM in their session (§76), started by the agent;
no harness runs a window as SYSTEM in a logged-in session. `AttachThreadInput` from a higher integrity level to a lower one is
allowed, so it should behave the same — `TEST-3.6.md` section DF checks it on hardware. Leave the mouse and keyboard alone while
`consentfront` runs. `MicQuestion` (the tray app's microphone question) still uses the old `TopMost = false; TopMost = true`
pattern; it could use `ComeForward` too if it is ever reported behind.

**Deploy:** it changes the HOST, so a signed `Publish-Platform.ps1`; a machine that has had its one update by hand (§148) takes
it by itself, any other needs that update or a reinstall. No migration, no console re-download.

## 150. The name given at a support request names the machine — 2026-10-18

Clint: *"techs and staff are not immediately linking machines to clients, so very quickly the system can become messy. Can
we have it that as soon as a client puts their name in when requesting support, this is the user name that shows in the
console and portal for that machine. It then changes when the contact or client is created and the machine gets manually
linked to them."* His four answers, all the recommendations: **the latest name wins** (a shared reception PC shows whoever
asked last); **it is marked** as only what they typed; **linking suggests** people on file by that name and offers it as a new
contact — a person still chooses; **machines that asked before take it from their past tickets**.

**The rule is `Shared/OwnerNames.cs`, once:** the contact, else the client, else the name given (`Device.RequestedBy`,
`RequestedByUtc`), else Windows' sign-in. `DeviceInfo.OwnerName` and `ContactService.OwnerName` both ask it — they used to be
two copies that "must agree". `NamedByRequest` / `IsRequested` is the mark: only while the machine is linked to NOBODY. Linking
to a client alone replaces the name with the client's (Clint's words: it changes when the client is created and linked).
`Likeness` (2 same name, 1 every word of the shorter in the longer, 0) orders the suggestions; it never chooses.

- **Kept** by the hub on `RequestCallMsg` (`TenantHub.RememberRequestedByAsync` → `ContactService.RememberRequestedByAsync`),
  tidied and cut to 100 characters; a blank box changes nothing; every console gets a `DeviceUpdateMsg` at once. **It waits for
  the machine's stored record first (`WhenRecordReadAsync`)** — a first install that asks for help within a second of its first
  hello would otherwise have its name written to no row and lost (`requestedname` 33 of 42 with that line out). Loaded at start
  and put back into the live record in `PersistDeviceAsync`, so it survives a restart and a reinstall.
- **Console:** the Who cell is drawn muted and italic by `DashboardForm.RequestedName` (over the themed handler, from
  `DeviceDot`), with a tooltip saying what it is. The chat box's machine picker and the Processes/Performance window's title
  now say the Who name too, not Windows' sign-in. **The Link window** (`LinkDeviceDialog`, `given`): people on file whose name
  fits, best first, then *+ Add {name} as a new contact…*, which turns the list into *Which customer is {name} at?* (companies
  only, a way back). Save untouched still changes nothing — *Not linked to anybody* stays chosen.
  `DeviceLinkMsg.NewContactName` → `ContactService.LinkDeviceToNewContactAsync`, which goes through `CreateAsync` (a contact of
  that name at that client is REUSED) and then `LinkDeviceAsync` — still the one writer of a machine's owner.
- **Portal:** Devices' User column shows the name in italic (`.requested-by` — **site.css sets every `<em>` upright, so the
  class carries its own `font-style`**; the browser walk found the mark missing), Windows' sign-in under it; under the owner
  picker, a button per person on file it fits and *Add {name} as a contact at [client] — Add and link* (`OnPostAddContactAsync`).
  The dashboard's Unassigned machines card shows it too (`DashboardService.DeviceRow.RequestedBy`).
- **The backfill** (migration `RequestedByName`, both databases, the same SQL): each machine's most recent ticket opened by a
  support request (`Source` 1) with a name, **blanks only**. A reused ticket (the 30-minute window) keeps its FIRST caller's
  name, so a machine asked from by two people inside half an hour backfills the first — the next request corrects it.

`tools/requestedname` **43 of 43 on both databases**: the rule; then a real platform with pretend tray apps and a console —
the name arriving, the latest winning, a blank changing nothing, a first install asking before its record is saved (it proves
the timing: 0 rows when sent; `Testing:PersistDeviceGapMs` 800), a restart, a new contact at a client and the same name again
reusing it, a refusal with no client, unlinking back to the given name; the portal's page, its own form's antiforgery token
(§80), Add and link, the dashboard, the stylesheet's rule; and the backfill's SQL taken from each database's own migration
class (`UpOperations`) and run on that database. `dashtabs` **145** (the real Who cell and tooltip, the Link window's rows,
its new-contact step and the way back), `contactcheck` 34, `devicelink` 20, `requestwire` 20, `watchprobe` 68, `lookprobe`
348, `pgcheck` 20. Walked in the browser: Devices, Add and link by hand, the dashboard.

**Found on the way, NOT fixed: BUGS #13** — `/ws/device` drops anything a machine sends in the first milliseconds after its
hello. The harness's first attempt sent the request straight behind the hello and the request (and its ticket) vanished on
PostgreSQL. No real tray app does that — a person fills in a form first — so the harness waits for the console to see the
machine online.

**Deploy:** a signed `Publish-Platform.ps1` (migration `RequestedByName` — the backfill runs then), then the console (it
updates itself since §148, or re-download). **No client reinstall**: every tray app already sends the name.
`TEST-3.6.md` section DG, 744–750.

## 151. Tickets by email: Sign in with Microsoft — 2026-10-19

§79 left Microsoft 365's own sign-in *"later, by Clint's decision"*: a 365 company could only forward, which its
administrator must first allow outside the organisation. Microsoft no longer takes a mailbox password from a program like
ours — basic authentication is gone for IMAP, and SMTP AUTH with a password is off by default for existing tenants from the
end of December 2026 (MC786329) — so for more and more IT companies' own mailboxes forwarding was the only way. This is the
third way in. **One-time steps for Clint (register the app, the secret, publisher verification): `docs/MICROSOFT-365.md`.**

### What it is

- **Portal → Tickets by email** has three ways now: *We check your mailbox* (a password), **Microsoft 365 — sign in with
  Microsoft**, and *You forward it to us* (still the fallback, unchanged). Choosing Microsoft shows its own part: who is
  signed in (and who pressed it, when), **Sign in with Microsoft** (or *…again*, or *…as another account*), **Disconnect**,
  and the approval link for an administrator. Above the button, until somebody is signed in, **Before you sign in**: tick IMAP
  and Authenticated SMTP for the mailbox (and the organisation-wide SMTP AUTH switch) — many 365 tenants have SMTP AUTH off.
  The *Fill in for: Microsoft 365* button now chooses it. **Owner and
  supervisors only, as the page always was** (`Program.cs` page policy — the way back, `/Portal/MailIntakeMicrosoft`, is on
  the same list).
- **The mailbox read is ALWAYS the support address typed on the page.** The account that signs in is that mailbox, or a
  person who may open it — a **shared mailbox** (no password of its own) is read through a person with Full Access, and
  replies from it need Send as. IMAP: XOAUTH2 with `user=` the support address and the person's token. SMTP: XOAUTH2 as the
  person, From the support address. If Exchange says *SendAsDenied*, the reply goes from ours and the log says Send as.
- **Sign in with Microsoft saves the form first** (the support address must pass `CheckAddressAsync`, switched on or not),
  then sends the browser to Microsoft; a good answer **switches email on** (pressing the button said so) and the page tests
  at once, as Save and test does. **Disconnect deletes the token.** **Saving another way in, or another support address,
  deletes it too** — a live key to their mailbox is kept only while it is the way in, for the mailbox it was given for.
- **When Microsoft refuses the sign-in** (password changed, sessions revoked, permission withdrawn, unused too long, a new
  MFA or conditional-access step): **the dead token is deleted, checking stops, and it is not asked again** — §79's rule
  for a refused password. The status line says *stopped — Microsoft no longer accepts the sign-in; sign in again*, the reason
  is in words (`MicrosoftSignIn.Explain` maps the AADSTS codes), and the button reads *Sign in with Microsoft again*. The
  account it was for is kept so the page can say who; **signing in again as the same account carries on from where it
  stopped** (UIDs kept), so mail that arrived meanwhile becomes tickets and nothing older does. Client updates (§123) stop
  being offered meanwhile — a reply could not come back.
- **When Microsoft refuses OUR app** (`invalid_client`: the secret ran out or was deleted): *ours to fix, not yours* on every
  affected company's page, a warning in the log, **their token kept and checking NOT stopped** — it backs off like any
  server trouble and carries on by itself once the secret is replaced. `microsoft-app show` says when the secret runs out.
- **The IMAP/SMTP side, with a good token**: a refusal there is the MAILBOX saying no — IMAP or Authenticated SMTP switched
  off for it, or no Full Access to a shared mailbox — and `MailWire.Explain` says which and where to switch it on. Reading
  refused stops checking (tried once) but keeps the sign-in; saving starts it again.
- **The command line**: `microsoft-app show` (client id, secret stored or not, when it runs out, the redirect URI, the
  scopes — never the secret) and `microsoft-app set --client-id GUID [--expires yyyy-mm-dd]` with the secret in
  `RSP_MS_CLIENT_SECRET`. **`deploy\Set-MicrosoftApp.ps1`** is how it gets there from this PC (PayFast's pattern: a
  `Get-Credential` window, ssh standard input, `sudo -E`). Stored encrypted in `PlatformSettings` (`MsClientId`,
  `MsClientSecretEnc`, `MsSecretExpiresUtc`), its own Data Protection purpose.
- **`/.well-known/microsoft-identity-association.json`** names our app (404 until `microsoft-app set`), so Entra can verify
  theremotesupportprogram.com as the app's publisher domain — the step before publisher verification. Caddy's holding page
  never covers it.

### The rules that matter, and why

- **Delegated scopes only, and only these** (`MicrosoftSignIn.SignInScopes`): `openid profile email offline_access` plus
  `https://outlook.office.com/IMAP.AccessAsUser.All` and `…/SMTP.Send`. Never an application permission such as Mail.Read or
  full_access_as_app, which would open every mailbox in their organisation; m365check fails if one appears. The refresh asks
  only `offline_access` + the two mail scopes, against **their own tenant id** (the id_token's `tid`), not `organizations`.
- **The way back is bound four ways** (`MicrosoftSignIn.CheckReturn`): the state is Data Protection, time-limited to 15
  minutes, and names the company AND the person; the `rsp_ms` cookie (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax — Microsoft returns with a
  top-level GET, which Lax allows; the portal cookie is Lax too) carries the nonce and the **PKCE verifier**; the nonce in the
  state must equal the cookie's (constant-time); and the id_token's nonce must match. Another company's browser, a tampered
  state, or one start's state with another start's cookie all come back *expired* without the code ever being redeemed. The
  cookie is deleted on every way back, so a refresh of the address does nothing.
- **Codes, not words, in the address** (§105): the way back redirects to `/portal/mailintake?ms=connected|declined|admin|
  account|ours|expired|noaccount|approved|failed`; `MicrosoftSignIn.CallbackWords` is the sentence. Microsoft's own
  `error_description` never reaches our address bar or our page.
- **Microsoft hands out a new refresh token with each refresh, and it is stored** — only over the one it came from, so a new
  sign-in made meanwhile is never overwritten by the old one's heir. Access tokens are cached per company in memory (until
  five minutes before they run out) and forgotten on Connect, Disconnect and a refusal. The refresh token is Data
  Protection under `RemoteSupport.MicrosoftMailToken.v1` — its own purpose, not readable with the mail-password protector.
- **Every §79 rule still holds**: EXAMINE and BODY.PEEK only, found by UID, "last UID 0" is an empty mailbox, a refusal
  tried once, backing off 2…30 minutes for anything else. The Microsoft way always reads INBOX.
- **Not built**: personal Outlook.com accounts (the authority is `organizations`; `Microsoft:Tenant` could change it);
  revoking at Microsoft on Disconnect (there is no per-token revoke for this — the page says how to delete the app in Entra).

### Where it lives

`Services/MicrosoftSignIn.cs` (the only file that talks to Microsoft's identity platform: the authorize address, the code
and refresh grants, the cache, `Explain`, `CallbackError`/`CallbackWords`, the id_token read). `Services/TicketIntake.cs`
(`ReadsMailbox`, `MicrosoftConnected`, `ReaderAsync`, `SenderAsync`, **`MicrosoftTokenAsync` — the refusal rule**,
`ConnectMicrosoftAsync`, `DisconnectMicrosoftAsync`; `TestAsync`, `CheckMailboxAsync` and `SendAsCompanyAsync` ask them).
`Services/MailWire.cs` (`MailServer.AccessToken`/`SignedInAs`, `SignInAsync` — XOAUTH2 or a password — and the Microsoft
words in `Explain`). `TicketIntakeSweep` reads microsoft-way companies that are connected. `ClientUpdateService.Ready` asks
`ReadsMailbox`. Pages: `Portal/MailIntake` (`OnPostMicrosoftAsync`, `OnPostDisconnectAsync`, `SaveEmailAsync` shared by
Save and test and the button), `Portal/MailIntakeMicrosoft` (the way back). Data: `TicketIntakeSettings.Ms*` (refresh token,
account, tenant, when, by whom), `PlatformSettings.Ms*`; migration **`MicrosoftSignIn`** on both databases. Configuration,
for harnesses only: `Microsoft:Authority` (refused unless https or loopback), `Microsoft:Tenant`, `Microsoft:ImapHost/Port`,
`Microsoft:SmtpHost/Port` (defaults outlook.office365.com 993 SSL, smtp.office365.com 587 STARTTLS).

### How it is proved

| | |
|---|---|
| `tools/m365check` | **103 of 103 on SQLite and on PostgreSQL.** In-process: the scopes (and none wider); a token refusal in words for each family (password changed, consent withdrawn, MFA, OUR secret, Microsoft's trouble); the way back's errors as codes; a good token refused by the mailbox (IMAP off, Full Access, SMTP AUTH, Send as); the id_token read. Then a real platform with a **fake Microsoft token endpoint, a fake 365 IMAP and a fake 365 SMTP** in the harness that accept only XOAUTH2 with a token the fake Microsoft issued: the app put on by the command line (encrypted, never printed), the publisher-domain file, the page as owner (with the *Before you sign in* note above the button: IMAP and Authenticated SMTP, gone once connected) and refused to a technician (page and way back), the authorize address (our app, the redirect URI, exactly the scopes, PKCE S256, state, nonce, login_hint, `select_account`), the cookie, three hostile ways back (another company's browser, a tampered state, crossed starts) with **no code redeemed**; the real way back, the code redeemed with the matching verifier, the page tested at once, the token kept encrypted, refreshes against their tenant with only the mail scopes, **rotation stored** (RT-1 → RT-2 → RT-3…); a real email made a ticket by the real timer and the auto-reply sent by XOAUTH2 from support@, **no password login ever**, read-only; IMAP off said once and not retried; OUR app refused — said to be ours, token kept, not stopped; **THEIR sign-in refused — token deleted, stopped, said on the page and the status line, Microsoft not asked again over three ticks**, mail meanwhile unread, then signing in again picking it up; a shared mailbox without Full Access, with it, without Send as (reply from ours, Send as named), with it; Disconnect (token and account gone, nothing more asked or read); another way in deleting the token; declined, admin approval (with the link), approved. **93 of 100 with the refusal rule taken out of `MicrosoftTokenAsync`** (Microsoft asked 7 more times in 9 s, token kept, nothing said); **96 of 100 with `CheckReturn`'s company and nonce checks taken out** (a crossed start's code redeemed). |
